¶ **To the arguments.** To the first argument regarding natural propagation instituted by God between male and female, it is said: that just as by God's permission the **sacrament of marriage** can be corrupted by the work of the devil through **witchcraft** <term>maleficia: harmful magic or spells intended to cause injury or impotence</term>, as was shown above, so by similarity and all the more so in any other venereal act between male and female. 

But if you ask: Why is the devil permitted to exercise witchcraft more in and upon the venereal act than upon other human acts? It is said that multiple causes are assigned by the doctors <note>theologians and scholars of the Church</note>, which will be discussed below in that part concerning **divine permission**. For the present, the cause touched upon earlier suffices: namely, that the power of the demon is in the loins of men. Because among all struggles, the battles of this contest are harder, where there is continuous fighting and rarely victory. 

Nor is the argument valid which says that the work of the devil would then be stronger than the work of God, since matrimonial acts instituted by God could be corrupted. For the devil does not corrupt through violence; rather, since he can infect nothing unless he is permitted by God, his **impotence** is instead concluded through this. 

¶ **To the second argument.** It is true that procreating a human is an act of a living body. But when it is said that demons cannot give life, because life flows formally from the soul—again, this is true. However, because life is materially drawn from the seed, the **incubus** demon can inject that by God's permission through intercourse—and not as if drawn from himself, but through the seed of some man taken for this purpose. This is as the **Holy Doctor** says in the *Summa*, Part 1, Question 51, Article 3: namely, that the same demon who acts as a **succubus** to a man becomes an **incubus** to a woman, just as they also take the seeds of other things for the generation of certain things.

As Augustine says in Book 3 of *On the Trinity* <note>original: "iij. de trini."; referring to De Trinitate, where Augustine discusses how angels can manipulate matter</note>. Wherefore, if it is asked whose son a child born in this way is, it is clear that he is not the son of the demon, but of that man from whom the seed was taken. But when it is urged that nothing is superfluous in the works of angels, just as in the works of nature, this is granted. Yet, when it is inferred that a demon can invisibly both receive and infuse seed, this is true. However, it rather works this visibly as a **succubus** <note>a demon taking female form to collect seed from a man</note> and an **incubus** <note>a demon taking male form to infuse seed into a woman</note>, so that through such filth it may infect both the body and the soul of both persons—namely, the woman and the man—as was touched upon regarding the body.

Furthermore, demons could do many more things invisibly which they are nevertheless not permitted to carry out, even if they wished. For instance, because the demon assigned to the woman would receive seed from the other demon assigned to the man, so that each one may exercise the 

<margin>witchcraft</margin>

Or, it may be that invisibly, in the place of a man to women, it may introduce its seed—that is, the seed which the incubus received—by invisibly interposing itself with the woman. To make such an interposition is not against its nature or power, since even in an assumed body it can interpose itself invisibly and without being felt, as was clear above concerning that youth who had betrothed the idol <note>A reference to a popular medieval legend where a youth places a ring on a statue of Venus, and a demon inhabiting the statue claims him as its husband</note>. 

¶ To the third point: As for the claim that the power of an angel is infinite with respect to those things above it, this is because its power cannot be fully grasped by those below it, but rather always exceeds them. Thus, it is not limited to only one effect. And this is because the highest things among beings have more universal powers. Wherefore, because its power is infinite 

<column-break/>

above, it cannot be said that it can produce every effect indifferently, for then it would also be called infinite below just as it is above. Finally, because there must be a proportion between the agent <note>the thing doing the action</note> and the patient <note>the thing receiving the action</note>, and since there can be no proportion between a purely spiritual and a corporal substance, the demons themselves could not produce any effect except by means of some other active principle. 

Hence it is that they use the **seeds of things** <note>original: "seminibus rerum"; a philosophical concept (seminal reasons) referring to the latent potential or "blueprints" within matter that allow things to grow or change</note> to produce effects, according to Augustine in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*. Wherefore, this argument flows back into the preceding one, nor is it strengthened unless one wished to have a declaration as to why **intelligences** <note>a scholastic term for angels or spiritual beings</note> are asserted to have infinite powers above and not below. This is understood from the order of corporal things and celestial bodies, which of themselves could influence many and infinite effects. But this does not happen because of the weakness of the lower things. 

It is concluded that although demons can make transmutations in seeds without assuming bodies, this argues nothing against what is intended here concerning **incubi** and **succubi**, whose acts they cannot exercise except in assumed bodies, according to what was touched upon above. 

To the fourth point: That demons cannot move bodies locally, and thus cannot move seed, etc., which is proved there concerning the soul by a comparison. It must be said that it is one thing to speak of the spiritual substance of the angel or demon itself, and another of the soul itself. For the soul cannot move a body locally unless the body is vivified by it, or through the contact of that body with another non-vivified body. This is because the soul holds the lowest rank in the order of spiritual substances, from which it also happens that the body it must move (even by contact) must be proportioned to it. But it is not so with demons, whose power entirely exceeds corporal power. 

¶ To the fifth point: It must be said that the contact of a demon with a body of seed, or any other body, is not a corporal contact but a **virtual contact** <note>original: "contactus virtualis"; contact through the application of power/virtue rather than physical touching</note>. It happens according to a convenient proportion for both the mover and the moved, so that the body which it moves does not exceed the proportion...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the physical limits of demonic power. Having previously established that demons can manipulate matter through local motion, the text now addresses why they cannot move celestial bodies or the entire earth, and then moves into the specific mechanics of how they facilitate human procreation through the roles of incubi and succubi.</meta>

the power of a demon, such as the celestial bodies and even the entire earth or the elements of the world. And why do I say they exceed it? As **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text's theology.</note> says in the *Disputed Questions on Evil*, question 16, concerning demons. This is either because of the condition of their nature or because of the damnation of their guilt. For the order of things is arranged according to their nature and according to their motion. Just as the higher celestial bodies are moved by higher spiritual substances, such as the good **angels**, so the lower bodies can be moved by lower spiritual substances, such as **demons**. And indeed, this happens to them according to the condition of their nature, according to what some used to claim—that demons were not among those higher angels, but from those who are assigned by God to this earthly order, as was the opinion of the **philosophers** <note>Referring to the Platonic or Neoplatonic idea of "daemons" as spirits of the middle air.</note>. Or even if it happens because of the penalty of sin, as is the opinion of the **theologians**, then having been thrust down from the celestial seats into this air as a punishment, they are not able to move the air or the earth itself. These things are added because of two arguments which are silently resolved: namely, concerning celestial bodies, that they could also move them if they were able to move bodies locally, because they are more closely related to them, as even the final argument suggests. For he responds that this is not valid: because those bodies exceed the proportion of their power, if indeed the first opinion holds. If, however, it does not, but the second does, then again they cannot move them because of the penalty of sin. There is also an answer to the argument where someone might object that the motion of the whole and the part is the same—such as the whole earth and a clod of earth—according to the third book of the **Physics** <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book 3, discussing the nature of motion.</note>. Thus, if demons could move a part of the earth, they could also move the entire earth. This is not valid, as is clear to anyone looking at the distinction. Moreover, to collect the **seeds of things** <note>term: "semina rerum" (seeds of things); a Stoic and Augustinian concept that the potential for all life exists in hidden "seeds" within the elements.</note> and apply them to certain effects does not exceed their natural power, God permitting them, as is self-evident. Let it be concluded in summary that despite what some say—that demons in assumed bodies can in no way procreate, and that by the "sons of God" are meant the sons of **Seth** and not **incubus angels**, just as by the "daughters of men" are meant those

<column-break/>

who descended from the lineage of **Cain** <note>A common medieval interpretation of Genesis 6:1–4 to avoid the idea of angels having sex with humans.</note>. Because, however, the contrary is asserted by many, as has been shown, and because it seems so to many, it cannot be entirely false, according to the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> in the seventh book of the *Ethics* and at the end of *On Sleep and Waking*. Furthermore, even in modern times, the deeds and words of **witches** <note>original: "maleficarum"</note> who truly and actually carry out such things bear witness to this. Therefore, let us say three things. First, that through such demons, the most filthy venereal acts are performed, not for the sake of pleasure, but for the sake of infecting the souls and bodies of those for whom they act as **succubi** or **incubi**. Second, that through such an act, a complete conception and generation by women can occur, insofar as they can place human seed in the appropriate place of the woman’s womb near the proportionate matter existing there. By a similar logic, just as they can collect the seeds of other things to complete certain effects. Third, that in such procreation, only that which is **local motion** is attributed to the demons, but not the generation itself, the principle of which is not the power of the demon or of the body assumed by him, but the power of him whose seed it was. Wherefore, the one born is not the son of a demon, but the son of some man. And through these points, the response is clear to the arguments where someone might wish to argue that demons cannot procreate for two reasons. First, because generation is completed through the **formative power** <note>The biological force believed to reside in semen that shapes the embryo.</note> which is in the seed released from a living body; and since a body assumed by demons is not such, therefore, etc. The response is clear: because the demon, by the power of the seed, replaces the formative power in the proper place, etc. Second, if it is said that seed has no power of generating unless the **heat of the soul** <note>original: "calor anime"; the "vital heat" or spirit required for life to begin.</note> is retained in it, which nevertheless must evaporate when carried over a great distance. The response is that demons can store something to preserve the seed so that the vital heat does not evaporate. Or also because they move extremely quickly due to the victory of the mover over the thing moved. Therefore, it cannot evaporate so easily.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of demonic interaction with the physical world. While the previous page discussed the limits of demons' physical strength—specifically their inability to move celestial bodies—this section transitions into their internal hierarchy and whether all demons engage in the "unclean" acts of incubi and succubi.</meta>

**W**hether it is a Catholic view to assert that the acts of **incubi** and **succubi** <note>In medieval demonology, an "incubus" was a demon in male form seeking sex with women, and a "succubus" was a demon in female form seeking sex with men.</note> demons are common to all unclean spirits indiscriminately and equally. And it seems that it is so, because to assert the opposite would be to affirm a certain order of "goods" among them <note>The argument here is that "order" is a characteristic of good things; therefore, some believe evil beings should be entirely chaotic and without any internal ranking.</note>. This is proved: Just as mode and order belong to the nature of good—<margin>**Augustine**, in the first book of *On the Nature of Good* <note>original: "de natura boni"</note></margin>—so disorder belongs to the nature of evil. But in the good **angels** nothing is disordered; therefore, in the evil ones, nothing can be ordered. Hence, they must engage in such acts indiscriminately. From this also comes the saying: *where no order but everlasting horror dwells*, namely in the land of misery and darkness. <margin>**Job** 10</margin>.

Furthermore, if all do not engage in these acts indiscriminately, this would belong to them either by nature, or by guilt, or by punishment. It is not by nature, because after their sin, all are indiscriminately—as touched upon in the previous question—impure spirits in their nature, though not "unclean" in a way that diminishes their natural goods <note>In Scholastic theology, even demons retain their "natural" angelic powers (like intellect and will), but their "moral" nature is corrupted.</note>. They are subtle in wickedness, eager to harm, puffed up by pride, etc. Therefore, it belongs to them regarding their guilt or punishment. Thus: where there is greater guilt, there is greater punishment. But the higher angels sinned more; therefore, as part of their punishment, they must engage more in these filthinesses. If this is not the case, another reason must be given why they do not engage in those acts indiscriminately.

Furthermore, where there is no subjection and obedience, there all work indiscriminately. But among **demons**, there is no subjection or obedience, which is proved because those things cannot exist without harmony, and in demons there is no harmony. <margin>**Proverbs** 13 <note>The OCR reads "puer," likely a scribal shorthand or error for "Proverbia."</note></margin>: *Among the proud there are always quarrels.*

Furthermore, just as all will be thrust into hell equally because of their guilt after the Day of Judgment, so also before that time they are held in the misty air because of their duty/office. Nor do we read that there is inequality regarding their confinement; therefore, there is no inequality regarding their duty and temptation.

But on the contrary: <margin>Gloss on **1 Corinthians** 15</margin> *As long as the world lasts, angels are over angels, men over men, and demons over demons.* Also, in <margin>**Job** 40</margin> it is said concerning the scales of

<column-break/>

the **Leviathan**—by which the members of the devil are signified—that *one clings to another*. Therefore, between them, there is a diversity of both order and action.

Incidentally, it is asked: whether the demons themselves are sometimes hindered from carrying out such filthinesses by the good angels or not. And it must be said that because angels are called **"powers"** <note>One of the nine traditional "choirs" or ranks of angels, specifically thought to restrain evil forces.</note> under whose authority the adverse forces are subjected—as **Gregory** says and **Augustine** in book 3 of *On the Trinity* <note>original: "de trini."</note>—the spirit who is a deserter of life and a sinner is ruled by the spirit of life that is rational, pious, and just. And just as those creatures have influence over others who are more perfect and closer to God—because the whole order of **prelacy** <term>prelatio: the system of hierarchy or being "set over" others</term> is first and originally in God and is shared by creatures according to how much they approach Him—therefore, the good angels, who most closely approach God because of His enjoyment (which the demons lack), have authority over the demons themselves, and the demons are ruled by them.

And when it is argued that demons, through the permitted means, do many evils: either they are not hindered because they are not subject to the good angels who could hinder them, or if they are subject, then since the evil things done by subjects seem to reflect the negligence of the one presiding, it would seem that there is some negligence in the good angels. 

It is answered that the holy angels are ministers of Divine **Wisdom**. Hence, just as Divine Wisdom permits some evils to be done by evil angels or men because of the goods He draws out of them, so also the good angels do not totally restrain the evil ones from harming either men or demons.

**The Response:** It is Catholic to assert that a certain order of internal and external actions exists among demons, even through a kind of hierarchy. Hence, certain filthinesses are perpetrated by some of the lowest ones, from which the higher ones are secluded because of the nobility of their nature. And this is declared first generally from a triple suitability by which such things suit their nature, Divine Wisdom, and their own wickedness. Finally, more specifically: From nature indeed. For it is established that from the beginning of creation, certain spirits were superior to others by nature, since they differ among themselves by species.

...flowing down, because it flows back, that is, it falls specifically and locally. The names of the **demon** also include "wise" over blood, <note>The author uses a traditional medieval etymology where "demon" is linked to the Greek *daimon*, interpreted here as "knowing" or "wise."</note> or "bloody," namely regarding the sins for which he thirsts and which he procures by a triple knowledge in which he excels: namely, the subtlety of his nature, the experience of ages, and revelations from good spirits. He is also named **Belial**, which is interpreted as "without a yoke" or "without a lord," because he fights with all his might against the One to whom he ought to be subject. He is also called **Beelzebub**, which is interpreted as "man of flies," <note>original: *vir muscarum*</note> that is, of sinning souls who have abandoned their true spouse, Christ. Likewise **Satan**, which means "adversary." Hence:
> **1 Peter 5**: Your adversary the devil goes about, etc. <note>original: *aduersarius vester diabolus circuit*</note>
Likewise **Behemoth**, which means "beast," because he makes men beastly. However, the demon of fornication and the prince of that filth is called **Asmodeus**, which is interpreted as "the work of judgment," because on account of this type of vice a terrible judgment was brought upon Sodom and four other cities. Just as the demon of pride is called **Leviathan**, which is interpreted as "their addition," because **Lucifer**, in tempting our first parents through pride, promised them the "addition" of divinity. Concerning which the Lord says through **Isaiah**:
> I will visit Leviathan the old and crooked serpent. <note>original: *Uisitabo sup leuiathan serpentē vettrē et tortuosum*</note>
And the demon of greed and riches is called **Mammon**, whom Christ also specified in the Gospel of **Matthew 6**:
> You cannot serve God and Mammon, etc. <note>original: *Nō potestis deo seruire*</note>
To the arguments: To the first, it is said that one thing can be found without evil, but evil is never found without good, because it is founded upon a creaturely nature which is good in itself. Therefore, insofar as demons have a good nature, they are ordered both in their natural states and in their actions. To that point from **Job**, <note>A reference to Job 10:22, which describes the afterlife as a land of "no order." The author argues this refers to the loss of the "order of grace," not the "order of nature."</note> it can be said that those demons assigned to the testing of men are not in hell, but in this murky air. Hence they possess an order among themselves here which they will not have then in hell. Or it can also be said that even now all order ceases in them regarding the attainment of blessedness, since they have fallen irrecoverably from such an order. And it can be said that even in hell there will be an order of power and of the affliction of punishments among them, insofar as

<column-break/>

some will be assigned to afflict souls and others will not. But this order will be more from God than from themselves, just as their torments are. To the third point, when it is said that the superior demons—since they sinned more and are punished more—ought to insist more on these unclean acts: The answer is that guilt is ordered through punishment and not through a natural act or operation. Therefore, they do not insist on those impurities because of the nobility of their nature, not because of their guilt or punishment. And although all are impure spirits and eager to do harm, nevertheless one is more so than another to the extent that his superior natural gifts have been darkened. To the fourth point, it is said that there is a concord among demons—not of friendship, but of wickedness, through which they hate men and resist God's justice as much as they can. For such a concord is found among the impious: that they join and subject themselves to those they see are more powerful in strength, in order to carry out their own wickedness. To the fifth point: although being held as prisoners is reckoned equally for all, first in the air and later in hell, nevertheless the natural things in them are not for that reason ordered toward equal punishments and equal offices. Rather, the more noble they are in nature and the more powerful in office, the more heavily they are subject to torment. Hence **Wisdom 6**:
> The mighty shall suffer torments mightily. <note>original: *Potentes potēter tormenta patientur*</note>
¶ There is, therefore, a question regarding the influences of the celestial bodies, in which three other errors are refuted; and it is the fifth in the order of questions. But for a fuller declaration of the aforementioned things, one must also confront any alleged objections. Inquiry is made into the works of **sorcerers** <term>malefici: literally "evil-doers," referring here to practitioners of harmful magic or witchcraft</term> regarding a fivefold cause: refuting four of them from which such effects cannot flow, and concluding with the fifth—namely, the intellectual power from which they do flow, which, although good by nature, is nonetheless evil by will. Now, four causes are refuted against those who deny either the existence of sorcerers or their works: these are the influences of celestial bodies; the movers of those bodies and spheres; the overflowing malice of men; and the efficacy of images, characters, and words.

Here it might also be considered in a general sense that the origin and multiplication of works of witchcraft <term>maleficia; harmful magic or sorcery</term> proceed from the influences of celestial bodies <note>The stars and planets</note> or from the over-abounding malice of men, and not from the filth of <term>incubi and succubi; demons believed to take male or female forms to engage in sexual acts with humans</term>. And it seems that it comes from one's own malice. **For Saint Augustine, in his book *Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*,** says that the cause of a person's depravity returns to their own will, whether they were led into it by someone else or by no one at all. But a practitioner of witchcraft is depraved through sin; therefore, the cause of it is not the devil but the human will. Regarding the same point, he says in his book **On Free Choice** <note>original: *li. ar.* or *De libero arbitrio*</note> that everyone is the cause of their own malice, which is also proven by reason. The sin of man proceeds from **free will**; but the devil cannot move the **free will**, for this would be contrary to liberty. Therefore, the devil cannot be the cause—neither of that sin nor of any other. Furthermore, in the book **On Ecclesiastical Dogmas** <note>A work traditionally attributed to Saint Augustine, but now usually assigned to Gennadius of Marseilles</note> it is said: "Not all our evil thoughts are stirred up by the devil, but sometimes they emerge from the movement of our own choice." Finally, it is proven that these works can arise from the influences of celestial bodies and not from demons. Just as every multitude is reduced to one, so every manifold thing is reduced to some uniform principle. But human acts are varied and manifold, concerning both vices and virtues. Therefore, it seems they should be reduced to some principles that move and are moved uniformly. But such things cannot be assigned except to the motions of the heavens, which are uniform. Therefore, those bodies are the causes of such actions. Furthermore: if celestial bodies were not the cause of human acts regarding virtues and vices, **astrologers** would not so frequently predict the truth about the outcomes of wars and other human acts. Therefore, they are in some way the cause. Furthermore, celestial bodies are moved by spiritual substances according to all theologians and philosophers; but those spirits are superior to our souls just as the celestial bodies are superior to our bodies. Therefore, both together must make an impression on the soul and body of a man to cause any human acts whatsoever. Furthermore, celestial bodies can impress—

<column-break/>

—upon the demons themselves to cause certain works of witchcraft; therefore, even more so upon humans. This assumption is proven by three points. First, certain men who are called **lunatics** <note>original: *lunatici*; literally "moon-struck," referring to those whose illnesses or behaviors were thought to cycle with the moon</note> are infested by demons more at one time than at another. This would not happen—rather, they would molest them at all times—unless the demons themselves were unsettled during certain phases of the moon to inflict such things. It is also proven from **necromancers** <note>original: *nigromanticis*; practitioners of "black magic" or spirit-summoning</note> who observe certain constellations for invoking demons, which they would not do unless they knew those demons were subject to the celestial bodies. It is also proven from what **Saint Augustine says in Book X of *The City of God*:** that demons are drawn to certain inferior bodies, namely herbs, stones, animals, and certain sounds, words, and figures. But since celestial bodies are more powerful than these inferior bodies, they are much more subject to the actions of the celestial bodies. And again, the works of witches are even more subject to this, as they may come from the influences of those bodies and not from the assistance of evil spirits. This argument is strengthened by **1 Kings, chapter 16** <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 16</note> where Saul, who was vexed by a demon, was relieved when David played the harp before him, and the evil spirit departed. But on the contrary: it is impossible to produce an effect without its cause. But the works of witches are such that they cannot be done except by the work of demons; this is clear from the description of the works of witches. From **Isidore of Seville’s Book VIII of the *Etymologies*:** "Witches <note>original: *Malefici*</note> are so called because of the magnitude of their crimes. For these people shake the elements, disturb the minds of men, and without any draft of poison, kill souls by the force of their songs alone," etc. However, effects of this kind cannot be caused by the influences of celestial bodies with a human acting as the intermediary. Furthermore, **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics* inquires with difficulty into what the principle of operation in the soul might be. And he shows that it must be something external. For everything that begins anew has some cause. For a man begins to do what he wants. He begins to want because he has deliberated beforehand; but if he deliberates beforehand, it is because of some...

preceding deliberation. Therefore, either there is a process of preceding to infinity, or one must posit some external principle that first moves a human to deliberate—unless, perhaps, someone says this happens by chance <note>original: *a fortuna*</note>, from which it would follow that all human acts are accidental, which is absurd. Therefore, the principle in good people toward good things is said to be God, who is not the cause of sin. In evil matters, however, when a human begins to act, will, and deliberate toward sinning, it is necessary that there also be some external cause for this. And there can be no other cause except the devil, especially in the case of practitioners of witchcraft <term>maleficis; those who perform harmful magic</term>, as was shown above, because celestial bodies cannot influence such acts. Therefore, the truth is evident. Furthermore, the power that controls the motive force also controls the motion itself, because the motive force causes the motion. Now, the motive force of the will is something perceived through the senses or the intellect, both of which are subject to the power of the devil. For **Saint Augustine** says in his *Book of Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*: "This evil"—meaning that which comes from the devil—"creeps through all the sensory inlets; it presents itself in shapes, adapts itself to colors, clings to sounds, lurks in anger and in the deception of speech, subjects itself to odors, and infuses itself into flavors. And with certain clouds, it fills all the passages of the intelligence." Therefore, it seems that it is in the power of the devil to move the will, which is the direct cause of sin. Furthermore, everything that is inclined toward either of two options <note>original: *ad utrumlibet*; a technical term for the neutrality of the will before it chooses</term> requires something to determine it so that it may proceed into action. But the **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium</term> of man is inclined toward either of two options, namely toward good or evil. Therefore, in order to proceed into an act of sin, it requires being determined toward evil by something. This is seen to be done chiefly by the devil, especially in the works of those who practice witchcraft, since his will is fixed on evil. Therefore, it seems that the evil will of the devil is the cause of an evil will, particularly in practitioners of witchcraft. And this reasoning can be strengthened by the fact that just as a good angel relates to good, so an evil angel relates to evil. But the former leads humans back to good; therefore, the latter leads them to evil. For as **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian philosopher</note> says, the law of divinity is immovably established so that the lowest things are perfected by the highest.

**Response.** Because the question regarding the origin of the works of witchcraft is based upon the

<column-break/>

influence of the celestial lights <note>The sun, moon, and stars</note>, the author demonstrates this by the rejection of three errors held by those who attempt to assert this: namely, the errors of the "planet-watchers," the **casters of birth charts** <term>genethliacorum; astrologers who predict a person's fate based on their birth</term>, and those who posit a fixed order of fate. He shows that this is not possible regarding the first point. For if it is asked whether the vice of practitioners of witchcraft is caused in humans by the impression of the celestial lights, then, while attending to the diversity of customs and preserving the truth of the faith, one must distinguish. Namely, that the idea that human morals are caused by the stars can be understood in two ways: either *necessarily and sufficiently*, or *dispositively and contingently*. If it is meant in the first way, then it is not only false but even heretical, because it is so repugnant to the Christian religion that the truth of the faith cannot be preserved in such an error. The reason is: while one posits that all things happen by necessity because of the stars, one then removes merit and, consequently, demerit. It also removes grace and, consequently, glory. Furthermore, because the integrity of morals suffers prejudice through this error, while the fault of the sinner is shifted back onto the stars, the license to practice witchcraft is granted without rebuke, and man is bent toward praying to and worshiping the stars. If, however, it is said that human morals are varied by the dispositions of the stars *dispositively and contingently*, this can be true, as it is repugnant neither to reason nor to faith. For it is plain that a varied disposition of the body contributes much to the variation of the soul's affections and morals. For the soul, for the most part, imitates the physical temperaments <note>original: *complexiones*</note> of the body, as is stated in the **Book of Six Principles** <note>A standard medieval textbook on logic and categories</note>. Hence, those who are **choleric** 
<margin>Thus [the soul follows?] through the body <unclear>smita</unclear> <unclear>p</unclear> <unclear>cōp⁹</unclear></margin>
are prone to anger, and the **sanguine** are kind, and the **melancholy** are envious, and the **phlegmatic** are lazy. But this is not by necessity. For the soul rules its own body, and especially when it is aided by grace. For we see many choleric people who are gentle and melancholy people who are kind. Since, therefore, the power of the celestial bodies brings about the mixture and quality of the physical temperaments, it follows that in a certain way, it contributes to the quality of morals—yet only from a great distance.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into whether celestial bodies (the stars and planets) can be the cause of human malice and the works of witchcraft. The previous page argued that while the devil can influence the senses, he cannot directly compel the human will. This section specifically addresses the limits of astrological influence on human behavior and free choice.</meta>

The power of inferior nature contributes more to the quality of the temperament <term>complexio; the specific balance of humors in an individual's body</term> than does the power of a star. Hence, **Saint Augustine** in the fifth book of *The City of God*, in solving a certain question concerning two brothers who fell ill and were cured at the same time: when it was asked why this should be so, he commended the reasoning of **Hippocrates** more than that of the astronomer. For Hippocrates replied that this occurred because of the similarity of their temperament <note>original: "similitudinem complexionis"</note>, while the astronomer replied that it was because of the identity of their constellation. The physician <note>original: "phisicus"; referring here to Hippocrates</note> replied better, because he provided a cause that was more proximate and more immediate. Therefore, it should be said that the impressions of the stars in some way dispose one toward the malice of sorcerers <note>original: "maleficorum"; those who practice harmful magic</note>, provided that some celestial influence dominates in their bodies toward such unspeakable acts rather than toward any other works, whether vicious or virtuous. However, such a disposition must not be called a necessary, primary, and sufficient cause, but rather a remote and contingent one. 

Nor is it valid if someone were to object using the Philosopher <note>Aristotle; though the work cited is likely the pseudo-Aristotelian "On the Properties of the Elements"</note> in the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, where it says that kingdoms were made empty and lands depopulated at the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn. The argument would be: because such things depended on the free will of men, the influences of the luminaries must therefore have efficacy over free will. For it is answered that the Philosopher does not intend to imply that those men could not have resisted the influence of that constellation which inclined them toward discord, but rather that they were unwilling to do so; for as **Ptolemy** says in the *Almagest*: "A wise man will rule the stars" <note>original: "sapiens homo dominabitur astris"</note>. For although the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn might incline men toward anger or discord—because Saturn has a melancholic and evil influence while Jupiter has a very good one—men can nevertheless resist that inclination through the freedom of their will, and quite easily with the help of God’s grace. 

Again, it is not valid if someone were to object to the saying of **John of Damascus** <note>original: "damascenus"</note> in his second book, chapter six, where he says: comets and certain signs of the deaths of kings are often established. For it is answered that even following the opinion of Damascene—who, as is clear in the aforementioned book, held an opinion contrary to the philosophical path—nothing is concluded by this regarding the necessity of human acts. For Damascene is of the opinion that a comet is neither naturally

<column-break/>

generated, nor is it one of the stars placed in the firmament. Hence, its significance is not natural, nor is its influence. For he says that comets are not among those stars which were created in the beginning, but are established by divine command according to the needs of the time and are again dissolved; thus says Damascene. Moreover, God foretells the death of a king through such a sign more than the death of others, both because a king is a public person <note>original: "persona communis"</note> and because a disturbance of the kingdom can arise from his death. Angels are more solicitous for the guardianship of the kingdom for the sake of the common good; by their ministry, these signs are both generated and dissolved. 

But the opinion of the philosophers does not stand in the way either, for they say that a comet star is a "hot and dry impression" generated in the upper part of the air near the region of fire. From the hot and dry vapor of this region, a small globe of gathered vapor makes the body of the star appear. The parts of that vapor, either continuing around that globe or extending long at its ends and joined to that globe, are like its hair <note>original: "come"; the Greek and Latin root for "comet" implies "long-haired star"</note>. According to this position, a comet signifies and causes mortality—not through itself, but by accident—resulting from infirmities that are hot and dry <note>such as fevers</note>. And because, for the most part, the wealthy nourish themselves with hot and dry things, many wealthy people die at such a time, among whom the deaths of kings and princes are more notable. 

This position does not differ from the position of Damascene, if one considers it well, except regarding the operation and cooperation of an angel, which even the philosophers cannot exclude. Indeed, where vapors would never concur in their dryness and heat to generate a comet, they must often concur by the operation of an angel for the reasons aforesaid. Such was the star that indicated the transition <note>original: "transitu"; his death or passing into heaven</note> of the doctor **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, which certainly did not flow from the higher stars placed in the firmament, but was formed by the operation of an angel from some pre-existing matter and, its office performed, was again dissolved. Hence we see that according to any of these opinions, the luminaries of heaven have absolutely no dominion over free will. Consequently, they have no power over the malice and morals of men. Note, moreover, why astronomers often predict truths, and why their judgments for the most part concern a province or...

occur to the people of a single land. The reason for this is that because [astrologers] take their judgments from the stars—which have a greater influence that is more probable but not necessitating—in acts of nature as well as the will, and in the general acts of men (such as a whole nation or province) rather than in the particular acts of one person. This is because a greater effect of the stars is impressed upon an entire people than upon one man, and because the greater part of a single nation follows natural bodily inclinations more than a single, individual man does. Thus the matter stands; but this has been touched upon incidentally.

The **Second Way** by which our aforementioned Catholic assertion is declared is through the rejection of the errors of the "genethliacs" <term>genethliaci; astrologers who cast horoscopes based on the hour of birth</term> and of those "mathematicians" <note>In the Middle Ages, "mathematici" often referred to those who practiced forbidden divination or judicial astrology.</note> who worship the goddess Fortune. Concerning these, **Isidore** says in the eighth book of his *Etymologies*, chapter nine, that they are called "genethliacs" because of their consideration of the stars at birth, whom the common people call mathematicians. Truly, as is said in the same work in chapter two, Fortune is said to take her name from "fortuitous" events, as if she were a certain goddess mocking human affairs with various and chance occurrences. Whence they also call her blind, because she rushes upon anyone at random without any examination of their merits, coming to both the good and the evil. So says Isidore.

But to believe in such a goddess, or to believe that the injuries to bodies or creatures resulting from the works of sorcerers <note>original: "maleficorum"</note> proceed not from the sorcerers themselves but from the goddess Fortune, is idolatry. Likewise, to assert that witches themselves were born for this purpose—so that such things could be carried out by them in the world—is alien to the faith and even to the common tradition of the philosophers. If anyone pleases, let them look to the **Holy Doctor** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> in the third book of the *Summa Contra Gentiles*, question 88 and following, and they will find more. 

However, one point should not be omitted for the sake of those who perhaps do not have a wealth of books: namely, that there are three things in man (as noted there) which are directed by three celestial causes: the act of the **will**, the act of the **intellect**, and 

<margin><image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand) indicates the start of the next section.</image-desc></margin> the act of the **body**. The principle of the first is directed by God alone and immediately; the second by an angel; and the third by a celestial body. For choices and wills are 

<column-break/>

immediately directed by God in good works, as the Scripture says in Proverbs 21: *The heart of the king* (implying that he who seems able to resist with greater power is less able to than others) *is in the hand of the Lord, and he shall turn it whithersoever he will.* And the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in Philippians 2:13</note> says: *It is God who works in us both to will and to perform according to his good will.*

Truly, human intellectual knowledge is ordered by God through the mediation of angels. But those things which pertain to bodily matters—whether they be external or internal—that come into the use of man are dispensed by God through the mediation of angels and celestial bodies. For the **Blessed Dionysius** says in chapter seven of *On the Divine Names* that celestial bodies are the causes of those things which happen in this world, though they do not impose necessity. 

And since man is ordered according to the body under celestial bodies, but according to the intellect under angels, and according to the will under God, it can happen that a man, having spurned the inspiration of God toward the good and the illumination of the good angel, is led by bodily affection toward those things to which the influence of the heavenly lights inclines him. Thus, both the will and the intellect become involved in malice and errors. 

However, it is not possible to be entangled in the types of errors with which sorcerers are ensnared [solely] by the influences of the heavenly lights—even though one might be inclined by them toward the shedding of blood, or theft, or robbery, or even the perpetration of the worst incontinencies <note>original: "incontinentias"; referring to sexual sins or lack of self-control</note>, just as one might be inclined toward certain other natural things. Also, as **William [of Auvergne]** says in *On the Universe*, it is known through experience that if a prostitute <margin>Note</margin> strives to plant an olive tree, it is not made fruitful, yet one planted by a chaste woman is made fruitful. And a certain physician <margin>will not love</margin> in healing, or a farmer in planting, or a soldier in attacking, may achieve certain things due to the impression of a celestial body which others possessing the same arts cannot achieve.

The **Third Way** is taken from the rejection of "fatal" effects. Here it should be noted that asserting something to be "fate" in one way is Catholic, while to assert it in another way is entirely heretical. For if they estimate fate to be according to the estimation of certain [pagans]...

It rejects the idea of "born witches" or "Fortune" as the cause of evil, emphasizing that astrology only creates inclinations, not necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of fatalism, moving from a general discussion of astrology to a specific theological definition of "fate" as distinct from "divine providence," specifically addressing whether the acts of sorcerers are subject to these forces.</meta>

of the pagans and also of certain **mathematicians** <note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers specifically to practitioners of judicial astrology or divination.</note> who thought that from the power of the position of the stars, a diversity of morals was infallibly caused. Thus, a person would necessarily be made either a **sorcerer** <term>maleficus; one who performs harmful magic</term> or virtuous in their habits, because the power contained in the disposition of the stars under which that person was conceived or born would cause them to be so. And they called this power by the name of **fate**.

But this opinion is not only false, it is indeed heretical and entirely to be detested because of the inconsistencies that would necessarily follow, as was touched upon above regarding the rejection of the first error. Namely, it would take away the logic of merit and demerit—and indeed of grace and glory—and it would make God the author of our evils, among many other errors. Therefore, **fate** understood in this way is entirely refuted because it is nothing; just as **Gregory** says in his *Homily on the Epiphany*: <note>original: "Absit a fidelium cordibus vt fatum aliquid esse dicant."</note> "Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to say that fate is anything."

And although this opinion seems to be the same as the first one concerning the planets—and this because of the same inconsistencies perceived in both—they are nevertheless different, just as the specific power of the stars and the general influence of the seven planets differ from one another. If, however, **fate** is estimated to be a certain disposition or ordering of secondary causes for producing effects provided by God, in this way fate truly is "something," because the providence of God executes its effects through intermediary causes. This applies to those things which are subject to secondary causes, though not in other things such as the creation of souls, glorification, and the bestowing of grace. Although even angels can cooperate in the infusion of grace by illuminating and disposing the intellect and the capacity of the will. 

And so, a certain ordering of effects is called **providence** and **fate** as one and the same thing. For if it is considered as it exists in God, it is called **providence**; but if it is considered according to how it exists in the intermediary causes ordered by God to produce certain effects, then it has the logic of **fate**. It is in this way that **Boethius**, speaking of fate in the fourth book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, says: <note>original: "Fatum est rebus mobilibus inherēs dispositio per quā prouidētia suis queq[ue] nectit ordinibus."</note> **Fate** is a disposition inherent in mutable things, through which Providence binds each thing to its own orders.

<column-break/>

But nevertheless, the **Holy Doctors** <note>The "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theological teachers like Augustine or Aquinas.</note> refused to use this name because of those who twisted it to refer to the power of the position of the stars. Whence **Augustine** says in the fifth book of *The City of God*: "If anyone attributes human affairs to fate for the reason that they call the very will or power of God by the name of fate, let them hold their opinion but correct their language." <note>Augustine argues that while God's will governs all, using the word "fate" is dangerous because it implies the stars have power over the soul.</note>

From the preceding points, a silent response is also clear regarding the question of whether all things are subject to fate, and whether even the **works of sorcerers** are subject to it. Because if "fate" is defined as the ordering of secondary causes toward effects provided by God—that is, where God has arranged to produce such effects through secondary causes—then I say they are subject to fate, meaning they are subject to secondary causes so ordered by God, such as the influences of the celestial bodies. 

However, those things which are done immediately by God, such as the creation of things, the glorification of spiritual substances, and other things of this sort, are not subject to fate. And this is what **Boethius** says in the place cited above: that those things which are near to the primary Deity exceed the mobility of the fatal order. Whence the **works of sorcerers**, because they are not subject to secondary causes—since such things happen outside the common course and order of nature—are therefore not subject to fate, but must be subject to other causes regarding their origin.

Consequently, it follows that the works of such sorcerers cannot arise or be caused by **separate substances** <term>substantiis separatis; spiritual beings like angels or demons who exist apart from physical matter</term> which are the movers of the spheres or celestial bodies. This was the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>An influential Persian philosopher and physician (980–1037 AD).</note> and his followers, moved by this reasoning: because those separate substances are of a higher power than our souls, and since our own body is sometimes changed by the soul through its imagination alone—concerning a certain internal apprehension regarding something external—and sometimes even someone else's or an external body is changed. 

For example: someone walking upon a **beam** placed high up falls easily, because they imagine the fall out of fear; yet they would not fall if that beam were placed upon the ground, where the fall could not be feared. Likewise, by apprehension alone...

<summary>This page discusses the theological definition of "fate," distinguishing the heretical view of stellar determinism from the Boethian view of fate as the unfolding of Divine Providence through secondary causes. It concludes that while natural events may be subject to fate, the supernatural works of sorcerers and direct acts of God are not.</summary>

<margin>Note</margin> However, that creature by whose help magical operations are performed—if they are good by nature—nevertheless cannot be good according to their **will**. To lead away from these, therefore, and to draw them toward other minimal goods is the mark of an improperly disposed intellect. 

By these arts, however, men do not acquire any progress in the goods of reason—which are the sciences and the virtues—but rather in certain minimal things, such as the discoveries and activities of thieves and a thousand other harms. In conclusion: just as such arts cannot arise from the celestial bodies, they also cannot arise from their movers. And since they must necessarily arise from some power granted to some creature—and that creature also cannot be good according to its will, though it is good by nature—and such creatures are the **demons** themselves, it remains that these things are done by their power. 

Unless, perhaps, there still stands in the way the frivolous opinion that these things follow from the **malice of men** concurring with the threatening words of sorcerers and magic items placed in a certain location by the power of the stars. For example: when a sorcerer, while placing an image, says, "I will make you blind or lame," and this happens, it would happen because such a person was granted such a power from their birth by the influence of the stars above other men. In that case, even if others uttered the same words and were trained by instruction to utter them, they still could not be effective in such works. 

In responding to each of these points, it will be declared: First, that such effects cannot be caused by the **malice of men**. Second, that they cannot be caused by the errors of any men...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the causes of witchcraft, moving from celestial influences to the role of human malice and the distinction between divine miracles and demonic works. And first, that such works of **sorcerers** <term>maleficorum; those who perform harmful magic or witchcraft</term> cannot arise from human **malice** <term>malitia; a deliberate will to do evil</term>, however great it may be, is declared thus: For human malice—whether it be **habitual** (insofar as one acquires a habit through frequent acts that inclines them toward committing **sins** <term>peccata; moral offenses</term>, not out of ignorance or weakness, and thus is judged to be from sheer malice) or whether it be **actual malice** (which is called the very choice of evil, also termed the **sin against the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "peccatū in spiritū sanctum"; considered an unpardonable sin because it involves a conscious rejection of divine grace</note>)—can never achieve so much through the sorcerer alone that such works, like the changing of the elements or the infliction of injuries upon the bodies of humans and cattle alike, could occur without the assistance of some higher power. This is declared first on the part of the cause, and second on the part of the effect of the sorcery.

For if a human cannot achieve something without malice—that is, through their own natural powers—they are even less able to achieve it through those natural powers when they are diminished. It is clear that an active power is weakened when it is diminished. But a human, through sins committed by malice of any kind, is diminished in their natural gifts. This is proven by both authority and reason. For **Dionysius** <note>original: "dio. iiij. ca. de di. no."; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite’s "On the Divine Names," chapter 4</note> says: 

<margin>Chapter 4 on the Divine Names.</margin>
Evil is a defect of a natural habit. And he is speaking of the evil of **guilt**. Hence, no one who knows evil performs it as evil; if they do perform it, they do so out of a defect. The reasoning is this: as the good of grace is to the evil of nature, so the evil of guilt is to the good of nature. But through grace, the evil of nature—such as the "kindling" of sin—is diminished; therefore, by an even stronger logic, the good of nature is diminished by guilt.

Nor is it an obstacle if one speaks of **fascination** <term>fascinatio; the "evil eye" or the power to harm through a look</term>, which is sometimes brought about by the gaze or looking of some malicious old woman staring at a child, whereby the child is changed and fascinated. Because, as was touched upon above, this can only happen to children on account of their tender complexion. Here, however, we are speaking of the bodies of any humans and cattle, and even the changing of the elements into hailstorms. If

<column-break/>

anyone wishes to understand this more broadly, let them look to the **Holy Doctor** <note>original: "doctorem sanctum"; referring to St. Thomas Aquinas</note> in his *Disputed Questions on Evil*, specifically on whether sin can corrupt the whole of the good of nature. Finally, this is declared from the side of the effects of sorcery. For from the effects, one arrives at the knowledge of the cause. Thus, just as those effects which, relative to us, are done outside the order of created nature known to us, are performed by the power of a creature unknown to us—though these are not strictly **miracles** <term>miracula; events that transcend all created nature</term> like those done outside the order of *all* created nature, which are performed by the power of Him who is above the entire order of all created nature, namely **God the Blessed**—according to which definition it is said: *You alone are the one who does great wonders.* So too, the effects of sorcery are called "miraculous" insofar as they are produced by some cause unknown to us and outside the order of created nature known to us.

<margin>Augustine in the Book of 83 Questions.</margin>
From this, it is gathered that the bodily power of a human cannot extend itself to causing such works, for a human power always has this quality: that the cause, along with its natural effect, is naturally known without wonder. And it is clear from the effects themselves that the works of sorcery can in some way be called miracles, insofar as they exceed human knowledge, since they do not happen naturally. This is also clear through all the Doctors, especially **Augustine** in his *Book of 83 Questions*, where he says that through magical arts, miracles are often performed similar to those miracles performed by the servants of God. And again, in the same place, he says: **Magicians** perform miracles through **private contracts** <term>private contracts; secret agreements with demons</term>; good Christians perform them through **public justice** <term>public justice; the universal law and authority of God</term>; and evil Christians perform them through the signs of public justice. All of these things are declared thus: For divine justice is in the whole universe like the public law in a city. The power of any creature in the universe is like the power of a private person in a city.

Therefore, good Christians, insofar as they perform miracles through divine justice, are said to perform miracles through "public justice." A magician, however, because he works from a **pact** entered into with a **demon** <term>daemonem; a fallen angel or evil spirit</term>, is said to work through a "private contract," because he works through a demon who, by his natural power, can do something outside the order of created nature known to us.

### Finally, [these things occur] neither through the words of any men, even with the concurrence of any constellation, nor upon any images.

For since the human intellect is of such a disposition that its knowledge is caused by things—since it is necessary for the one who understands to look upon **phantasms** <term>fantasmata; mental images or sensory perceptions used by the mind to form thoughts</term>—it is not in its nature that its intrinsic conception or intellectual operation could cause external things simply by expressing them through words. Nor is it the case that the conception of the intellect, when expressed through words, should have the power to change physical bodies. Indeed, such humans who possessed such a power would not be of the same species as us; they would be called "humans" in name only.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that they achieve these things through words by the power of the stars concurring at their birth—whereby it happens that they achieve something through words while others, speaking the same words, cannot effect any transformation because the power of the stars at their birth did not serve them—it is clear from the preceding arguments that this is false. This follows from the rejection of three errors: those of the planetarians, the casters of horoscopes, and those who posit a fatalistic order.

Moreover, since words express the concept of the mind, and celestial bodies cannot impress upon the intellect, nor even can the **movers** <note>The "movers" were believed to be spiritual intelligences (angels or spirits) that guided the motion of the planets and stars.</note> of those bodies—unless they wished to illuminate the intellect by themselves without the motion of the celestial bodies—and this would only be done for good works. Because

<column-break/>

for the perpetration of evil, the intellect is not illuminated but rather darkened, which is not the office of good spirits but of evil ones. Therefore, it is clear that if their words achieve anything, it is not by the vigor of any celestial body, but by the assistance of some intellectual power which, even if it is good by its nature, cannot be good by its **will** <term>voluntate; the faculty of choice</term>, insofar as it always schemes for evil. And such a being is a **demon**, as was shown above.

And they cannot achieve such things through **images** <note>Likely referring to talismans, wax figures, or astrological amulets.</note> as if the celestial bodies were infusing something into them. For images of this kind, no matter how much they are marked with characters and figures, are the effects of a human operating through **art** <term>artem; here meaning human skill or craft, as opposed to nature</term>. Celestial bodies, however, cause natural effects, and the effects of sorcerers (which are called "maleficial") are not of this kind. For example, they burst forth into the harming of creatures beyond the accustomed order of nature; hence, this is irrelevant to the proposal.

Furthermore, it was also shown above that there are two types of images: **astrological** and **magical**. These are even intended for obtaining some private good and not for corruption. However, the images of **sorcerers** <term>maleficorum; those who practice harmful magic</term> are of an entirely different kind, since they are always intended for the injury of creatures and are hidden in some place at the instigation of demons, so that those walking over them or sleeping near them may be harmed, as the **witches** <note>original: "malefice"; the female form of the word for sorcerer, reflecting the text's specific focus on women in later sections.</note> themselves confess. Therefore, they achieve whatever they cause through the demons themselves and not from the influences of celestial bodies.

Regarding the arguments: To the first, the saying of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> must be understood to mean that the cause of human depravity returns to the human will as the "perfecting" or direct cause, which is properly called the cause. The devil is not a cause in this way, but rather as a "permitting," "disposing," "palliating," or "preceptive" cause. In these ways—palliating, disposing, and commanding—the devil is called the cause of sin and depravity. God, however, is a cause only in a "permissive" sense, as He permits evils for the sake of good, according to **Augustine in the Enchiridion** <note>The *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Love*, a handbook on Christian theology.</note>. The devil disposes internally by suggesting, persuades internally and externally by sharply stimulating; but he only seizes upon these...

For every cause of limited power can produce a more intense effect upon matter that is predisposed than upon matter that is not. For instance, the devil can harass more intensely with a **melancholic passion** <term>passio melancolica; an excess of "black bile," associated in medieval medicine with depression and vulnerability to demons</term> a person already predisposed to it than a person...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into whether natural objects like herbs or music have power over demons. ...of a contrary disposition. It is certain, moreover, that **herbs and harmonies** <term>armoniae; here referring to musical arrangements and the mathematical proportions of sound</term> are very capable of changing the disposition of the body, and consequently, the movement of the **sensuality** <term>sensualitas; the part of the soul concerned with sensory perception and appetite</term>. This is evident regarding herbs, since some incline a person toward joy, others toward sadness, and so on for other states. This is also clear regarding harmonies according to **the Philosopher** <note>original: "phm̄" referring to Aristotle</note> in the eighth book of the *Politics*, where he maintains that different harmonies have the power to provoke different passions in humans. **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher and musician.</note> also reports this in his work on music. Furthermore, the author of *The Origin of the Sciences* <note>Dominicus Gundissalinus, a 12th-century translator and philosopher.</note>, when speaking of the utility of music, says that it is effective for curing or alleviating various infirmities. And thus it can be seen that, all other things being equal, the **reason** <term>ratio; the rational faculty of the soul</term> is made weaker.

However, I do not see how herbs or harmonies could cause a disposition in a person by which that person could in no way be harassed by a demon, if the demon were permitted to do so. For the devil, by moving only with **local motion** <term>motus localis; movement from one place to another</term> the **vapors and the spirits** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" and "vapors" were subtle substances that circulated in the blood and nerves to carry out the functions of the soul.</note> themselves in a disordered movement, could greatly harass a person. Herbs or harmonies could cause no disposition in a person through their own natural power by which a demon would be prohibited from causing the aforementioned commotion. It happens, however, sometimes that the devil is not permitted to harass a person unless the reason is so small that it might be totally removed by some strong disposition toward the contrary; and then certain herbs or harmonies could so dispose a person’s body toward the contrary that the reason for the harassment would be totally removed. For example: the devil might sometimes be able to harass a person through the reason of sadness so weakly that through certain herbs or harmonies—which have the power to cause the dilation and diffusion of the spirits (which are movements contrary to sadness)—that sadness would be totally removed. 

Regarding this, **Augustine** in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine* condemns **bindings** <term>ligaturas; amulets or charms tied to the body</term> and certain other things about which he writes more extensively there, attributing this to the **magical art** <note>original: "arti magice"</note>. This is because they cannot achieve such things through their own natural power, which is evident from what he says: "To this class belong all bindings and remedies which the discipline of physicians condemns." In this it is clear enough that he condemns them regarding their use in respects for 

<column-break/>

which they have no efficacy through their natural power. 

As for what is found in **the first book of Kings, chapter sixteen** <note>This refers to 1 Samuel 16 in modern Bibles.</note>, that **Saul**, who was harassed by a demon, was relieved when **David** struck the **lyre** <note>original: "cytharā"</note> before him and that the evil spirit departed, etc.: It should be known that it is quite true that through the playing of the lyre, by the natural power of that harmony, Saul's affliction was somewhat alleviated, insofar as that harmony in some way sweetened his appetite through the sense of hearing; through which sweetening he was rendered less fit for that harassment. 

But the fact that the evil spirit departed when David played the lyre was due to the power of the **Cross**, which is stated quite expressly in the **Gloss** <term>Glossa Ordinaria; a standard collection of biblical commentaries</term>, where it says: "David was learned in musical songs, a rational and moderate concord of diverse sounds. It signifies the unity of essence which resonates daily in various ways. ### Question: Whether witches are able to change 
### the minds of men toward love or hatred. 
### And this is the seventh in order.

<margin>
<unclear>Ma</unclear> <note>Likely "Materia" (Subject Matter).</note>
</margin>
It is asked whether demons, through these witches, are able to change and incite the minds of men toward inordinate love or hatred. And it is argued that they cannot, based on what has been said before. There are three things in man: the will, the intellect, and the body. The first [the will], God has to rule by Himself; for "the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord." <note>Proverbs 21:1</note> Likewise the second [the intellect] He rules by enlightening it through an angel, and the body itself He directs through the influences of celestial bodies. Furthermore, demons cannot be inside bodies to change them; therefore, they are even less able to be within the soul's powers to instill hatred or love. The consequence is clear, because by nature they have greater power over bodily things than over spiritual things. And indeed, that they cannot change these things has appeared above in many places, because they can induce no form, whether substantial or accidental, except by the aid of some other agent, just as any other craftsman does. Also to the same point is Canon 26, Question 5, *Episcopi*, at the end: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or for the worse except by the Creator of all Himself is worse than an infidel and a pagan." <note>The *Canon Episcopi* was an influential 10th-century legal text that argued witchcraft was a delusion or hallucination; the authors of this manuscript often struggle to reconcile their views with it.</note> Furthermore, every agent acting by purpose knows its own effect. If, therefore, the devil were able to change the minds of men toward hatred or love, he would be able to see the internal thoughts of the soul,

<column-break/>

which is contrary to what is said in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: "The devil cannot see internal thoughts." <note>This work was traditionally attributed to the early Christian writer Gennadius of Marseilles.</note> And again in the same place: "Not all our evil thoughts are excited by the devil, but sometimes they emerge from the movement of our own free will." Furthermore, love and hatred concern the will, which is rooted in the soul; therefore they cannot be caused by the devil by any art whatsoever. The consequence holds, because to "glide into the soul" <note>original: "illabi anime"</note>, as Augustine says, is possible only for Him who created it. Furthermore, if it is said that he can move the internal sensitive powers and thus consequently the will, this is not valid, because the sensitive power is more noble than the nutritive power. But the devil cannot form an act of the nutritive power, such as forming flesh or bone; therefore he also cannot cause any act of the internal powers of the soul. But on the contrary: the devil is said to tempt men not only visibly but also invisibly. This, however, would be false unless he could cause something internally concerning the soul and its powers. Furthermore, [John] Damascene says in his *Sentences*: "All malice and all uncleanness have been devised by the devil." And Dionysius in chapter 4 of *On the Divine Names*: "The multitude of demons is the cause of all evils, both to themselves and to others." 

**Response.** Here, first, a distinction regarding "cause" must be given; and second, how he is able to change the internal powers of the soul, which are called the "internal sensitive powers"; and thus, thirdly, the proposition will be concluded. Regarding the first point, it must be considered that a thing can be called the cause of something in two ways: in one way, directly; in another way, indirectly. Indirectly, indeed, as when some agent causes some disposition toward some effect, it is said to be the occasional and indirect cause of that effect; as if it were said that he who cuts wood is the occasion for its burning. And in this way we can say that the devil is the cause of all our sins, because he himself instigated the first man to sin, and from that sin followed in the whole human race a certain proneness toward all sins. And the words of Damascene and Dionysius are to be understood in this way. Directly, however, something is said to be the cause of another insofar as it works directly toward it...
