...concluded, and in this way the devil is not the cause of every sin. For not all sins are committed at the devil's instigation, but some arise from the **freedom of the will** <note>original: "libertate arbitrii"</note> and the corruption of the flesh. As Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) whose works were widely cited in the Middle Ages.</note> says: Even if the devil did not exist, humans would still have an appetite for food and for sexual matters <note>original: "venereorum," referring to Venus, the goddess of love; hence, sexual acts.</note> and the like. Many disorders occur regarding these things unless such an appetite is restrained by reason, especially given the presupposed corruption of human nature. To restrain and order such an appetite falls under the domain of **free will**, over which the devil has very little power.

But because we cannot, through this distinction, discern how **passionate love** <term>original: "amor hereos," a medieval medical/psychological condition of obsessive erotic desire, often considered a form of melancholy.</term> or **love-sickness** <term>original: "philocaprio," a term for being ensnared or captivated by lust, often through magical means.</term> can sometimes be procured through witchcraft <note>original: "maleficio"</note>, it must be further noted that although the devil cannot be the cause of that inordinate love by directly forcing a person's will, he can nevertheless act by way of persuasion.

This happens in two ways: visibly and invisibly. Visibly, as when he appears in some human form to the witches themselves, speaks to them sensibly, and persuades them to sin—just as he tempted our first parents in Paradise in the form of a serpent, or Christ in the desert by appearing in some visible form. And since it is not to be thought that he persuades humans only in this way (for it would follow that no other sins would be committed by the devil’s instruction except those he persuaded by appearing visibly), it must be said that he also invisibly instigates humans to sin.

This invisible instigation happens in two ways: by way of persuasion and by way of disposition. By way of persuasion, as when something is proposed to the cognitive faculty as a good. This can happen in three ways: either it is proposed to the intellect, or to the internal senses, or to the external senses. Regarding the intellect: the human intellect can be aided by a good angelic intellect to know something by way of a certain illumination, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher.</note> says. The reason is that, according to "the Philosopher" <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note>, understanding is a kind of "undergoing" or being acted upon. Therefore, an angel can impress a certain species upon the intellect from which the act of

<column-break/>

understanding is named. And if it were said that the devil could also do this by his natural power (which is not diminished, as is clear from what was said before), it must be answered that he cannot do so by way of illumination, but only by way of persuasion. The reason is that the human intellect is of such a condition that the more it is illuminated, the more it knows the truth; and the more it knows the truth, the more it can guard itself against deception. Since the devil ultimately intends this deception, none of his persuasion can be called "illumination."

However, it can be called "revelation" insofar as he might impress something upon the internal or external sensitive powers where he would visibly persuade. Thus, intellectual knowledge would be persuaded to perform some act. Regarding how this can be done—namely, how he can impress something upon the internal powers—it must be noted that corporeal nature is naturally suited to be moved **locally** <note>original: "localiter," meaning physical movement from one place to another.</note> by a spiritual nature. This is evident in our own bodies, which are moved by our souls, and likewise in the celestial bodies. However, corporeal nature is not suited to be formed by spirit immediately. We speak here especially of forms that remain outside, not of those that inform the substance itself. Therefore, a corporeal agent must concur, as is proven in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book VII, which discusses the nature of substance and change.</note>.

Corporeal matter naturally obeys a good or bad angel regarding local motion. Because of this, demons can use local motion to collect "seeds" <note>A reference to "seminal reasons," a concept where demons gather the hidden biological components of things to produce rapid effects.</note> and join or apply them to certain effects to perform wonders, as happened with Pharaoh's magicians <note>Exodus 7:11-12, where the Egyptian magicians turned staffs into serpents.</note> who produced serpents and real animals by joining appropriate active things to appropriate passive things. Therefore, whatever can happen through the local motion of corporeal matter, there is nothing to prevent it from being done by demons, unless they are divinely hindered.

Furthermore, if we wish to understand how they can incite the human imagination and internal sensitive powers to appetites and impetuous acts through local motion, it must be noted that "the Philosopher" [Aristotle], in his book *On Sleep and Waking*, assigns the cause of the appearance of dreams to local motion. This occurs because when an animal sleeps and much blood descends to the sensory source, there also descend...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how demons interact with the human mind. It focuses on the Aristotelian and Thomistic understanding of "internal senses"—fantasy, imagination, and memory—to explain how obsessive love (amor hereos) can be psychologically manipulated by spiritual entities.</meta>

...movements or impressions left behind by past motions of the senses, which have been preserved within the spirits <note>original: "spiritibus"; in medieval physiology, these were subtle vapors that carried sensory information through the nerves.</note> or the interior sensitive powers. These powers are fantasy or imagination, **which** <gloss>which</gloss> are the same thing according to Saint Thomas [Aquinas], as will be shown. In fantasy or imagination, there is a kind of treasury of forms received through the senses. From this, it happens that they move the apprehensive principle—that is, the power that preserves the mental images <term>original: "specierum," the formal likenesses of objects stored in the mind.</term>—in such a way that these things appear in fantasies as freshly as if the sensory power were being newly affected by the external things themselves. It is true that not everyone understands these things; but if anyone wished to occupy himself with considering them, he would find the number and the function of the internal senses. According to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to European scholasticism.</note> in his book *On the Soul*, he says there are five: namely, common sense, fantasy, imagination, estimation, and memory. However, according to Blessed Thomas in the first part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], question 78, he says there are only four, because he considers the imaginative power and fantasy to be one and the same. A lengthy explanation is avoided here for fear of being tedious, especially since these matters are discussed at length in many other places. It is enough to say this: fantasy is a treasury of forms. If it seems to someone that memory is this same kind of thing, one must make a distinction: fantasy is the treasury or conservatory of forms received through the senses, but memory is the treasury of **intentions** <note>original: "intentionum," meaning the perceived qualities of a thing that the five senses cannot detect, such as whether it is dangerous or useful.</note> which are not received through the senses. 

For who, seeing a wolf, flees from it? He does not flee because of the ugliness of its color or its shape—which are the forms received by the external senses and stored in the fantasy—but he flees because the wolf is an enemy to his nature. He knows this through a certain "intention" and apprehension from the **estimative power** <note>The faculty that allows animals and humans to instinctively judge a situation as harmful or beneficial.</note>, which perceives the wolf as harmful and the dog as a friend. The conservatory of those intentions is the memory. This is because, in physical things, the act of receiving and the act of retaining are traced back to different principles; for instance, moist things receive impressions well but retain them poorly, while the opposite is true for dry things. 

Regarding the matter at hand: this occurs in those who are sleeping, through the appearance of dreams coming from the spirits—that is, the mental images stored in the conservatories. This happens

<column-break/>

from a natural local motion, due to the stirring of the blood and the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> toward those principles, which is to say, toward the internal sensory powers. And we call this an "intrinsic local motion" within the head and within the cells of the brain. This can also happen from a similar local motion procured **by demons**. This occurs not only in those who are sleeping, but also in those who are awake, in whom demons can move and stir the internal spirits and humors so that the images preserved in the conservatories are drawn out from the "treasuries" toward the sensory principles—that is, to the imaginative and fantastic powers—so that such a person imagines certain things. This is called an **interior temptation**. It is no wonder that a demon can do this by his natural power, since any person who is awake and has the use of reason can, by a voluntary stirring of the preserved images, draw out these images from their treasuries (namely, the conservatories), so that he may imagine certain things at his own pleasure. 

Because this is established, the matter of **obsessive love** <term>original: "amore hereos"; also known as "heroic love," a medical diagnosis for extreme erotic obsession.</term> can now be clearly understood. Since demons, as has been said, can stir up these images, etc., they do so in two ways. Sometimes they do it without "binding" the use of reason (as was said regarding temptation), and an example of this is the voluntary dwelling on a thought that sometimes happens. At other times, however, the use of reason is **totally bound**. We can see examples of this in certain natural defects, such as in those who are frenzied <note>original: "freneticis," referring to those suffering from brain inflammation or acute delirium.</note> or drunk. Therefore, it is no wonder if demons, with God's permission, can so bind the use of reason; and such people are called **seized** <note>original: "arreptitij," from "arripio" (to snatch or seize); a term for those whose minds have been overtaken by a spirit.</note>. This happens in two ways: either without a witch or witchcraft, or with them. 

As the Philosopher <note>Standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the aforementioned book: a person who is in the grip of a passion is moved by even a slight resemblance, just as a lover is moved by a slight resemblance to the beloved, and similarly for one who feels hatred. Therefore, demons—who learn through human actions which passions people are most subject to—instigate them toward such inordinate love or hatred. They do this all the more strongly by effectively impressing what they intend into the person's imagination, doing so as easily as they are able.

They can do this more easily when the lover more easily draws out a reserved hope toward the sensitive principle—that is, the imagination—and dwells more delightfully in the thought of her. ### The method of proposing the premises concerning obsessive love <note>original: "amore hereos"; a medical and psychological term in the Middle Ages for a pathological, obsessive love that was considered a form of melancholy or mental illness.</note> in sermons to the people.

The aforementioned proposers move the question thus: Whether it is Catholic to assert that witches are able to change the minds of men toward an inordinate love of foreign women and so inflame their hearts that by no outpouring of blows, words,

<column-break/>

or deeds are they able to be forced to resist; and similarly to incite hatred between those joined in matrimony so that they can find no place for the rendering or demanding of the "marriage debt" <term>The "marriage debt" refers to the theological obligation of spouses to engage in sexual intercourse for the procreation of children.</term> for the sake of offspring; rather, it sometimes behooves them to run to their mistresses in the dead of night through many distances of land. If the preacher wishes, he may take some arguments regarding this from the preceding question. If not, let him merely say that these questions suffer from difficulties because love and hatred are founded in the will, which in its act is always free and cannot be forced by any creature except by God, who can rule it. Hence, neither a demon nor a witch by his power seems to be able to force the will toward love or hatred. Likewise, because the will, just like the intellect, exists subjectively in the soul, and to "glide into" the soul <note>original: "illabi animae"; a theological term meaning to enter the internal essence of the soul, a power reserved for God alone.</note> is possible only for Him who created it. Therefore, the question suffers difficulty regarding the truths to be enunciated in its parts. Notwithstanding these things, it must be said first concerning love-charms <note>original: "philocaptōem," from the Greek for "love-catching."</note> and hatred; and second, concerning the bewitchment of the generative power. Regarding the first: although the demon cannot operate immediately upon the intellect and will of man, yet according to all the doctors of theology in the *Fourth Book of Sentences*, <note>Referring to the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages by Peter Lombard.</note> they are able to act upon the body and the powers of the body (whether they be internal or external senses) by the power of the demon and with God's permission. This is proved by authority and reason from the preceding question. If it pleases the preacher, he will find it; if not, let him state the authority and reason from Job, chapter 2. God said to the demon: *Behold, he is in your hand*—that is, in your power—and this was regarding his body, which is clear because He did not want to give over his soul; hence He said: *Nevertheless, save his soul*—that is, keep it unharmed. The reason is that because his power reaches the body, it also reaches all the powers bound to the body, such as the five external senses and the four internal senses: namely, **Common Sense**, **Fantasy** or **Imagination**, **Estimation**, and **Memory**. If it cannot be declared otherwise, let the example of pigs and sheep be given, where pigs know how to return home through the memorative power, and sheep discern the wolf and the dog from natural imagination—one as an enemy, the other as a friend to its nature.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into how demons and witches manipulate human psychology, focusing specifically on the corruption of the intellect and the will to produce obsessive "heroic" love. Consequently, since all our intellectual knowledge originates from the senses—for, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On the Soul*, it is necessary for the intellect to observe mental images <term>phantasmata: the sensory images or "ghosts" of objects stored in the imagination</term>—it follows that just as a demon can alter the internal imagination, so he can also darken the intellect. And this will not be an immediate action upon the soul, but rather one occurring through the mediation of these mental images. Furthermore, because nothing is loved unless it is first known—take, for example, gold, which the miser loves because he understands its value—so, when the intellect is darkened, the will and its affections will also be darkened. 

A demon can do this both without a witch and with a witch; indeed, it can even happen solely from the carelessness of the eyes. We shall provide examples of each. For as it says in the first chapter of James: "Each one is tempted by his own desire, being drawn away and enticed. Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death." <note>James 1:14-15</note> Thus Sychem, when he had seen Dinah going out to see the women of that region, fell in love with her, seized her, and slept with her, and his soul was knit to hers (Genesis 34). According to the gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval biblical commentary</note>: This happens to weak souls when, neglecting their own affairs like Dinah, they busy themselves with the affairs of others; they are seduced by habit and become one in sense with illicit things.

Regarding the second point—that this may also arise without witches, primarily through the temptation of demons—it is explained thus: For Amnon fell in love with his most beautiful sister, Tamar, and despaired over her so greatly that he fell ill because of his love (2 Samuel 13). <note>The original cites 2 Kings 13, following the Vulgate numbering</note> For no one would leap into such a great crime of ravishment unless he were totally corrupt and heavily tempted by the devil. Hence the gloss on that passage: This warns us, and God permitted it so that we might always act cautiously, lest vices dominate us and the prince of sin <note>The Devil</note>—who promises a false peace to those in danger—finds us unprepared and slaughters us suddenly. The *Book of the Holy Fathers* <note>The *Vitae Patrum*, a collection of stories about the early Christian desert hermits</note> is full of this second type of love; it relates that although they had withdrawn from every temptation of carnal desire, they were sometimes tempted by the love of women beyond what can be believed. Hence the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 12: "A thorn of my flesh was given to me,

<column-break/>

an angel of Satan to buffet me." On which the gloss says: "It was given to me to tempt me toward lust." However, temptation to which one does not consent is not a sin, but rather material for the exercise of virtue. This is understood as temptation coming from the enemy, not from the flesh—for temptation from the flesh is always at least a venial sin, even if it is not consented to. The preacher may provide some examples of this if he wishes. 

Regarding the third point—that passionate love <term>amor hereos: a medieval medical and psychological term for obsessive, "heroic" love or lovesickness, often treated as a disease</term> may result from the witchcraft of demons—this has been discussed above, and it is this temptation of which we speak. And if anyone should ask how one can discern that such inordinate love proceeds from witchcraft alone and not simply from the devil, it must be said that it can be known by many signs. 

First, if the man so tempted has a beautiful and honorable wife, while the opposite is true of the other woman <note>Meaning the man is inexplicably attracted to an "ugly" or "lowly" woman over his virtuous wife</note>. Second, if the judgment of his reason is so entirely bound that no blows, words, deeds, or even public shames can induce him to resist her. And third, most especially, when he cannot contain himself, but must sometimes unexpectedly transport himself over a long distance—regardless of the harshness of the journey, as anyone can learn from the confessions of such people—whether by day or by night. 

For as Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, an early Church Father</note> says in his commentary on Matthew 21 regarding the donkey which Christ rode: when a demon possesses the human will through sin, he drags it where he pleases at his whim. He gives the example of a ship at sea that has lost its rudder, which is tossed at the whim of the wind; or like a man who sits powerfully upon a horse, or a tyrant king in possession of a territory. Fourth, it is discerned by the fact that they are sometimes transported and changed so unexpectedly and suddenly that nothing can stand in their way. It is also gathered from the ill-repute of the person herself. 

Before we proceed to the further question concerning witchcraft and the generative power <note>The ability to procreate or perform sexually</note>, which is also connected, the initial arguments must be resolved.

The solution is clear: for just as the intellect is only illuminated by a good angel toward the knowledge of the truth—from which follows the love of the good, because truth and being are interchangeable <note>original: "verum et ens convertuntur" — a core scholastic principle that anything that truly exists is inherently "true" and "good" in its being</note>—so also the intellect can be darkened by the evil one toward the knowledge of an apparent truth. And this happens through the confusion of the mental forms <term>species: the cognitive "images" or "forms" through which the mind understands objects</term> represented to the sensitive principles—that is, to the internal sensitive virtues and powers. From this follows an inordinate love of an apparent good, such as bodily pleasure, which such people also seek.

To the second argument—that they cannot be inside bodies by changing them—this is partly true and partly not, regarding a threefold change. For they cannot change those bodies as far as the drawing out of any form, whether substantial or accidental <note>Substantial forms define what a thing is (e.g., a human); accidental forms define its properties (e.g., being tanned or tall)</note>; this should rather be called production than change, and cannot happen without the help of some other agent or without divine permission. 

But if we speak of a qualitative change, such as health and sickness, then, as is clear from what has been said before, they can inflict various illnesses, even to the point of the binding of the reason <term>ligamen rationis: a state where the rational mind is "tied up" or blocked, preventing clear thought or free will</term>, and thus procure hatred and inordinate love. A third type of change can also be added: when a good or evil angel enters the body. We say that God alone enters into the soul—that is, into the very essence of the soul. But when we say an angel enters a body, especially an evil one as in the case of the possessed, he does not enter within the boundaries of the body’s essence. Because in that way, only He who gives being—namely, God the Creator—can enter, and He is contained as one who has intrinsic operation within the soul. 

However, an angel is said to enter the body when he performs some work upon the body, because he is where he acts, as John of Damascus <note>original: "Damascenus," an 8th-century theologian</note> says. And then he acts within the boundaries of bodily quantity and within the boundaries of the body’s essence. From this it is inferred that the body has boundaries of a twofold nature: of quantity and of essence. And there is a distinction here, just as there is between the individual person <term>suppositum: the individual "subsistence" or underlying personhood</term> and nature. Therefore, just as they

<column-break/>

can enter bodies, so they can also enter the powers attached to the bodily organs, and consequently they can make impressions upon these powers. Wherefore, by accident <note>In philosophy, "by accident" means indirectly or through a secondary property, rather than by the thing's primary essence</note>, such operation and impression results in the intellect, since its object is the mental image <term>phantasma: the sensory "ghost" or image stored in the imagination that the mind uses to think</term>, just as color is the object of sight, as is said in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s "De Anima"</note>. 

And consequently, this results by accident even in the will, because the will receives its object from the intellect under the aspect of the good, according to how the intellect apprehends something under the aspect of a true or an apparent good.

To the third argument: knowing the thoughts of the heart can be understood in two ways: either in their effect or as they are in the intellect. In the first way, not only an angel but even a man can know them, though an angel does so more subtly, as will be shown. For sometimes a thought is known not only through an external act, but even through a change in facial expression; even doctors can know certain affections of the soul by the pulse. Wherefore Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note>, in the book *On the Divination of Demons*, says that they learn men’s dispositions with total ease, not only when spoken aloud but even when conceived in thought, when certain signs from the soul are expressed in the body. 

Though in his book of *Retractions*, he says this should not be asserted; I believe he retracts the explanation of "how" this happens, lest anyone should think he meant that demons could know thoughts directly in the intellect. In the second way, thoughts can be known as they are in the intellect, and affections as they are in the will. In this way, God alone can know the thoughts of hearts and the affections of wills. The reason for this is that the will of a rational creature is subject to God alone, and He alone can work within it, for He is its principal object and final end. Therefore, those things which are in the will, or depend on the will alone, are known only to God. Moreover, it is manifest that it depends on the will alone that someone actually considers something. An angel cannot flow into the soul <note>original: "illabi animae"</note>, therefore it cannot by its very nature see those things that are within the soul, so long as they remain in the innermost part of the soul. Therefore, when it is argued that a demon cannot see the thoughts of the heart, and consequently cannot incite the hearts or minds of men toward love or hatred, it is said that just as the demon knows the effects—and in a much more subtle way than a human does—so also can he change a person toward hatred or love in a more subtle way by agitating **mental images** <term>phantasmata: the sensory images or "ghosts" in the mind that medieval scholars believed were necessary for thought</term> and by darkening the intellect.

There is also something to be noted for the consolation of those with fearful and virtuous consciences: that the physical and bodily change of the external senses which accompanies a person’s thoughts is sometimes so slight and indeterminate that the devil cannot come to a certain knowledge of the thought through it. This is especially true when people occupy themselves with studies or good works at intervals; in such cases, the devil vexes them more in their dreams, as experience teaches. Sometimes, however, the change is so strong and determinate that the demon can know the thought as far as its "species"—for instance, whether one is thinking about envy or about lust. But whether he can know with certainty all the circumstances—as for example, whether the thought is about this or that person—we leave as a matter of doubt, just as we find it in the texts. Nevertheless, it is true that he can later know such circumstances from the person's subsequent actions.

Regarding the fourth point, it is clear that while entering the soul belongs to God alone, "flowing into" the body—and consequently into the powers connected to the body in the manner touched upon above—can happen through an angel, whether good or bad. Hence, love and hatred can be caused in such a person. 

Regarding the argument that the sensory power is more noble than the **nutritive power** <term>nutritive power: the biological function of digestion and growth</term>, which nonetheless cannot be changed by the demon: it must be said that, on the contrary, he could even affect the nutritive power, so that something is directed into the mouth or the flesh more quickly or slowly. But he does not cooperate with that power as much as he does in hindering or agitating the internal or external sensory powers; he does this for his own "profit," which he pursues mostly through the deception of the senses and the illusion of the intellect.

**S**econdly, the same truth—namely that witches exist for the sake of adulterers, fornicators, etc.—is further shown through the sorcerous impediment placed upon the act of the generative power. If this is granted, then since marriage is a work of God and witchcraft is a work of the devil, the work of the devil would be stronger than the work of God. 

If, however, it is granted that it only happens to fornicators and not the married, then the opinion returns that witchcraft is nothing in reality, but exists only in the opinion of men—the opposite of which was touched upon in the first question. Or, a reason must be given as to why it can happen to these people and not those. But that this position is false is clearly proven by Saint Thomas in the same place: because some operations of demons are found which in no way [can be explained by natural causes].

And so, others were forced by the mentioned inconveniences to propose that demons exist, although they fell into various other errors; some claimed that the souls of men exiting their bodies become demons. Whence many **soothsayers** <note>original: "arusperices," referring to diviners who read signs in entrails</note> killed boys so that they might have their souls as their co-operators. Many other errors are recited in that place. Whence it is clear that the **Holy Doctor** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for the authors</note> does not without merit say that such an opinion proceeds from the root of infidelity. If it pleases anyone, let them read **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430)</note> in books 8 and 9 of *The City of God* regarding the various errors of the unfaithful concerning the nature of demons. Therefore, the reasoning of all the doctors alleged in the aforementioned distinction against those wandering in error—namely, those who deny that witchcraft is anything—is of great efficacy in its judgment, though brief in its words. There they say that those who assert witchcraft is nothing in the world contradict the opinions of all the doctors and the declaration of Holy Scripture that demons exist and that demons have power over bodies and over the imaginations of men, God permitting. Whence, through them, sorcerers can work wonders concerning creatures. Whence also the instruments of the demons themselves—at whose insistence the demons sometimes work to the harm of creatures—are rightly called **sorcerers** <term>malefici: literally "evil-doers," the technical term for those who practice harmful magic</term>. And indeed, while in the rejection of this first error by the doctors no mention is made of those joined in marriage, this is nevertheless clear through the rejection of the second error. For they say that the error of others was that, although witchcraft existed and abounded in the world even against the **carnal act** <term>carnalem copulam: sexual intercourse within marriage</term>, yet because no such witchcraft can be judged perpetual, it would never annul a marriage already contracted. Behold, mention is made here of those joined in marriage. In disproving this error—though declaring this may not serve our immediate purpose—nevertheless for the sake of those who do not have a wealth 

<column-break/>

of books, it should be noted that they disprove this by saying that to assert such things is against experience and against the **ancient and new laws** <note>referring to the *Decretum Gratiani* and the subsequent *Decretals* of canon law</note>. Whence the Catholic doctors give such a distinction: that impotence procured by witchcraft is either temporary or perpetual. If it is temporary, then it does not impede the marriage. It is presumed to be temporary when, cohabiting within the space of three years and giving as much effort as they can, they can be healed either through the **ecclesiastical sacraments** <note>such as confession, prayer, or exorcism</note> or through other remedies. If, however, they are not healed by any remedy, from then on it is presumed to be perpetual. And then, it either precedes the contract and consummation of the marriage, and thus it prevents a marriage from being contracted and annuls one already contracted; or it follows the contract of the marriage but not the consummation, and thus also, as some say, it annuls a marriage already contracted. For it is said in **Case 23, Question 1, Chapter 1** <note>a citation from the Decretum of Gratian</note> that a marriage is confirmed by its office, namely that of the flesh, as the **gloss** <note>the standard marginal commentary on canon law</note> says. Or, it follows a consummated marriage, and then the matrimonial bond is not dissolved. Many things are noted there in the section **"On the frigid and those under spell"** <note>original: "extra de frigid. re." referring to the Decretals of Gregory IX, Book 4, Title 15</note> by **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Susa</note> and **Goffredus** <note>Goffredus de Trano (c. 1200–1245), a canon lawyer</note> and the doctors, including the theologians mentioned above. As for the arguments: the first is clear enough from what has been said. For as to the first point, that God's works can be destroyed by the works of the devil if witchcraft could occur between spouses, the objection is not valid; rather, the opposite is clear, since the devil can do nothing except with God permitting. Likewise, because he does not destroy by violence like a tyrant, but through a certain **extrinsic art** <note>magic that works on the body from the outside rather than changing the soul</note> as was shown above. To the second point, it was shown above why God permits this over the act of lust rather than over other acts; he can also permit it over others when he wills. Whence it does not follow that he would destroy the world. To the third, it is similarly clear from what has been said.

### **Question Nine: Whether witches, through glamour and illusion, operate around the male organs as if they were entirely torn away from the bodies.**

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the powers of witches and demons, specifically focusing on the perceived removal of male genitalia. It follows a classic "disputed question" format: presenting arguments for a position, followed by a counter-argument, and finally a resolution that clarifies the nature of the phenomenon as a diabolical illusion rather than a physical transformation.</meta>

### Third, the same truth is declared through diabolical operations concerning the male members.

To make the truth of this matter shine more brightly, it is asked: Whether **witches** <note>original: "malefice"</note> are able, by the power of demons, to truly and actually remove male members, or whether they do so only through a **deceptive appearance** <term>prestigiosa apparitōne: a "glamour" or optical illusion caused by demonic influence on the senses</term>. 

It is argued that it happens truly and actually, by an argument from the stronger case:
1.  Demons can do greater things, such as kill men or transport them from place to place, as was shown previously regarding **Job** and in the Book of **Tobit** <note>Tobit 3:8, where a demon kills seven husbands of Sarah</note> regarding the seven men who were killed; therefore, they can also truly and actually remove a man's members.
2.  Furthermore, the **Gloss** <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> on the Psalm says: "Inflictions through evil angels." God punishes through evil angels, just as He often punished the people of Israel with various diseases truly and actually inflicted upon their bodies; therefore, He can also inflict such infirmities upon that specific member.
3.  If it is said that this happens by **divine permission**, then, as stated in the preceding sections, God permits the generative power to be more subject to witchcraft because of the first corruption of sin <note>The Fall of Adam and Eve</note> which comes down to us through the act of generation; therefore, He also permits more power over the member of that generative power, so that it may be totally removed.
4.  Furthermore, the conversion of **Lot’s wife** into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19) was a greater thing than removing a male member. But that was a true and real conversion, not a mere appearance, since (it is said) that statue still visibly remains. And this was done through an evil angel, just as those who were struck with blindness so they could not find the door of the house were coerced by Lot; as were the other punishments of the **Sodomites**. The Gloss also asserts there that she was infected by that same vice; therefore, they can also do these things.
5.  Furthermore, whoever can introduce a natural form can also take it away. But demons have introduced natural forms many times, as is seen with the **magicians of Pharaoh** who, by the power of demons, produced frogs and serpents.
6.  Also, **Augustine** in the book *Eighty-Three Different Questions* says that all things which happen visibly can also be done by the inferior powers of the air. It is not considered absurd that this can happen. But men can do this—removing a member by some art or incision; therefore, demons can also do these things invisibly which others do visibly.

<column-break/>

**But on the contrary:** 
**Augustine** says in Book 18 of *The City of God*: "It is not to be believed that even the body of a man can be converted into the features of a beast by the art or power of demons." Therefore, by a similar reasoning, he cannot remove that which belongs to the truth of the human body. Also, in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, he says: "It must not be thought that this matter of visible things serves these transgressing angels at their whim, but God alone."

**Response:** 
There is no doubt that certain witches perform wonders concerning male members, as is established from the things seen and heard by many—and indeed from public fame—regarding how the truth of that member was perceived through the senses of sight or touch. As to how this can happen, it must be said that although it could happen in two ways—namely, truly and actually (as the first arguments suggested) or by a deceptive operation—nevertheless, those things which are done by witches in this regard are done only through a **deceptive illusion** <note>original: "prestigiosa illusione"</note>. 

However, this illusion does not only take place in the **imagination** of the sufferer. For the imagination of a person can truly and actually judge a thing not to be present, even though the person perceives it is not present through no operation of the exterior senses, such as sight or touch. Hence, it can be called a "true removal" of the member from the perspective of the sufferer's imagination, although not from the perspective of the reality of the thing. 

Regarding how this is so, several things must be noted. First, there are two ways in which these things can happen. It is no wonder that the devil can deceive the human exterior senses, since he can delude the interior senses (as touched upon above) by drawing out stored forms to their sensory origins. He captures them in their natural operation, so that what is visible becomes invisible to them; what is tangible becomes intangible; what is audible becomes inaudible, and so on with the others. Yet, in reality, this does not mean nothing exists on the part of the object; rather, it all happens through a change in the organs that serve sight or hearing, such as the eyes and hands, by which the judgment of the senses is deceived through the change. 

We can demonstrate these things from certain natural phenomena. For just as sweet wine seems bitter to a person with a fever because of an infection of the tongue, the taste is deceived not because of the thing itself, but because of the **humors** <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and perception</note>. So too for you: there is no actual removal on the part of the thing, for the **rod** <note>original: "virga," a common euphemism for the penis</note> is still there.

Furthermore, reason suggests that such a deceptive illusion in the one seeing and touching occurs not only through the interposition of some smooth, un-membered body, but also by the way in which certain **spirits** or **images** <term>species: mental representations or "forms" of objects stored in the mind</term> are drawn out to their interior sensory principles—namely, to the **imagination** and **phantasy**. Secondly, other easier ways for understanding and preaching this must be noted. For as **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), author of the *Etymologies*, a medieval encyclopedia</note> says in the *Etymologies*, Book 8, Chapter 9, a **glamour** <term>prestigium: often translated as "prestige" or "juggling," here meaning a demonic illusion</term> is nothing other than a certain delusion of the senses, and especially of the eyes. Hence it is named from "binding" <note>original: "a prestringo"</note> because it binds the sharpness of the eyes so that things seem to be otherwise than they are. And as **Alexander of Hales** <note>A 13th-century Franciscan theologian</note> says in the Second Part: "Prestige," properly taken, is that illusion of the demon which does not have a cause on the part of a change in the thing itself, but only on the part of the one perceiving it, who is deluded whether in regard to the interior senses or the exterior senses. Therefore, speaking generally, let us say that even regarding the human art of illusion, it can be done in **three ways**. One is without demons, and that is rather called a **delusion** <note>original: "delusio"</note>, because it is done artificially by the agitation of men showing or hiding certain things, as happens in the **sleight of hand** <note>original: "traiectionibus"</note> by jugglers or mimes. Another way happens also without the power of demons, namely naturally, by the power of natural bodies or even minerals; those who possess these can, according to a certain power implanted in such things, show a thing or make it appear not as it is. Hence **Thomas** in the First Part, question 114, article 4, and many others say that a certain **herb**, when set on fire or lit and smoking, makes beams appear to be **serpents**. The third way of delusion is that which is done by demons, yet with God's permission. For demons have by nature, as has been shown, a certain power over certain lower things, which they can exercise upon them when God allows, so that then things appear otherwise than they are. Regarding which it should be noted...

Thirdly, it must be said that the **demon** can delude a person in five ways, so that they judge a thing to be otherwise than it truly is. First, by **artificial sleight of hand** <note>original: "artificiali traiectione"</note>, as has been said: because whatever a human knows through the arts, the demon himself can know much better. In the second way, by the **natural application** of some thing, as was said regarding the interposition of some body so that another is hidden, or even by disturbing the **imagination** <term>fantasia: the mental faculty that processes sensory images</term> of men. In the third way, as when he shows himself in an **assumed body** to be some thing which he is not, just as **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD)</note> narrates in the first book of the *Dialogues* concerning a **nun** who ate a lettuce, which—as the demon himself later confessed—was not a lettuce, but the demon in the appearance of a lettuce, or rather he was within the lettuce itself. This also happened to **Anthony** <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356 AD), a desert hermit famously tempted by demons</note> with the mass of gold which he found in the desert. Or even when the demon covers a true man and makes him appear as a **brute animal**, as will be discussed later. In the fourth way, as when he disturbs the **organ of sight** so that a clear thing appears cloudy, or vice versa, so that an **old woman** appears as a **young girl**. For even after weeping, light appears differently than it did before. In the fifth way, by operating on the **imaginative power** and by making a transformation of the **sensible images** <term>specierum sensibilium: the mental forms or "pictures" of objects perceived by the senses</term> through the movement of the **humors** <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and temperament</note>, as touched upon above; thus, new and fresh appearances are caused in those sensitive powers. And so, in these three last ways, the demon can delude the senses of a man by the **art of glamour** <term>prestigiosa arte: deceptive magical illusion</term>, and also in the second way. Hence, there is no difficulty in his wishing to hide the **male member** by this art of glamour. Evidence or experience of this matter, which was revealed to us while we were performing our duties in the **Office of the Inquisition**, will be set down below where more of these and other deeds are recounted in the second part of the treatise.

### How witchcraft can be distinguished
### from a natural defect.

An incidental question arises along with certain other difficulties. Hence, if it is asked: the member has been taken from **Peter**, but he does not know whether it was taken by **witchcraft** <term>maleficium: harmful magic or a "spell"</term> or otherwise by divine permission through the power of a demon—are there ways of knowing and distinguishing between these? It can be answered that there are. First, because those to whom such things happen are for the most part **adulterers** or otherwise **fornicators**. Thus, when they

<column-break/>

do not serve their **mistresses** <note>original: "amassijs"</note> at their whim, or wish to leave them to cling to others, then the women procure such things in **vengeance**, or otherwise cut off the power of that member. Secondly, it is known by this: that it is **not durable**. For if it does not happen from witchcraft, then it is not lasting but will return eventually. But here again a doubt arises: whether it is part of the nature of witchcraft that it is not durable? It is answered that it can be **perpetual** and last until death, just as the **canonists** <note>Experts in Church law (Canon Law)</note> and **theologians** judge concerning the **impediment of witchcraft** in marriage: that it is found to be both temporary and perpetual. For **Goffrey** <note>Goffredus de Trano (c. 1200–1245), a famous jurist and canonist</note> says in his *Summa*: "Witchcraft cannot always be undone by the one who made it; either because they are dead, or because they do not know how to delete it, or because the charm is lost." Hence, by analogy, we can say that the witchcraft inflicted upon Peter will be perpetual, either because that **witch** <note>original: "malefica"</note> who did it cannot heal him. For there are three kinds of witches: some who heal and harm; some who harm but cannot heal; and some who only seem to heal, that is, to remove the injuries, as will be seen below. For this happened to us: two witches were quarreling with each other, and while one was insulting the other, she said: "I am not as wicked as you, because I know how to heal those whom I harm." Or it will also last if the witch should depart before his healing, either by changing location or by departing from this life. For even **Saint Thomas** says: "Any witchcraft can be so perpetual that it cannot have a **human remedy**; because even if it has a remedy, it is nevertheless not known or lawful to man. Although God can provide a remedy through a **holy angel** by removing the demon, though not by forcing the witch." Nevertheless, the **supreme remedy** against witchcraft is the **Sacrament of Penance** <note>The ritual of confession and absolution</note>, according to the chapter *concerning the frigid* <note>original: "extra de frigid." — a reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding impotence in marriage</note>. For even bodily infirmity often comes from sin, as in the chapter *on penance*, "Since infirmity." How witchcraft is to be removed will be made clear in the third part of the treatise, and in the second part, chapter six, three other differences are touched upon.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the illusions of witches, specifically resolving previous arguments about the physical reality of "missing" limbs before moving into a new question regarding the transformation of humans into animals.</meta>

<margin>
# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill other humans when God permits it, they can also truly and physically remove a limb or other body parts. However, in those cases, **demons** are not operating through the **witches** <note>original: "maleficas"</note> currently under discussion. This also provides the solution to the second point. But as for the claim that because God permits the **generative power** <term>vim generativam: the biological ability to procreate</term> of witches more than other powers, He therefore permits that a limb be truly and physically removed—this is not a valid rule for every case. Such an act would not be performed by way of **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficii"</note>, nor do witches even desire this when they perform their works, because they want to retain the power to restore the limb whenever they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that the limb is not truly removed, but is taken away through the **art of illusion** <term>prestigiosa arte: the demonic skill of creating deceptive appearances</term>.

Regarding the third point about the transformation of **Lot's wife** <note>The biblical story from Genesis 19 where Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt</note>, we say that this was a real transformation and not done through the art of illusion; however, we are currently speaking of the deceptive arts. To the fourth point—that demons can introduce certain **substantial forms** <term>substantial forms: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "human-ness" or "snake-ness")</term> and therefore can also remove them—it is said regarding the **magicians of Pharaoh** <note>In Exodus 7, these magicians mimicked Moses's miracles</note> that they produced real serpents. Indeed, demons can produce certain effects regarding some "imperfect" creatures with the help of some other agent; however, they cannot do this to humans, for whom God has greater care. According to the scripture: *Is it for oxen that God is concerned?* <note>original: "Nunquid deo cura est de bobus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note> Nevertheless, as has been stated, they can always harm humans truly and physically, or through the art of illusion, if God permits it. This also makes the solution to the final argument clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into bestial forms through the art of illusion.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared regarding where humans are transformed into beasts. As to how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. In the **Canon Law** <note>original: "xxvi. q. v. Epi." referring to the Canon Episcopi, a famous 10th-century legal text on witchcraft</note> from the Council of Ancyra: "Whosoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is beyond doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan."

<column-break/>

Let us also use the arguments of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian</note> in the *Second Book of Sentences*, distinction 8, on whether demons can make impressions upon the **bodily senses** by deluding them with illusions. There, he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere. But it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not possess any **sensory image** <term>speciem: a mental representation of an object</term> unless it is received from real things. Furthermore, according to the legal authority cited above, there is no real beast there. Nor, again, can the form be in the thing that is seen (as when a woman appears to be a beast), because two **substantial forms** cannot exist in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that beastly form which is seen can exist nowhere, no **illusion of prestige** <term>illusio prestigiosa: a deceptive trick or hallucination</term> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that the form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be. Firstly, because the air is not capable of receiving a specific form or shape. Secondly, because the same air does not always remain around that person due to its fluid nature, especially when they are moving. Thirdly, because such a transformation would then be seen by everyone—which is not the case, since demons do not seem to deceive the visions of holy men, at the very least.

Furthermore, the sense of sight or the power of vision is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. Now, the active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one that originates the act (namely, the **object**), and another that conveys it (namely, the **medium**). But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor can it be the medium conveying it. Regarding the first—that it cannot be the object—this is because it cannot be derived from any real thing (as touched upon in the preceding argument), since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a real thing, nor is it in the object itself, nor even in the air as a conveying medium (as touched upon in the third argument). Furthermore, if the demon moves the internal **cognitive power**, he either does this by presenting himself as an object...

<summary>This page addresses theological objections regarding the physical reality of demonic transformations, concluding that while God may allow real physical harm, most "transformations" of humans into animals are demonic illusions that deceive the senses rather than changing a person's actual essence.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, illusion, substantial form, Thomas Aquinas, Canon Episcopi, metamorphosis, sensory perception, Pharaoh's magicians, Lot's wife</keywords>

to the cognitive faculty. It does this either by changing the faculty itself or by presenting itself to it. However, it does not do this by presenting itself, which would require it to either take on a body—and thus it could not enter internally into the **organ of imagination** <term>organum imaginationis: the physical part of the brain where medieval scholars believed mental images were processed</term>, since two bodies cannot occupy the same place simultaneously—nor by taking on a **phantasm** <term>fantasma: a mental image or sensory impression</term>, which is also impossible because a phantasm cannot exist without physical dimension. A **demon**, however, lacks all dimension. 

Similarly, a demon cannot do this by changing the faculty through alteration, as it seems impossible to perform; for all alteration happens through active qualities which demons lack. Or, it might change it through transmutation or by local movement, which seems inappropriate for two reasons. First, because the transmutation of the organ could not happen without a sense of **pain** <note>original: "voloris," likely a scribe's error for "doloris" (pain)</note>. Second, because according to this, a demon would show a person only things already known to them, yet **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the primary theological authority for this text</note> says that he shows humans forms both known and unknown. Thus, it seems that demons cannot in any way reach the human imagination or sense.

But on the contrary, **Augustine** says in the 18th book of *The City of God* that the transformations of humans into brute animals, which are said to be done by the art of demons, were not real in truth, but only according to appearance. This could not happen if demons could not transmute human senses. Furthermore, the authority of Augustine in his *Book of 83 Questions*, which was also cited previously, alludes to this: "This evil of the demon creeps through all the sensory pathways," etc.

**Response.** If the reader wishes to look into the method of transmutation, they will find various modes in the second part of this work, chapter 6. For now, proceeding in a **scholastic** <note>scholastic: refers to the formal, academic method of argument used in medieval universities</note> manner: let us state the opinions of three Doctors who agree that the devil can occupy the **fantasy** <term>fantasia: the mental faculty that stores and combines sensory images</term> of a man so that a man appears to be a true animal. Among these, the last is more subtle than the others, which is the opinion of **St. Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian</note>. 

The first opinion is that of **Lord Antoninus** <note>Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), an archbishop and theologian</note> in the first part of his *Summa*, title 5, chapter 6, paragraph 5, declaring that the devil sometimes works upon the human fantasy for the purpose of receiving [images], especially regarding the illusion of the senses; he explains this by natural reason, by the authority of the **Canon** <note>Canon: a rule of church law</note>, and by a multitude of experiences. First, thus: Natural bodies are by nature subject to and obedient to

<column-break/>

**angelic nature** regarding local motion. Even though **evil angels** have lost their grace, they have not lost their natural power, as has been touched upon above. Since the **fantastic** or **imaginative power** is physical—that is, attached to a physical organ—it is naturally subject even to evil spirits, so that they can transmute it by causing various phantasms through the drawing back of **humors** <term>humors: the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, etc.) believed to govern health and temperament</term> and **spirits** <term>spirituum: subtle "vapors" in the body thought to carry sensory information to the brain</term> to the sensory source, as procured by them. 

This is what he [Antoninus] says, and he adds: This is also clear from the **Canon** <note>original: "xxvi. q. v. episcopi" – referring to the Canon Episcopi, a 10th-century decree incorporated into church law which is a foundational text for medieval views on witchcraft</note>. For Satan himself transforms himself into the likenesses and appearances of various persons, and deluding the mind which he holds captive in sleep, he leads it through various devious paths.

For very often men are physically transported across many lands against their will and without being **sorcerers**. 

But because it can happen in both ways <note>i.e., both physically and through mental illusion</note>, it follows in the aforementioned *Summa* and in the chapter "No wonder" <note>original: "c. nec mirum"</note> in the same Question: **Augustine** recounts that it is read in the books of the pagans about a certain sorceress named **Circe** <note>the famous sorceress from Homer's Odyssey</note> who had changed the companions of **Ulysses** into beasts; this was fashioned through magical **illusions** <term>prestriigiis: deceptive tricks or glamours that fool the eyes</term> rather than being completed in reality, by altering human phantasms. This is also clear through many examples: for it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "vitaspatrū" – a collection of stories about early Christian monks</note> that a certain young woman, because she would not consent...

But if a difficulty should arise as to whether such deeds of demons should be called **miraculous works**, the answer was made clear from what preceded: that even demons can perform certain true miracles, provided they are things to which the particular power of nature can extend. The solution to the other argument regarding the "subject of the form" is also clear. The form of the beast that is seen is neither in the air nor in the object itself, as has been shown, but in the **sense** <note>the faculty of perception</note> itself, according to the opinion of **Saint Thomas Aquinas** as was

<column-break/>

declared above. Regarding the point that every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it, this is granted. And when it is further argued that the form which is seen cannot be the object originating the act because it is not taken from any real thing, it is said that, on the contrary, it *is* from a real thing. This is because it comes from a **sensible species** <term>species: a mental "image" or form of an object stored in the memory</term> reserved in the **imagination**, which the demon can draw out and offer to the imagination or even to the sensitive power, as was said above. To the final point, it must be said that a demon does not change the sensitive and imaginative power by presenting himself to it as an object, as has been shown, but by **transforming** it. He does not do this by altering it essentially, but only through **local motion** <note>physical movement within the body</note>. This is because he cannot, by his own power, imprint new "species" or mental forms, as was said. He changes them by transforming—that is, by moving them locally. And again, he does this not by dividing the substance of the organ (which would result in the sensation of pain), but by moving the **spirits and humors** <note>the internal fluids and vapors thought to govern human physiology and psychology</note>. Furthermore, it is objected that it would follow that a demon could not demonstrate anything new to a person through **imaginative vision**. To this, it must be said that something "new" can be understood in two ways. One way is something **totally new**, both in itself and in its principles. In this way, a demon cannot show anything new to a man through imaginary vision. For he cannot make a man born blind imagine colors, or one born deaf imagine sounds. In another way, something is called new according to the **form of the whole**. For example, if we say it is "new" in the imagination when someone imagines **mountains of gold** which he has never seen. Because he has seen both gold and a mountain, he can, by a natural movement, imagine the phantasms of a golden mountain. And in this way, a demon can offer something "new" to the imagination.

An incidental question concerning wolves, who sometimes snatch men and children from their homes and devour them, running about with such great cunning that they cannot be harmed or captured by any skill or power. Regarding the first cause, **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a prominent Dominican theologian and scientist</note> says in his *On Animals* that this can happen for five reasons: sometimes due to an increase in hunger, just as deer and other beasts sometimes approach humans; sometimes due to the ferocity of their strength, particularly in cold regions or when they have cubs. And **Deuteronomy 32**: "I will send the teeth of beasts upon them with fury," etc. 

As to the manner of this—whether they are true wolves or demons appearing in such forms—it is said that they are true wolves, but they are possessed by demons or driven by them in two ways. One way is without the operation of witches, as happened to the forty-two children killed by two bears coming out of the woods, who slaughtered them for the mockery they made of the prophet **Elisha** <note>original: "heliseo"</note> by saying: "Go up, bald head," etc. And regarding the lion who killed the prophet of God who did not fulfill the command in **1 Kings 13** <note>original: "tercio Reg. xiij"</note>. Also the story of the **Bishop of Vienne** <note>Saint Mamertus (d. c. 475), who instituted the Rogation Days</note>, who instituted the **Minor Litanies** <term>letanias minores: processions and prayers for divine protection, often called Rogation Days</term> before the Ascension of the Lord, because wolves entering the cities were publicly devouring men. 

The second way is through the illusion of witches, as **William of Auvergne** <note>original: "Guilhel. vbi supra"; William was the Bishop of Paris (d. 1249)</note> relates above concerning a certain man who thought he was transformed into a wolf at certain times, during which he lay hidden in caves. For he went there at a set time, and meanwhile, while he remained there as a wild beast, it seemed to him that he himself had become a wolf and was going about devouring children. And while in reality only a demon, possessing a certain wolf, performed these acts, the man falsely thought in his dreaming that he was the one prowling

### Question II: How midwife-witches destroy the conceptus in the womb in various ways, procure abortions, and when they do not do this, offer the newborn infants to demons.

In the fifth, sixth, and seventh place, the aforementioned truth is proved through four horrendous acts which they perform regarding infants both in the womb and outside the mother’s womb. To these are added a third and fourth way: that where they do not procure an abortion, they then consume the infant or offer it to a demon. Regarding the first two ways, there is no doubt, since a person can procure through natural means without the help of demons—such as through herbs or other impediments—that a woman might not be able to generate or conceive, as was touched upon above. ### On the Third Main Point of this First Part
#### Touching on Divine Permission

It is asked: Whether it is so "Catholic" to commend Divine Permission in these works of witches that to argue the opposite—that is, to refute it—is entirely heretical. And it is argued that it is not heretical to assert that God does not permit such great power to the devil in these kinds of witchcraft. For to refute those things which can result in an insult to the Creator is Catholic and not heretical. But to assert that such power of harming humans is not permitted to the devil is Catholic, which is proven thus: to assert the opposite seems to result in an insult to the Creator. 

For it would follow that not all things are subject to Divine Providence <note>original: "diuine prouidentie"</note>, because every wise provider excludes defect and evil as much as possible from those for whom he cares. However, if the things done through witchcraft are permitted by God, they are not excluded by Him. And if they are not excluded by Him, God Himself would not be a wise provider, and thus not all things would be under His providence. Since this is false, it is also false that God permits these things. 

Furthermore, one permits something to happen which he could prevent if he wished, or which he cannot prevent even if he wished; but neither of these can be applied to God. Not the first, because such a person is judged to be envious; not the second, because such a person is judged to be powerless. Then it is asked incidentally: this witchcraft truly happens, and God could have prevented it and did not. Therefore, God is envious or has no care for all things. If, however, He could not prevent it even if He wished, then He is not omnipotent. To assert any of these is inappropriate. 

Furthermore, whoever is left to himself <note>is responsible for his own acts</note>, and if witchcraft occurs by God's permission, the master of his own acts is not subject to the permission or providence of any governor. But humans are left to themselves by God according to that passage in Ecclesiasticus 15: "God established man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel." Specifically, also, the wicked are left to their own works according to the passage: "He gave them up to the desires of their hearts." Therefore, not all evils are subject to Divine Permission. Furthermore, Augustine says in...

<meta>The previous page introduced the terrifying crimes of witches, specifically their practice of killing and devouring infants, and cited the testimony of the Inquisitor of Como and the writings of Johannes Nider. This page transitions into a complex theological debate regarding why a providential God would allow such vile acts to occur at all.</meta>

In the *Enchiridion* <note>original: "Enchirio."; a handbook on faith, hope, and love by St. Augustine</note>, as also the Philosopher <note>A common medieval shorthand for Aristotle</note> says in the fourth book of his *Metaphysics*: It is better not to know certain things than to know them, even if they are useful. But everything that is better must be attributed to God; therefore, God does not involve Himself in these most vile works of witches <note>original: "maleficorum"</note>, whether to permit them or not. To the same point, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says in 2 Corinthians 9: "God has no care for oxen." By the same reasoning, He has no care for other irrational creatures. Hence, whether they are bewitched <note>term: "maleficiantur" (to be harmed by magic or witchcraft)</note> or not, it is of no concern to God; nor are these acts subject to His permission, which proceeds from His providence. Furthermore, things that happen by necessity do not require a providential permission, any more than they require prudence. This is clear from the Philosopher in the sixth book of his *Ethics*: "Prudence is the right reason of contingent things about which there is counsel and choice." But many effects of witchcraft happen by necessity—for example, when illnesses or other things we judge to be witchcraft occur due to some cause or the influence of celestial bodies <note>Refers to the medieval belief that the stars and planets could cause physical ailments</note>. Thus, they are not always subject to divine permission. Furthermore, if humans are bewitched by divine permission, the question arises: Why is it permitted against one person rather than another? If it is said that it is because of sins, which are more abundant in one than in another, this seems to be false, because then the greatest sinners would be the most bewitched. Yet the contrary is apparent, in that they are punished less in this world. According to the saying <note>Jeremiah 12:1</note>: "It is well with all who transgress," so they are also less often victims of witchcraft. Finally, it is clear from the fact that innocent children and other just people are more frequently bewitched. But on the contrary, God permits evil to be done, even if He does not will it, and this is for the perfection of the universe. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian mystic</note> says in the third chapter of *On Divine Names*: "Evil will be for the sake of all," meaning it contributes to the perfection of the universe. And Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: "From all things, both good and evil, the admirable beauty of the universe is composed." Insofar as that which is called evil—when it is well-ordered and placed in its proper location—more eminently commends the good things, so that they please us more and are more praiseworthy when compared to evils. Likewise, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the dominant theologian of the Middle Ages</note> disapproves of the opinion of those...

<column-break/>

...who say that although God does not will evils—because no creature desires evil, whether by natural, animal, or intellectual appetite (which is the Will, the object of which is the Good)—He nevertheless wills that evils exist or happen. Thomas says this is false. For God neither wills that evils happen, nor does He will that they do not happen. Rather, He wills to *permit* evil to happen, and this is good because of the perfection of the universe. As for why it is erroneous to say "God wills evils to exist or happen for the good of the universe," he says: Because nothing is to be judged good except according to that which belongs to it essentially <note>original: "per se"</note> and not accidentally <note>original: "per accidens"</note>. Just as a virtuous man is judged "good" in his intellectual nature and not merely his animal nature. Evil, however, is not ordered toward the good essentially, but only accidentally. For a good result arises beyond the intention of those who work evil; just as it was beyond the intention of witches, or beyond the intention of tyrants, that the patience of the martyrs should shine forth through their persecution. **The Response:** This question is as much more useful for preaching as it is more difficult to understand. For this is the primary argument among not only the common people <note>original: "laicorum"</note> but even some wise men: that acts of witchcraft so horrendous as those mentioned above are not permitted by God. They remain ignorant of the causes of this divine permission. Because of this ignorance, witches are not suppressed through the punishment they deserve, and they now seem to depopulate the whole of Christendom. Therefore, so that both the learned and the unlearned may be satisfied according to the opinion of theologians, we must respond by discussing two difficulties. First: Is the world so subject to divine providence that God Himself provides for all things immediately? Second: That God justly permits the totality of evils that occur—whether the evil of guilt <note>sin</note>, punishment, or loss—based on the first two "permissions" regarding the fall of the angels and our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note>. From this it will be clear that to stubbornly disagree on these points savors of heresy <note>term: "haeresim sapit" (to have the flavor of or verge on heresy)</note>, as such a person entangles himself in the errors of the infidels. Regarding the first point, it should be noted that, presupposing that...
