<meta>The previous page introduced arguments regarding whether God’s providence and permission extend to the "vile works" of witches. It touched upon the idea that some might believe God does not concern Himself with the suffering of irrational creatures (like oxen) or that certain events happen by necessity or celestial influence rather than divine will. This page continues that investigation by refuting errors and establishing the scope of divine providence.</meta>

providence belongs to God. According to that passage in 
Wisdom 14: "But you, Father, govern all things by providence" <note>original: "Sapient. xiiij. Tu aut pater gubernas omnia prouidētia."</note>. It is also necessary to assert that all things are so subject to His providence that He provides for all things immediately. To make this clear, let us show it first by the rejection of a certain contrary error. For regarding that passage in Job 22: "Clouds are his hiding place, and he walks about the vault of heaven, and he does not consider our affairs" <note>original: "Nubes latibulum eius ⁊ circa cardines celi ꝑambulat nec nostra considerat."</note>. Some have been of the opinion—following the doctrine of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian</note> in the First Part, Question 22—to propose that only incorruptible things are subject to divine providence, such as separate substances <note>term: "substantie separate" (beings without physical bodies, specifically angels)</note> and the celestial bodies, along with the species <note>The "types" or "categories" of things, rather than the specific individuals</note> of lower things, which are also incorruptible. But they said that the individuals of these species, because they are corruptible, were not subject to it. Hence they said that all lower things done in the world were subject to divine providence only in a universal sense, not in a particular or singular sense. 

But because this seemed inappropriate to others—specifically, that God should have no more care for man than for other animals—therefore Rabbi Moises <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), a Jewish philosopher highly respected by Christian scholastics</note>, wishing to hold a middle ground, agreed with the former group. He said that all corruptible things, as they are individuals, are not subject to divine governance at all, but only the universals and the other things already mentioned. However, he excepted man from that generality of corruptible things, and this because of the splendor of the intellect, which humans share with the separate substances. And so, according to this opinion, whatever might happen to men by means of witchcraft <note>term: "maleficijs" (harmful magic or sorcery)</note> would be by God's permission; however, this would not apply to whatever happens to animals or the fruits of the earth. 

And although this opinion is closer to the truth than the one which denied God's providence over the affairs of the world entirely—asserting that the world was made by chance, as did Democritus and Epicurus—yet it is still not without great falsehood. This is because it is necessary to say that all things are subject to divine providence, not only in universal terms but also in particular. Thus, not only the witchcraft practiced against men, but also against beasts and the fruits of the earth, happens by divine and provident permission. This is shown as follows.

<column-break/>

The providence and ordering of things toward an end extends as far as causality itself extends. We see this by similarity in things subject to someone's lordship: they are subject to that person’s providence insofar as they are subject to them. Since God's causality, as the first agent, extends to all beings—not only regarding the principles of their species but also their individual principles, and not only to incorruptible things but also to the corruptible—it follows that just as all things have their being from God, so all things are provided for by Him; that is, they are ordered toward some end. 

The Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> touches on this in Romans 13: "The things that are from God are ordained" <note>original: "Que a deo sunt oꝛdinata sunt." In a modern context, "ordained" here means "ordered" or "set in place."</note>. It is as if he were saying: Just as all things are from God, so also all things are ordered by Him, and consequently subject to His providence. For God's providence is known to be nothing other than the *ratio* <note>term: "ratio" (the underlying reason or logic)</note> or cause of the order of things toward an end. Therefore, all things, insofar as they participate in being, are to that extent subject to divine providence. 

Furthermore, God knows all things not only in a universal sense, but indeed in particular. And since God's knowledge is compared to created things as the knowledge of an art is to the works of that art, just as all works of art are subject to the order and providence of the art, so all things are subject to the order and providence of God. 

But because these points do not sufficiently explain how God justly permits evils and witchcraft to happen in the world—even though we understand Him to be the provider governing all things—it follows that if He is the provider, He should exclude every evil from those for whom He cares. Among men, we see that a wise provider excludes defect and evil as much as possible from those they care for. Therefore, to understand why God does not exclude all evils, it must be noted that it is one thing to speak of a *particular* provider and another of a *universal* provider. A particular provider must exclude evil as much as possible because he cannot draw good out of evil. But God, since He is the universal provider of the whole world, can draw very many goods out of particular evils, just as from the persecution of tyrants comes the patience of the martyrs, and...

It refutes the views of Maimonides and Epicurus, explaining that God permits specific evils because, as a universal provider, He can transform them into greater goods.</summary>

...from the works of sorcerers <note>original: "maleficorum"</note>, there comes a purification or a testing of the faith of the just, as will become clear. Therefore, it is not God's part to prevent all evils, lest many good things should happen to be missing from the universe. Regarding this, Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* <note>A handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love written by St. Augustine around 420 AD</note>: "Almighty God is so merciful that He would not allow any evil to exist in His works unless He were so almighty and good that He could even bring good out of evil" <note>original: "Adeo misericors est omnipotens deus q^d non sineret aliquod malum esse in operibus suis nisi adeo esset omnipotens & bonus ut benefaceret etiam de malo."</note>. 

We also have an example of this in the actions of natural things. For the corruptions and defects that happen in natural things—even though they are against the intention of that *particular* nature, such as when a thief is hanged or when animals are killed for human food—are nevertheless part of the intention of *universal* nature. This is so that, clearly, humans may be preserved in life and in goods, and thus the good of the universe is maintained. For in order for the species <note>The general "type" or "category" of a living thing</note> of things to be preserved, it is necessary that the corruption of one be the preservation of another. Indeed, the killing of animals preserves the life of lions.

<margin>It is explained, regarding the aforementioned divine permission, that God could not grant a creature the ability to be impeccable by its very nature.</margin>

As for the second point—that God justly permits a multitude of evils, whether in faults <note>sins</note> or in punishments, and especially now as the world grows cold and declines toward its end—it is explained by two propositions that must necessarily be presupposed. The first of these is that God cannot make (or rather, to speak with the fear of God, it is not possible) a created nature, such as a human or an angel, to have the quality of being unable to sin <term>impeccable: from the Latin 'impeccabilis', meaning 'not capable of sinning'</term> by the very condition of its nature. The second proposition is that God justly permitted man to sin or to be tempted. 

Given these points, and since it belongs to divine providence that each and every creature be left to its own nature, it must be said that from the premises, it is impossible that God should not permit acts of sorcery <note>original: "maleficia"</note> to be done by the power of demons. And regarding the first point—that it was not possible to communicate to a creature that it could not sin by the condition of its 

<column-break/>

nature—this is shown by the Holy Doctor <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential theologian of the Middle Ages</note> in the *Second Book [of the Sentences]*, distinction 44, article 1. He argues that if this could have been communicated to any creature, God would certainly have communicated it, because all other communicable goodnesses and perfections of creatures have been communicated, at least in some kind. Examples include the personal union of two natures in Christ, the motherhood and virginity in Mary, the first grace given freely to wayfarers <note>term: 'viatores' refers to humans currently living on Earth, 'on the way' to the afterlife</note>, the beatific union in the elect, and so on with others. 

Therefore, since we do not read of this being communicated to any creature, neither man nor angel—according to that passage: "And in his angels he found wickedness" <note>original: "Et in angelis suis repperit prauitatē" - a reference to Job 4:18</note>—it is certain that it cannot be communicated to man to be impeccable by nature, although they may find this through grace. 

Secondly, regarding the same point: if it were communicable and yet not communicated, the universe would not be perfect. The perfection of the universe consists in this: that all communicable kinds of goodness are shared among creatures. Nor is the argument valid that since God is supremely powerful and created humans and angels in His own likeness, He could have also granted that a creature, by the condition of its nature, would be unable to sin. Or even that He could have made that "habit of grace" (which causes one to be confirmed in goodness) an essential part of the nature of an angel or a man, so that by its own natural principle and natural condition, it would be confirmed in good so as not to be able to sin. 

For the first argument does not hold. Although God is supremely powerful just as He is supremely good, He nevertheless cannot grant this—not out of any imperfection in His power, but out of the imperfection of the creature. This imperfection is considered first in this way: that a human or angel cannot, and could not, receive this. The reason is that since it is a creature, its "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> depends on the Creator just as an effect depends on its cause. To "be" and to "create" is to make something out of nothing; therefore, if the creature is left to itself, it fails. It is only preserved as long as it receives the influence of its cause. 

Take the example of a candle, which shines only as long as it has wax. This being the case, it is known that God created man and "left him in the hand of his own counsel" <note>original: "reliquit eum in manu cōsilij sui" - citing Ecclesiasticus 15:14 (though the text notes chapter 18)</note>. And He did similarly with the angel from the beginning of creation.

And this was done through free will <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note>, whose specific property it is to act or to omit acting, just as it is its property to withdraw from its cause or not to withdraw. And because the "power to sin" is the power to withdraw from God through the freedom of will, therefore neither man nor angel could receive this <note>the inability to sin as a natural trait</note>. Nor could it be communicated to them by God such that they would possess the inability to sin by their very nature.

Another perspective on why this could not be communicated to man or angel is because it implies a contradiction. Because such things are not "doable" in themselves, we say God cannot do them. But rather, it should be said that creatures cannot receive them—just as something cannot be alive and dead at the same time. In the same way, it is a contradiction for someone to have free will—by which they can cling to their cause or not cling to it—and yet be unable to sin. For if one cannot sin, one cannot "not cling" to their cause, since sin is the clinging to changeable things while scorning the unchangeable Good <note>A classic Augustinian definition of sin as "aversio a Deo, conversio ad creaturam"—turning away from God and toward the created thing</note>. To scorn or not to scorn is an act of free will.

Furthermore, the second argument is not valid. For if the grace of confirmation <note>A theological state where a soul is so strengthened by God that it can no longer choose to sin, as the blessed in Heaven</note> were turned into the creature's nature so that it held the inability to sin through its essential principles, then it would not possess this through some accidental good and grace, but would have it by nature—and then the creature would be God, which is absurd.

Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> touches upon this solution where cited above, in the solution to the final argument. He says that whenever an accident <note>A "property" that is not part of a thing's essential nature, like the color of a coat</note> belongs to a nature only because of an influence from a superior, the inferior nature cannot have that accident by itself unless it were transformed into that superior nature. For example, if air is illuminated in reality by fire, it cannot be bright by its own nature unless it actually becomes fire. I say, therefore, that since "confirmation" belongs to a rational creature only through grace—which is a kind of spiritual light and a likeness of the Uncreated Light—it is impossible for any creature to have confirmation or grace by its nature unless it were made to be of the divine nature by its very being. This is entirely impossible. Let us...

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion of why God permits evil and sin, focusing on the fall of the angels (led by Lucifer) and the subsequent fall of humanity. ...and many other things, which if they were taken away, much would certainly be subtracted from the perfection of the universe. It was also fitting that he <note>Referring to the first falling angel, Lucifer</note> should sin with no one suggesting it from the outside, but should take the occasion for sinning from within himself. This he did when he wished to be equal to God. This must be understood not simply and directly, nor indirectly, but only **in a certain respect** <note>original: "secundum quid" — a scholastic term meaning "in a qualified sense" rather than in every possible way</note>. This is clarified by the authority of **Isaiah 14**: *I will ascend into heaven... and I will be like the Most High.* 

He did not desire this simply and directly, because then he would have had a "bound" and erroneous intellect by desiring something that was impossible for him. For he knew himself to be a creature and created by God, and therefore he knew it was impossible for him to become equal to his Creator. Nor did he desire it indirectly, because since the total good of an angel and every creature lies in being subject to God—just as the total clarity of the air lies in its being subjected to the rays of the sun—the angel could not have desired to lose this, as it would be desiring something against his own nature. 

Rather, he desired equality not absolutely, but **in a certain respect**. It happened in this way: since God possesses two things by His very nature—blessedness and goodness—and is the source from which all blessedness and goodness is poured into every creature; the angel, seeing the dignity of his own nature by which he stood out above all other creatures, wished and desired that blessedness and goodness should be derived from himself into all lower creatures. He wanted this to happen through his own natural powers, so that he would possess those qualities first by his own nature, and thus other creatures would receive them from the nobility of his own nature. And because he also desired these things from God and while remaining under God (provided he possessed these powers), he did not even wish to be equal to God in the *manner* of possessing them, but only in that specific respect. 

Furthermore, because he attempted to bring his desire into action, he immediately exposed his desire to the others. And because the other angels' vision of his desire and their own perverse consent to it was also instantaneous, the sin of the first angel exceeded and preceded the sins of the others in the magnitude of the fault and in causality—though not necessarily in duration. Thus it is said in **Revelation 12**: *The dragon falling from heaven dragged a third part of the stars.* And he is represented in the figure of **Leviathan** <note>A biblical sea monster often used as a symbol for the devil</note>: *He is king over all the children of pride.* He is called "king" according to **Aristotle** in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "secundum philosophum v. metha."</note> because he is a "beginning" or principle insofar as he moves those subjects to himself through his own 

<column-break/>

will and through the wicked. 

Therefore, his own sin was the occasion of sinning for the others, so that he, being the first and tempted by no external force, tempted the others externally. Indeed, what has been said—that an instantaneous operation occurred in all these matters—is illustrated by sensible things. For the illumination of the air, the seeing of a color, and the discerning of the thing seen all happen at the same moment of time. 

I have set these matters out at length so that, by considering such a stupendous divine permission regarding the most noble of creatures <note>The angels</note> on account of only **one sin of ambition**, we might understand how God admits "particular permissions" regarding the works of **witches** <note>original: "maleficorum"</note> on account of even greater sins in certain circumstances. For the sins of witches in various circumstances exceed the sin of the angel and of our first parents, as will become clear in the second question. 

However, it is also quite clear from what has been said about the transgressing angels that the providence of God justly permitted the first man to be tempted and to sin. For just as man and angel were created for the same end and left in the freedom of their own will, so too—in order that they might receive the reward of blessedness not without merit—the angel was not preserved from his fall. This was done so that the power of sinning from the one side, and the power of the grace of confirmation from the other, might be made manifest for the beauty of the universe; the same principle had to be observed regarding man. 

Hence, **Saint Thomas Aquinas** <note>original: "sanctus Tho."</note> in the second book [of the *Sentences*], distinction 9, article 2, says: *That by which God appears praiseworthy should not be completely hindered.* But even in sins, God appears praiseworthy, since He spares through mercy and punishes through justice. Therefore, He ought not to have hindered sin. 

Briefly then, and by way of recapitulation, let us return to the point and say that man was permitted to fall into these things by the just providence of God for many reasons. 
**First**, to show the power of God, who alone is unchangeable, while every creature is changeable. 
**Second**, to declare the wisdom of God, which knows how to bring good out of evil—which could not have happened unless God had permitted the creature to sin. 
**Third**, to manifest the clemency of God, in which Christ liberated lost man through His death. 
**Fourth**, to show the justice of God, which not only gives rewards to the good but also punishments to the wicked.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic defense of Divine Providence. The previous page explained that the fall of the angels and the permission of sin were necessary for the "perfection of the universe," allowing God's attributes like mercy and justice to be displayed. This page concludes those arguments and begins specific rebuttals to common objections against God's control over evil and the natural world.</meta>

Fifthly, it is so that man would not be of a worse condition than other creatures, all of whom God governs in such a way that He allows them to act by their own motions. Whence He also ought to leave man to his own <term>free will</term> <note>original: "proprio arbitrio"</note>. Sixth is human praise; for the praise of a just man is that he was able to transgress and yet did not transgress. Seventh is the **beauty of the universe**, because just as a triple evil is found—of fault, of punishment, and of loss—so on the opposite side a triple good is found, namely the honorable good, the delightful good, and the useful good. Through these, the universe is adorned: for through fault, honor is adorned <note>That is, the honor of God's law is highlighted by the contrast of sin</note>; through punishment, delight; and through loss, the highest utility. And through these points, the response to the arguments is clear.

## Solutions to the arguments

Regarding the first point, where it is asserted that to say the devil is permitted the power of harming men is heretical: the opposite is rather evident. Just as it is heretical to assert that God does not permit man to sin out of his freedom of will when he wishes, so it is heretical to assert that God leaves sin unpunished. He permits this power of harming men for the vengeance of the wicked and for the beauty of the universe. This is according to **Augustine** in his book *Soliloquies*: "You are just, O Lord, and so it is that the disgrace of fault is never without the beauty of vengeance." Finally, the proof of the argument concerning a "wise provider"—who excludes defect and evil as much as he can—is not valid here. There is a difference between one who has a particular care <note>such as a parent or a local official</note> and the **Universal Provider** (God). For the former cannot elicit good from evil, whereas the Universal Provider does so, as was shown in the preceding points. 

To the second, it is clear that both the power, the goodness, and the divine justice are made manifest in the fact that He permits evils. Whence, when it is asked, "Either God can prevent evils or He cannot," the answer is that He can prevent them, but He ought not to for the reasons already stated. Nor is the objection valid if one says, "Therefore He wants evils to happen since He can prevent them and does not." For, as was touched upon in the arguments for the truth: God cannot will evils, nor does He will evils to happen, nor does He will evil *not* to happen; rather, He wills to **permit** evil to happen, and this for the perfection of the universe. 

To the third, **Augustine** and **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> speak of human knowledge, for which it is better not to know evil and vile things for a twofold reason. First, because through them we are sometimes hindered from the consideration of **better things** <note>original: "maloz," likely a scribal error for "meliorum" (better things)</note>;

<column-break/>

and this happens because we cannot understand many things at once. Also, it is for the reason that the thought of evils sometimes turns the human will toward evil. These things, however, have no place in God, who understands all the works of men and evildoers without any defect. 

To the fourth, **the Apostle** <note>St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 9:9</note> removed God's care from oxen to show that because a rational creature possesses mastery over its own acts through free will, God has a **special providence** over him. This is so that something may be imputed to the human being for fault or for merit, and punishment or reward may be rendered accordingly. God does not provide for irrational things in this same special way. However, to wish to assert that individual irrational creatures do not belong to divine providence at all would be heretical. It would be to assert that not all things are subject to divine providence, contrary to the proclamation of Holy Scripture concerning Divine Wisdom, which *reacheth from one end to another mightily and disposeth all things sweetly* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 8:1</note>. To hold otherwise would be the error of **Rabbi Moses** <note>Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher who argued that individual providence only extends to humans</note>, as was shown in the arguments for the truth. 

To the fifth, it is because man is not the creator of nature, but merely uses the natural works of art and virtue for his own use. Therefore, human providence does not extend to the "necessary" things that come from nature (such as whether the sun will rise tomorrow); however, the providence of God does extend to these, because He Himself is the Author of nature. Whence even natural defects—even if they arise from the natural course of things—would still be subject to divine providence. For this reason, **Democritus** and other natural philosophers erred by attributing whatever happened in the lower world to the necessity of matter alone. 

To the last point: although every punishment is inflicted by God on account of sins, nevertheless evils are not always inflicted upon the greatest sinners. This may be because the devil here does not wish to afflict or tempt those whom he sees he already possesses by a "just title" <note>meaning those already firmly in his grasp</note>; or it may be so that they do not hasten back to God, according to the verse: *Their infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they made haste* <note>Psalm 16:4</note>. And that every punishment is inflicted by God on account of sins is clear from what follows, because...

It is declared that the sins of <term>sorcerers</term> <note>original: "maleficorum," referring here to those practicing harmful magic or witchcraft</note> are graver than the sins of the fallen angels and the <term>first parents</term> <note>Adam and Eve</note>. Whence, just as the innocent are punished because of the faults of their parents, so also now many innocents are harmed and bewitched because of the sins of sorcerers.

### The Fourteenth Question: and the entire matter is suitable for preaching.

But regarding the enormity of these crimes, it is asked: Whether the outrages of sorcerers exceed all the evils that God permits to happen—and has permitted from the beginning of the world until now—both in terms of <term>faults</term> <note>moral guilt</note> and in terms of punishments and losses? 

And it seems that they do not, especially regarding the fault. For a sin that someone commits which they could have easily avoided exceeds a sin committed by another who could not avoid it so easily. This is clear through **Augustine** in *The City of God*: "Great is the iniquity in sinning where there is such great ease in not sinning." But **Adam** and many others who sinned from a state of perfection or even <term>grace</term> <note>divine assistance</note> could have more easily avoided sin because of the help of grace—especially Adam, who was created in grace—than many sorcerers who have not received such gifts. Therefore, the sins of the former exceed all the outrages of sorcerers.

Furthermore, regarding punishment: a greater punishment is owed to a greater fault. But the sin of Adam was punished most severely, in that (as is clear) the punishment is shown along with the fault in all his descendants through the transmission of <term>original sin</term>; therefore, his sin is graver than all other sins. 

Furthermore, regarding loss: for according to **Augustine**, a thing is evil precisely because it takes away a good. Therefore, where more of a good is lost, a greater fault must have preceded it. But the sin of our first parents brought about a greater loss both in <term>natural goods</term> <note>faculties like reason and health</note> and <term>gratuitous goods</term> <note>spiritual gifts like divine favor</note>, where it deprived us of innocence and immortality, which

<column-break/>

no other subsequent sins have brought about. Therefore, etc. 

**But on the contrary:** That which includes more reasons for evil is more evil. But the sins of sorcerers are of this kind. For they can procure all manner of evils in the goods of nature and fortune, God permitting, as is deduced from the <term>Papal Bull</term> <note>This refers to the *Summis desiderantes affectibus* issued by Pope Innocent VIII in 1484, which authorized the authors' inquisitorial activities.</note>. 

Furthermore, Adam sinned only by doing that which is evil because it was prohibited, and which was not evil in itself <note>The act of eating a fruit is not inherently evil, but became so because God forbade it.</note>. But sorcerers and other sinners sin by doing that which is evil in both ways: both in itself and because it is prohibited, such as homicides and many other forbidden acts. Whence their sins are graver than other sins. 

Furthermore, a sin that comes from certain <term>malice</term> <note>premeditated wickedness</note> is graver than a sin through ignorance. But sorcerers, out of great malice, despise the faith and the sacraments of the faith, as many have confessed.

**Response:** I respond that the evils perpetrated by modern sorcerers exceed all other evils that God ever permitted to happen, according to what is touched upon in the title of the question. And this is true regarding the sins that occur in the perversity of morals, although it may be otherwise for sins opposed to the other <term>theological virtues</term> <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note>. This can be shown in a triple way:
1.  **First, in general:** by comparing their works indifferently to any outrages in the world.
2.  **Second, in particular:** by comparing them to the types of superstition arising from any pact entered into with demons.
3.  **Third:** by comparing them to the sins of the fallen angels or even the first parents.

Regarding the first point: Since there is a triple evil—namely, of **fault**, of **punishment**, and of **loss**—because there is a triple good to which these are opposed, namely: the **honorable**, the **delightful**, and the **useful**. <note>This follows the Aristotelian and Thomistic classification of goods: *bonum honestum* (virtue), *bonum delectabile* (pleasure), and *bonum utile* (utility).</note> To fault is opposed the honorable; to punishment, the delightful; to loss, the useful. 

That the fault of sorcerers exceeds all other sins appears thus: according to the teaching of **Saint Thomas** in the *Second Book of Sentences*, distinction 42, article 2: although many things can be considered in a sin from which the gravity or even the lightness of the sin can be drawn...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological classification of the sins of sorcerers, specifically focusing on how their "apostasy" (falling away from the faith) is defined and categorized by Church authorities like Thomas Aquinas and Raymond of Penyafort. ...they have received. Concerning the second point, which is also called **apostasy**. For according to **Thomas [Aquinas]** in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 12, apostasy implies a certain turning back from God and from religion, which occurs through the various ways in which a person is joined to God: either through faith, or through a will subjected to obedience, or through religion and the clerical state.

According to what is also said by **Raymond [of Penyafort]** and **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Segusio, a prominent 13th-century canon lawyer</note>, an apostate is one who makes a "rash departure from the state of faith, or of obedience, or of religion." And since when the prior thing is removed, that which follows it is also removed (but not the other way around), the first type exceeds the other two. That is to say, apostasy from the faith precedes apostasy from religion or from the clerical order. Concerning this, see Distinction 18, *quantumlibet*, and Question 16, Causa 1, *legi non debet* <note>These are references to the Decretum Gratiani, the foundational collection of Canon Law</note>.

However, according to **Raymond**, a person is not judged an apostate or a fugitive even if they wander far away for a long time, unless they live in such a way that shows they have set aside the intention of returning. <note>original Latin: "ff. de re. milit. l. desertorem" — a reference to the Digest of Roman Law concerning military deserters</note>. This would be the case if he were to take a wife or something similar.

Likewise, there is the apostasy of **disobedience**, where someone willfully despises the commands of the Church and its prelates. <note>original: "ij. q. iiij. alieni" — another Canon Law reference</note>. Such a person is rendered <term>infamous</term> <note>a legal status of disgrace that stripped a person of certain rights</note>, is rejected from giving testimony, and ought to be excommunicated.

Therefore, the apostasy of which we speak—the apostasy of **witches**—is called the **apostasy of perfidy** <note>meaning a total breach of faith or "bad faith"</note>. This is all the more grave because it is carried out through an **express pact** with the enemy of the faith, of reason, and of salvation. For this is what witches must do, and this is what that enemy demands, either in whole or in part. Indeed, we <term>Inquisitors</term> have discovered women who had denied every article of the faith; others, however, denied only a certain number, yet they still maintain a true and sacramental confession. <note>The authors are noting a paradox where some witches still attempt to participate in Church rites like confession while practicing their craft.</note>

Hence, the perfidy of **Julian the Apostate** <note>The Roman Emperor who tried to revive paganism after Christianity had been established</note> does not seem to have been so great, even though in other matters he exercised greater cruelties against the Church.

If someone were to ask incidentally: what if they held the faith in their mind and

If, however, it is by a simple deed, then it is apostasy of deed." And because in all these things there is always an **insult to the faith**—since that which ought to be expected from God is expected from a demon—it is therefore always judged as apostasy. See how clearly he distinguishes the two-fold...

### ¶ Question Fifteen: Declaring that because of the sins of witches, the innocent are often harmed, although sometimes also because of their own sins.

But as to this—that by divine permission many innocent people are harmed and punished in the aforementioned injuries because of the sins of others (namely witches) and not because of their own faults—lest this seem unfitting to anyone, **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** shows in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 107 <note>In modern editions of the Summa Theologica, this argument about collective punishment is found in Question 108</note>, that this is done justly by God. Speaking of the punishments of the present life, he gives a threefold reason. ¶ First, indeed, because one person is the "property" <note>original: "res" — in a legal or feudal sense, someone who falls under the ownership or responsibility of another</note> of another; and just as someone is punished in their possessions, so also can someone be punished as a penalty for another. For children, according to the body, are a certain property of the fa-

<column-break/>

-ther, and servants and animals are the property of their masters. And thus children are sometimes punished for their parents, just as the son born of the adultery of David died sooner, and the animals of the Amalekites were ordered to be killed, although in such things there is also a mystical reason, as is held in Question 1, Part 4, under "little ones." ¶ Second, because the sin of one is derived to another, and this in two ways. ¶ By imitation, just as children imitate the sins of parents, and servants and subjects the sins of masters, so that they might sin more boldly; as happens in things wrongly acquired in which children succeed [to the inheritance], or servants in robberies and unjust wars where they are often killed. And the subjects of prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> sin more boldly when they see them sinning, even if they do not commit the same sins; hence they are also justly punished. ¶ A sin is also derived from one to another by way of merit <note>In this context, it means "what is deserved" by a community</note>, as that of subjects results in an evil prelate—that is, the sins of the subjects deserve a sinful prelate, according to that passage in **Job**: "He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people" <note>Job 34:30</note>. ¶ A sin is also derived—and consequently a punishment—through someone's consent or turning a blind eye <note>original: "dissimulationem"</note>. This is when superiors do not rebuke sins; then very often the good are punished with the wicked, as **Augustine** says in the first book of *The City of God*. ¶ An example: where among us inquisitors, one found a certain town almost destitute of people by mortality, and where a rumor was flying that a certain buried woman was gradually swallowing the shroud <note>original: "lintheamen"</note> in which she was buried, and the plague <note>original: "pestis"</note> could not cease unless she had consumed the shroud entirely into her belly. ¶ Having taken counsel on the matter, the mayor <term>original: "scultetus" — a local administrative official or magistrate</term> with the prefect of the city, digging up the grave, found almost half of the shroud driven through the mouth and neck even into the stomach and consumed. ¶ Having seen this, the mayor, being moved, drew his sword and, by cutting off the head, threw it out of the pit; and so the plague suddenly ceased. From which things it is clear that by divine permission the sins of that old woman were [visited] upon the innocent because of the turning of a blind eye by the presiding officials...

And therefore, it leads to their own damnation, just as He now punishes His people through the Turks, and many times before through foreigners even in the Old Law. **B**ut note that for whatever reason someone suffers, if they do not endure the punishments patiently, then they are scourges not for satisfaction <note>The theological act of making amends for sin</note> but for vengeance only—that is, for punishment.
**A**ccording to that passage in Deuteronomy 32: A fire—namely of temporal punishment—is kindled in my fury, that is, in punishment; because otherwise there is no "fury" in God. And it shall burn even unto the lowest parts of hell; that is, the vengeance will begin here and burn until the final damnation, as Augustine explains. And it is found in the section "On Penance" [dist. 4]. But if those scourges are borne patiently and the sufferer is in a state of grace <note>The spiritual state of being free from mortal sin</note>, they take the place of satisfaction, as Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says in the *Fourth Book of Sentences*. Even if someone were punished by a judge because of a crime committed, or even a witch, and this according to more or less depending on the devo-

<column-break/>

-tion of the sufferer and the nature of the crime. **H**owever, natural death, since it is the most terrible of final things, is not in itself "satisfactory" <note>sufficient to pay the debt of sin</note> because it became a part of our nature as a penalty for original sin. Although according to Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, a Franciscan theologian</note>, if it is expected voluntarily and with devotion and offered to God in its bitterness, it can in some way become satisfactory. Yet a violent death—whether a person deserved it or not—is always satisfactory if it is sustained patiently and in a state of grace. And these things indeed pertain to penalties inflicted because of the sins of others. However, God also scourges in this present life because of one's own sins, and specifically regarding the casting of spells <note>original: "maleficia"</note>. **F**or in Tobit 6 <note>The text says 7, but the reference to demons and lust is typically Tobit 6:17</note>, the devil receives power over those who abandon themselves to lust. This was also clear from the preceding sections explaining spells regarding the limbs and the powers of procreation, which God allows to be bewitched more frequently. **N**evertheless, for the sake of preaching to the people, it should be noted that despite the aforementioned punishments—according to which God punishes because of the faults of others or one's own—he should hold this legal rule as a foundation and propose it to the people: **N**o one is to be punished without fault unless there is a sufficient cause. This is found in the section "On the Rules of Law" [in the *Decretals*], and this rule has a place in the judgment of heaven <note>original: "iudicio poli" — literally the "judgment of the pole," referring to God's court</note> and in the judgment of the court <note>original: "iudicio fori" — referring to human secular or ecclesiastical courts</note>. **E**xplain regarding the judgment of heaven: for since God punishes with a twofold penalty, spiritual and temporal: In the first, it is found that He never punishes without fault. In the second, it is found that He sometimes does so without fault, but not without cause. **R**egarding the first, the spiritual penalty, which is threefold: namely, the withdrawal of grace (from which follows hardening in sins), it does not happen without one's own fault. **S**econdly, the penalty of loss—that is, the deprivation of glory—this too is never inflicted without one's own fault (as in adults) or contracted fault (as in children dying in original sin). **T**hirdly, the penalty of the senses—that is, the torment of hellfire—is also clear. **W**hence that which is said in Exodus 20: *I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation*, is understood...

<meta>This page continues the theological and legal analysis of why God permits suffering and punishment. ...of those who imitate their fathers' crimes, as explained by Gratian <note>original: "Gratianus"</note> in the first part of the *Decretum*, question 4, paragraph "Quibus," where he also provides other explanations. Regarding the second type of punishment—temporal punishment <note>Punishment that occurs within time (this life), as opposed to eternal punishment in the afterlife.</note>—God inflicts it in several ways. First, because of the fault of another, as touched upon above, for a three-fold reason. Or it may be without anyone's fault—neither another's nor one’s own—but not without a cause. Or it may be due to one’s own fault rather than another’s. If you wish to know the reasons why God punishes even without the fault of another or oneself, you may look to the five modes set down by the Master <note>The "Master" refers to Peter Lombard, the 12th-century author of the *Sentences*, the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> in Book Four, Distinction 15, Chapter 2. Take the first three causes as such; the remaining two should be taken as pertaining to one's own faults. For he says God lashes man in this present life, or inflicts penalties, for five reasons:

**F**irst, so that God may be glorified. This occurs when the penalty or "lash" is miraculously removed. An example of this is the man born blind in John 9, and the resurrected Lazarus in John 11. 

**S**econdly, if the first reason is absent, punishment is sent so that merit may be accumulated through the exercise of patience, and also so that a virtue hidden within may be manifested to others. Examples of this are found in Job 1 and Tobit 2. 

**T**hirdly, so that virtue may be preserved through the humbling effect of these lashes. An example is found in Paul, who, as he says of himself in 2 Corinthians 12: "Lest the greatness of my revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan," <note>original: "stimulus carnis mee angelus fathane"</note> and so on. This "thorn," according to the scholar Remigius, was a certain physical infirmity. These are the causes that exist without fault.

**F**ourthly, punishment is sent so that eternal damnation may begin here on earth—that is, to show in some measure what the person will suffer in hell. Examples include Herod in Acts 12 and Antiochus in 2 Maccabees 9. 

**F**ifthly, so that a person may be purified, either by the expulsion of guilt—as when one is moved to contrition by these lashes—an example being Miriam <note>original: "maria"</note>, the sister of Aaron, in Numbers 12, who was infected with leprosy; and the Israelites prostrated in the desert, according to Jerome. Or, it is for the satisfaction of the penalty. An example of this is David, who, after the guilt of his adultery was forgiven, was expelled from his kingdom as a penalty, as is seen in 2 Samuel. This is noted by Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> regarding the repentance of David. It could also be said that every penalty we suffer proceeds from our own fault—at least from the original sin <note>The inherited state of sin in Christian theology, believed to stem from the Fall of Adam and Eve.</note> with which we are born, since it is the cause of all causalities.

<column-break/>

Regarding the third penalty, which is the "penalty of loss" <note><term>Penalty of Loss</term>: The theological concept of *poena damni*, the pain of being eternally separated from the vision of God.</note>, speaking of that eternal damnation which they will sustain in the future: let no one doubt that they will be tortured with sensible pains above all the damned. For just as grace leads to the vision of God in the fatherland <note>A common medieval term for Heaven.</note>, so does mortal guilt lead to the penalty of hell. And just as the degrees of blessedness in the fatherland are measured according to the degree of charity and grace held during life, so too is the measure of punishments in hell according to the measure of crimes committed during life. This is what is said in Deuteronomy 25: "According to the measure of the sin shall be the manner of the stripes."

While this applies to all other sins, it is especially true for witches <note>original: "maleficis"</note>, as touched upon in Hebrews 10: "How much worse punishment do you think he deserves who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, and has counted the blood of the covenant, by which he was sanctified, an unholy thing?" This is characteristic of witches, who deny the faith and perform many evil deeds by misusing the most divine sacrament, as will be made clear in the second part of this work.

### Chapter Fourteen: The aforementioned truth is declared in detail by comparing the works of witches to other species of superstition.

The aforementioned truth regarding the enormity of the crimes of witches is finally proved by comparison to the other works of mages and diviners. For since there are fourteen species of superstitious works arising from three types of divination <note><term>Divination</term>: The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note>:

The **first** type occurs through the manifest invocation of demons. 

The **second** occurs through a tacit consideration of the disposition or movement of some thing, such as the stars, days, winds, and such. 

The **third** occurs through the consideration of some human act to inquire into something hidden, which are called "lots" <note>original: "fortium"</note>. 

The species of the first type of divination, which occurs through the express invocation of demons, are: 
1. Prestidigitation <note>Illusion or "glamour" magic.</note>
2. Divination by dreams
3. Necromancy <note>original: "Nigromancia"; communication with the dead.</note>
4. Pythonic divination <note>Prophesying through a spirit of possession.</note>
5. Geomancy <note>Divination by dots on the ground or earth.</note>
6. Hydromancy <note>Divination by water.</note>
7. Aeromancy <note>Divination by air/atmospheric phenomena.</note>
8. Pyromancy <note>Divination by fire.</note>
9. And the cult of soothsayers <note>original: "ariolorum cultus"</note>. 

See Thomas Aquinas, *Secunda Secundae*, Question 95.

Preparation, however, occurs after the calming of both external and internal movements, such as when the nights are silent and the movements of <term>vapors</term><note>Latin: "fumositatū." Medieval physiology held that vapors from digestion rose to the brain to induce sleep.</note> have settled. This typically happens around dawn when digestion is complete. I say this regarding us sinners and those like us, to whom angels, out of divine piety and in the execution of their office, reveal certain things; or perhaps during a time of study at dawn, when an angel informs the intellect regarding the hidden secrets of the scriptures. For a good angel presides over the intellect just as God presides over the will, and as the celestial bodies preside over our physical bodies. To others who are more perfect, however, an angel can reveal things at any hour, whether they are awake or sleeping. According to the <term>Philosopher</term><note>Aristotle.</note> in his book *On Sleep and Waking*, such people are more fit to receive revelations, as has been said, at one time or another, just as other <term>magi</term><note>Wise men or practitioners of high sciences.</note> were accustomed to do.

Regarding the second point, note that from the natural concern of nature for the governance of the body, it happens that certain future events have a natural cause within the dreaming person. In such cases, those dreams or visions are merely **signs** and not the **causes** themselves, as was stated previously. This applies to future events happening to a person, such as health, sickness, or danger, etc. And this is the opinion of Aristotle in the work mentioned above. For nature represents to the soul in sleep certain dispositions that are in the body, from which sickness or something else later occurs. For example, if someone dreams of "fiery" activities, it is a sign that <term>choler</term><note>Yellow bile, associated with fire and a hot/dry temperament.</note> predominates in them. If they dream of matters of the air, such as flying and the like, it is a sign of the <term>sanguine</term><note>The blood humor, associated with the air.</note> temperament. If they dream of water or another watery liquid, it is a sign of <term>phlegm</term>. If they dream of earthy things, it is a sign of <term>melancholy</term><note>Black bile, associated with the earth.</note>. And therefore, through dreams, physicians are sometimes helped to recognize the dispositions of the body, as the Philosopher also says in the same book.

### ¶ The seventeenth [point] is a declaration of the fourteenth gravity of the crime, by comparing it to any sins of the demons.

But such is the magnitude of their crimes that they even exceed the sin and the fall of the bad angels. And if they exceed them in guilt, why not also in the punishments of hell? It is indeed not difficult to demonstrate this regarding guilt for various reasons. First: for although the demon's sin is irremissible <note>Unforgivable.</note>, this is not because of the magnitude of the crime in relation to their natural state—especially according to the opinion of those who say they [the angels] were created only in a state of nature and never in a state of grace. And since the good of grace exceeds the good of nature, therefore the sins of those who fall from a state of grace—just as witches exist by denying the faith they received in baptism—certainly exceed their [the demons'] sins. If, however, we say they were created in grace though not confirmed in it, even so, witches—though not created in grace—nevertheless fell from grace of their own will, just as he [Lucifer] sinned willingly.

¶ Second, it is demonstrated: for although his [the demon's] sin is irremissible for various other reasons—for instance, according to **Augustine**, because he sinned with no one suggesting it; therefore, he ought to return with no one repairing him. Or because, according to **Damascene**<note>St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a key figure in Eastern theology often cited in Western medieval scholasticism.</note>, he sinned with his intellect against the form of God; and the more noble the knowledge, the worse is the error. For "the servant who knows the will of his master," etc. <note>A reference to Luke 12:47: "That servant who knows his master’s will and does not get ready or does not do what his master wants will be beaten with many blows."</note> Or again, according to the same Damascene, because he is not capable of repentance, and therefore not of pardon; and this is due to his nature, which, because it is purely spiritual, is capable of only a single turning: for he turns himself entirely, which does not happen in man, where the flesh always fights against the spirit. Or again, because he sinned in a high place, namely in heaven, while man sins on earth.

First, in this: that according to **Anselm**<note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), famous for his ontological argument and theories on the Fall of the Devil.</note> in a certain prayer, he sinned through pride with no preceding punishment for a crime to warn him. Witches, however, despite so many punishments often inflicted on many other witches—and even after the punishments they see inflicted upon the devil in the Church because of his fall—scorn all these things. They do not hasten toward the least mortal sins like other sinners who sin out of weakness or malice without a habit of wickedness, but rather they hasten toward horrendous outrages out of a deep malice of the heart.

Second, because although the state of the bad angel is threefold—Innocence, Guilt, and Misery or Punishment—he only fell once from innocence and was never restored to it. Third, he [sinned] against the Creator; but we, and above all witches, sin against the Creator and the Redeemer, etc. Fourth, he abandoned God who merely permitted him to sin and did not pursue him with mercy; but we, and above all witches, are distanced by our sins from a God who permits it yet continually pursues us with mercy and anticipates us with many benefits. ¶ Fifth, he persists in malice while God rejects him and does not offer His grace, [while] we wretched ones run...

**R**egarding the arguments. To the first, the answer is clear through the points touched upon at the beginning of the body of the question: namely, on what basis a certain sin should be judged more serious than another, and how the sins of witches are more serious than all others in terms of guilt. To the other point regarding punishment, it must be said that just as Adam’s <term>guilt</term><note>Latin: "culpa."</note> is considered in two ways, so is his punishment: either regarding his person or regarding his whole nature—that is, the entire <term>posterity</term><note>All future generations of humanity.</note> following from him. In the first way: just as greater sins were committed after him, because he sinned only by doing what was evil not in itself but because it was forbidden <note>Referring to the eating of the forbidden fruit, which was a "positive" law rather than a "natural" law.</note>. Fornications, however, adulteries, and homicides are evil in both ways—namely, in themselves <note>By natural law.</note> and because they are forbidden—therefore a heavier punishment is also due to them. In the second way: although the greatest punishment followed the first sin, this occurred indirectly; specifically, insofar as through him all posterity was infected with <term>original sin</term><note>The Christian doctrine that all humans are born with a tainted nature inherited from Adam.</note>, because he was the first parent of all, for whom only the Son of God could make <term>satisfaction</term><note>The theological concept of "paying the debt" for sin through Christ's sacrifice.</note> through His ordained power. Yet, regarding his personal part, he repented by divine grace and was saved after the payment made by Christ. However, the sins of witches incomparably exceed [Adam’s] in gravity; they are not content with their personal sins and destructions, since they also continually draw countless others after them. Regarding the third, it must be said from what precedes that it was <term>accidental</term><note>A philosophical term meaning a secondary quality rather than the essential nature of the act.</note> to Adam’s sin that it caused greater harm. This is because he found human nature <term>whole</term><note>Unblemished by previous sin.</note> and was forced to transmit it corrupted—by necessity of nature, not by a specific act of will. Hence, it does not follow that his sin was simply more 

<column-break/>

grave than the others. This is also because subsequent sins would have done the same if they had found nature in such a state. Just as a <term>mortal sin</term><note>In Catholic theology, a grave sin that destroys the state of grace in the soul.</note> does not deprive one of grace if it does not find grace [already present], yet it would deprive one of it if it found it there. This is the solution of <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for the author's arguments.</note> in the *Second Book of the Sentences*, distinction 21, article 2, and in the solution to the second argument. If anyone wishes to understand this solution fully, he must consider that if Adam had maintained <term>original justice</term><note>The state of perfect harmony and grace before the Fall.</note>, he would not have transmitted it to his descendants, as <term>Anselm</term><note>Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), an influential theologian and philosopher.</note> thought, because someone after him could still have sinned. See the words of the <term>Doctor</term><note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> in distinction 20: "Whether children would have been born confirmed in grace." Also, in <term>Quodlibet 11</term><note>A "Quodlibet" was a formal academic debate on "any given topic." This refers to Aquinas's Quodlibetal Questions.</note>, article 1: "Whether the same people who are now saved would have been saved if Adam had not sinned."

...permits. Whence some argue that **witchcraft is nothing in the world.** This claim is based on five perspectives. First, from the side of God. Second, from the side of the devil. Third, from the side of the witch. Fourth, from the side of the disease. Fifth, from the side of the preachers and judges who preach and judge against such women, for these men would surely never be safe if witchcraft were real.

**First**, the argument is this: God can punish man for his sins, and he does so with the sword, with famine, and with <term>mortality</term><note>Meaning plague or widespread fatal disease.</note>. Likewise, he punishes with various other diverse and innumerable infirmities to which the human condition is subject. Since he has no need to add other punishments, he does not permit witchcraft.

**Second**, from the side of the devil: if the things being preached were true—namely, that they can impede the <term>generative power</term><note>The ability to conceive children.</note> so that a woman does not conceive, or if she does, that they cause a miscarriage, or if not a miscarriage, that they kill the children immediately after birth—then surely they could destroy the whole world. Furthermore, it could be said that the works of the devil would then be stronger than the works of God—specifically the sacrament of matrimony, which is God’s work.

**Third**, from the side of man: For we see that if witchcraft were to be something in the world, then some people would be bewitched more than others. If one asks why, the answer given is that it is due to the punishment of sins. But this is false; therefore, the claim that witchcraft exists in the world is also false. The falsity is proven by this: that then the greatest sinners would be punished the most. However, this is false, as they are often punished less than some who are just—which is even seen in innocent children who are said to be bewitched.

**Fourth**, another argument can be added from the side of God: namely, that he who could prevent something but does not, but rather permits it to happen, is judged to have willed it by his own choice. But since God is supremely good, he cannot will evil; therefore, he cannot permit an evil to happen which he himself can prevent.

Likewise, from the side of the disease: the defects and infirmities that people call "witchcraft-induced" are also similar to natural defects and infirmities—that is, those which proceed from a defect of nature. For that someone limps, is blinded, loses their reason, or even

<column-break/>

dies, can happen from a natural defect. Whence these things cannot safely be ascribed to witchcraft.

**Lastly**, from the side of the judges and preachers: if they preach and practice such things against witches, they would never be safe because of the immense hatred conceived against them by the witches.

**But against these arguments**, one should take from the first question regarding the third principal point of the first part of this treatise <note>The author is cross-referencing an earlier part of the *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note>; and let them propose those things which are more suited for the common people: namely, how God **permits evils to happen** even though he does not *will* evil to happen.

He permits it for the sake of the **admirable perfection of the universe**, which is considered in this: that good things are more eminently commended, are more pleasing, and are more praiseworthy when they are compared to evils. There are authorities on this point <note>Referring to traditional theological citations, likely from St. Augustine.</note>. Likewise, the depths of divine wisdom, justice, and goodness shine forth in ways that would otherwise be hidden.

And briefly, for the sake of clarifying the question, various lessons for the information of the people can be gathered from what is touched upon there: namely, that God justly permitted two "falls"—that of the angels and that of our first parents <note>Adam and Eve.</note>. Since these are greater than all other falls, it is no wonder if other, lesser ones are permitted. They are "greater" in terms of their causality <note>Meaning they caused the fall of the entire human race and the existence of demons.</note>, not necessarily in other circumstances, according to which the sins of witches (as touched on in the third question) exceed the sins of the fallen angels and our first parents. Why God justly permitted those first falls is addressed in the second question, from which a preacher can gather many points and expand upon them as he pleases.

Therefore, he has very often acted outside of those things to punish sins, bringing about plagues and other things beyond any influence of the [celestial] bodies, as in the punishment of the sin of Su-

Therefore, just as it is not fitting to completely block the malice of the devil, but rather it is proper to permit it to act insofar as it can serve the good of the universe—even though it is continually restrained by the good angels so that he cannot do as much harm as he would wish—so too it is not fitting to restrain **human malice** regarding those things which a person can do out of **free will**, such as denying the faith and devoting oneself to the devil. **Third**, God justly permits those evils to happen through which the devil is also indirectly tormented the most and receives the greatest displeasure. Through those evils which are done by witches by the power of demons, the devil is indirectly tormented most of all when God, against the devil’s will, uses all those evils for the **glory of His name**, for the commendation of the faith, for the **purgation of the elect**, and for the accumulation of their merits. For it is certain that among all the grievances which the devil feels because of the pride he always raises against God—according to the scripture: *The pride of those who hate you ascends always* <note>Psalm 74:23</note>—this one is the greatest: that he is displeased that God converts all his schemes into His own glory and so forth. Therefore, God justly permits all things.

This is also illustrated by the **serpent**, who was the devil’s first instrument, and so forth.

Regarding the **third** point, it must be said that just as the devil’s intention and desire to tempt the **good** is greater than his desire to tempt the **wicked**—even though, on the part of the person being tempted, he tempts the wicked more than the good (meaning there is a greater capacity in the wicked to receive the demon’s temptation than there is in the good)—so too he desires more to harm the good than the wicked, even though he finds a greater capacity for being harmed in the wicked than in the good. And the reason for this is that, according to **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great, a major authority in medieval theology.</note>, the more frequently someone subjects themselves to the devil, the more intolerable the devil makes it for them, so that they cannot resist him. But since the wicked more frequently subject themselves to the devil, temptation becomes more intolerable and frequent for them, as they do not have the **shield of faith** with which to protect themselves. Regarding this shield, the Apostle says in Ephesians 6:

Therefore, he strives more to draw the **just** whom he does not have into his dominion through tribulation than he does the sinners he already possesses—just as an earthly prince rises up more against someone who takes away his rights or harms his kingdom than against those who do not oppose him. <meta>This page continues the theological justification for why God permits the existence of evil and the actions of witches. It transitions from abstract scholastic definitions of "God's will" to the practical problem of how to distinguish a supernatural curse from a natural medical condition.</meta>

...[God] does not will for evil to be done, nevertheless [He wills] that evil happen [by permitting it]. Beyond the points already touched upon, a preacher can explain this through the **five signs of the divine will**, which are: **Precept**, **Prohibition**, **Counsel**, **Operation**, and **Permission**. See **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note>, especially in the first part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], where he explains it more clearly in Question 19, Article 12. For although there is only one will in God—which is God Himself, just as His essence is one—nevertheless, in relation to His works, His will is indicated and signified to us in many ways, as the **Psalmist** also says: *Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all His wills* <note>Psalm 111:2; original: "Magna opera domini exquiſita in omnes voluntates eiꝰ".</note>.

Hence, the "will" in God is distinguished not by the reality itself, but by its effects. Thus, the will properly so-called is called the **will of good pleasure** <term>voluntas beneplaciti</term><note>This refers to God's ultimate, hidden will that governs everything that actually happens.</note>. The will metaphorically so-called is called the **will of the sign** <term>voluntas signi</term><note>The outward instructions God gives humans, like laws or advice, which humans may choose to follow or ignore.</note>, insofar as it is indicated to us through signs and metaphors that God wills this. 

By way of analogy: just as the **head of a household** <term>paterfamilias</term>, having one internal will, demonstrates it in five ways: namely, by himself and through another. By himself in two ways: directly and indirectly. **Directly**, when he performs an action, and then it is "Operation." **Indirectly**, however, when he does not hinder one who is acting; as it is also said in the fourth book of the *Physics* <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *Physics*, which was a standard textbook in medieval universities.</note>: "The one who removes a hindrance is an accidental mover." In this regard, the sign is called "**Permission**." 

Through another, the head of the household declares that he wills something in three ways. Either insofar as he orders someone to do something necessarily and by prohibiting the contrary—and thus there are **Precepts** in commands and **Prohibitions** in affirmative and negative commands. Or insofar as he orders someone persuasively toward something by way of advice, and this pertains to **Counsel**. And just as the human will is manifested through these five, so is the will of God. For that Precept, Prohibition, and Counsel are called the "will of God" is clear through that passage in **Matthew chapter six**: *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven* <note>original: "Fiat volūtas tua ſicut in celo et in terra".</note>; that is, that on earth we may fulfill His precepts, avoid what is prohibited, and fulfill His counsels as much as possible. And similarly, that Permission and Operation...

<column-break/>

...are called the will of God is clear through **Augustine**, who says in the *Enchiridion*: *Nothing happens unless the Almighty God wills it to happen, either by allowing it to happen or by doing it* <note>original: "Nihil ſit niſi omnipotens deus fieri velit. vel ſinendo vt fiat vel faciendo".</note>. To the point: when it is said that "something which a person could hinder but does not hinder is judged to have proceeded from their will," this is true. 

But when it is inferred that "God is supremely good, therefore He cannot will for evil to be done," this is also true regarding the **will of good pleasure** and the four signs of this will. For He cannot perform evil, nor command evil, nor fail to prohibit evil while persuading toward the **works of supererogation** <note>original: "bona ſuperoꝛgationis"; these are virtuous acts that go beyond what is strictly required by God's law.</note>. However, He can will to **permit** evil to be done.

Regarding the other question: how are illnesses distinguished from one another, so that one is caused by **witchcraft** <term>maleficialis</term> and the other is **natural**, resulting, for instance, from a defect of nature? It is answered that this is done in various ways. 

**First**, by the judgment of **physicians** <note>The text cites Canon Law: *Decretum Gratiani*, Case 26. These specific laws dealt with magic and healing.</note>, where the words of **Augustine** from the second book of *On Christian Doctrine* are found: "To this kind of superstition belong all the amulets and remedies which the discipline of physicians condemns, involving things to be hung or tied on." By analogy, where physicians—judging from circumstances such as age, a previously healthy complexion, and a sudden change as if in the blink of an eye—see that the illness did not occur from a defect of the blood, the stomach, or the side, they judge that it did not happen from a defect of nature, but from an **external source**. And it is from an external source when it is not from a poisonous infection (because in that case the blood and stomach would be filled with bad humors). Thus, by a process of elimination <term>ex ſufficienti diuiſione</term>, they judge the effect to be caused by **witchcraft**.

**Second**, when the illness appears **incurable** to them, so that the sick person cannot be relieved by any medicines; indeed, they rather see the condition grow worse. 

**Third**, because it sometimes happens so suddenly that the judgment of the sick person concurs with this. A case that occurred became known to one of us. For a certain man, one of the noblemen of the city of **Speyer** <note>Speyer is a major city in the Rhineland, Germany, where the authors were active.</note>, had a wife of an exceedingly stubborn will, to such an extent that although he was eager to please her in all things, she nevertheless resisted him in almost all his desires and with insulting words...

...always strove to trouble him. It happened then that upon entering his home one day, while the woman, in her usual manner, was quarreling with him with insulting words, he wished to give way to her anger and leave the house. However, she—anticipating him with a quick run—blocked the door through which he had to exit, and shouting, she protested that unless he beat her, no integrity or honesty would remain in him. At these harsh words, he extended his hand, not with the intention of hurting her, and touched her lightly upon the shoulder with his fingers spread. Suddenly, he collapsed to the ground and lost all his senses; for many weeks afterward, he lay in bed, held by a most grave infirmity. In this matter, it can be considered that the illness did not happen from a natural defect, but came upon him through the woman's **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficium"</note>. 

Many, indeed almost innumerable similar acts have occurred and have become known to many. There are some who, through certain practical experience of the matter, understand it in this way: they hold **molten lead** <note>original: "plumbum liquefactum"</note> over the sick person and pour it into a bowl full of water; if any solid image is seen to form, they then judge that the infirmity occurred due to witchcraft. And when those who practice such things are asked whether such an image emerges by the work of demons or by a natural power, they are accustomed to answer that by the power of **Saturn** over lead (which is otherwise considered an "evil" planet), just as the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the Sun is associated with Gold, and Saturn with Lead.</note> acts upon gold, it is able to reveal the witchcraft by its own power. 

But what should be felt concerning these things—namely, whether the practice is licit or not—will be discussed in the third principal part of this treatise. To the **Canonists** <note>Experts in Church law.</note> it seems licit, on the grounds that "vanities may be crushed by vanities"; however, to the **theologians**, the opposite seems entirely true, since evil things are not to be done so that good things may result. 

Finally, where various questions are asked: First, why are witches not made rich? To the first, it must be said that 

<column-break/>

for the most part, witches are not enriched so that, according to the desire of the demon and to the insult of the Creator, they may be "purchased" for the cheapest possible price. Secondly, it is so that they are not noticed because of their wealth. To the second point—why they do not harm princes—the cause is manifest: because as much as is in their power, they do this to keep the princes in their friendship. And if it is asked why they do not harm their enemies, the answer is that a **good angel** on the other side hinders this witchcraft. This is according to the book of **Daniel**: *The prince of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days* <note>Daniel 10:13. Medieval commentators often interpreted the "Princes" in Daniel as guardian angels of nations.</note>. Hence the Doctors, in the second book of the *Sentences* <note>A standard theological textbook by Peter Lombard.</note>, discuss how a battle occurs between good angels. To the third point, it is said that they cannot harm **Inquisitors** or other officials because these men exercise **public justice**. Various examples could be brought forward for this, but the length of time does not permit it.
