...progress in the manner of operating and the **horrendous observance** <note>original: "horrenda observantia," referring to the terrifying rituals of witches</note>. Third, the beneficial and preservative obstacles. And because we are now safe within the realm of moral matter, there is no need to insist everywhere upon arguments and formal declarations, since those things which follow in the chapters have been sufficiently discussed in the preceding questions. Therefore, we pray to God for the reader not to seek a rigorous demonstration in all things where a fitting probability suffices, by reducing those things to what is established as true either by sight or hearing from one's own experience, or by the reports of trustworthy people. 

Concerning the first part, however, two principal things will be touched upon: First, the various ways the demon himself entices the innocent; Second, the various ways of professing the **heresy** <note>The authors treat witchcraft not just as magic, but as a formal heresy involving a pact with the Devil.</note> itself. Concerning the second part, six things will be touched upon in order regarding the manner of proceeding and curing: First, about those things practiced by **witches** <note>original: "maleficis"</note> for themselves and their own bodies. Second, about those things they perform toward other people. Third, about those toward beasts. Fourth, about those by which they harm the fruits of the earth. Fifth, concerning the **witchcraft of men** only—namely those witchcrafts in which only men and not women engage. Sixth, concerning the action for removing witchcrafts and the ways in which the bewitched are cured. Therefore, the first question is divided into thirteen and eight chapters, since they vary and multiply in their rites by just as many ways.

### Question I
**Whether anyone can be so blessed by good angels that they cannot be bewitched by witches through any of the ways written below.**

It seems not. Because through the preceding arguments it has been declared that even the blameless, the innocent, and the just are many times afflicted by demons—as was **Job** and many innocent children who are seen to be bewitched along with many other just people; although they are not afflicted in the same way as sinners (since it is not for the perdition of their souls), they are nevertheless afflicted in their worldly goods and their bodies. 

On the contrary is the confession of witches,

<column-break/>

namely that they are not able to harm everyone, but only those whom they see—through information provided by demons—to be destitute of divine help. 

**Response:** There are three kinds of people blessed by God whom that most wicked race cannot harm with their witchcrafts. 

The first are those who exercise **public justice** against them, or who persist against them in some public office. 

The second are those who protect themselves by the observed and venerated **rites of the Church**, such as by the sprinkling of holy water, the consumption of consecrated salt, the lawful use of candles on the day of **Purification** <note>Candlemas (February 2nd), when candles were blessed for use against storms and evil spirits.</note>, and of branches blessed on **Palm Sunday**; for the Church exorcises such things for this purpose, so that they may diminish the powers of the demon, as will be made clear later. 

The third are those who are blessed by the holy angels in various and infinite ways. 

Regarding the first group, a reason is given which is proven by various acts and deeds; for since "all power is from God" and "carries the sword" (according to the **Apostle** <note>referring to St. Paul in Romans 13:4</note>) for the punishment of evildoers and the reward of the good, it is no wonder that demons are kept at bay by angelic power when justice is exercised for the punishment of that horrendous crime. 

The **Doctors** <note>Learned theologians and legal experts of the Church.</note> note to the same effect that the power of the demon is hindered in five ways, either in whole or in part: 

1. First, by the limit imposed on his power by God, as is touched upon in the first and second chapters of the **Book of Job**. 'He has good faith,' the demon said, 'and diligently protects himself with the sign of the cross; therefore, I cannot harm his body, but only the eleventh part of his crops in the field, if it pleases you.'" 

2. Second, it is hindered by an external impediment applied, as in the case of **Balaam's donkey** in the Book of Numbers, chapter 22. 

3. Third, by a miracle of impossibility performed externally. And there are those who are blessed by a singular privilege. Of which thirdly...

...the kind of men who cannot be **bewitched** <note>original: "maleficiari," meaning to be harmed by magic or sorcery</note>. This will be clear. Fourth, by the judgment of God, who singularly arranges an obstacle by means of a **good angel**—as was the case with the demon Asmodeus killing the husbands of the virgin Sarah, but not being able to harm Tobias <note>This refers to the Book of Tobit, where Sarah's first seven husbands are killed by a demon on their wedding night, but Tobias is protected through the guidance of the Archangel Raphael.</note>. Fifth, sometimes through the devil’s own caution; for sometimes the devil does not wish to strike, fearing that a worse result for him might follow. For instance, he might refrain from troubling the **excommunicated** <note>Those officially cast out of the Church.</note>, just as he troubled the man in Corinth who was excommunicated (1 Corinthians 5), yet he does not always do so, lest he strengthen the faith of the Church in the **power of the keys** <note>The "power of the keys" is the spiritual authority of the Church to forgive or withhold forgiveness for sins.</note>. 

Therefore, by analogy, we can also say that even if they were not restrained by divine power when public justice is exercised, they still often voluntarily withdraw their hand or protection from witches. This is because they either fear the witches’ conversion or because they desire and wish to hasten their damnation. Finally, these things are proven by acts and deeds. For the aforementioned **Doctor** <note>Likely referring to Nider or another authority cited by the authors.</note> reports that witches have given true testimony from experience: the moment they are captured by officials of public justice, all the power of their witchcraft is immediately weakened. 

For this reason, a certain judge named **Peter** <note>Likely Peter of Bern, a judge who figures prominently in the stories told within this manual.</note>, who was mentioned above, wished to capture a certain witch named **Stadlin** using his servants. Such a great trembling was struck into their hands, and such a foul stench entered their nostrils, that they almost despaired of daring to attack the witch. But the judge urged them, saying: "Attack securely, for once he is touched by **public justice**, he will lose all the strength of his wickedness." And so the outcome proved the fact: for he was captured and burned at the stake because of the many acts of witchcraft he had committed, which are recorded here and there throughout various subjects. 

But many other things occurred to us as **Inquisitors** <note>The authors, Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger, frequently insert their own personal experiences to validate their claims.</note> while laboring in our office of the Inquisition; if it were profitable to recite them, they would surely turn the reader's mind to wonder. But because praise in one’s own mouth becomes foul, it is better to pass over them in silence than to incur the mark of **vainglory** <note>Pride in one's own achievements.</note>—except for those things which have been brought to light by God and cannot be hidden. For example, in the town of **Ravensburg**, 

<column-break/>

when the **consuls** <note>City officials or magistrates.</note> were interrogating witches who were about to be burned, they asked why they had not inflicted any witchcraft upon us Inquisitors as they had upon other men. They responded that although they had attempted to do this many times, they were unable to. And when the officials asked for the cause, they replied they did not know, except that they had been so informed by the **demons**. 

Indeed, we cannot sufficiently describe how often, by night and by day, they were hostile toward us. At times they appeared as **monkeys**, and at other times as **dogs** or **goats**, disturbing us with their cries and insults. At night, when we rose for our prayers (however devout they might have been), something would strike with a most violent blow just outside the window—which was at such a height that it could only be reached by the longest of ladders—aiming directly at the head. They even inserted **needles** into the linen cloth covering the head; these were found by us when we rose, as if they had wished to thrust them into our heads by **magical art**. 

But praise be to the Most High, who in His piety and without our merits, preserved us as his servants—unworthy though we are—as public officials of the **justice of the Faith**. 

Concerning the second point, the reasoning is self-evident. For this purpose, the Church performs **exorcisms**, and these are the most effective remedies for preserving oneself from the attacks of witches. If it is asked in what manner one ought to fortify oneself, it must first be said of those things which are done without the binding of **sacred words**, and finally of the sacred charms themselves. 

Regarding the first, it is lawful to sprinkle **holy water** <note>original: "aqua benedicta"</note>—and indeed any honest places of men and cattle—with the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity and the Lord's Prayer for the salvation of men and livestock. For thus it is said in the exorcism: "that wherever it is sprinkled, it may be free from all uncleanness and delivered from harm; let no pestilential spirit reside there," etc. For the Lord saves both men and livestock, as the Prophet says, each according to his measure. 

Second, just as the first is a matter of necessity, so this second—namely, lighting a **blessed candle**—is a matter of fitness; to sprinkle, for instance, the inhabited places with such a candle. Third, **consecrated herbs**...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how individuals can protect themselves against witchcraft. Having previously categorized those who are immune, the text now provides specific historical examples and practical remedies used by the faithful to ward off demonic influence.</meta>

To join or to fumigate with these herbs in some hidden, habitable place is very beneficial. For instance, in the city of **Speyer** <note>original: "Spirensi," a historic city in southwest Germany</note> in the same year this book was begun, it happened that a certain devout woman had words with a woman suspected of being a **witch** <note>original: "malefica," a woman practicing harmful magic</note>, as is the custom among quarrelsome women. At night, when she wished to place her nursing infant in the cradle, she thought back on the dealings she had during the day with the suspect. Fearing for the child's safety, she placed **blessed herbs** <note>Herbs consecrated by a priest, often on the Feast of the Assumption.</note> under the boy, sprinkled him with holy water, put a little **exorcised salt** <note>salt that has been ritually purified and blessed to drive away evil spirits</note> in his mouth, protected him with the sign of the cross, and carefully secured the cradle.

And behold, around the middle of the night, she heard the child crying. When she went to touch the child and move the cradle—which was positioned high near the bed—she moved the cradle, but could not touch the child because he was gone. Trembling, the poor woman, grieving deeply over the loss of her child, lit a light and found the infant crying under the bed in a corner, yet without any injury. In this matter, one can perceive how much power lies in the **exorcisms** of the Church against the snares of the devil. Furthermore, the mercy and wisdom of God are clear, reaching from one end to the other, strongly and sweetly disposing even the **wicked deeds** <note>original: "maleficia"</note> of these worst of men and demons. Thus, where they seek to diminish and weaken faith, they actually strengthen and root it more firmly in the hearts of many. Many benefits come to the faithful from such evils, as faith is strengthened, the malice of the demon is seen, God's mercy and power are made manifest, people are moved to protect themselves, and they are drawn to the revered **Passion of Christ** and the ceremonies of the Church.

In those same days, a **bailiff** <term>schultetus</term> <note>a local administrative official or magistrate</note> of a certain village called **Wiesental** <note>original: "Wissental"</note> was being afflicted by witchcraft with the most severe pains and twistings of the body. <column-break/>

by experience. For he said that every Sunday he used to protect himself by taking **blessed salt and water**. However, because he had neglected this one day on account of a wedding celebration, he was bewitched on that very day.

Finally, what about that man in **Ravensburg** <note>original: "Ravenspurg," a city in Upper Swabia</note>? When he was solicited by the devil in the form of a woman for a carnal act, he was very anxious. While he did not wish to resist, the thought came to that poor man that he should protect himself by taking salt, as he had heard in a sermon. When he took the **blessed salt** at the entrance of the room, the woman looked at him with a grim face and suddenly vanished, mocking him by asking who among the demons had taught him this. In this case, the devil was present either by himself in the image of a witch, or with the bodily presence of a witch, as he is able to do both with God's permission.

Consider also those three companions walking along a road; two of them were struck by a bolt of lightning. The third, terrified, heard voices crying in the air, "Let us strike him too!" But another voice replied, "We cannot, for today **the Word was made flesh**" <note>original: "verbum caro factum est," a reference to the Incarnation of Christ</note>. He understood that he was preserved for this reason: he had heard Mass, and at the end of the Mass, he had heard the **Gospel of John** <note>The prologue of the Gospel of John (1:1-14) was traditionally read at the end of Mass and used as a protective blessing.</note>: "In the beginning was the Word," etc.

Thus, people are preserved by **sacred words** tied to the body, which are protective in a wonderful way, provided that seven conditions are observed. Mention of these will be made in the last question of this second part. Just as we treat protective remedies here, we will treat healing remedies there. And those sacred words tend not only toward preserving but also toward curing those who are bewitched. The most effective protection for the places of men and cattle are the words of the **triumphal title of our Savior** <note>The "titulus," or the inscription placed on the Cross of Christ (INRI).</note>, namely, when they are written in the four parts of a place in the form of a cross: **Jesus + of Nazareth + King + of the Jews +** <note>original: "Jesus + Nazarenus + Rex + Judaeorum +"</note>, or by adding the name of the Virgin Mary, or...

<meta>This page continues the technical and theological explanation of how certain people are immune to witchcraft. The previous page concluded a story about a child protected by holy salt and herbs; now the text moves into a scholarly classification of the types of divine and angelic protection that shield the "elect" from demonic influence.</meta>

...of the evangelists, or even the words of John:
> The Word was made flesh. <note>original: "Verbum caro factum est" (John 1:14)</note>

The third type of person who cannot be harmed by sorcerers is the most unique: namely, those protected by a special angelic guard, both internally and externally. Internally, this occurs through the **infusion of grace**; externally, it occurs through the protection of the **celestial virtues** <note>In medieval theology, "Virtues" are a specific rank or "choir" of angels</note>—that is, through the **movers of the celestial spheres** <term>motovers orbium: the angelic beings believed to physically move the planets and stars in their orbits</term>. 

And this type is divided into two kinds of the elect. For they are either protected against all types of witchcraft so that they can be harmed in no way, or they are specifically protected regarding their **procreative power** <note>original: "generatiuam potentiam"; the text focuses heavily on the idea that witches interfere with fertility or sexual function</note> so that they are preserved in purity by the good angels themselves, just as evil spirits inflame certain wicked people toward one person or make them "cold" <note>impotent</note> toward another through their sorcery.

The first point regarding internal and external protection through grace and the influence of celestial bodies is explained as follows: For although God pours grace into our minds by Himself—such that no creature’s power can reach such an infusion, according to the verse:
> The Lord will give grace and glory. <note>original: "Gratiam et gloriaz dabit dominus" (Psalm 84:11)</note>

—yet he does so as a **disposition** <note>a preparatory state of being</note>, as **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian</note> teaches in a certain place in the *Third Book of the Sentences*. When God wishes to infuse some notable grace, a good angel cooperates. And this is what **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian philosopher</note> suggests in the fourth chapter of *On the Divine Names*: "It is a law of the divinity, immutably established, that the lowest things are perfected by the highest through those in the middle." This means that whatever good flows into us from the source of all goodness, we receive it entirely through the ministry of the good angels.

For although in the **conception of the Word of God** in the most blessed Virgin—through which God became man—only divine power was efficiently present, nevertheless, by angelic ministry, the mind of the Virgin was greatly moved or predisposed toward the good through the angel's salutation and through the strengthening and informing of her intellect. For the opinion of the aforementioned doctor [Aquinas] is that there are three things in man, as we see: namely, the **will**, the **intellect**,

<column-break/>

and other internal and external powers attached to the limbs and bodily organs. In the first [the will], God alone is able to act, because "the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord." However, a good angel acts as a **disposition**, insofar as he further illuminates the intellect toward the recognition of the true and the good. Thus, both God and the good angel can act upon the second [the intellect] by illuminating it. 

And similarly, in the third [the bodily powers], the good angel acts for the good, while the evil angel—though only with God's permission—can impress **evil influences**. Nevertheless, it is within the power of the human will to accept or reject such influences, which a person can always repel by invoking the grace of God.

Concerning the **external protection**, which is communicated by God through the **movers of the spheres**: it is a common tradition, and one more in harmony with both Holy Scripture and **natural philosophy**, that all celestial bodies are moved by angelic power and are called "movers of the spheres." By Christ and the Church, they are called the "**virtues of the heavens**," and consequently, all physical things in this world are ruled by celestial influences. This is witnessed by the **Philosopher** <note>The standard medieval way of referring to Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "metixorum," a scribal error for "Metaphysicorum"</note>. 

Therefore, we can also say that since God has a singular **providence** for His elect, although He subjects some to the evils of this life (namely, punishments), He nevertheless preserves others so that they can be harmed in no way. And they receive this gift either from the good angels assigned by God for their protection, or from the influences of the celestial bodies, or from the movers of those spheres. 

Furthermore, it should be noted that although some are protected against all witchcraft, and some against some but not all, there are nevertheless some who are uniquely preserved in purity by good angels regarding their **procreative power**, such that they can in no way be bewitched by evil ones in that regard. But to write about these things seems partly superfluous, though partly necessary, because those who are bewitched in their procreative power are deprived of angelic protection because they are always in mortal [sin]...

For it happened thus with the holy **Abbot Serenus**, of whom Cassian writes in the *Collations of the Fathers* <note>original: "colla. patrū"; a 5th-century work by John Cassian on monastic life</note>, in the first collation of Abbot Serenus. Here, he says, by unwearyingly persisting in nocturnal and daily prayers, fasts, and vigils for the internal chastity of his heart and soul, he finally perceived that he had extinguished all the heat of carnal concupiscence <note>sexual desire</note> within himself through divine grace. Then, being inflamed with a greater zeal for chastity and having used the aforementioned remedies, he asked of God that the chastity of the "inner man" might overflow into his body by God's gift. 

At last, an angel came to him in a vision of the night. It seemed to open his belly and pluck out a certain **inflamed growth of flesh** <term>ignitaz carnis strumam: metaphorically, the "tumor" of lustful desire</term> from his vitals; then, having restored all the intestines to their places as they had been, the angel said: "Behold, the **incitements of your flesh** <note>original: "incentina carnis"</note> are cut away, and know that on this day you have obtained perpetual purity of body, according to the vow by which you asked that you might no longer be stirred even by that natural movement which is excited even in small children and infants."

So also it is said of the blessed **Abbot Equitius** by the Blessed Gregory in the first book of the *Dialogues*: "In the time of his youth," he says, "when the sharp struggles of the flesh's incitements were wearying him, the very hardships of his temptation made him more diligent in the study of prayer. And when he sought a remedy for this matter from Almighty God with continuous prayers, one night, with an angel standing by, he saw himself being **made a eunuch** <note>original: "eunuchari se vidit"</note>. In that vision, it appeared that the angel cut away all movement from his genital members; and from that time forward, he was as far removed from temptation as if he had no gender in his body." Behold, what a great

<column-break/>

benefit of **becoming chaste** <note>original: "castificationis"</note>! Relying on this virtue by the help of Almighty God, just as he had previously presided over men, he began afterward to preside over women. 

So too, in the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "vitaspatrū"</note> collected by the most religious man **Saint Heraclides** in his book which he calls *The Paradise*, he mentions a certain holy father and monk whom he calls **Elias**. This man, moved by mercy, gathered three hundred women into a monastery and began to rule them. But after two years had passed, being now thirty-five years of age, he was tempted by the flesh and fled into the desert, where he fasted for two days, praying: "Lord God, either kill me or free me from this temptation." 

In the evening, therefore, sleep crept over him, and he saw three angels coming to him. When they asked why he had fled from the monastery of virgins, and he—out of shame—did not dare to answer, the angels said: "If you are freed, will you return to take care of the women?" He replied that he would do so gladly. Then, having received from him the oath they demanded, they **made him a eunuch**. For one seemed to hold his hands, another his feet, and the third appeared to cut away his testicles with a razor—not that it was truly so, but that it appeared to be so. When they asked if he felt the remedy, he replied that he felt greatly unburdened. Wherefore on the fifth day he returned to the mourning women; and through the forty years in which he survived afterward, he never again felt a spark of the former temptation.

We read that a no less benefit was conferred upon **Blessed Thomas**, the Doctor of our order <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the famous Dominican theologian</note>. Because he had entered the said order, he was imprisoned by his kinsmen. He was tempted so that he might be seduced back to the world by a **prostitute** <note>original: "meretricem"</note>, who was sent in by his relatives in the richest clothing and finery. When the Doctor had looked upon her, he ran to the physical fire, snatched up a **burning brand** <note>original: "titionem ignitum"</note>, and chased the temptress of burning lust out of the prison. Immediately prostrating himself in prayer for the gift of chastity, he fell asleep. Then two angels appeared to him, saying: "Behold, on behalf of God, we gird you with the **girdle of chastity** <note>original: "cingulo castitatis"</note>, which..."

These must be discussed in order first, so that it may be more clearly debated by which remedies the bewitched might be relieved; and so that the eighteen modes themselves might be more clearly evident, they will be reduced into as many chapters. 

First, concerning the "entry" of witches, the various ways will be made clear by which the witches themselves attract innocent young girls to the increase of that perfidy <note>betrayal of faith</note>.

Sixth, concerning the mode by which they are accustomed to impede the generative power <note>causing infertility or impotence</note>.

Twelfth, concerning certain infirmities in particular. 

Thirteenth <column-break/>

Fifteenth, concerning the mode by which they are accustomed to stir up hailstorms and tempests, and to strike men and beasts with lightning. 

Sixteenth, Seventeenth, and Eighteenth, concerning the three modes by which only men, and not women, are intent upon sorceries.

Nor should anyone think that they can grasp a complete knowledge of these things just because these various modes of inflicting various sorceries are recited. <meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding how humans are protected from or subjected to supernatural harms. It transitions from the previous discussion on divine protection (the three types of men who cannot be bewitched) into a scholastic explanation of how God, angels, and stars influence human health and will, concluding with the start of Chapter 1 on how witches recruit new members.</meta>

...are directed immediately by God. According to the Apostle <note>Paul the Apostle, specifically Philippians 2:13</note>: "It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish for his good pleasure." Furthermore, human intellectual knowledge is ordered by God through the mediation of angels. Therefore, even all physical things—whether they are internal, such as virtues and sciences acquired through internal physical powers, or external, such as health and sickness—are dispensed by the celestial bodies <note>the stars and planets</note> through the mediation of angels. Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher</note> touches upon this in the fourth chapter of *The Divine Names*, stating that celestial bodies are the causes of those things that happen in this world. However, these things are to be understood regarding natural health and sickness. Regarding those sicknesses that are supernatural—on account of the demonic power that inflicts them upon those whom God permits—we cannot say that it happens due to the influence of the celestial bodies that someone is bewitched <term>maleficiatur</term> <note>literally "made evil," but here meaning to be the victim of a harmful spell or witchcraft</note>. Just as it can rightly be said that, by the influence of the celestial bodies, it is possible for someone *not* to be bewitched.

And if it is said that opposites must occur concerning the same thing—and just as the proposition stands in the affirmative, so does the opposite in the negative—the response is that where someone is preserved from these supernatural infirmities by the power of the celestial bodies, this does not happen by the power of the celestial bodies immediately. Rather, it happens by angelic power, which can strengthen that influence so that the enemy <note>the Devil</note> cannot prevail over them with his witchcraft. That angelic power can be derived either from the mover of the celestial sphere <note>an Aristotelian concept of the intelligence that moves the planets</note>—as if someone were about to die at a specific point according to their natural lifespan, God, by his power (who always works through such intermediary causes), can change this by instilling a preservative power instead of a natural defect and its influence. Thus, we can say the same regarding one who could be bewitched: that in such a way they are preserved from witchcraft. Or, such preservation is performed by the angel assigned for protection, which is the most principal of all protections. And what is said in Jeremiah 22: "Write this man down as sterile, a man who shall not prosper in his days" <note>original: "Scribe virum istum sterilem qui in diebus suis non prosperabitur"</note>, this is understood in regards to the choices

<column-break/>

of the will, in which one man prospers and another does not. This can also happen from the influences of the celestial bodies. For example: someone is inclined by the impression of the celestial bodies toward certain useful choices, such as entering a religious order or something similar; and when his intellect is illuminated by the light of an angel to do those very things, and his will is inclined by divine operation to follow through, such a person is said to "prosper well." Or likewise, when someone is inclined toward some art or toward practicing something useful. On the contrary, he will be called "ill-fated" <note>original: "male fortunatus"</note> when his choice is inclined toward the opposite by higher causes.

Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher</note> speaks of these opinions and many others in the *Summa Contra Gentiles*, book three, and in many other places, explaining how it differs to say someone is "well-born" or "ill-born," "well-fated" or "ill-fated," and "well-governed" or "well-guarded." Because of the disposition left by a celestial body, someone is said to be well-born or ill-born, and likewise well-fated. But according to how one is illuminated by an angel, one is said to be well-guarded (and not poorly, if one follows those illuminations). But according to how one is directed by God toward a good end, one is said to be "well-governed." However, these choices do not have a place here, because we do not intend to focus on them as much as on the preservation from the infliction of witchcraft. Concerning which, let it suffice for the present, as we move on to the ceremonies which are practiced by them <note>the witches</note>. And first: by what modes they allure the innocent to their perfidy <note>a "betrayal of faith," specifically the renunciation of Christianity</note>.

...[is accustomed] through weariness from the troublesome loss of temporal goods. For as Saint Gregory says: "The Devil frequently tempts so that he may at least conquer through weariness." Understand this, however, to be within the strength of the tempted person; and regarding divine permission, explain that God permits it so that men do not grow sluggish with sloth. In a figure of this, Judges 2 says: "God did not destroy these nations so that He might instruct Israel through them." <note>Judges 2:21–22</note>. This refers to the neighboring nations of the Canaanites, Jebusites, and others. And now the <term>Hussites</term> <note>Followers of the reformer Jan Hus, who were considered heretics by the Church at this time</note> and other heretics are permitted because they cannot be fully destroyed. In the same way, demons, through witches, afflict neighbors and innocent people with such great losses in their worldly goods that, as if coerced, they are driven first to implore the help of witches and finally to submit themselves to their advice.

Experience has often taught us this. We knew an innkeeper in the Diocese of **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustensi"</note> who lost fourteen horses in succession within a single year. His wife, overcome by weariness, consulted witches; and following their advice—which was certainly not wholesome—she preserved from further spells the other horses her husband had bought, as he was a carrier by trade. Finally, how many women have complained to us while we were performing the office of the **Inquisition**? They reported that when they had consulted suspected witches regarding losses to their cows—such as the deprivation of milk—and other harms to their beasts of burden, they had even received offered remedies, provided they were willing to promise something to a certain spirit. And when these women asked what they ought to promise, the response was that it was a small matter, provided they agreed to follow the instructions of that master <note>the demon</note> regarding certain observances to be performed during the time of divine services in church, or by keeping certain things silent during their confessions to priests.

It should be noted here that, as touched upon above, that "artificer of a thousand deceits" <note>the Devil</note> begins with very small and few things: such as spitting on the ground during the elevation of Christ's Body <note>the Host during Mass</note>, or closing their eyes, or uttering certain useless words. We knew a woman who still survives, protected by the secular arm <note>civil authorities</note>, who, during the solemnities of the Mass,

<column-break/>

when the priest greets the people saying, "The Lord be with you," she always adds in the common tongue: "Turn my tongue around in my backside" <note>original: "ker mir die zung im arsz vmb"</note>. Or they might utter similar things in confession after absolution has been given; or they never confess fully, especially mortal sins. And thus, they are led little by little to a total denial of the faith and a sacrilegious profession. This method, or any similar one, is observed by witches toward honorable matrons who are less given to carnal vices but more eager for earthly comforts. But toward young girls more given to ambition and the pleasures of the body, they observe another method: namely, through carnal desires and bodily pleasures.

You should note that just as the Devil's intention and desire to tempt the good is greater than his desire to tempt the evil—although on the part of the tempted, he tempts the evil more than the good—that is to say, a greater capacity is found in the evil for receiving the demon's temptation than is found in the good. Thus, the Devil also tries more to seduce the holier virgins and girls; for which there is plenty of experience and also reason. For since he already possesses the evil but not the good, he therefore tries harder to seduce the just (whom he does not have) into his dominion than those evil ones he already possesses. Just as any earthly prince rises up more against someone who takes away more of his rights than against others who do not oppose him.

**Experience**: For in the town of **Ravensburg**, out of two women who were burned to ashes—as will also be shown below where the method they use to stir up storms is discussed—one of them, a bath-woman, among other things she had confessed, also recounted this: she had suffered many injuries from the Devil because she was supposed to seduce a certain devout virgin—the daughter of a very wealthy man whom it is not necessary to name, since she too is now deceased, Divine Mercy having disposed that malice should not corrupt her heart—in such a way that on a festive...

...on a certain day, she might invite him so that the <term>demon</term> <note>Latin: *demon*; in this context, a fallen angel or malevolent spirit</note> himself, in the form of a young man, could hold conversations with her. There is another virgin living in the **Diocese of Strasbourg** <note>Latin: "diocesi argentinensi"</note> who, having confessed to one of our brothers, asserted that one Sunday, while she was walking alone in her father's house, a certain old woman of that town came to visit her. Among other scurrilous words she uttered, she finally suggested that if the girl liked, she would lead her to a place where young men, unknown to any of the townspeople, were staying.

The girl said, "When I had given my consent and followed her to the house, the old woman added: 'Behold, we shall ascend the stairs to the upper chamber where the young men stay, but take care not to arm yourself with the **sign of the cross**.'"

The girl continued: "Because I had told her I would do as she said, while she went ahead and I followed up the stairs, I secretly armed myself with the sign of the cross. Thus it happened that when we were both at the top of the stairs and in front of the room, that old woman, with a **horrible face** and an angry soul, turned and looked at me, saying: 'Behold, cursed one, why have you signed yourself with the cross? Depart from here in the name of the devil!' And so I returned to my own home unharmed."

From this, one can gather with what crafts that ancient enemy rages for the seduction of souls. Finally, the aforementioned **bathhouse attendant**, who was **burned** <note>Latin: "incinerata"; she was executed by fire following a witchcraft trial.</note>, asserted in this manner that she had been seduced by another old woman. However, her companion was seduced in a different way: she had found a demon on the road in human form while she was intending to visit her lover for the sake of fornication. When she was recognized by the disguised demon and asked if she knew him, she asserted she did not know him at all. He replied: "I am a demon, and if you wish, I will always be ready at your pleasure,

<column-break/>

nor will I desert you in any necessities." When she had assented to this, she served those **diabolical filthinesses** for eighteen years—right up to the end of her life—along with a total denial of the faith.

And there is a **third way** of enticing people through the path of sadness and poverty. For when young girls are corrupted and then rejected by the lovers to whom they had immodestly joined themselves based on promises of marriage, and they find themselves frustrated in all hope and considered infamous on every side, they turn to any diabolical perfidy. They plot either for the sake of **revenge** by **bewitching** <note>Latin: "maleficiando"; casting a harmful spell or curse</note> that lover or the woman he eventually married, or by submitting themselves to all manner of filthiness.

Just as the number of such young girls is countless, as easy experience teaches, so too is the number of **witches** rising from among them. Let us relate a few examples from many. There is a place in the **Diocese of Basel** <note>Latin: "diocesi Bazin," likely referring to Basiliensis</note> where a young man told of such a case regarding his **bewitched wife**. 

He said: "In the time of my youth, I loved a certain woman. While she constantly insisted that I should join her in marriage, I despised her and married another woman from a different lordship. However, wishing to please her out of friendship, I invited her to the wedding."

When she arrived, while the other honest women presented their wedding gifts or offerings, this invited woman, lifting her hand in the hearing of the other women standing around, said: "**You will have few healthy days after this day.**" 

The bride was terrified. Since she did not know the woman—having been married from another lordship as mentioned before—she asked those standing by who it was who had uttered such threats. The others affirmed that she was a wandering and dissolute woman. Nevertheless, what she predicted followed exactly in that order. For after a few days, the bride was so **bewitched** and deprived of the use of all her limbs that even to the present day, after more than ten years, the effects of the witchcraft are visible in her body...

For a certain Count, of noble lineage from the territory of **Westrania** <note>Latin: *Westraniensis*; likely referring to a district in the Alsace or Rhine region.</note> near the borders of the **Diocese of Strasbourg**, married a young woman of similarly noble birth. However, after the wedding was celebrated, he was unable to know her carnally <note>A common euphemistic phrase for sexual intercourse.</note> for three years, as he was hindered by a **bewitchment** <term>maleficiali impedimento</term> <note>Specifically, an "impediment of witchcraft," which theologians believed could cause physical impotence through demonic interference.</note>, as the outcome of the matter proved. Anxious and not knowing what to do, and continually calling upon God's saints, it happened that he traveled to the city of **Metz** <note>An important city in the Lorraine region of France.</note> to settle certain business matters. 

While he was walking through the streets and squares there, surrounded by his servants and household, he encountered a certain woman who had been his concubine in the years prior. Upon seeing her, while thinking very little of the witchcraft inflicted upon him, he unexpectedly spoke to her kindly out of their old friendship, and asked how she was doing and if she was well. She, seeing the Count’s kindness, in turn inquired diligently about the health of his body and his status. 

When he responded that everything was going well and prosperously for him, she stood astonished and silent for a moment. Seeing her astonishment, the Count approached her with more kind words, inviting her to a conversation. When she asked about the state of his wife, he gave a similar answer: that she was doing well in all things. Then she asked if they had fathered any children. The Count said, "I have three male children; she has borne one every year." At this, she was even more stunned and fell silent for a short while. 

The Count said: "I ask you, dearest, tell me why you inquire so diligently? For I do not doubt that you congratulate me on my happiness." Then she said: "Truly I do congratulate you; but cursed be that old woman who offered to **bewitch** <note>Latin: *maleficiare*</note> your body so that you would be unable to perform the carnal act with your wife. As a sign of this, 

<column-break/>

the well which is in the middle of your courtyard contains at the bottom a pot holding certain **witchcraft items** <note>Latin: *res maleficiales*; these were often physical objects like bones, hair, or herbs used as a focus for a curse.</note>. It was placed there for this reason: that as long as it remained there, you would suffer from impotence. But behold, all these things are in vain, for which I am glad," etc. 

The Count did not delay; having returned home, he had the well drained. He found the pot, and by burning everything, he suddenly recovered that lost power. Wherefore, the Count once again invited all the nobles to a new wedding feast, declaring that she was now the mistress of that castle and domain, who had remained a virgin for so long. For the sake of the Count's honor, it is not expedient to name the castle and domain; for right reason persuades us of this, so that the substance of the fact may be revealed for the detestation of such a great crime. 

From these things, the various methods used by **witches** <note>Latin: *maleficis*</note> to increase their perfidy are made plain. For the aforementioned woman—because she had been expelled by the Count's wife—had inflicted this witchcraft upon the Count based on the instruction of another witch. For this reason, innumerable witchcraft effects follow.

### Chapter II

The manner of the **sacrilegious profession** <note>This refers to the formal oath or "profession" of faith made to the devil, mimicking a religious vow.</note> based on an express pact of loyalty with demons is varied, just as the witches themselves persist in various practices regarding the infliction of witchcraft. To understand this, it must first be noted that just as there appear to be three kinds of witches in general (as touched upon in the first part of this treatise)—namely, those who harm but are unable to heal; those who heal and, by some singular pact entered into with a demon, do not harm; and those who both harm and heal—so also among those who harm, there exists one supreme type. Those within this class are able to perpetrate all the other witchcrafts that the others perform sporadically. Wherefore...

And this is the **supreme species** <note>The highest or most extreme category of witches according to the authors' hierarchy of evil.</note> in the practice of sorcery. They can strike a great trembling into the hands and minds of those who capture them. They reveal hidden things to others and predict certain future events based on the information of demons—specifically those which can have a natural cause. See the question of whether demons are able to foreknow the future in the **second book of the Sentences, distinction VII** <note>Referring to Peter Lombard's "Sentences," the standard university textbook for medieval theology.</note>. They can see absent things as if they were present; change the minds of men to inordinate love or hatred; and occasionally kill whom they wish, or even other men and cattle, by a stroke of lightning. They take away the **generative power** <note>The ability to conceive or father children.</note> or even the power of sexual intercourse; procure abortions; and kill infants in the mother's womb by a mere external touch. Sometimes, by sight alone without touch, they bewitch men and cattle and bring about death. They dedicate their own infants to demons and, in short, perform all those pestilential acts that other witches are known to procure separately, whenever God's justice permits such things to happen. Those existing in that supreme class know how to perpetrate all these things, but not vice-versa. This, however,

Therefore, through their manner of initiation, those in the supreme class can easily grasp the methods of other witches. Such people existed in the territories of **Savoy** <note>original: "subaudie"</note> toward the domain of the **Bernese** <note>The people of Bern, Switzerland.</note> about thirty years ago, as **Nider** recounts in his **Formicarius** <note>Johannes Nider’s "The Anthill," an early and influential work on witchcraft written in the 1430s.</note>. Now, however, they are in the borders of **Lombardy** toward the domain of the Duke of Austria, where the **Inquisitor of Como** <note>original: "inq̃sitoꝛ cumanꝰ"</note>—as was mentioned in the preceding part—caused **forty-one witches to be burned** <note>original: "incinerari"; literally "to be turned to ashes."</note> in a single year. That was the year of our Lord 1485, and he still continues to labor in his inquiry. Now, the manner of initiation is twofold. One is **solemn**, through a vow made in a formal ceremony. The other is **private**, which can be done at any hour for the demon. The solemn ceremony takes place among them where the witches come to a certain assembly on a fixed day and see the demon in the assumed shape of a man. While he exhorts them to keep faith with him, promising earthly prosperity and long life, those who are present recommend the **novice** who is to be received. And if the demon finds the novice or disciple willing—once they have renounced the faith and the most Christian worship, and the **Woman of the Height** <note>original: "extensa muliere"; a derogatory or coded demonic reference to the Virgin Mary.</note> (for so they call the most Blessed Virgin Mary), and once they have sworn never to venerate the sacraments—then the demon extends his hand, and in turn, the disciple or novice, with hand grasped, promises to keep these things. And once these promises are made, the demon immediately adds that these are not enough. And when the disciple asks what more must be done, the demon seeks **homage** <note>A feudal term for a vassal's pledge of submission to a lord.</note>, which consists of the disciple belonging to him eternally in soul and body, and desiring to bring as many others of both sexes as possible into his association. Finally, he adds that they must prepare certain **ointments** from the bones and limbs of children—especially those reborn at the baptismal font—through which, with his assistance, they will be able to fulfill all their desires. We Inquisitors have learned of this manner through the evidence of experience in the town of **Battenheim** <note>original: "Basiaco"; likely Battenheim in the Diocese of Basel.</note> in the Diocese of Basel, by taking full information from a young girl who was a witch but had converted; her maternal aunt had also been burned in the **Diocese of Strasbourg**.

She added that the manner by which her **maternal aunt** <note>original: "matertera"</note> had first tried to seduce her was as follows. She also asserted that she had often been transported over long distances of land at night, even from **Strasbourg** <note>original: "argentina"</note> all the way to **Cologne**. This is the case through which we promised in the first question to declare whether witches are truly and bodily transported from place to place by demons. She reported many other things after taking an oath to tell the truth, just as she had recounted. Finally, her words regarding the manner of her profession were granted indubitable faith, even through those things which the distinguished doctor **Johannes Nider** <note>A 15th-century theologian whose work "Formicarius" (The Anthill) was a major source for the Malleus Maleficarum.</note> recites in his *Formicarius*. He was famous in our times for his wonderful writings, and he based this on the report of the **Inquisitor of the Diocese of Autun** <note>original: "inquisitoris edvensis"</note>, who had investigated many accused of sorcery in that diocese and had them burned. For he says: "I learned from the report of the aforementioned inquisitor that in the **Duchy of Lausanne** <note>A region in modern-day Switzerland.</note>, certain witches had snatched and eaten newborn infants."

<column-break/>

The manner of learning such an art was, as he said, that the witches came together in a certain assembly, and through their work, they likely saw a demon in the assumed image of a man. The disciple was required to give his word to renounce **Christianity** <note>original: "christianismo"</note>, never to adore the **Eucharist** <note>The consecrated bread used in the Catholic Mass.</note>, and to trample upon the cross whenever he could do so secretly. Another example from the same source follows. There was, moreover, a common report from **Peter, the judge in Boltigen** <note>original: "petro iudice in boltingen"</note>, reporting that in the land of the Bernese, thirteen infants had been devoured by witches, for which reason public justice had burned quite harshly against such murderers. When Peter asked a certain captured witch in what manner they ate infants, she responded: "This is the way. For we especially lie in wait for infants who are not yet baptized, or even baptized ones, especially when they are not fortified by the **sign of the cross** <margin>note</margin> and prayers." Reader, take note that they especially lie in wait for the unbaptized by the instinct of the devil so that they may not be baptized. She continued: "We kill them in their cradles or lying at the sides of their parents by our ceremonies. After people think they have been smothered or died of other causes, we secretly steal them from their graves and cook them in a **cauldron** <note>original: "caldaria"</note> until all the flesh is pulled from the bones and becomes almost drinkable. From the more solid matter, we make an **ointment** <note>original: "vnguentum"</note> suitable for our desires, arts, and transportations. ## Regarding the declaration of homage to be performed, some things are to be noted.

<gloss>Note: how homage is performed <unclear>by the witches</unclear></gloss>

Concerning this point that the **Devil** receives homage, some things are to be noted: namely, for what reason and in what different ways he does this. And first: for although he does this principally for the sake of the greater offense to the **Divine Majesty**—by usurping for himself a creature dedicated to God and for the greater certainty of that person's future damnation, which he most greatly desires—yet it has often been found by us that he has accepted such homage for a certain number of years along with the profession of faith. Sometimes he has deferred the profession and homage for a certain term of years. 

And let us say that the **profession** <note>A formal declaration of loyalty or faith.</note> consists in a total or partial **renunciation of the faith**. It is **Total**, as was touched upon above, when the faith is renounced in its entirety. It is **Partial** when, by an entered pact, one has to observe certain ceremonies against the statutes of the Church: such as **fasting on Sundays**, or **eating meat on Fridays**, or concealing certain crimes in **confession**, or perpetrating something similar. 

But let us say that **homage** consists in the surrender of body and soul. For which reason such things are practiced, we can assign four causes on the part of the demon. For since, as was declared above in the first part of the treatise regarding the second principal point—whether demons can change the minds of men toward hate or love—it was clear that they cannot penetrate the **secrets of the heart**, since this belongs to God alone. And yet they come to a knowledge of them through conjectures, as will also be clear below. 

Therefore, that crafty enemy, if he considers a novice to be difficult to bring to consent at the start, then he approaches them mildly, requiring little, so that he might lead them gradually to greater things. **The second cause**: For since among those renouncing the faith a diversity of belief is to be found—some doing so with the mouth but not the heart, and some with both mouth and heart—the Devil, wishing to test whether one professes to him with the heart as with the mouth, grants a term of years so that in that time he may investigate the person's mind through their works and conversation. **The third cause**: For if during such a space of time he should recognize that she is less willing to execute whatever he commands and that she adheres to him now with the mouth and not the heart, and he presumes that divine mercy will be shown to her on account of the protection of a **good angel**, which the demon can experience in many...

A demon conjectures what is or will be in the soul more astutely than even a wise man. For they know, by instinct, what actions are likely to follow and, consequently, what kind of works will result. Eighth, they know the acts and writings of the prophets better than humans do, and many future events depend upon those writings. Therefore, they can predict many future things from them. This is also noted in canon law <note>original: "xxvi.q.iiij. sciendum"; referring to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of Church law, specifically Case 26, Question 4.</note>. Hence, it is no wonder if a demon can know a person’s **natural lifespan** <note>original: "periodum hominis... naturalē"</note>, although it is different regarding an "accidental" end, such as being **burned to ashes** <note>original: "incinerationem"</note>, which the demon ultimately procures. As has been said, the demon does this when he finds his victims are becoming involuntary and fears their return to the faith and conversion; yet, he defends others whom he knows are voluntary in their service until their natural death. Let us give examples of both cases which we have discovered and recorded.

In the diocese of Basel, in a village situated above the Rhine named **Oberwil** <note>original: "oberwyler"</note>, there was a **parish priest** <note>original: "plebanum"</note> of honest conversation. He was, however, of the opinion—or rather the error—that **witchcraft** <term>maleficium: harmful magic or sorcery</term> was nothing in the world but existed only in the opinion of men who attributed such effects to poor women. God wished to purge him of his error in such a way that the other dealings of demons regarding the pre-fixed end of a witch's life might be made clear. 

While he was hurrying to cross a bridge to expedite some business, he encountered a certain old woman with similar urgency. When he would not give way to her at the entrance of the bridge, but continued forward unyielding, he accidentally pushed the old woman into the mud. Indignant, she broke out into insulting words and said to him: "**Priest** <note>original: "pfaff"; a German term for priest, often used here with a sharp or disrespectful tone.</note>, you shall not pass unpunished!" Although he paid little attention to her words, that night, while he was trying to get out of bed, he felt himself **bewitched** <note>original: "maleficiatuʒ"</note> from the waist down. He became so debilitated that he always had to be supported by the arms of others when he wished to visit the church. He remained in this state for three years, under the domestic care of his biological mother. When this time had passed, the old woman fell ill. Because of the insulting words and threats she had made, the priest had always 

<column-break/>

suspected her of the witchcraft inflicted upon him. It happened that, as she grew weaker, she sent for him to hear her confession. The priest said, though perhaps harshly, "Let her confess to the devil, her master!" However, at the insistence of his mother, he went to her, supported between the arms of two villagers, and sat at the head of the bed where the witch lay. 

The two villagers wanted to eavesdrop from outside near the window—for the room was situated on the ground floor—to hear if she would confess to the witchcraft inflicted on the priest. It happened that, although she made no mention of the witchcraft during the formal confession, once the confession was finished, she said: "Do you know, **priest** <note>original: "pfaff"</note>, who bewitched you?" When he gently replied that he did not know, she added: "You suspect me, and rightly so. Know that I brought this upon you for the reason mentioned before." When he urged her to release him, she said: "Behold, the appointed time has arrived and I must die; but I will arrange it so that a few days after my death, you will be healed." And so it happened. For she died at the time set by the demon, and within thirty days, the priest found himself entirely healed one night. The name of the priest is said to be Priest Heflin.

A similar thing happened in the diocese of Strasbourg <note>original: "argentinensi"</note>, and also in the diocese of Basel in the village of **Bühl** <note>original: "buhel"</note> near the town of **Guebwiller** <note>original: "gewiler"</note>. A certain woman was captured and finally **burned to ashes** <note>original: "incinerata"</note>. For six years she had kept an **incubus** <term>incubum demonem: a male demon believed to have sexual relations with women</term> demon, even while her husband slept beside her in the bed. This occurred three times a week: on Saturdays, Thursdays, and Tuesdays, or on other holier nights. She had offered such **homage** to the devil that after the seventh year, she would be perpetually dedicated to him in body and soul. 

However, God intervened. For in the sixth year, she was captured and sentenced to the fire. Having truly and fully confessed, it is believed she received mercy from God. For she was very much willing to face death, asserting that even if she could be freed, she would rather choose death provided she could escape the power of the demon.

# Concerning the manner in which they are locally transported from place to place.
## Chapter III

Now we must approach their ceremonies and the methods by which they proceed in their works. And first, concerning those things they perform upon themselves and their own persons. And because being transported from place to place corporally is one of their principal carnal actions—along with insisting on filthy lusts with **incubus** <note>A demon in male form who seeks to have sexual intercourse with women.</note> demons—we will deduce something about each. And first, about their corporal transportation. Where it should be noted that this transportation suffers from a difficulty—as has been frequently touched upon—from one particular passage of scripture, namely, *Canon 26, Question 5, Episcopi* <note>original: "xxvi.q.v.Episcopi"; referring to the 'Canon Episcopi,' a 10th-century legal text that was central to the medieval debate on witchcraft. It claimed that women who believed they flew with Diana were suffering from delusions.</note>. Where it is said from the Council of Ancyra: It must not be omitted that certain wicked women, having turned back after **Satan** <note>original: "sathan"</note> and being seduced by the illusions and phantasms of demons, believe and profess that during the night hours they ride upon certain beasts with **Diana** <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, often associated with the moon and night.</note>, the goddess of the pagans, or with **Herodias** <note>original: "herodiade"; the biblical figure responsible for the death of John the Baptist, often linked in medieval folklore with Diana as a leader of the "night-ride."</note> and an innumerable multitude of women, and cross many spans of the earth in the silence of the dead of night, and obey her as their mistress in all things, etc. Therefore, the priests of God ought to preach to the people so they may know these things are entirely false, and that such phantasms are not from a divine spirit but are inflicted upon the minds of the faithful by a malignant spirit. Indeed, **Satan** himself transforms himself into the likeness and appearance of various persons, and by deluding the mind which he holds captive in sleep, he leads it through vain things, etc. And for this purpose, examples are sometimes publicly preached by some concerning **Saint Germanus** <note>A 5th-century bishop of Auxerre; legends about him included exposing "night-visitors" as demons.</note> and another who watched over his daughter regarding this, as if it were entirely impossible for these things to happen. And these examples are indiscreetly applied to **witches** <term>maleficas: women who practice harmful magic</term> and their works, as if individual acts of theirs—such as the injuring of humans, cattle, and the fruits of the earth—should not be attributed to them, because, just as they are deluded in their transportations, so too are they deluded regarding the injuries to creatures.

<column-break/>

This opinion, since it was condemned as heretical in the first question—as it works against the divine permission regarding the power of the devil, which can extend to greater things than this—similarly militates against the intention of **Sacred Scripture** <note>The Bible.</note>, etc., to the intolerable damage of the Holy Church. For many years now, they have remained unpunished because of this pestiferous opinion, which cuts off the ability of the **secular arm** <note>The civil or government authorities responsible for physical punishment, as the Church could not shed blood.</note> to punish them. Hence, they have grown so immensely that it is no longer possible to eradicate them. Therefore, the diligent reader will consider what was stated there for the destruction of that opinion, and for now, will observe how they are transported and in what ways this is possible, with responses to the examples they bring forward. That they can, therefore, be corporally transported is shown in various ways. And first, from other operations of magi. For if they could not be transported, it would be either because God would not permit it, or because the devil could not do it because the creature [human nature] would resist it. Not the first, because greater and lesser things can certainly be done by God's permission. And greater things, both in children and in men, have very often been done, even to the just and those established in grace, as is clear. <margin>On how changelings are made by God's permission.</margin> For where they ask whether **changelings** <term>camphiones puerorum: literally "champions of children," here meaning infants swapped by demons</term> can be made by the work of demons, and whether a demon can locally transport a person from place to place even against their will—to the first, they respond that it is so. Such children are always miserable and wailing; and although four or five mothers would scarcely suffice to nurse them, they never grow fat, but are heavy beyond measure. However, because of the great terror women might conceive, these things should neither be affirmed nor denied; they should be instructed to seek the judgments of the learned. He <note>Likely referring to a specific theologian or a scriptural gloss mentioned previously.</note> means to say that they do not only besiege, but indeed horribly torture, such as those who are described in the Gospel of **Matthew 8**. <note>original: "Mat. viij."; refers to the story of the Gerasene demoniacs and the herd of swine.</note> From these things we can conclude, first, that it should not be said that witches are not locally <term>localiter: physically moved from one place to another.</term> transported on the grounds that God would not permit it. For if He permits it over the righteous and innocent, or even over magicians or other wanderers, how would He not permit it over those who devote themselves entirely to the devil? Let us speak with fear: Did not the devil lift up our Savior, lead him, and set him here and there, as the Gospel testifies? <note>original: "euangelium testatur"; referring to the Temptation of Christ in the wilderness (Matthew 4, Luke 4).</note> Nor can it be denied according to the arguments of opponents, as if the devil were unable to do this; for as was evident in the aforementioned things, so much natural power <note>original: "virtus naturalis"</note> is in him, exceeding all bodily things, that no earthly power can be compared to him. According to that scripture: **There is no power upon earth, etc.** <note>original: "Non est potestas super terram &c."; quoting Job 41:33 (Vulgate 41:24).</note> Indeed, in **Lucifer** himself there is such natural power or virtue that no greater exists even among the good angels in heaven. For just as he exceeded all angels in natural gifts, these natural gifts were not diminished by his Fall, but only the gifts of grace were lost. Therefore, these powers still remain in him, though darkened and bound. Whence the gloss on that passage, **There is no power upon earth, etc.**, says: "And if he surpasses all things, yet by his merits he is subject to the saints." <note>An explanation that while the devil's natural power is supreme among creatures, the spiritual 'merit' of a holy person can overcome him.</note> Nor is it valid if someone were to object with two points: First, that the human soul could resist; and second, that the text seems to speak of one individual, namely Lucifer, since it speaks in the singular. And because it was he who tempted Christ in the desert and seduced the first man, but is now bound, and other angels are not of such great power since he exceeds them all.

¶ Therefore [they argue] other evil men cannot be locally transported through the air. These objections do not hold. First, let us speak of the angels. Even the least angel incomparably exceeds all human power. Reasons are taken from several points. First, because spiritual power is stronger than bodily power, just as the power of an angel or even of the soul is superior to bodily power. Second, regarding the soul: Since every bodily form

<column-break/>

is a form individualized by matter and determined by "here and now," <note>original: "hic et nunc"; a standard scholastic phrase referring to the specific physical presence of an object.</note> just as our soul currently consists. However, immaterial forms are absolute and intelligible. Whence they also have absolute and more universal power. Therefore, the soul when "joined" <note>original: "anima cōiuncta"; referring to the soul while it is united with the living body.</note> cannot so suddenly transport its body locally nor raise it on high. But it would certainly do so when it were separated [from the body], God permitting; all of which a spirit that is entirely immaterial—such as an angel, whether good or bad—can do with even greater force. Just as the good angel also transported **Habakkuk** in a moment from Judea to Chaldea. <note>original: "abacuc"; referring to the story in the deuterocanonical portion of Daniel (Daniel 14:33–36), where an angel carries the prophet by the hair to Babylon.</note> And for this reason, it is also concluded that those who are carried through high buildings at night in their sleep <note>A 15th-century explanation for sleepwalking.</note> are not carried by their own souls, nor by the influences of the celestial bodies, but by some more excellent power, as was shown above. Third, that bodily nature is thus born to be moved immediately by spiritual nature according to place; both because local motion is the "first of motions" according to the eighth book of **Physics**, <note>original: "viij. phi."; referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book 8.</note> and because it is the most perfect among all bodily motions, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> proves there by this reason: because a thing moved according to place is not in potentiality to anything intrinsic, but only to something extrinsic. Whence it is concluded not only by the holy doctors but also by the philosophers that the supreme bodies—namely the celestial ones—are moved by spiritual and separate substances, which are good by both nature and will. Also, because we see that the soul primarily and principally moves the body with local motion. Therefore, it must be said that neither the condition of the human body nor that of the soul prevents either from being moved suddenly, God permitting, from place to place by a spiritual substance. This substance is good by both will and nature when the righteous established in grace are transported; or it is good by nature but not by will when the wicked are transported. As it pleases **Saint Thomas** to see in the First Part, question 110, through the three articles there, or even in his *Questions on Evil*, or in his commentary on the *Second Book of Sentences*. <note>original: "sanctum tho... in .ij. senten."; referring to Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa Theologica*, *De Malo*, and *Scriptum super Libros Sententiarum*.</note>

## Distinction 8: On the power of demons over bodily effects.

The method of transportation is as follows. As has been shown in the preceding sections, they are accustomed to manufacture an ointment from the limbs of children—especially those they have killed before baptism. At the instruction of a demon, they smear a seat or a piece of wood with this ointment, and once this is done, they are immediately carried into the air. This occurs either by day or by night, and they may be visible or, if they wish, invisible. This is because a demon can hide a body by placing another body as an obstacle in front of it, as was explained in the first part of this treatise regarding the deceptive appearance of the works of demons. <note>original: "prestigiosa apparitione"; referring to the demonic ability to create illusions or "prestiges" that trick the human eye.</note> Truly, although a demon usually employs such an ointment for this purpose—primarily so that he may deprive infants of the grace of baptism and salvation—he has nevertheless been seen to achieve this many times without such aids. In these cases, they are transported by animals which are not true animals, but demons existing under those forms; or sometimes they are transported solely by the power of a demon operating invisibly without any external assistance.

The following is an account of a visible and daytime transportation. 
<margin>Example</margin>
In the town of **Waldshut** <note>A town in modern-day Germany on the Rhine river.</note> on the Rhine river in the Diocese of **Constance**, there was a certain witch who was greatly hated by the townsfolk. She had not been invited to a celebration for a certain wedding, even though almost all the other townspeople were present. Indignant and seeking to avenge herself, she summoned a demon and opened to him the cause of her sorrow. She petitioned that he might stir up a hailstorm to scatter everyone from the wedding dance. The demon agreed and lifted her up, transporting her through the air to a mountain near the town in the sight of certain shepherds. As she later confessed, when she lacked water to pour into a pit—a method they observe when they wish to stir up hailstorms, as will be shown later—she put urine in place of water into a small hole she had made. With the demon standing by, she stirred it with her finger according to her custom. The demon suddenly raised that liquid upward and sent a violent hailstorm consisting of stones falling only upon the dancers and the townspeople. When these people had been scat-

<column-break/>

-tered and were conferring with one another about the cause of the storm, the witch entered the town, which made their suspicions even heavier. But when the shepherds recounted what they had seen, their strong suspicion grew into a violent certainty. Consequently, she was captured and confessed that she had committed these acts because she had not been invited; for this and many other crimes she had committed, she was reduced to ashes. <term>incinerata: a legal term for being burned at the stake, the standard punishment for witchcraft in this period.</term>

And because public reports of this kind of transportation are constantly circulating even among common people, it is not necessary to insert more accounts here to prove the point. Let these suffice against those who either entirely deny these physical transportations or who attempt to affirm that they occur only in the imagination and as a fantasy. Indeed, if they were left alone in their error, it would be a small matter; one might not even need to take notice of them, provided their error did not tend toward an insult to the Faith. However, we must take notice because, not content with that error, they strive to insert and publish others to the increase of witchcraft and the detriment of the Faith. They assert that all the crimes of witches—which are truly and realistically imputed to them as the instruments of demons—should only be imputed to them as imaginary and illusory things, just like their "fantastic" transportation, as if they were harmless. Because of this view, many have repeatedly remained unpunished, to the great insult of the Creator and the now-grievous increase of the witches themselves.

Nor can the arguments they bring forward from the beginning support them. For first, when they allege 
<margin>Canon Episcopi, Case 26, Question 5</margin>
the chapter of the **Bishop** <note>original: "capitulum episcopi"; refers to the *Canon Episcopi*, a 10th-century legal text that was the primary source for those arguing that witchcraft was merely a delusion.</note> (Case 26, Question 5), where it is asserted that they are only transported in fantasy and imagination, who is so foolish as to conclude from this that they cannot *also* be physically transported? For just as it is stated at the end of that chapter: "he who believes that a human being can be changed for better or for worse, or transformed into another species, is to be judged worse than an infidel and a pagan"—who could conclude from this that humans cannot be transformed into beasts by a deceptive illusion, or even from health into sickness (as if from a better state to a worse)?

### Chapter IV

witches <note>original: "malefice"; specifically female witches.</note> submit themselves to

First, regarding the material and quality of the assumed body: it must be said that he assumes an aerial body, which is in some way earthly insofar as it possesses the property of earth through condensation. This is explained as follows: Because air
