In its own nature, air cannot take a specific shape unless it is contained within the boundaries of another body in which it is enclosed. Therefore, it is not limited by its own borders, but only by those of something else, and one part of the air is continuous with another. Thus, strictly speaking, a demon cannot assume an **aereal body** <term>corpus aereum: a body made of air, a common concept in medieval demonology to explain how spirits appear to humans</term> in its simple state. However, it must be noted that air is highly changeable and can be transformed into anything. A sign of this is that certain people, attempting to cut or pierce a body assumed by a demon with a sword, were unable to do so, because the parts of the divided air immediately joined back together again. 

Therefore, it is clear that air is, in itself, a suitable material. But because it cannot be shaped unless some other terrestrial element is added to it, it is necessary that the air be **thickened** <note>original: "inspissatus"; meaning condensed or made more dense</note> in some way, approaching the properties of earth, while still maintaining the true nature of air. Demons and departed souls can perform this condensation using thick vapors raised from the earth, and through their **local motion** <term>motus localis: the ability of a spirit to move physical objects or matter from one place to another</term>, gathering and shaping them. In these bodies, the demons remain only as **movers** <note>original: "motores"; they act like a pilot, rather than a biological soul</note> and not as **informers** <note>original: "informatores"; in medieval philosophy, the soul "informs" the body, giving it life and essence. A demon does not give the air-body "life" in this way.</note> who formally provide life to that body, as the soul provides life to a joined body. They are in their assumed and shaped bodies just like a **sailor in a ship** that he moves. 

Therefore, when it is asked what kind of material the body assumed by a demon is, it must be said that it is one thing to speak of it at the beginning of the assumption, and another at its completion. At the beginning, it is air. At the completion, it is **thickened air** approaching the properties of earth. Demons can do all these things, with God’s permission, by their nature, since spiritual nature is superior to corporal nature. Hence, corporal nature must obey the spiritual in regards to local motion—though not in regards to receiving natural forms (either accidental or substantial), except perhaps in some small creatures, and this only with the help of some other agent, as was touched upon above. Through local motion, no form is placed 

<column-break/>

in distant things. Thus, they can move things at their will when other circumstances are met. 

If someone were to ask incidentally what should be thought when a good or evil angel performs the works of life through true, natural bodies (not aereal ones)—such as in **Balaam's donkey** <note>Referencing the biblical story in Numbers 22:28, where an angel causes a donkey to speak.</note> through which an angel spoke, or where demons agitate the bodies of those who are **possessed**—it must be said that those bodies are not called "assumed," but merely **occupied**. One should look at the sayings of the Doctors in the second book, eighth distinction, on whether angels assume bodies. 

But let us stay on our subject. Demons in assumed bodies speak, see, hear, eat, and procreate with witches. How these things are to be understood is the second part of this primary difficulty. Regarding the first point, it must be said that for **true speech**, three things are required. First, the lungs, along with the drawing in of air, which is not only for the sake of the voice but also for the cooling of the heart (this is why even the mute have this necessary inhalation). Secondly, it is required that a sound be formed from the striking of a body in the air, just as when someone strikes the air with a piece of wood, or a bell makes a sound, whether great or small; because the material is in itself capable of sound, and when it is struck with a sounding instrument, a sound is produced according to the size of the body, and it is received in the air and multiplied until it reaches the ears of the listener. (If the listener is far away, there is a delay in time before it arrives). Thirdly, the **voice** is required. It can be said that what is called "sound" in inanimate bodies is called "voice" in animate bodies. There, the tongue strikes the air that has been breathed in and then sent out again, using an instrument and a vessel naturally cast by the living God, which is not the case with a bell. Therefore, what is sound in a bell is called voice in a living being. This third point can be exemplified by the way preachers deliver their message to the people. Fourthly, it is required that the one who forms the voice wishes to express a **mental concept** to another through that voice so that the other may understand. Therefore, he "organizes" that voice—that is, he distinguishes it successively in the mouth by striking the tongue and teeth...

They willingly offer themselves to men under these resemblances so that they may manifest their properties, which they possess naturally—namely, seeing, hearing, and speaking spiritually—through these kinds of works. For this reason, the holy angels often appeared to the **Fathers** <note>The Patriarchs or early leaders of the Church</note> by God’s ordinance and His permission. To evil men, demons manifest themselves so that men, recognizing their properties, might associate with them—here in their faults, and elsewhere in their punishments. But as for **eating**: let us say that a complete definition of eating involves four things: the division of food in the mouth, its passage into the body, the power of the body to digest it, and fourthly, the conversion of necessary nourishment and the expulsion of the superfluous. Angels, in their assumed bodies, perform the first two when eating, but cannot do the third and fourth. Instead of digestive and expulsive power, they possess another power by which they suddenly **dissolve** the food into the surrounding matter. In Christ, there was also true eating in all respects, because He possessed the power of nutrition and conversion; however, he did not convert it into his body because those powers were **glorified** <term>glorificate: the state of the body after resurrection, perfected and no longer subject to decay</term> just as his body was, hence it was also dissolved...

## How in modern times witches perform carnal acts with **incubus** <term>incubus: a demon in male form that seeks sexual contact with women</term> demons and how they are multiplied by these.

But regarding the carnal acts which are our primary focus—those which they perform with witches as **incubi** in assumed bodies—no difficulty remains from the previous arguments, unless perhaps someone should doubt whether modern witches are actually intent on these kinds of filthiness, and whether the very origin of witches is derived from such filth. In responding to these two doubts, let us say regarding the first: whatever may have been the case with previous witches before the year of our Lord’s incarnation **1400** or thereabouts—namely, whether they were enslaved to these filthinesses as the witches of today are—is unknown. However, history has now clearly taught us through experience. For no one who travels through historical accounts can doubt that witches have always existed, and that many lessons have come to men, cattle, and the fruits of the earth from their wicked works; nor can one doubt the existence of **incubus** and **succubus** <term>succubus: a demon in female form that seeks sexual contact with men</term> demons, since the traditions of the Church laws and the holy doctors have left behind and handed down many accounts of them for hundreds of years. There is, however, this difference: in times past, **incubus** demons were hostile to young women against their will, as **Nider** <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), author of the Formicarius, an influential book on witches</note> relates in his *Fornicarius* <note>The Ant-Hill</note>, and as **Thomas of Brabant** <note>Thomas of Cantimpré (1201–1272), a Dominican monk and author of "On the Universal Good of Bees"</note> recounts in many places in his book *On the Universal Good or On Bees*. But our opinion does not adhere to this position—that modern witches are infected by these diabolical filthinesses—so much as do the proven testimonies of the witches themselves. These women have made all these things credible; they no longer submit with unwilling minds as in the past, but voluntarily subject themselves to this most foul and miserable slavery for the sake of pleasure. For however many

<column-break/>

of them were left to the **secular arm** <term>secular arm: civil authorities responsible for carrying out the physical punishment, such as execution, decreed by the Church</term> by us to be punished in various dioceses—especially in **Constance** and the town of **Ravensburg** over many years—they have clung to these filthinesses for certain periods, some for twenty, others for twelve, or others for thirty years. And always, as all the inhabitants there can testify, they did so with a renunciation of the faith, in whole or in part. For, not counting those who did secret penance and returned to the faith, no fewer than **forty-eight** were handed over to the fire in five years. Nor was faith only placed in them, but credit was given to those who voluntarily returned to penance; for they all agree on this point: that they must persist in these kinds of filthiness for the increase of this perfidy. We shall treat these cases individually in the second part of this work, where their particular deeds will be described. All things are therefore established either by sight or hearing through our own experience, or by the reports of trustworthy people. As to the second doubt, where it is questioned whether these witches themselves take their origin from these filthinesses, let us say according to **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of the Western Church</note> that it is certainly true that all superstitious arts took their origin from a "pestiferous society" of men and demons. For he says this in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine* <note>original: "de doc. xpiana"; De doctrina christiana</note>, and it is held in Case 26, Question 2, paragraph "That which is" <note>A reference to the Decretum Gratiani, the basis of medieval Canon Law</note>: "All arts of this kind, whether frivolous or harmful superstition, established from a certain pestiferous society of men and demons—as if a pact of unfaithful and deceitful friendship—are to be utterly repudiated." With this in mind, it is manifest that just as there are diverse species of superstition or magic art, so too are there diverse societies between them. And just as the species of "witchcraft" <note>original: "maleficozum" (maleficium)</note> is the worst among the fourteen species of that art—because it is not through a silent pact but an **express pact** <note>original: "pactum expressum"; a formal, spoken or written agreement with the devil</note>, and beyond this, they must offer the worship of **latria** <term>latria: supreme worship due to God alone</term> to the demons themselves through the renunciation of the faith—it is therefore also the worst in its turning away...

### Whether an **incubus** demon always approaches a witch with the release of semen.

There is also the question: "Does the infusion of semen always occur when the demon approaches the woman, etc.?" It is answered that he has a thousand ways and arts of harming, as one who from the beginning of his fall has tried to tear apart the **unity of the Church** and turn the human race away in every way. Therefore, an infallible rule cannot be given for these things, but a probable distinction can be made: namely, whether the witch is aged and sterile, or not. 

If she is, then he certainly approaches her without the release of semen, since it would be of no use, and the demon—just like nature—avoids superfluity in his works as much as possible. Or, even if she is not sterile, he may approach her for the sake of causing pleasure on the part of the witch. 

If, however, she is disposed toward pregnancy, then if he can conveniently obtain seed released from a man, he does not hesitate to approach her with it for the infection of the offspring. 

Furthermore, if anyone should ask whether semen emitted through **nocturnal pollution** <term>nocturnal pollution: a "wet dream" or involuntary nighttime emission</term> could be collected in the same way as that released through the carnal act, a probable reason can be given that it is not, although the opposite might seem true to others. For, noting that demons (as stated before) look for the generative power of the seed, and such force is more fully poured out and preserved in the seed through the carnal act, whereas seed released through nocturnal pollution is taken only from superfluous fluid and is not released with such great generative power. Therefore, it is believed that they use it less for the generation of offspring, unless perhaps the demon understands that generative force is present. But we also cannot entirely deny that a married witch might be impregnated by her husband...

# On the manner in which they are accustomed to take away the male organs.

### Chapter VII

But regarding this matter as well, that they are accustomed to take away the male organs—not indeed by stripping the human bodies of them in actual reality, but by hiding them through an illusory art <note>original: "prestigiosa arte"; refers to demonic trickery that deceives the senses without changing physical reality.</note>, as was declared above in the question touched upon—let us bring forward some accounts into the open. In the town of Ravensburg <note>original: "Rauenspurg"</note>, a certain young man had an affair with a young woman; wishing to leave her, he lost his male member—certainly through an illusory art—so that he could see or touch nothing except a smooth body. Anxious because of this, he went to a certain cellar to buy wine, and while sitting there for a little while <margin>conis <note>The Latin here is likely a contraction for "companions" or "at the table."</note></margin>, he revealed the cause of his sadness to a woman who happened to come by, telling her everything in detail and showing his body to demonstrate that it was so. That clever woman inquired whether he held anyone in suspicion. And he indeed identified the woman and manifested the matter by telling the story. She said, "It is necessary that you use some form of violence to induce her to restore your health, since kindness does not help you." But the young man, in the twilight of the night, watched the path the witch <note>original: "malefica"</note> was accustomed to cross and, finding her, begged her to return his bodily health. When she claimed ignorance

<column-break/>

and asserted that she knew nothing, he attacked her, tightly squeezing a towel around her neck and saying: "Unless you restore my health to me, you shall perish by my hands." Whereupon she, because she could not cry out and her face was already swollen and turning black, said: "Let me go, and I will heal you." And when the young man loosened the knot or the tightness, the witch touched him between the thighs or the groin with her hand, saying: "Now you have what you desire." And as the young man later reported, he had remarkably felt, even before he confirmed it for himself by sight or touch, that the member had been restored to him solely by the touch of the witch. A similar story is often told by a certain venerable father, illustrious for the integrity of his life and his knowledge, in the order and convent of Speyer <note>original: "spirensi"</note>. He says: "One day, while I was busy hearing confessions, a certain young man approached and, during his confession, lamentably claimed that he had lost his male member." I, the father, marvelling at this and being unwilling to believe his words easily—for he who believes easily is judged light-hearted by the wise—learned by experience through sight, seeing nothing when the young man showed the place by uncovering his clothes. Whereupon, using sound judgment, I inquired whether he had anyone in suspicion who might have cast such a spell <note>original: "maleficium"</note> upon him. And the young man asserted that he suspected one woman, but she was absent and living in Worms <note>original: "wormacia"</note>. Then I enjoined him: "I command you to go to her as soon as possible and strive to soften her as much as you can with promises and flattering words." Which he did. For after a few days, he returned, giving thanks to me and asserting that he was healthy and had recovered everything. And thus I believed his words, being certified once more by the experience of sight. There are, however, some things to be noted here to understand more clearly what was touched upon above concerning the same matter. First, that it is by no means to be believed that such organs are pulled out or separated from the bodies, but are hidden by an illusory art <note>original: "prestigeosa arte"</note> through a demon, so that they can neither be seen nor felt. And this is by authority and reason...

...though it was touched upon above where Alexander of Hales <note>A 13th-century Franciscan theologian known as the "Irrefragable Doctor."</note> says in the second part: **Illusion** <note>original: "Praestigium"; refers to a demonic "glamour" or trick that deceives the senses without altering physical reality.</note>, properly understood, is that deception of a demon which does not have its cause in a change of the object itself, but only on the part of the perceiver who is deluded. This applies to the external senses. Regarding these words, it must be noted that here two external senses are deluded, namely **sight** and **touch**, and not the internal senses such as the common sense, phantasy, imagination, estimation, and memory. This is despite the fact that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the dominant philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> only posits four internal senses as touched upon above, because he considers phantasy and the imaginative sense as one, and rightly so, for there is little difference between imagining and fantasizing (Thomas, *Summa Theologica*, Part I, Question 79). And these senses are changed—and not the external ones alone—when nothing is hidden or revealed, either while waking or sleeping. While waking, this occurs when a thing is seen differently than it is in itself; for example, when someone sees a horse with a rider passing by, or a man transformed into a beast, or someone who thinks they are a beast themselves and ought to walk among beasts. For then the external senses are deluded and occupied by the internal ones. Because by the power of demons, <term>sensory images</term> <note>original: "species sensibiles"; these are the mental "data" or pictures stored in the brain that represent physical objects.</note> long ago stored in the treasury of sensory images—which is the memory (not the intellectual memory in which <term>intelligible species</term> <note>original: "species intelligibiles"; abstract concepts or ideas</note> are preserved, but the memory which is the preserver of sensory images, which is also in the back part of the head)—are drawn out by the power of demons (God sometimes permitting it) to the common imaginative sense. And they are so strongly impressed that, just as the person is compelled to imagine a horse or a beast by the impetuous act by which the demon draws the image of the horse or beast from the memory, so too he is compelled to think he sees such a beast with his external eyes. In reality, the thing from the outside is not a beast, but through the impetuous operation of the demon using those images, it is seen as such. Nor should it seem strange that demons can do this, since...

<column-break/>

Those with "frenzy" <note>A medieval medical term for acute mental disturbance or brain inflammation.</note> think they have seen wonders and see beasts and other horrifying things, though in truth there is nothing there. See above in the question "Whether witches can change the minds of men to love or hate," where more notes are given. Finally, the reason is clear in itself. For since the demon has a certain power over certain lower things, by taking away only the soul <note>The text likely suggests the demon has power over the physical/animal soul or the body, but not the higher rational soul unless permitted.</note>, therefore <margin>by</margin> he can also perform some changes around these things when God allows it, so that things appear otherwise than they are. And this occurs, as I said, either by disturbing or deluding the organ of sight, so that a clear thing looks cloudy—just as after weeping, because of the collected humors, light appears differently than before—or by working on the imaginative power through the transformation of sensory images, as was said, or by moving various humors so that things appear fiery or watery which are actually earthy or dry. Some act in such a way that everyone in a house strips off their clothes and stands naked, thinking they are swimming in water. Furthermore, beyond the manner described above, if it is asked: Can these kinds of illusions happen indifferently to the good and the bad, just as (as will appear below) other bodily infirmities can be inflicted by witches even upon those existing in a state of grace? On this, adhering to the words of Abbot Serenus in the second Conference of Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), an influential Christian monk and theologian.</note>, it must be said that no. Hence all those who are thus deluded are presumed to be in mortal sin. For he says—and it is clear from the words of Anthony <note>St. Anthony the Great, the early Christian hermit who famously fought demonic visions.</note>—that a demon can in no way invade the mind or body of anyone, nor has he the power to break into the soul of any person, unless he has first stripped it of all holy thoughts and rendered it empty and naked of spiritual contemplation. Philosophy <note>Refers to Lady Philosophy, the personification in Boethius's *The Consolation of Philosophy*.</note> agrees with this in the first book of the Consolation to Boethius, saying: "We had bestowed such weapons upon you that..."

<meta>This page continues the theological and philosophical defense of the reality of witchcraft. After discussing the "theft" of male organs through illusion on the previous page, the author now addresses legal and scriptural counter-arguments, specifically interpreting the "Canon Episcopi"—a famous medieval law that many used to argue that witchcraft was merely a fantasy.</meta>

<sig>b 4</sig>

It has been sufficiently declared how **witches** <note>original: "malefice" - female practitioners of harmful magic.</note> are able to effect these things. However, because this question might be too obscure for some, given its various arguments and solutions—especially since the actual deeds and trials concerning these matters have not been fully recounted—and because the **manner** in which they transform themselves is not explicitly stated, the present declaration must be added to resolve several doubts.

First, that law—**Canon 26, question 5, "Episcopi"** <note>The "Canon Episcopi" was a 10th-century church decree that claimed women who believe they fly through the night with the goddess Diana are deluded by the devil. Skeptics used it to argue all witchcraft was an illusion.</note>—is not to be understood so "nakedly" <note>interpreted literally without nuance</note> as many men, even learned ones (though I wish they were truly learned), receive it. These men do not fear to assert publicly in their sermons that these types of **glamour-filled transformations** <note>original: "transmutationes prestigiosas" - illusions that trick the physical senses.</note> can in no way be performed even by the power of demons. This is certainly to the great detriment of the faith, as has often been mentioned, and it provides comfort to witches, who greatly rejoice in such sermons. This happens to such preachers because they labor over the "bark" and not the "marrow" <note>a metaphor for looking at the surface of words rather than their deep meaning</note> of the words of the Canon, as was touched upon above. 

For when it says: *"Whoever believes that any creature can be made, or transmuted for better or worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things, is beyond doubt an infidel."* 

Here the pious reader should attend to two principal points. First, regarding the word **"made"** <note>original: "fieri"</note>. Second, regarding the words **"converted into another likeness."** Concerning the first, let it be resolved that "to be made" is understood in two ways: namely, for "to be created" and for the "natural production" of a thing. In the first sense, it belongs to God alone, as is well known, who by His infinite power can create something from nothing. In the second sense, we must distinguish between creatures. For they are either **perfect creatures**, such as a human, a donkey, etc., or they are **imperfect**, such as serpents, frogs, mice, etc., which are called "imperfect" because they can also be generated from decay <note>Medieval science believed in "spontaneous generation," where simple animals were born from rotting organic matter without parents.</note>. Although the Canon always speaks of the former, it does not speak of the latter. This is evident from what **Albertus Magnus** <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> says in his *Book on Animals* where he asks if demons can make true animals.

<column-break/>

And he responds that they can, but only regarding **imperfect animals**. Even then, there is this difference: they do not work in an instant, as God does, but through a certain movement, though a sudden one. This is evident regarding the magicians in **Exodus, chapter 7** <note>Referring to Pharaoh’s magicians who turned their staffs into snakes to mimic Moses's miracle.</note>. If it pleases you, look at the things noted in the question touched upon in the first part of this work and in the solution to the first argument.

Regarding the second point, where it is touched upon that they cannot "transmute" any creature: you should say that there are two types of **transmutation**: **Substantial** and **Accidental**. And this Accidental type is again two-fold: for it is either through a natural form inherent in the thing seen, or through a form not inherent in the thing seen, but inherent in the **organs and powers** of the person seeing it. 

The Canon speaks of the first type, and especially of formal or quantitative transmutation, where one substance is changed into another. Only God, who is the creator of such essences, can do this. It also speaks of the second type, although a demon can effect that insofar as, through illnesses sent by divine permission, some accidental form is induced in the body, as when a **leprous face** might appear or something similar. 

But because we are not strictly speaking of these, but of a **glamourous appearance** <note>original: "prestigiosa apparitione"</note> by which things seem to be transmuted into other likenesses, we say that the aforementioned Canon cannot exclude these. This is proven by authority, reason, and experience together from those things which are reduced from certain experiences that **Augustine** reports in the **eighteenth book, seventeenth chapter of *The City of God***. 

These are declared through various questions. For among other glamour-filled transformations, he reports that the most famous sorceress, **Circe**, changed the companions of **Ulysses** into beasts. For it was also the opinion of some, as **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> relates in his commentary on the *Second Book of Sentences* (Distinction 8, Article 2), that any angels, whether good or bad, never truly assumed bodies. Rather, they held that everything read in the scriptures about their appearances happened through **illusions** or in an **imaginary vision**. In these words, a difference is noted by the Holy Doctor between an illusion and an imaginary vision. 

Because an **illusion** <note>original: "prestigium"</note> can have an external thing presenting itself to the bodily sight, although it is seen to be something other than it actually is. An **imaginary vision**, however, does not necessarily require this—that is, that an object be presented from the outside. Whence, following the opinion of those men, the companions of Diomedes were not represented by demons in assumed bodies and the likeness of birds, but only by a phantasmic and imaginary vision, namely through the bringing back of those sensory images, and so on, as stated above. The text of Holy Scripture also agrees more with such bodily appearances than with imaginary or illusory ones. ### How demons exist within bodies and
### heads without injury when they
### perform illusory transformations

### Chapter IX

If it is further asked concerning the manner of **illusory** <note>original: "prestigiofe"</note> transformation: whether the **demons** then exist within the bodies and heads, and whether such people are to be considered **possessed** <term>obsessed/possessed: in medieval theology, this refers to a demon acting upon a person from within the body, though not necessarily controlling the soul</term> by **demons**. And how it can be possible that, without injury to the internal powers and strengths, they can move **species** <term>species: mental "blueprints" or images of objects stored in the mind that allow for recognition</term> from one internal power to another. And whether such a work ought to be judged a miraculous deed or not.
Regarding the first point, it is necessary to distinguish concerning **illusory** <note>original: "prestigiosa"</note> deception according to what has been stated. That deception sometimes happens to the external senses, and sometimes to the internal senses even reaching the external sense. The first type, therefore, although it can happen without the **demons** entering and occupying those external powers—but only by deluding from the outside, as when he wishes to hide some body by placing another body in between or by any other way, or where he assumes a body for himself and presents himself to the sight. The second type, however, cannot happen unless he occupies the head and the principal powers. And this is shown by authority and reason. Nor can it be an obstacle that two created spirits cannot be in one and the same place, and that the soul is in every part of the body. For there is the authority of **John of Damascus** <note>original: "Damasceni," an 8th-century theologian</note> on this: "An angel is where he ope-

<column-break/>

-rates." The reasoning of **Saint Thomas Aquinas** <note>original: "sancti Thome"</note> in the second book of *The Sentences*, distinction 6, article 5: All angels, both good and evil, by their natural power (which is surely more excellent than any corporeal power), have the power of transforming our bodies. This is clear not only because of the excellence and nobility of their nature, but also because the entire machine of the world and every corporeal creature is administered by angels. **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> says in the fourth book of his *Dialogues*: In this visible world, nothing can be disposed except through an invisible creature. Whence all corporeal things are ruled by angels, just as the **movers of the spheres** <note>The spiritual beings believed to rotate the celestial orbits</note> are asserted to be, not only by the holy doctors but also by all the philosophers. It is also clear from the fact that all human bodies are moved by souls, just as all other things are moved by the celestial bodies and by their own movers. If it pleases anyone, let him see **Saint Thomas** in the first part, question 110, article 1. From which it is concluded that because **demons** are where they operate, therefore when they disturb the **fantasies** <note>original: "fantasias," referring to the faculty of imagination</note> and internal powers, they also exist there.
Likewise, although to **glide into the soul** <note>original: "illabi anime"</note> is possible only for Him who created it, nevertheless **demons** can also glide into our bodies if God permits. And because they can then make impressions on the internal powers attached to the bodily organs, therefore through those impressions, just as the organs are changed, so the operations of the powers are changed. This happens in the manner described: that they can draw out **species** <term>species: mental images</term> reserved in a power attached to an organ. For example, from the **memory** which is in the back part of the head, he draws out the **species** of a horse by locally moving that **phantom** <note>original: "fantasma"</note> as far as the middle part of the head, where the cell of the **imaginative power** <note>original: "virtutis imaginatiue"</note> is located; and finally, consequently, to the **common sense** <term>common sense: the "sensus communis," believed to be a physical faculty in the front of the brain that integrates sensory data</term> whose residence is in the front part of the head. And yet they can suddenly change and disturb all things in such a way that these forms are necessarily estimated as if they were presented to the external sight. An example is seen in the natural defect found in **frenetic** <note>original: "freneticis," meaning those suffering from brain fever or delirium</note> and other manic people.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mechanics of demonic illusions, specifically addressing how demons can inhabit the human head to manipulate perception without causing physical pain or displacing the soul. It transitions from neurological mechanics to the theological distinction between demonic wonders and divine miracles.</meta>

If it is asked how a **demon** can achieve this without causing a headache, the answer is easy. First, because he does not divide or change the physical organs themselves, but only moves the **species** <term>species: mental images or "blueprints" stored in the brain that represent objects</term>. Second, because he does not cause an alteration by introducing any active quality <note>In medieval science, "active qualities" refer to physical properties like heat or cold that would cause a bodily reaction.</note> from which suffering would necessarily follow; for the **demon** himself lacks all bodily quality, and therefore can perform such operations without pain. Third, because—as has been stated—he only creates changes through local motion from one organ to another, and not through other types of movement from which harmful alterations are sometimes caused.

Therefore, the point that creates difficulty is how two **spirits** can be in the same place (specifically in a "definitive" sense) <note>definitive presence: a theological term for how a spirit occupies a specific space without taking up physical volume.</note>. Since the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> also exists in the head, how then can **demons** exist in the same location? It must be said that the residence of the **soul** is assigned to the center of the heart, from which it communicates life to all the members. An example is given of a spider in the middle of its web, which feels a touch from every side. However, because of the saying of **Augustine** in his book *On the Spirit and the Soul* <note>original: "Augustini in libro de spiritu et anima"</note> that the soul is "entirely in the whole and entirely in every part of the body," even if it is granted that the soul is in the head, the **demon** can still operate there. This is because his operation is different from the operation of the soul. The soul's operation in the body is to give it form and life; hence it is there as form is in matter, not as something in a physical location. A **demon**, however, is in such a part of the body and such a location by changing and operating upon the sensible **species**. Since there is no confusion of operations between them, both can exist simultaneously in the same part of the body. 

Regarding whether such people should be considered **possessed** <note>original: "obsessi"</note> and "seized"—that is, seized by **demons**—this requires a specific declaration: namely, whether it is possible through the work of **witches** <note>original: "maleficorum"</note> for someone to be **possessed** by a **demon**, meaning that the **demon** truly and corporally possesses them. Therefore, this specific subject matter will be treated in the following chapter, for it has its own particular difficulty: whether by the works of **witches**

<column-break/>

they are able to make this happen. Regarding the point of whether such works of **witches** and **demons** are to be judged as **miracles** <note>original: "miracula"</note>, so that they ought to be esteemed as miraculous works: It must be said that they are so in as much as they happen outside the order of created nature known to us, even though they are not properly **miracles** like those which happen outside the order of the *entirety* of created nature—which are the **miracles** of God and the saints. See what was touched upon in the first part of this work under the fifth question and the rejection of the third error. 

To this must be added something for the sake of those who might challenge such works, as if they should not be judged as miraculous works but simply as "diabolical works," because **miracles** are given for the confirmation of the faith and should not be granted to an enemy of the faith. Also, because the signs of the Antichrist are called "lying signs" by the Apostle. But it must be said to the first point that performing **miracles** is a gift of grace freely given. Thus, just as they can be performed through evil men, so too can they be performed through evil **spirits** in those matters to which their power can extend. Hence, **miracles** performed by the good are distinguished from those performed by the evil in at least three ways. 

First, by the efficacy of the power operating; for signs performed by the good are done by divine power, even in those matters to which the power of active nature in no way extends—such as raising the dead and similar things, which **demons** in truth cannot do. They can only do so in **illusions** <note>original: "prestigijs"</note>, just as **Simon Magus** <note>A biblical figure who attempted to buy spiritual power and was famous for using magic to deceive crowds.</note> did with a dead man whose head he made move, though such things cannot last long. Second, by the utility of the signs; for signs performed by the good are for useful things, such as the curing of infirmities and such. But signs performed by **witches** are for harmful or vain things, such as flying in the air or making the limbs of men become numb, and the like. This difference is assigned by the **Blessed Peter** in the *Itinerary of Clement* <note>The "Clementine Recognitions," a popular medieval narrative about the travels of St. Peter.</note>. The third difference concerns the end goal.

...because signs of the good are ordained for the edification of faith and good morals. But the signs of the evil are for the manifest harm of faith and honesty. They also differ in their manner of operation: for the good perform wonders through the invocation of the divine name piously and reverently. But sorcerers and the evil perform them by certain delusions and the invocation of demons. 

Another point does not stand in the way, namely that the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 2 Thessalonians 2:9.</note> calls the works of the devil and the Antichrist <term>signa mendacia: lying signs</term>. For then those wonders which will be done by him by divine permission are both true and false in different respects. They are **true** in those things which are done by the power of the **demon**, to which his power can extend. They are **false** when he performs those things to which his power cannot extend, such as raising the dead or giving sight to the blind. For in the first case, where he attempts to do so, he will either enter the body of the deceased or remove it and, in its place, present himself in an assumed body made of air. And likewise in the second case, he takes away sight by a prestidigitator’s art <note>The "art of the juggler" or illusionist; a deceptive manipulation of the eyes.</note>, or he will heal other illnesses suddenly by ceasing to cause the injury, rather than by rectifying the internal qualities of the body, as is stated in the legend of **St. Bartholomew**. 

All the wonderful works of the **Antichrist** and of **witches** <note>original: "maleficarum"</note> can also be called "lying signs" insofar as they are done only to deceive now, just as the Antichrist will operate then. These are the words of **Thomas Aquinas** in *Distinction 7* <note>original: "di. vij." referring to his commentary on the Sentences</note> concerning the power of demons in their operations. One could also bring in here the distinction regarding miracles found in the *Compendium of Theological Truth* <note>original: "compendio theologiche veritatis"</note>, and the difference between a **marvel** and a **miracle**. For a miracle properly requires four things: first, that it be done by **God**; second, that it be done outside the workings of nature; third, that it be done against the order of nature; and fourth, that it be for the strengthening of faith. Since the works of **witches** lack at least the first and the last of these, they can be called "marvelous works" <note>original: "mira opera"</note> but not "miracles" <note>original: "miracula"</note>. For that reason as well, even if they can in some way be called miracles, yet some are **above**

<column-break/>

nature, some are **against** nature, and some are **beside** nature. Those **above nature** are things for which there is no likeness in nature or its power, such as a virgin giving birth. **Against nature** are those which are done by a use contrary to nature but result in something conforming to nature, such as the giving of sight to the blind. And **beside nature** are those things done similarly to the order of nature but not through a natural principle, as in the changing of rods into serpents—which nature could have done through a long process of rot because of **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons: the medieval scientific belief that the "seeds" or blueprints for all physical things are hidden in matter and can be accelerated by spiritual beings</term>. In this way, the works of magicians shall be called wonders.

It is helpful to narrate an event that occurred and to dwell a little on its explanation. There is a town in the **Diocese of Strasbourg** <note>original: "argentinensi"</note> whose name the order of charity and honesty requires me to hide. In this town, a certain laborer was cutting wood to burn in his house one day, when a certain **cat** <note>original: "cattus"</note> of no small size strove to trouble him by throwing itself persistently in his path. When he drove it away, behold, another of even larger size joined the first, and together they attacked him more fiercely. When he tried to repel them again, behold, three of them together began attacking him, jumping toward his face and tearing at him with bites between his shins. 

Terrified and—as he later reported—never more perplexed by great anxiety, the man drove them away by protecting himself with the **sign of the cross** and abandoning his work. And behold, an hour later, while he was again busy at his work, two servants of the town councilors seized him like a criminal and wanted to lead him before the bailiff or judge. The judge, looking at him from a distance and refusing to grant him a hearing, commanded that he be thrown into the depths of a certain tower or prison where those condemned to death were confined. The man wailed, asking why he should suffer such things when he was guilty of no crime...

rebuker of crimes, the holy man called him aside after the sermon finished. When he asked the reason for this, the demon responded: "Behold, I speak the truth knowing that while the listeners are hearers of the word but not doers, God is further offended and my profit is increased."

### On the manner by which demons sometimes
### substantially inhabit a man through the
### works of witches. Chapter X.

Since it was touched upon in the preceding chapter how demons can also occupy the heads of men or other parts of the body, and enter them, and move internal perceptions from place to place, someone might wonder: Can they entirely <term>possess</term> <note>original: "obsidere"; to besiege or obsess, used here for demonic possession</note> men at the urging of witches? 

Regarding the various modes of possession and the urging of witches, three points must be explained for the sake of clarity. First, concerning the different modes of possessing. Second, that by God's permission, demons sometimes possess people in all those modes at the urging of witches. Third, the actual deeds and events regarding this must be recounted. 

Regarding the first point: excluding that general way in which the devil inhabits a man through any mortal sin—concerning which mode <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian whose work provides the logical framework for this text</note> wrote in the third book of <gloss>Quodlibetal Questions</gloss>, question 3, under the doubt: "Whether the devil always substantially inhabits a man whenever he sins mortally." 

The cause of his doubt arises because, since the Holy Spirit always inhabits a man through grace—according to the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3: *You are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you*—and since guilt is the opposite of grace, and opposites must occur regarding the same subject. There, he also declares that "inhabiting a man" can be understood in two ways: either regarding the soul or regarding the body. In the first way, since it is not possible for the devil to inhabit the soul (because God alone enters the mind), and since the devil is not the cause of guilt in the same way the Holy Spirit is the cause of grace (which the Holy Spirit effects in the soul by working through Himself), the comparison does not hold. As for the body, however, we can say that the devil can inhabit it in two ways...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of demonic influence on humanity. ...humanity. Just as people are found in two states—either existing in sin or in grace—we must speak of the first way. Because of any mortal sin, a person is handed over to the slavery of the devil, insofar as the devil sometimes suggests sin from the outside, either through the senses or through the imagination. Therefore, he is said to "inhabit" a person’s disposition when that person is moved by every impulse of temptation, like a ship at sea without a pilot. 

The devil can also substantially inhabit a person, as is evident in the <term>possessed</term> <note>original: "arrepticiis"; literally "those snatched away," referring to individuals whose bodies have been seized by a spirit</note>. And because this pertains more to the nature of punishment than to fault (as will be shown), and since bodily punishments do not always follow guilt but are sometimes inflicted on both sinners and the innocent alike, it follows that those in a state of grace and those outside of it can be substantially inhabited by demons, according to the depth of God’s incomprehensible judgments. 

This mode of possession, although it is not the focus of our current study, is nevertheless included so that it does not seem impossible to anyone that, by God’s permission, humans are sometimes substantially inhabited by demons at the instigation of <term>sorcerers</term> <note>original: "maleficorum"; practitioners of harmful magic</note>. We can say, therefore, that there are five ways demons can harm and possess humans on their own without the use of magic; and in all those ways, at the instigation of <term>witches</term> <note>original: "maleficarum"; specifically female practitioners</note>, God is further offended, and thus the demon is granted a greater power to rage against humanity through these witches. 

Briefly recited, these modes are:
1. When they sometimes harass people in their external goods and fortune.
2. When they harm only people's own bodies.
3. When they harm the bodies and the internal powers <note>the "internal powers" usually refer to the imagination, memory, and cognitive senses</note> at the same time.
4. When they only tempt from within and without.
5. When they deprive some of the use of reason for a time, or render others like irrational beasts.

Let us speak of each individually. But first, let us put forth the causes for which God permits humans to be possessed, as the subject matter demands we maintain this order. For sometimes a person is possessed for

<column-break/>

his own greater merit. Sometimes for another's light fault. Sometimes for one’s own venial sin. Sometimes for another’s grave sin. And sometimes for one’s own great crime. Regarding all these causes, there is no doubt that God sometimes permits similar things to happen through demons at the instigation of witches. 

It is useful to prove each of these to you from the Scriptures and not through "new deeds," since new things are always strengthened by the old. Regarding the first cause—greater merit—this is clear in the *Dialogue* of <term>Sulpicius Severus</term> <note>original: "seueri"; a 5th-century Christian writer</note>, the beloved disciple of the <term>Blessed Martin</term> <note>St. Martin of Tours</note>. There, it is told of a certain father of a most holy life who flourished so greatly in the grace of expelling demons that they were put to flight not only by his own words but even by his letters and his <term>hair-shirt</term> <note>original: "cilicio"; a garment of rough animal hair worn for penance</note>. 

When this father became most celebrated before the world, he felt himself tempted by <term>vainglory</term> <note>original: "vana gloria"; the sin of taking pride in one's own holiness or reputation</note>. Although he resisted this vice manfully, in order to be humbled further, he prayed to God with his whole heart that he might be possessed by a demon for five months. This was done; for he was immediately possessed, and it became necessary to bind him in chains and apply all the treatments common to the demonic. When the five months were finished, he was entirely liberated from all vainglory and from the demon. (However, whether someone can be possessed by another's magic for this specific reason is not found in writing, and thus is not affirmed here—though as stated before, the judgments of God are incomprehensible).

Regarding the second cause—being possessed for another’s light fault—the <term>Blessed Gregory</term> <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> provides an example concerning the Blessed Eleutherius, a most simple-hearted Abbot. While he was staying overnight near a monastery of nuns, they arranged (without him knowing) for a small boy who was tormented every night by a demon to be placed in his cell. But that same night, the boy was freed from the demon by the father’s presence. When the Abbot learned what had happened and the boy had been placed in the holy man's monastery, many days passed. Becoming a little too immoderately joyful over the boy's liberation, he said to his brothers: "The devil was just playing with those sisters; but when he came to the servants of God, he [did not dare] approach this boy..."

Regarding possession due to one’s own venial sin, this is made clear by <term>Cassian</term> <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435), a monk and theologian whose "Conferences" (Collationes) are cited here.</note> in his first conference with Abbot Serenus. The Lord seems to have brought this lash upon him for the sake of purification, so that not even the stain of a momentary fault would remain in him; this was made clear by his miraculous cure. For as soon as Abbot Macarius offered a humble prayer, the wicked spirit was quickly driven out and departed from him. 

A similar case is reported by <term>Gregory</term> <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose "Dialogues" were a primary source for medieval stories of the supernatural.</note> in the first book of his *Dialogues* concerning a nun who ate a piece of lettuce without first protecting herself with the sign of the cross. She was later freed through the prayers of the holy father Equitius.

All these examples have been touched upon, as we said, so that it does not seem impossible to anyone if people are also possessed at the instigation of witches due to their crimes.

Therefore, whenever any angel, whether good or bad, operates within the boundaries of the body, he operates within the boundaries of the bodily quantity. And thus he also glides into the body by operating around the quantitative powers. Thus also the good angels [produce] imaginary visions in good people.

But it is never said that they glide into <note>original: "illabi," a technical term used in scholastic theology to describe a spiritual substance entering into the very essence of another substance</note> the essence of the body, because they cannot glide in either as a part or as a power. Not as a part, because the essence of each is distinct in both cases. Not as a power, as if giving being, because the body has its own being through creation by God. Wherefore He alone has the power of working within the essence and of preserving it for as long as it shall please His mercy to preserve it. From this it is concluded that all other perfections or defects—speaking of "goods" in regards to perfections and "evils" in regards to defects—when they operate, if they operate upon the body and its parts, such as upon the head, they glide into <note>original: "illabuntur"</note> such a body only within the limits of its physical size and its quantitative powers. But if they operate upon the soul, then again both <note>meaning both good and bad angels</note> operate from the outside, but in different ways. And they are said to operate upon the soul by representing those phantasms <term>phantasmata: mental images or sensory perceptions stored in the imagination</term> or species to the intellect, and not only to the judgment of the common sense and the external senses. From these operations follow temptations from the evil angels, and evil affections and thoughts, by operating indirectly upon the intellect. But from the good angels follow the enlightenments <note>original: "illustrationes"</note> of these mental images to know things that should be revealed by them. Hence, there is this diversity: that good angels can even directly impress mental images into the intellect by enlightening them. Evil ones, however, are not said to enlighten mental images but rather to cloud <note>original: "obfuscare"</note> them. Likewise, they cannot impress them directly, but only indirectly, insofar as it is necessary for the one who understands to gaze upon these mental images. Through these things, however, even a good angel is not said to glide into the soul, even though he illuminates it; just as a superior angel is not said to glide into an inferior one, even though he illuminates him, but he only operates and cooperates externally in the manner described. ...and in what matters. And as for the first point, it was answered as was clear from the first question of the first part of the treatise. It is also proven by **Isidore** [of Seville] describing the operations of **sorcery** <term>malefica: harmful magic</term> in the seventh book of his *Etymologies*, chapter nine. **Sorcerers** <term>Malefici: those who perform harmful magic</term> are so called because of the magnitude of their crimes. For these people shake the elements—namely by the work of demons—to stir up tempests. They disturb the minds of men in the ways touched upon above, namely by either completely hindering the use of reason or severely clouding it. He adds: and without any drinking of poison, they kill souls by the violence of a **spell** <term>carminis: a song, incantation, or ritual chant</term>, namely by taking away life. It is also proven by **Saint Thomas** [Aquinas] in the second book of his commentary on the *Sentences* around distinctions seven and eight, and in the fourth book, distinction thirty-four. And it is commonly held by all theologians writing there that sorcerers can procure injuries in men and their things in every way with the cooperation of a demon, in which the demon alone can hurt or receive—namely in property, reputation, the body, the use of reason, and in life. He [Aquinas] means to say that in those things in which a demon can hurt by himself without a sorceress, he can also do so with a sorceress. Indeed, he can do so with **greater ease** because of the greater offense to the Divine Majesty, as was touched upon above. For regarding property, this is clear from **Job**, chapters one and two, as was shown above. Regarding reputation, it is clear in the legend of **Blessed Jerome**, as **Johannes Andreae** relates in his *Hieronymianum*: that the devil transformed himself into the form of **Saint Silvanus**, the Bishop of Nazareth and a friend of Jerome. This demon first began to woo a noblewoman at night in her bed and provoke her to lust with words. And then, having done so, he solicited her to evil. When she cried out, the demon, under the appearance of the holy bishop, hid himself under the woman's bed. When he was sought and found, through lewd words he lied, saying he was Bishop Silvanus. On the following day, therefore, the devil having disappeared, the holy man was most gravely defamed. This infamy was finally purged at the tomb of Saint Jerome when the devil confessed while in a possessed body. Regarding the body, it is clear in **Blessed Job**, who was struck by a demon with a

<column-break/>

most evil **sore** <note>original: "vlcere pessimo." This is the biblical "boils" or "sores" afflicted upon Job by Satan.</note> which is explained as leprosy. **Sigebert** and **Vincent [of Beauvais]** also relate in the *Mirror of History* <note>original: "in spe. histo." referring to the Speculum Historiale.</note>, book twenty-five, chapter thirty-seven, that in the time of the **Emperor Louis II**, in the parish of **Mainz** <note>original: "moguntina."</note>, a certain demon first frequently threw stones and struck houses as if with a mallet. And then, by speaking publicly, revealing thefts, and sowing discords, he disturbed many. Then he incited everyone against one man, whose lodging he burned wherever he stayed. And he [the demon] affirmed that everyone suffered because of that man's sins. For which reason, he [the man] could finally only have fields for his lodging. Because of this, when the priests celebrated the litanies, the demon injured many with the throwing of stones even to the point of bloodshed. Sometimes he was quiet; sometimes he raged; and he continued these things for three years until all the buildings there were consumed by fire. Likewise, concerning the harm to the use of reason and the vexation of the internal senses, it is proven from the possessed and the seized even through the **Gospel stories**. Likewise, concerning death and how he also deprives some of life: this is clear from the book of **Tobit** <note>original: "Tho." likely shorthand for Tobit.</note> concerning the seven husbands of the virgin **Sarah** who were killed; because of their lustful affection and unbridled appetite for the virgin Sarah, they were not worthy of marriage. Therefore, it is concluded that just as they [demons] can do so by themselves, they can do so even more through **witches** in all things, provided they are permitted to harm men. Truly, where it is asked whether injuries of this sort are to be imputed rather to demons or to witches, it is answered that just as demons work by their primary and immediate action in sending infirmities, so also the injuries are principally to be imputed to them. But because they seek to perform these things through witches for the contempt and offense of the **Creator**, and at the same time for the perdition of souls, knowing that through such a method, just as God is more provoked, so also He permits them more power of raging. For in fact, innumerable acts of witchcraft are perpetrated which the devil would not be permitted to inflict on men if he sought to hurt men by himself alone; yet these things are permitted by the just and hidden judgment of God through **witches**...

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the culpability of witches. It transitions from discussing how demons can harm humans independently to explaining why the human witch is nonetheless held responsible for crimes where the demon is the primary supernatural actor.</meta>

...witches <term>maleficas: women who perform harmful magic</term> on account of their treachery and their abnegation of the Catholic faith. Therefore, in a just judgment, such **sorceries** <term>maleficia: harmful acts of magic</term> are imputed to the accused secondarily, however much the devil is the principal actor. For example, consider a broom which a woman might dip into water so that it may rain, splashing the water upward into the air; although this action does not in itself cause rain, nor could the woman be blamed for it on its own merit, nevertheless, because of the **pact** <term>pactum: a formal agreement or contract with a demon</term> entered into with the demon—where she now acts as a sorceress—even if it is the demon who actually causes the rain, she is deservedly blamed. This is because she serves the devil in bad faith and through her own work, handing herself over to his service.

So it is also when a sorcerer makes a **wax image** or something similar to bewitch someone, or when an image appears in water or lead through someone's sorcery. Whatever harm is inflicted upon such an image is likewise experienced by the person represented—that is, the bewitched human—such as a prick or any other injury. 

¶ Although the injury is actually inflicted upon the image by the witch or another person, and the demon invisibly harms the bewitched person in the same way, the act is nevertheless deservedly imputed to the witch. This is because, without her, God would never permit the devil to inflict the injury, nor would the devil have attempted to harm the person on his own. 

But because it was said concerning **reputation** <note>original: "fama"</note> that demons can harm men by themselves without the cooperation of witches, a doubt might arise: Could demons also, by themselves, defame honorable women so that they are regarded as witches, perhaps by appearing in their likeness while bewitching someone? In such a case, an innocent person would be defamed. 

**The Response:** Several things must be premised. 

¶ First, as was said, the demon can effect nothing without **divine permission**, as is clear in the first part of this work near the final question. It was also touched upon that there is not as much permission granted over the just and those living in a state of charity as there is over sinners, over whom the devil certainly has greater power, according to the saying: *When a strong man armed keeps [his house],* etc. <note>A reference to Luke 11:21, implying the devil's control over the "house" of a sinner's soul.</note> Thus, many more things are permitted by God for the affliction of sinners

<column-break/>

than for the just. Finally, although they can harm the just in external things like reputation and bodily health if God permits, they know this results in an increase of the victim's merits; therefore, they desire to harm them less. 

From these points, it can be said that in this difficulty, one must look at several factors: 
¶ First, to divine permission. 
¶ Second, to the person who is considered honorable; for such people are not always living in a state of grace, even if they are reputed to be honorable. 
¶ Third, to the crime for which an innocent person would be defamed; for that crime, from its very root, exceeds all the shames of the world. 

Therefore, it must be said: Although by divine permission any innocent person—whether they are in a state of grace or not—can be harmed in their fortune and reputation, yet, having respect for the crime itself and the gravity of the offense (since sorcerers are so named because of the magnitude of their crimes, according to **Isidore** [of Seville] whom we have often cited), it can be said that it is not quite possible for an innocent person to be defamed by a demon in the aforementioned way, for several reasons:

¶ First, because defamation regarding common vices is one thing—vices which are perpetrated without an express or tacit sin involving a demon, such as thefts, robberies, and carnal acts. 
¶ It is another thing regarding defamation for vices that can in no way be imputed to a person or performed by them except through an **express pact** entered into with a demon. Such are the works of witches, which are not performed except by the power of demons—for instance, when humans, cattle, or the fruits of the earth are bewitched. These cannot be imputed to a person in any other way. 

¶ Therefore, although a demon might be able to defame a person for other vices, it does not seem quite possible for him to defame them for a vice that cannot be committed without his own cooperation. 

¶ Furthermore, until now it has never happened, nor has it been found, that any innocent person was so defamed by a demon. If they had been, they would have been sentenced to death because of such defamation; on the contrary, where a person suffers only from a bad reputation, they are punished with no penalty except that a **canonical purgation** <note>A legal process where the accused clears their name by swearing an oath of innocence, often supported by neighbors who act as "character witnesses."</note> is enjoined upon them, as will be seen in the third part.

It will be clear in the part of the work concerning the second way of perceiving witches. And although it is contained there that, in a case where a defendant fails in their **purification** <note>purgatione: a trial by ordeal or a formal oath-taking to prove innocence</note>, they should be held as guilty, nevertheless, an **abjuration** <term>abiuratio: a formal renunciation of heresy under oath</term> would still be enjoined upon them before proceeding further regarding the penalty due to a **relapsed** <term>relapsus: a person who falls back into heresy after having previously renounced it</term> person. But because we are working with contingencies that have never actually been perpetrated, there is no doubt that divine permission will not allow them to happen in the future. Furthermore, and even more so, because of **angelic protection** <note>angelicam custodiam: the belief that guardian angels protect the innocent</note>, which does not permit the innocent to be defamed in other minor crimes—such as thefts and the like—it will allow it even less here. Indeed, the angel will even more strongly preserve the person assigned to his care from the infamy of such outrages. 

Nor is it valid if someone were to object by citing the deeds of **Saint Germain** <note>Saint Germanus of Auxerre (c. 378–448), a bishop famous for battling paganism and demonic illusions.</note>, when demons in assumed bodies—while the real women were sleeping with their husbands—represented those women sitting at a table, mocking the host as if those women were coming to eat and drink in their own bodies. This objection fails because even there, those women are not excused as if they were entirely innocent, but rather it is noted that such things often happen to women, as recorded in the Church canons <note>original: "c.xxvi.q.v.episcopi" referring to the Canon Episcopi, a medieval legal text regarding witchcraft and illusions.</note>. There, such women are rebuked because, while they are transported only in an **imaginary illusion**, they think they are truly and bodily transported; though, as mentioned above, they are sometimes also bodily used by demons. 

But concerning the fact that they can inflict all other physical infirmities, none excluded, by **divine permission** <term>diuina permissio: the theological concept that God allows the devil to act to test the faithful or punish the wicked</term>, this is the subject of the present investigation. Concluding from the aforementioned points: yes, they can, since no exception is made by the **Doctors of the Church**, and reason must agree, since otherwise demons exceed all physical things by their natural power, as has often been mentioned. Finally, the acts and deeds found by us affirm this. For although a greater difficulty might perhaps arise concerning **leprosy** or **epilepsy**—namely, whether they could inflict such things, since these usually arise only from long-term and prior internal defects of the body—

<column-break/>

nevertheless, it has been found that they are sometimes inflicted through **sorcery** <term>maleficium: harmful magic performed through a pact with the devil</term>. 

For in the **Diocese of Basel** <note>Basiliensi: modern-day Basel, Switzerland</note>, on the borders of the regions of Lorraine and Alsace, when a certain honest laborer had uttered some harsh words against a certain quarrelsome woman, she, being indignant, added threats that she would soon have her revenge on him. And although he made light of the threats, nevertheless that same night he felt a pustule grow on his neck. By rubbing and touching it a little, he felt his whole face and neck become swollen and puffed up, so much so that a horrible appearance of **leprosy** appeared over his entire body. He did not delay, but as quickly as possible, having called his friends and advisors, he told the story regarding the woman's threatening words, and stated that he wished to die in the faith and suspicion that the same witch had inflicted this on him by magic art. 

What more? The woman was captured, exposed to **interrogations** <note>questionibus: a legal euphemism often implying the use of judicial torture to extract a confession</note>, and confessed to the crime. But when the judge inquired more diligently about the manner and cause, she responded: "When that man attacked me with reproachful words, I was inflamed with anger. When I arrived home, an evil spirit began to inquire into the cause of my sadness. When I had told him everything and insisted that I might avenge myself, he inquired, saying: 'What then do you want me to do to him?' And I replied: 'I would like him to always keep a swollen face.' And so the spirit departed and inflicted that infirmity on the man beyond what I had asked; for I had by no means hoped that he would strike him with such leprosy." Because of this, she was **burned** <note>incinerata: literally "reduced to ashes," the standard execution for witchcraft</note>. 

Finally, in the **Diocese of Constance** <note>constantiensi: a region encompassing parts of modern Germany and Switzerland</note>, between Basel and Freiburg, a certain leprous woman used to tell many people—unless she has already **paid the debt of all flesh** <note>debitum vniuerse carnis: a Latin idiom meaning to die</note> within the last two years—that for a similar reason a controversy had been stirred between herself and another woman. While she had gone out of the house at night and tried to do some work before the door, a certain hot wind from the house of the other woman, which was opposite her house, suddenly blew upon her face.

-ture, when water was poured into a certain dish, the water itself ascended into another pot, with other ceremonies which it is not necessary to recite. And so, being stupefied, when I asked the master what should be done, he ordered me to throw everything into the fire. I threw them in. And behold, suddenly, not after the space of an hour...

I began to have suspicions. This sick woman used to recite these things; but if I wished to recount every single thing found in that town alone, a whole book would certainly have to be written. For how many blind, lame, withered, and those ensnared by various infirmities—following the legal form and under the examination of suspicion—predicted such **spells** <term>maleficia: harmful magic intended to cause injury, illness, or death</term> upon them, either in general or specifically, and told them that they would soon feel such things, either for the rest of their lives or to face immediate death. And everything happened according to their predictions, whether regarding a specific infirmity or the death of others. 

Because that land abounds with vassals and men-at-arms, and idleness breeds vice, women there sometimes provoked them. When these men disposed to cast off the women they had provoked and marry other honest women, it was rarely without vengeance through a **spell** <term>maleficium</term> inflicted upon either the man or the wife when the rejected women saw themselves scorned. The marriage bed remained, but not for the men as much as for the women; for it can be piously estimated that with the husbands killed or withered away, their former lovers might seek them as suitors. 

For even a certain cook of the **Archduke** <note>Referring to Archduke Sigismund of Austria, who presided over the region at the time of these trials.</note>, when he had married a virtuous young foreign girl, his mistress—a **witch** <term>malefica: a female practitioner of harmful magic</term>—in the public street and in the hearing of other honest persons, predicted a spell and death for the young girl. Extending her hand, she said: "You will not enjoy your husband for long." <note>original Latin: "Non diu de tuo marito gaudebis"</note> Immediately the following day the girl took to her bed, and after a few days she paid the debt of all flesh <note>An idiom for dying.</note>, attesting in her final moments: "Look, I am dying thus because that woman, with God permitting her spells, is killing me; and surely for the better, God is arranging other nuptials for me in heaven." 

Thus, finally, by spells a certain knight was killed, as public fame testifies; and so too many others whom I omit to mention. Among these was a certain nobleman who, when he was unwilling to spend the night with his mistress at her whim and had sent word through his servant 

<column-break/>

that he could not spend the night with her that evening because he was hindered by certain business. She, indignant, ordered the servant: "Tell the nobleman: He will not vex me for long." <note>original Latin: "Non diu me vexabit"</note> And so, on the following day he fell ill, and after a few days he was buried. 

There are also such **witches** <term>malefice</term> who know how to bewitch judges by their look alone and the gaze of their eyes. They even boast publicly that the judges can bring no trouble upon them. Furthermore, for any who are detained for criminal cases and exposed to the gravest tortures to speak the truth, these witches know how to impose silence upon them so that they can never reveal their crimes. 

There are also those who, to perpetrate spells, have dishonored the image of the Crucified by striking it with whips and knives, using the most foul words against the purity of the most glorious Virgin Mary and the birth of our Savior from her untainted womb. It is not expedient to recite those words and individual acts, as they are too offensive to pious ears; nevertheless, they have been put in writing and stored. In this way, a certain baptized Jewish woman had led away other young girls, one of whom, named Walpurgis, was at the point of death in that same year. While she was urged by those standing by to confess her sins, she cried out: "I have surrendered my body and soul to the devil, and there is no hope of pardon for me." <note>original Latin: "Corpus et animam tradidi diabolo nec spes mihi adest venie"</note> And so she died. 

All these things are recorded not for ignominy, but for the praise and glory of the most illustrious Archduke, since indeed, as a Catholic prince and chief zealot of the faith, he labored greatly with the assistance of the Most Reverend Ordinary of **Brixen** <note>The Bishop of Brixen, whose diocese included Innsbruck.</note> toward their extermination. These things are recited rather to inspire detestation and hatred of such a great crime; for if men do not cease to avenge injuries against other men, how can they suffer injuries against the Creator and insults to the faith, even without regard for temporal losses? For this is the concern of all of them.

From these things, this sacrilegious offering effects three things in the boy. First, just as an outward offering is made to God in sensible things—namely in wine, bread, or the fruits of the earth—and this is a sign of due subjection and honor, according to that of Ecclesiasticus 35:
