...fire, that is, the torment of hellfire. <note>original: "fus id est cruciationis ignis infernalis"</note> For no one is ever punished with these [eternal] penalties without their own fault, either contracted through original sin or committed through actual sin. But the second authority <note>referring to a legal citation</note> is understood to apply to those who imitate the crimes of their fathers, as **Gratian** <note>Johannes Gratian, a 12th-century jurist who founded Canon Law</note> explains in Case 1, Question 4, at the section beginning "to whom." There he also gives other explanations. Therefore, by any other penalties in the judgment of God, a person is punished not only for their own fault—whether committed or to be committed (so that it may be avoided)—but also for the fault of another. 

Nor is the argument valid that a person is then punished without cause and without fault, which ought to be the cause of the penalty; for according to the rule of law, no one is to be punished without fault unless there is a cause. From this, we can also say that there always remains a cause, even a most just one, although it is unknown to us. As **Augustine** says in Case 23, Question 4: "Even if we cannot penetrate the depth of God's judgments regarding the action taken, nevertheless we know that what He said is true and what He did is just."

There is, however, a distinction regarding children who have been offered. When speaking of innocents who are not offered by **witch-mothers** <term>matres maleficas: women practicing harmful magic</term> but are stolen secretly by midwives and snatched away, as was said above, from the embraces and the womb of an honorable mother: it is piously to be believed that such innocents are not so abandoned as to become imitators of such great crimes, but rather imitators of their parents' virtues.

The second effect of this sacrilegious offering is this: just as in an offering where a man offers himself to God as a sacrifice, he recognizes God as his beginning and his end—which sacrifice is indeed more worthy than all other external sacrifices performed by him, according to that scripture:

> The sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. <note>Psalm 51:17</note>

And this pertains to the beginning of creation and the end of glorification. In the same way, the **witch** <term>malefica</term> offering a child to the devil commends its soul and body to him as to its beginning and its end of eternal damnation. Hence, it cannot

<column-break/>

be freed from the payment of such a great debt except by a miracle. A certain story—indeed, several—is usually recited concerning children unexpectedly offered by their mothers to demons from the womb, perhaps out of some passion or mental disturbance. It is told how, with the greatest difficulty in their adult age, they were able to be liberated from the jurisdiction of demons, which the demons had usurped by divine permission. 

The *Book of Examples of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary* is known to be filled with such accounts. Specifically, there is the story of one who could not be freed from the vexations of demons even by the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note>. He was finally sent to a certain holy man living in Eastern regions, and even then, with great difficulty, he was snatched from that jurisdiction through the intercession of the most glorious Virgin herself. 

Thus, regarding the vengeance following a single unexpected act—I will not call it an offering, but a "handing over"—where a mother, out of mere indignation regarding the carnal union to be performed with her husband, when the husband had said, "I hope for fruit [a child] to come from this," and she replied, "Let that fruit be given to the devil." The severity of divine punishment was so clear that it is believed to rage wherever such a great offense to the Divine Majesty is perceived.

The third effect of this sacrilegious offering is an habitual inclination toward performing such **witchcraft** <term>maleficia</term> against humans, cattle, and the fruits of the earth. The reason for this can be assigned from the things which, according to **Thomas [Aquinas]** in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 108, are reduced to the temporal punishment by which some are punished for the faults of others. 

For he says that because children are, according to the body, a certain "thing" belonging to the father, and slaves and animals are things belonging to their masters—and since a person is to be punished in all his "things"—therefore children are frequently punished for their parents. And this reason differs from the one touched upon above concerning the sins of fathers, where God "visits the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation." For as discussed there, this is understood to apply to those who imitate the crimes of their ancestors.

Furthermore, reason does not conclude that children should be punished for their parents where they do not imitate their father’s crimes in action through evil works, but only in their disposition. Also, the animals of the **Amalekites** <note>A biblical tribe frequently cited in legal texts regarding divine punishment extending to property and offspring</note> were ordered to be killed, although in such matters there is a mystical reason, as held in **Canon Law** <note>original: "I. q. iij. §. paruulos" referring to the Decretum Gratiani</note>. Finally, experience demonstrates that the daughters of **witches** <term>maleficarum: women who practice harmful magic</term> are always defamed as being similar imitators of their mothers' crimes; indeed, nearly the entire lineage is infected. And the reason for this and all preceding points is because they always have a successor to leave behind, and they strive with the greatest efforts to increase that faithlessness by means of a **pact entered into with a demon**. <note>original: "ex pacto cum demone inito"</note> For how else could it happen, as has very often been discovered, that young girls before the age of puberty—such as eight or ten years old—have stirred up storms and hailstorms, unless through such a pact and under such a sacrilegious offering to the devil, the mother, a witch, had raised the infant? For children could not perform such things by themselves through a denial of the faith (as adult witches have to do from the beginning) since they perhaps have no knowledge of any article of the faith. Let us bring forward some of these deeds into the open. For in the regions of **Swabia**, <note>A historic region in southwestern Germany</note> while a certain peasant had decided to look at the crops in the fields with his little daughter, barely eight years old, and because of

<column-break/>

the dryness of the earth, he was mulling over and wishing for rain, saying: "Alas, when will the rain come?" The girl, hearing her father's words, said out of the simplicity of her soul: "Father, if you desire rain, I will make it come quickly." But the father said: "How is this possible for you? Do you know how to procure rain?" The girl responded that she certainly knew how to stir up not only rain, but also hailstorms and tempests. And the father asked: "Who taught you?" She responded: "My mother. But she forbade me from telling this to anyone." Then the father asked again: "And how did she teach you?" She responded: "She committed me to a certain master, whom I can have at any hour for whatever things are requested." But the father asked: "Have you seen him?" She responded: "I have sometimes seen men entering and leaving to see my mother." And when she had asked who they were, she [the mother] responded: "They are our masters to whom I have also handed you over and committed you; they are great patrons and wealthy men." The father was terrified. He inquired whether she could stir up hail at that very hour. And the girl said: "Certainly, if I have a little water, I will do it." Then the father led the girl by the hand to a stream. "Do it," he said, "but only over our own field." Then the girl put her hand into the water and moved it in the name of her master according to the teaching of her mother. And behold, rain drenched only that field. Seeing this, the father said: "Make hail too, but only over one of our fields." When the girl had done this again, the father, being certain from the experience, accused his wife before a judge. She was captured, convicted, and **burned to ashes**; <note>original: "incinerata fuit"</note> the daughter was baptized anew and dedicated to God, and she was no longer able to perform those things.

...is concerning property, wishing by this to imply that although all things are subject to divine providence, both men and beasts—preserving each according to their measure, as the **Psalmist** says: *men and beasts Thou shalt preserve, O Lord* <note>Psalm 36:6; original Latin: "homines et iumenta saluabis domine"</note>—yet the children of men are governed more fully under the cover and protection of His wings. If, I say, men—the innocent, the just, and sinners alike—are afflicted by **witches** <term>maleficos: practitioners of harmful magic</term> through divine permission, and parents are even afflicted in their children (who are property pertaining to them); since the beasts of the earth and the fruits of the field are similarly among the property of men, no one should presume to doubt that various harms can be inflicted upon them by witches, provided divine permission concurs.

For thus was **Job** struck by the devil and lost all his livestock <note>Referring to the biblical story of Job's trials in Job 1:14-16</note>. Finally, there is not even the smallest village to be found where women do not cease to mutually infect cows, deprive them of milk, and very often kill them. Beginning with the smallest harm, which can be seen in the deprivation of milk: if it is asked by what means they are able to effect this, it can be answered that, according to **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher</note> in his work *On Animals*, milk is by nature similar to the menses in any animal. Just as any other flow in a female is restricted by some infirmity—either by natural condition or accidental illness—it is also sometimes restricted or taken away by the work of **witchcraft** <term>maleficiali opere: the work of harmful magic</term>. By natural condition, milk is restricted after the fetus is conceived. By accidental illness, it happens as if from the eating of some herb which by its nature restricts milk and alters the cow. 

By witchcraft, however, they procure such things in various ways. For some, during the night and with consecrations—certainly at the instigation of the devil to cause a greater offense to the Divine Majesty—place themselves in any corner of their house holding a jug between their legs. And while they fix a knife or some tool into the wall or a column and apply their hands as if for milking, they then invoke their **devil** <term>diabolum: the demon or familiar assisting the witch</term> who always cooperates with them in all things.

<column-break/>

They declare that they intend to milk such-and-such a cow from such-and-such a house, whichever is tastier and more abundant in milk. Then suddenly, the devil receives the milk from the udders of that cow and brings it to the place where the witch resides, making it flow from that tool. 

Indeed, in preaching these things to the people, no one is "informed" or taught how to do them, because no matter how much someone might invoke a demon and estimate themselves able to effect these things through bare invocation, they would only deceive themselves. This is because they lack the foundation of that treachery—namely, they have not performed **homage** <term>omagium: a formal ritual of submission to the devil</term> and have not **denied the faith** <note>original: "fidez nō abnegauit"</note>. Therefore, I have set this down because many believe these and other matters should not be proposed to the people due to the danger of providing "information" (instruction). Yet, it is impossible for anyone to be instructed through preaching for the reason touched upon. Rather, these things should be preached for the detestation of such a great crime, and so that judges might burn more fiercely for the punishment of such a great wickedness—that is, the denial of the faith. 

Although one need not always do so, secular people weigh these kinds of temporal losses more heavily, as they are more entangled in earthly affections than spiritual ones. This follows the determination of the **Doctor** <note>Referring to Peter Lombard</note> in the *Second Book of the Sentences*, distinction 8, regarding the difficult question: *Whether using the help of demons constitutes apostasy from the faith.* For while **Albertus Magnus** <note>13th-century polymath and theologian</note> agrees with other doctors, he states more explicitly that in such matters there is always an **apostasy of word or of deed**.

## Chapter XV

Finally, that demons and their disciples can stir up such witchcraft in the form of lightning, hail, and tempests—having received power from God in the case of demons, or His permission in the case of their disciples—is testified by the **Holy Scripture** in **Job**, chapters one and two. There, once power had been received from God, the demon immediately arranged for the **Sabeans** <note>A group from South Arabia mentioned in the Bible as raiders</note> to carry off five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred she-asses; then, fire descending from heaven consumed seven thousand camels. Finally, his seven sons and three daughters were killed by a violent wind and the collapse of the house. Also, many boys—that is, servants—perished, as one might report. Furthermore, the demon struck the holy man’s body with the worst sores and arranged for his wife and three friends to grieve him heavily. 

On this point, **Saint Thomas Aquinas** in his commentary <term>postilla: a marginal or biblical commentary</term> on Job speaks thus: "It must be confessed that, by God's permission, demons can bring about disturbances of the air, stir up winds, and make it so that fire falls from heaven." For although **corporeal nature** <note>The physical world</note> does not obey the will of angels—neither good nor bad—in the receiving of forms <note>Spirits cannot create life or change the fundamental "essence" of a thing, which only God can do</note>, but only obeys God the Creator; nevertheless, in terms of **local motion**, corporeal nature is born to obey spiritual nature. Evidence of this appears in man; for at the sole command of the will (which is subjectively in the soul), the limbs are moved to follow the work arranged by the will. Therefore, whatever can be done by local motion alone, these things can be done by natural power not only by the good [angels] but also by the evil ones, unless they are divinely prohibited. Winds, however, and rain and other things of this sort...

The points noted above regarding the question of whether witches must always cooperate with demons to inflict <term>maleficium: harmful magic or bewitchment</term> could also apply here. The "Doctors" <note>Theologians and scholars of the Church</note> also serve this point in their commentary on the Second Book of *Sentences*, distinction 6, regarding whether the "dark air" is considered a fitting place for bad angels to move. Since three things are considered in demons—their nature, their office, and their guilt—just as the highest heaven <note>The Empyrean</note> would correspond to their nature and hell to their guilt, so the dark air is suitable for their office, since they are "torturers" and ministers (as mentioned above) for the punishment of the wicked and the testing of the good. This is so that they do not infest us too much, which they would do if they lived among us in the lower world. Therefore, in the air and around the sphere of fire <note>In the medieval cosmos, the sphere of fire sat just below the moon</note>, they know how to join "active" elements with "passive" ones <note>A medieval scientific theory that demons could cause effects by bringing natural causes and effects together more quickly than nature could</note> where they are permitted by God; they even cause fire to fall from heaven or produce lightning and thunderbolts.

In the *Formicarius* <note>Johannes Nider’s "The Anthill," a famous 15th-century work on witches</note>, a story is told of a certain man captured by a judge. When he was asked how they proceeded to stir up hail and storms, and whether it was easy for them to procure this, he responded: "We procure hail easily, but we are not able to strike wherever we wish." **Note here the protection of the good angels.** For he added: "We can only strike those who are destitute of God’s help, and those who fortify themselves with the sign of the cross we cannot harm." This is our method: first, with certain words in the fields, we implore the prince of

all demons to send one of his followers to strike the place we designate. Then, when a specific demon arrives, we sacrifice a black chicken to him at a crossroads <note>original: "biuio"—a place where two ways meet, traditionally associated with magic</note> by throwing it high into the air. Once the chicken is taken by the demon, he obeys, and immediately stirs up the air—yet not always in the places we have designated, but rather he casts down hail and lightning according to the permission of the living God.

It is also narrated in the same place about a certain author or "heresiarch" <note>a leader of a heretical sect</note> of witches named **Stafus**. Living in the territory of Bern and the surrounding areas, he used to boast publicly that whenever he wished, he could make himself appear like a mouse in the eyes of all his rivals and thus slip away from the hands of his deadly enemies; and in this way, he had very often escaped the hands of those who sought his life. However, when Divine Justice wished to put an end to his malice, he was sitting near a window in a certain room <note>original: "stupa"—a heated room or bath</note> while his enemies were cautiously scouting for him. These two knew how to transfer a third part of the hay or grain—or any other thing—from a neighbor's field to their own field without anyone seeing, whenever they pleased. They could procure the most violent hail and harmful winds with lightning; they could throw infants walking near water into it without anyone seeing, even in the sight of their parents; they could cause sterility in men and beasts, reveal hidden things to others, and harm in whatever ways possible in both property and bodies. Sometimes they could kill whomever they wished with a stroke of lightning and procure many other pestilential things, wherever and whenever God’s justice permitted these things to happen.

It crushed all the fruits, crops, and vineyards over a width of one mile to such an extent that for three years the land was judged to be barely fertile.

### ->Concerning the three ways in which men, and not women, are found to be infected by harmful spells. In three chapters. And first, concerning the archer-sorcerers.<-

Turning now to the present type of sorcery by which men are infected in three species. It must first be noted concerning the gravity of the crime regarding the archer-sorcerers that it consists of seven horrendous atrocities. 

For first, on the most sacred day of the Lord's Passion, namely <note>original: "feria paraſceue"</note> Good Friday, during the solemnity of the Mass, they take a most sacred image of the Crucifix and shoot at it with an arrow as if at a target. What great cruelty and injury to the Savior! 

Second, although it is debated whether there is another <term>apostasy: the formal rejection of one's religious faith</term> beyond that of the work they do in entering a pact with demons, nevertheless, in whatever way it happens, no greater insult can be inflicted on the faith by a Christian. It can be estimated that he does this in denial of the Most Holy Trinity. With those three shots spent, he could only shoot arrows by chance like anyone else.

He fulfilled exactly what he predicted: for when everyone except one had been killed as promised, the castle was taken. He hung the ring on his own house in Rohrbach in the Diocese of Worms, and it is seen hanging there to this day.

When he confessed his crime to those inquiring about the event, he was moved from the place by the touch of <term>public justice: the official executioner or legal authority</term> and received a miserable death, a worthy vengeance for his committed crimes. <column-break/>

terrified by these things so as to refrain from similar outrages. For in the courts of the great, as it is said, such men are supported everywhere; they are permitted to boast of their outrages and brag of such things to the public contempt of the faith, the heavy offense of the divine majesty, and the insult of our Redeemer. Whence, are not such men, as well as those who receive, defend, and favor them, to be judged not only as heretics but as apostates from the faith? They are to be punished with the penalties written below, and this is the seventh atrocity. For first, they are excommunicated by the law itself, and the clergy who favor them are deposed and deprived of every office and benefice, nor are they restored to them without a special <term>indult: a specific grant of favor or exemption</term> from the Apostolic See. Likewise, the aforementioned harborers, after they have been publicized, if they remain in excommunication for a year with a stubborn soul, they are to be condemned as heretics. Each of these points is proven as follows: For in the chapter *Ut inquisitionis*, section *prohibemus*, of the <term>Liber Sextus: the "Sixth Book" of Canon Law, promulgated in 1298</term>, it treats of not hindering, directly or indirectly, the process and judgment of diocesans and inquisitors in cases of the faith, where the aforementioned penalty to be inflicted after a year is mentioned. For it says first: "We strictly prohibit..."—if it pleases anyone, let him read the chapter. Finally, that the sorcerers themselves along with their harborers are excommunicated by the law itself is clear regarding the heretics and their <term>maleficia: harmful sorcery</term> in the chapter *Ad abolendam* <note>original: "ad abolendā"</note> at the beginning, and in the chapter *Excommunicamus* <note>original: "excoicam⁹"</note>, first and especially, and more briefly in the second chapter *Excommunicamus* concerning heretics, where it says: "We excommunicate and anathematize all heretics, <term>Cathars: a dualist heretical sect</term>, <term>Paterines: another name for the Cathars or similar heretical groups</term>," and so on, "and others by whatever names they may be known." And note the phrase "by whatever names." Concerning believers, however, and harborers and the others mentioned above, it is held in the first chapter *Excommunicamus*, in the section *Credentes*, where it says: "Furthermore, we decree that the believers, harborers, defenders, and favors of such men are subject to excommunication," and so on. And in the second chapter *Excommunicamus*, several penalties are touched upon which they incur within a year along with the clergy themselves, where it says: "We decree that harborers, favors, and defenders are subject to excommunication, so that after any such person has been noted for excommunication, if he scorns to make satisfaction within a year, from then on he is <term>infamis: a legal status of infamy, losing civil and legal rights</term> by the law itself, nor is he to be admitted to public offices or councils, nor to electing others to such positions, nor to giving testimony..."

...caught in heretical depravity, as will appear below, shall face the **due penalty**. This is done so that he may grieve for his past actions and may never again harbor such people; as a Catholic prince should, he must remain firm in his soul.
¶ If it is asked: To whom should he be handed over? In what order should he be punished? And should he be judged as one manifestly rebuked for heresy? Regarding the first point, a difficulty is specifically touched upon at the beginning of the third part: namely, whether their punishment belongs only to the **secular judge** <note>a civil or royal judge, rather than a church official</note> and not to the ecclesiastical one. For it is manifest through the chapter *Ut Inquisitionis* <note>original: "c. vt inquisitōis"; a chapter in Canon Law regarding the Inquisition</note>, section *Prohibemus* in Book VI, that temporal powers and lords are forbidden from judging the crime of heresy in any way without the permission of the bishops or inquisitors, or at least one of them. However, the reason assigned there does not seem to apply to **sorcerers** <term>malefici</term> <note>those who practice harmful magic</note>. For it is stated there that they should not judge because the crime of heresy is purely ecclesiastical; yet the crime of sorcerers does not seem to be purely ecclesiastical, but also civil, because of the temporal damages they cause. Nevertheless, as will appear below, although it belongs to the ecclesiastical judge to acknowledge and judge the case, it belongs to the secular judge to execute the sentence and punish, as is clear in the chapters *Ad abolendam*, *Exgentis*, and *Excommunicamus*. Hence, even if the secular judge hands such a person over to the **Ordinary** <note>the local Bishop or official with standard jurisdiction</note> to be adjudicated, the secular judge must still punish the person himself after they have been handed back or left to him by the bishop. Alternatively, with the bishop's consent, the secular judge can do both: judge and punish. Nor is it valid to argue that such sorcerers are not heretics but rather **apostates** <note>those who completely renounce their faith</note>. For while both involve the faith, just as a heretic doubts the faith in whole or in part, so too does the reason of "sorcerer-apostates" dictate for itself. For since it is a graver matter to corrupt the faith—by which the soul has life—than to forge money—by which temporal life is supported—it follows that if counterfeiters of money or other evildoers are immediately handed over to a just death by secular powers, how much more so can such heretics and apostates be **justly killed** as soon as they are convicted. Hence, this provides the answer to the second point: by what order and by which judge they should be punished. But this will be treated more clearly in the third part of this work regarding the methods of sentencing, specifically how one manifestly rebuked for heresy is to be sentenced, regarding the eighth and twelfth methods. And regarding the

<column-break/>

doubt: what if he should repent? Would he still have to be killed? In truth, if a simple **relapsed heretic** <note>someone who has fallen back into heresy after previously recanting</note> repents, no matter how much he does so, he is still to be killed according to the chapter *Ad abolendam* cited above. This is reasonable according to **Thomas Aquinas** <note>original: "thomā"; the influential 13th-century theologian</note>, since this provides for the **common good**. For if returning heretics were always received back so as to be preserved in life and other temporal goods, this could prejudice the salvation of others—both because they might infect others if they relapsed again, and because if they escaped without penalty, others would more securely fall back into heresy. From the very fact of their relapse, their inconstancy regarding the faith is presumed. Therefore, they are justly killed. For this reason, it must be said here that if, due to the mere suspicion of inconstancy, the ecclesiastical judge must hand over a relapsed person to the secular court for execution, then all the more so—even if he does not wish to hand over an apostate or sorcerer to the secular court because of his repentance and conversion—he must nevertheless leave him to it and not impede the secular judge when that judge wishes to kill him according to the laws because of the temporal damages the sorcerer caused. However, the ecclesiastical judge must first **absolve** the repentant sorcerer from the **excommunication** <note>the act of being cut off from the Church and its sacraments</note> which he incurred because of the heresy of sorcery, even if the heretic is excommunicated according to the chapter *Excommunicamus*, and receive him into the bosom of the Church so that his spirit may be saved, as is said in the eleventh section. Other reasons are assigned below regarding the first question of the third part. Let this suffice for now. Only let the rulers of souls take heed: a harsh and strict account will be required of them by the **Tremendous Judge** <note>God at the Last Judgment</note>, since indeed a most severe judgment awaits those who rule, especially where they permit such people to live to the injury of the Creator.

These vary: for there are some who agree with the aforementioned **archer-sorcerers** in that they learn such things through insults offered to an image of the **Crucifix**. For example, if he wishes not to be harmed in the head by any iron or blow, he must remove the head of the image; if he wishes it for his neck, he removes the neck; if for his arm...

### The following is the second main section of this second part, concerning the methods of removing and curing witchcraft, beginning with the difficulty of the matter.

The question is whether it is lawful to remove **witchcraft** <term>maleficia</term> <note>the harmful effects or charms produced by a sorcerer</note> through other witchcraft or through any other illicit means. It is argued that it is not, because using the help of **demons** <term>demonum</term> is not lawful, as was shown above. It is commonly determined by the doctors in the second book of the *Sentences*, distinction seven, that such an act is **apostasy** from the faith. Furthermore, it is proved that witchcraft cannot be dissolved without the help of demons. This is because it is dissolved either by human skill, by diabolical skill, or by divine power. It cannot be the first, because an inferior power cannot break a superior one, since nothing acts beyond its own strength. Nor is it divine power, because that would be a **miraculous work**; God performs such works at His own will and not at the urging of men. This is similar to how Christ responded to His mother when she asked for a miracle to help with the lack of wine—as the doctors explain, Christ, desiring the miracle of conversion, replied: "Woman, what is that to me and to you?" <note>referring to the Wedding at Cana, John 2:4</note>, meaning they did not share a common purpose in the miraculous work. It also appears that people are very rarely freed, no matter how much they implore divine help and the intercession of the saints. Therefore, they can only be freed by the help of demons, which nonetheless is not lawful to seek. Furthermore, this practice is commonly tolerated in general use, even if it is illicit. For it is common practice that those who are bewitched run to **superstitious little women** <note>original: "mulierculas superstitiosas"; a derogatory term for folk healers or "cunning women"</note>

<meta>catchword: sas</meta>
<column-break/>

by whom they are very often freed, and not by priests or **exorcists**. This practice shows that witchcraft is removed by the help of demons. However, since seeking such help is illicit, it is also not lawful to remove witchcraft in this way; instead, one must suffer it patiently. Furthermore, according to **Thomas [Aquinas]** and **Bonaventure** <note>original: "Tho. et Iona."; while the OCR says "Iona," this is a standard citation of Bonaventure in the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, distinction thirty-four, regarding the impediment of witchcraft: witchcraft is so "perpetual" that it cannot have a human remedy. If it does have a remedy, it is either unknown to man or illicit. In these words, they give it to be understood that it is like an incurable and perpetually inherent infirmity. Whence they add: although God can provide a remedy by compelling the demon, and the person would be cured by the demon resisting its own work, the cure would still not be human. Therefore, unless God dissolves it by Himself, it is not lawful to seek its dissolution in any way whatsoever. Furthermore, in the same distinction and question, it is said that it is illicit to apply a remedy even through another act of witchcraft. Whence he says that even if another witchcraft could be applied as a remedy, it would nonetheless be considered "perpetual" even if the witchcraft were removed, because it is in no way lawful to invoke the help of a demon through witchcraft. Furthermore, the **exorcisms** of the Church are not always effective in repressing demons regarding all bodily troubles—the judgment of reality demands this. However, they are always effective against those infestations of demons against which they were principally instituted, such as against those who are possessed or regarding children to be exorcised. Furthermore, it does not necessarily follow that if power was given to the devil over someone because of sin, the power ceases once the sin ceases; for sometimes the punishment remains even when the guilt has departed. From these words, the two aforementioned doctors seem to feel that it is not lawful to remove witchcraft, but rather to permit it just as other incurable infirmities are permitted, and to commit it only to the Lord God, who can take it away at His pleasure. To the contrary: just as God and nature do not abound in superfluous things, so they do not fail in necessities. Therefore, it is necessary that not only **preventative remedies** (which were touched upon at the beginning of this second part) but also **curative remedies** have been given to the faithful against such assaults of demons, since otherwise they would not be sufficient...

<meta>This page continues the debate from the previous section regarding the morality of using "counter-magic" or superstitious rituals to undo the harmful effects of witchcraft. It presents the conflicting views of major medieval legal and theological authorities.</meta>

...it would have been better provided by God for the faithful, and the works of the **devil** would seem stronger than the works of God. Furthermore, the gloss on that passage in **Job 41** <note>Job 41:33: "There is no power on earth that can be compared with him."</note> says that this power surpasses all human strength, even if it is subject to the merits of the **saints**; thus, it is also subject to the merits of holy men in this life. Furthermore, **Augustine** says in *On the Customs of the Church* that no angel is more powerful than us when we are joined to God in our minds; for if power is a virtue, then a mind adhering to God is more sublime than the entire world. Therefore, the works of the devil can be dissolved by such people.

**Response.** There are two formal opinions here that appear to be contrary to one another. For there are certain **theologians** and **canonists** <note>experts in Church law</note> who agree with one another that it is lawful to remove **witchcraft** <term>maleficia</term> <note>harmful magic or spells</note> even through superstitious and vain practices. This opinion is held by **Scotus**, **Hostiensis**, and **Gotfridus**, and generally all the canonists. The opinion of the other theologians—especially the ancient ones and certain modern ones like **Thomas Aquinas**, **Bonaventura**, **Albertus Magnus**, **Petrus de Palude**, and many others—is that evil must in no way be done so that good may result. They argue that a person ought to die rather than consent to such things to free themselves through superstitious and vain works. But because their sayings can be reconciled by a single distinction, their views must first be examined.

For **Scotus**, in his fourth book, distinction 34, concerning the impediment of witchcraft or concerning those who are **impotent** and bewitched, considers it foolish to assert that witchcraft should not be removed even through vain and superstitious means. For he says: "Nor is there any **infidelity** <note>lack of faith or heresy</note> in this, because the one who performs the ritual does not assent to the works of the devil, but believes that the devil is able and willing to harass as long as such a sign lasts, because by his **pact** <note>the 'Demonic Pact' where the devil agrees to serve a witch in exchange for their soul</note> he does not assist except while that sign remains. And thus the destruction of that sign will put an end to such a vexation." Therefore, he says it is meritorious to destroy the works of the devil. And because he speaks of "signs," let us give an example:

There are certain women who identify **witches** <term>maleficas</term> by such a sign: if a cow is deprived of its abundance of milk by witchcraft, they hang a jar of milk over a fire and, while insisting on certain superstitious words, they strike the jar with a stick. And although the woman strikes the jar, the devil transfers all the blows

<column-break/>

to the body of the **witch**, by which the devil and the witch are thus harassed. Although the devil is not forced nor truly harassed, he performs these things so that he may entice the **Catholic** person who is striking the jar into worse sins; therefore, it remains dangerous. Otherwise, the opinion of such a great doctor would not seem to have any difficulty. Other examples could also be brought forward. 

**Hostiensis** <note>a famous 13th-century canon lawyer</note> says the same in his *Summa Copiosa* regarding the "impotence to procreate" and witchcraft, in the gloss on the chapter *Litere*. In the section "Regarding the Woman," he says that in this defect, one must turn to the remedies of **physicians**. And although certain remedies written against these things seem vain or superstitious, nevertheless every author must be believed in his own art. Indeed, the **Church** can sufficiently tolerate "beating back vanity with vanity." **Humbertinus of Venice**, in his fourth book on the aforementioned distinction, uses these words: "Witchcraft or potions can be destroyed either through the same arts by which they were made, or by others." 

To this same point, **Gotfridus** says in his *Summa* on the same title: "Witchcraft cannot always be undone by the person who performed it, either because they are dead, or they do not know how to undo it, or the object of the witchcraft is lost. If, however, they did know, they could lawfully undo it." And he is speaking of those who used to say that witchcraft could not provide an impediment to **carnal union** <note>sexual intercourse within marriage</note> because no such thing could be perpetual, and therefore it would not dissolve a marriage already contracted. Furthermore, those who were moved to assert that no witchcraft is perpetual were moved by these reasons: they thought every witchcraft could be removed either through another witchcraft, or through the **exorcisms** of the Church which are ordained to repress the power of demons, or through true **penitence**, since the devil has no power except over sinners. 

Thus, regarding the first point, they agreed with the opinion of the others that at the very least, they can be removed through superstitious means. The **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, however, is of the contrary opinion in his fourth book, distinction 34, saying as follows: "If witchcraft cannot be revoked except through something illicit, such as through the help of a **demon** or similar means, even if it were known that it could be revoked this way, it is nonetheless judged 'perpetual' because the remedy is not lawful." **Bonaventura** and commonly all theologians feel the same where they briefly touch upon the help of a demon, which they see as being invoked either silently or expressly; they feel that nothing should be used except lawful exorcisms and true [penitence]...

<summary>This page discusses the debate between medieval canon lawyers and theologians on whether "superstitious" rituals (counter-magic) can be used to break a witch's spell. Authorities like Scotus argue it is permissible to destroy the "signs" of magic, while Thomas Aquinas maintains that any remedy involving demonic cooperation is a sin and thus the curse must be considered permanent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether it is permissible to use superstitious means to undo witchcraft. ...penance, as in the chapter *If by sorceresses* <note>original: "si per sortiarias"; a reference to a specific decree in Canon Law regarding those who use magic</note>, it is argued that he should be removed from his office. This is based on the reasons noted at the beginning of the question. And because it is possible to reconcile such great **doctors** <note>authoritative scholars of the Church</note> in their contrary sayings—and this can be done through a single distinction—it should be noted that a **curse** <term>maleficium</term> <note>a harmful spell or act of witchcraft</note> is removed either by another curse, or through some other magical act; or it is removed not by a curse, but by harmful and illicit rituals. This, in turn, happens in two ways: either through rituals that are both illicit and vain together, or through rituals that are vain but not illicit. The first remedy is entirely illicit, both on the part of the person performing it and the remedy itself. This happens in two ways: either with harm to the person who cast the original spell, or without harm. Yet, if it is done through harmful and illicit rituals, it falls under the second category; namely, where the curse is removed not by another curse, but through harmful and illicit rituals. In that case, it is again judged illicit, though perhaps not as much as the first kind. In summary, we can say that a remedy is rendered illicit in three ways: first, when it is removed by another **curse** or by other spells—that is, by the power of some **demon**. Second, when it is removed not by a witch but by an honest person, yet in such a way that through superstitious remedies, the curse that is taken away from one person is cast upon another; this is also illicit. Third, when it is removed without being cast onto another, yet the **invocation of demons**, either express or tacit, is used; then it is again illicit. According to these methods, **theologians** say that death is to be preferred rather than consenting to such things. However, in the last two cases, the **canonists** <note>experts in Church law</note> argue that removing a curse can be either licit or at least not "vain" <note>spiritually empty or useless</note>. They argue these can be tolerated when the remedies of the **Church** previously attempted—such as the **exorcisms** of the Church, the implored help of the **saints**, and true penance—have achieved nothing. And so that there may be a clearer understanding of each of these, certain deeds and acts found by us should be recounted. In Rome, in the time of **Pope Nicholas**, a certain **bishop** from the regions of Germany arrived to settle certain business. The order of charity requires us to hide his name, although he has already paid the debt of all flesh <note>a euphemism meaning he has died</note>. This man fell in love with a certain young girl, and he had arranged to send her to his own diocese along with two servants and other things and **jewels** <term>clenodia</term> <note>precious ornaments or heirlooms</note>.

<column-break/>

The young girl, with a woman’s greed for the **jewels** she had received, which were precious, began to devise a way so that the bishop would die from a **curse** while on his journey, for she already had the jewels in her possession. And behold, on the following night, the bishop suddenly fell ill. Fearing he might have been poisoned, he was examined by physicians and cared for by his servants, though they despaired for his health. For such a great heat was in his chest that he could only be refreshed by continually rinsing his mouth with cold water. On the third day, when there was no longer any hope for his life, a certain **old woman** <note>original: "Vetula"; often implying a folk-healer or someone with secret knowledge</note> urgently sought entrance to the bishop and revealed that she had come for the sake of his health. Having entered, she spoke to the bishop and promised him health, provided he would comply with her persuasions. The bishop asked what he must comply with to recover the health he so greatly desired. The old woman replied: "Behold, this infirmity happened to you by a **curse**, and it cannot be cured except by another curse; namely, that the woman herself who brought this upon you shall die and be infected with your same infirmity." The bishop, astonished that he could be freed in no other way, and wishing to do nothing rashly, decided to consult the **Pope** by means of a petition. And the **Pontiff**, since he loved him most tenderly, and having learned that he could not be freed except through the death of the witch, agreed that between two evils, the lesser should be permitted <note>original: "inter duo mala minus permitteretur"; a legal principle used here to justify the witch's death to save the bishop</note>, and he signed the petition to this effect. Therefore, the old woman was summoned again, and she explained that both he and the Supreme Pontiff had consented to the death of the witch, provided he be restored to his former health. Thus the old woman departed and promised that he would be freed the following night. And behold, around the middle of the night, when he felt himself healthy and freed from all infirmity, he sent a messenger to inquire what had become of the young girl. And behold, the messenger arrived, affirming that the girl had suddenly fallen ill around midnight while sleeping at her mother’s side. By this event, it was understood that at that same hour and moment, the infirmity left the bishop and invaded the young witch through the other witch—the old woman. And so the **evil spirit**, ceasing from its injury to the bishop, seemed to restore him to health as a side effect <note>original: "per accidens"</note>.

The **Bishop** <note>original: "Eps," abbreviation for "Episcopus"</note> finally, when he proposed to visit her for the sake of piety, was received as he entered the chamber with horrible curses, as she cried out: "May you and your mistress, who taught you such things and liberated you, be cursed forever!" Here it should also be noted that the privilege of one does not create a common law. Therefore, a papal dispensation in this case does not prove that it is permitted for everyone. To this same point, **Nider** <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), a prominent theologian whose works influenced later witch-hunting manuals</note> refers in his *Formicarius* <note>original: "formicario"; literally "The Anthill," a famous treatise on the habits of society and the dangers of witchcraft</note>, saying: 

"The method of removing a curse, or of avenging oneself on a witch, is sometimes practiced in this way. Someone who is injured in himself or in his belongings comes to a witch, seeking to know the evildoer. Then the witch would sometimes pour molten lead into water until, by the work of the demon, some image appeared in the lead. When this was seen, the witch asked the inquirer: 'In what part do you wish your bewitcher to be harmed, so that you may recognize him by that same wound?' And when the inquirer chose a spot, the witch immediately placed a puncture or wound with a knife in that same part of the image that shone in the lead, and indicated the place where the guilty one could be found. She never revealed the name, however; but as experience testifies, the sorcerer was found to be harmed in all ways just as the leaden image had shown." 

These remedies and their like are certainly judged as those in which human fragility, under the hope of obtaining pardon from God, is too often entangled—being more fervent for the health of the body than

<column-break/>

for the health of the soul. 

Regarding the **second remedy**: concerning those witches who dissolve enchantments under an **express pact** <note>original: "expresso pacto"</note> entered into with a demon without harm to the person. What should be done with them and how they are recognized will be made clear below in the sixteenth method of passing sentence. For there are many of these, and they are always found within one or two **German miles** <note>original: "miliaria teuthonicalia"; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers</note>. Within that space, whatever other witches harm, these appear to cure. Some of them boast that they cure all those harmed by witchcraft simply and for all time. Some, however, can only cure with the consent of the witch who brought the curse. 

These are noted for having an express pact entered into with a demon because they are accustomed to manifesting hidden things to those who approach them for the sake of recovering their health. For they suddenly manifest the causes of their calamity, saying that because of quarrels and brawls held with a neighbor or another woman or man, they were harmed in themselves or in their relatives. Sometimes, to hide their crimes, they even enjoin pilgrimages or other works of piety. To approach these people for the recovery of health is all the more perilous than approaching those who seem to cure only through a **tacit pact** <note>original: "pactum tacitum"; an implied agreement with a demon rather than a spoken one</note>, as they offend more greatly against the faith. 

For while on one hand they propose bodily health to God, on the other hand, they shorten their own lives through the punishment of their crime as God strikes them. Thus did divine vengeance rage against **Saul**, when he had first removed the mages and soothsayers from the land, but later consulted them, whence he was killed in war with his sons (1 Samuel 28). And the guilt is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 10. For this reason also, the sick **Ahaziah** had to die (2 Kings 1). Such visitors of witches are also **infamous**; hence they should not even be admitted to provide testimony or accusation (Case 2, Question 8, "Whoever"). Likewise, according to the laws, such people are to be punished with the death penalty, as was touched upon in the first question of this work. 

But alas, Lord God, since all your judgments are just, who will liberate the poor bewitched ones who wail in continuous pains? Our sins demanding it, the enemy has prevailed too much. Where are those who are able to dissolve those works of the devil through lawful **exorcisms**? This seems to be the only remedy that remains.

In this way, innumerable superstitious works are practiced, though they differ regarding the offense against God, since in one work the offense to the Creator is greater than in another. Because he was certain of procuring health, and because he had to visit the patient for exactly as many days as the illness had lasted, and because he used no natural medicines yet restored the sick man to health as promised, he is judged not so much as a suspect but as one clearly caught—if not in an express pact, then at least in a tacit one entered into with a demon—and should be held as an associate and punished at least according to the second mode of sentencing contained below. ## Ecclesiastical remedy against
## Incubus and Succubus demons.

Because truly in the preceding

Therefore, concerning remedies of this kind, we shall not treat them at present, but in the final part of the work, where the twenty ways of proceeding and passing sentence against and upon <term>maleficae</term> <note>witches or female workers of harmful magic</note> persons will be deduced and discussed. For the present, however, it is necessary to focus on the remedies against their harmful magical effects, and first, how bewitched men are remedied; then how beasts; and finally, how the fruits of the earth are preserved.

Regarding bewitched men in relation to <term>incubi</term> <note>demons taking male form to sleep with women</note> or <term>succubi</term> <note>demons taking female form to sleep with men</note> demons: there are three kinds. First, those women who voluntarily submit themselves to incubi demons, such as witches. As for succubi in relation to men, it is found that this is not practiced so voluntarily, since by the natural vigor of reason by which men pre-eminently excel women, they abhor such things more. There is also a second kind: those who are involved with incubi or succubi by witches against their will. And there is a third kind, and this especially concerns certain virgins who are molested by incubi demons entirely against their will; regarding whom it is also often presumed that they are thus bewitched by witches—namely, that demons, at the instance of witches (just as they are very often accustomed to inflict other infirmities), present themselves as incubi to those persons so that they might even thus be able to entice them to their perfidy.

Finally, some examples: There is in the city of Koblenz <note>original: "confluentia"</note> a certain poor man so bewitched that in the presence of his wife, he performs the entire venereal act—just as men are accustomed to do with women—repeatedly by himself. Nor can he be turned away from these acts even at the urging and wailing of his wife; for when one or three acts are completed, he repeats the words: "We want to start again from the beginning, and again from the beginning." Yet no person is seen by bodily sight to lie under him. And so it happens that after long vexations of this kind, that poor man, collapsed on the ground, is destitute of all strength. And when, after recovering some strength, he is asked how and in what manner these things happen to him, and whether he had a person lying under him, he is accustomed to answer: "It seems so to me," but he is so captivated in mind that he is entirely unable to abstain. Namely, when a particular witchcraft occurs to the body by reason of some sin. And this indeed cannot be anything but the sin of incontinence <note>original: "peccatū incōtinentie"; refers to a lack of sexual self-control or lust</note>. The reason: for as it has been said, it is because of the foulness of that act. And because through that very first sin, God spreads more [judgment], He permits more over that act than over other human acts. Therefore, even among those joined in marriage—where they are deprived of divine help because of sin—they are permitted by God to be more bewitched regarding that generative power than others. 

If it is asked what kind of sins these are, it can be said that they are sins of incontinence among relatives, as they are varied. According to that saying of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, a 4th-century Church Father</note> which is held in the text: "He is an adulterer who is a more ardent lover of his own [wife]." <note>original: "Adulter est in propria amator ardentior"; a common medieval legal maxim suggesting that excessive lust even within marriage was sinful.</note> At the same time, such lovers are more frequently bewitched in the aforementioned ways. 

The ecclesiastical remedies are therefore twofold. One is practiced in the contentious forum <note>The public church court where legal disputes were settled</note>, the other in the forum of conscience <note>The private setting of confession and spiritual guidance</note>. 

First, if impotence caused by witchcraft is alleged in a trial, then a distinction must be made: for such impotence is either temporary or perpetual. If it is temporary, it does not impede [the marriage]. It is then presumed to be temporary when, within the space of three years of living together and making every possible effort, they can be healed either through the ecclesiastical sacraments or through other remedies. If, however, they are not healed by any remedy, from then on it is presumed to be perpetual. 

Likewise, it either precedes the contract and consummation of the marriage—and thus it prevents the marriage from being contracted and voids one already contracted—or it follows the contract of marriage but not the consummation. This is a common method of bewitching men when they reject their mistresses; for then, because they hoped to be joined in marriage and were defrauded, they cast spells on the men so that they are not able to mingle with others. In such a case, as some say, it voids a marriage already contracted unless they wish to live together in continence, like Mary and Joseph. And they have for their support the canon law which says to him <note>referring to Gratian's Decretum, Case 33, Question 1</note> that marriage is confirmed by the office, namely of the flesh, as the gloss says. And a little later it says that before it is confirmed, the impossibility of the office dissolves the bond of marriage. Or, it follows a consummated marriage, and then the matrimonial bond is not dissolved. Many other things are noted by the 

<column-break/>

doctors <note>Theological authorities and legal scholars</note>. But because they are not precisely within the scope of the present speculation—and are noted in various writings of the doctors where they treat the impediment of witchcraft—therefore one should stop here. 

Only if someone were to find it difficult to understand how that act can be hindered with respect to one woman and not with respect to another: Bonaventure <note>St. Bonaventure, a major 13th-century theologian</note> responds that this is either because the sorcerer directed the demon toward a specific person for this purpose, or because God does not permit the demon to hinder [the act] with respect to just any person. For a hidden judgment of God lies here, as in the case of the wife of Tobias <note>In the Book of Tobit, Sarah's first seven husbands were killed by a demon before the marriage could be consummated</note>. 

How the devil is able to do this is clear from what has been said previously. Bonaventure also says here that he hinders the generative power, not by an intrinsic impediment—by damaging the organ—but by an extrinsic one, by hindering its use. It is an artificial impediment, not a natural one. And so he can hinder it toward one woman and not toward another, either by taking away the arousal of desire toward one or the other, and this through his own power, or through an herb, or through a stone, or through some occult nature; and this agrees well enough with the sayings of Peter <note>Peter de Palude</note>. 

<margin>
The mode of the ecclesiastical remedy
</margin>

The ecclesiastical remedy in the forum of conscience is handed down in [Canon Law] Case 33, Question 8, "If by sorceries" <note>original: "si ꝓ sortiariaf"; referring to the canon 'Si per sortiarias'</note>, where it is said: "If through the arts of sorceresses and witches, by the sometimes hidden but just judgment of God permitting it and the devil preparing it, intercourse is followed [by failure], those to whom these things happen are to be exhorted so that, with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, they make a pure confession of all their sins to God and a priest. And with a pouring out of tears and more generous almsgiving, and with prayers and fastings, they should make satisfaction to the Lord." In these words, it is noted that such things happen only because of sins and to those existing outside of a state of grace. It follows also: "Through exorcisms and other protections of ecclesiastical medicine, the ministers of the Church should take care to heal such people, if the Lord permits, who healed Abimelech and his house through the prayers of Abraham." 

<margin>
Note the remedies which should be applied to the bewitched
</margin>

In summary, we can say that there are five remedies which can be lawfully applied to such bewitched men: namely, a pilgrimage to the shrines of certain saints; and there, a true confession of their sins with contrition; the frequent use of the sign of the cross and devout prayer; and a lawful exorcism using sober words. And how this ought to be done...

## Remedies Against Spells Concerning Inordinate Love or Hatred
### Chapter III

<margin>† Question regarding "heroic love" and why it is called "love"?</margin>
Just as a spell can affect the generative power, so love-entrapment <note>original: "philocaptio"; the act of being "captured" or "snared" by an obsessive love, often attributed to magic or potions</note> and hatred are caused within the will. It is expedient first to treat its cause, and finally, as far as possible, to run through its remedies. Love-entrapment, or inordinate love of one sex for the other, can arise from a threefold cause. Sometimes it comes from the mere carelessness of the eyes. Sometimes from the temptation of demons alone. Sometimes from the spells of necromancers and witches working together with demons.

Concerning the first cause, James 1 says: "Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence <note>original: "concupiscentia"; strong sexual desire or lust</note>, being drawn away and enticed. Then, when concupiscence has conceived, it brings forth sin; and sin, when it is completed, begets death." Thus Shechem, when he had seen Dinah going out to see the women of that region, fell in love with her, seized her, and slept with her; and his soul was knit to hers (Genesis 34). According to the Gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note>, this happens to a weak soul which, neglecting its own affairs, cares for the business of others; it is seduced by habit and becomes one in unity of consent with illicit things.

Concerning the second cause, love is provoked principally by the temptation of demons. Thus Amnon loved his sister Tamar, who was very beautiful, and he suffered so greatly in her regard that he became ill because of his love (2 Samuel 13). For he could not have been so entirely corrupt in mind as to commit such a great crime of debauchery if he had not been severely tempted by the devil. Regarding this kind of love, the Book of the Holy Fathers is full of accounts of those who sought to withdraw from all temptation of fleshly love into the wilderness, yet who were sometimes tempted by the love of women beyond what can be believed. Hence in 2 Corinthians 12, the Apostle says: "There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me." The Gloss says here: "the thorn was given to me by tempting through lust." Some say that temptation to which one does not consent is not a sin, but rather

<column-break/>

the material for the exercise of virtue. This is understood concerning temptation that comes from the enemy, not from the flesh, which is a venial sin even if it is not consented to. Various examples of these things are read in various places.

Concerning the third cause—how "heroic love" <note>original: "amor hereos"; a medieval medical and literary term for a pathological, obsessive love-sickness, often thought to be a physical ailment of the brain or a result of magic</note> results from the spells of demons and witches—the possibility of this spell was treated at length in the questions of the First Part: namely, whether demons, through witches, have the power to change and incite the minds of men to love or hatred. This is also proven through various deeds and acts discovered by us. Indeed, among all spells, this is considered the least [restricted] because of its commonness.

If it is asked whether a person who is "love-captured" in such a way knows whether it happened by the first, second, or third cause, the response is: hatred between spouses can occur through the crime of adultery and the cooperation of demons, where the fervor of fleshly desire and love involves and inflames someone to such a degree that they cannot be forced to resist by any shame, blows, words, or deeds. Likewise, it is a sign when someone often leaves a more beautiful partner to cling to a most foul one. Likewise, it is a sign when they are unable to rest at night, but are so driven out of their minds that they must wander through pathless places.

Nobles, prelates, and other wealthy men are very often involved in these miseries. This is indeed that "womanly age" of which Hildegard <note>St. Hildegard of Bingen, a 12th-century mystic and polymath</note> predicted (as Vincent refers to in his *Historical Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum Historiale"; an influential encyclopedia by Vincent of Beauvais</note>), saying it would not last as long as it had endured up to that point, since the world is now full of adultery, especially among the nobles. And what use is it to write about remedies for those who abhor the remedies? Nevertheless, so that the pious reader may be satisfied, I shall briefly touch upon some.

Regarding love-entrapment without a spell, Avicenna <note>A famous 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note> proposes seven remedies for when the person is made physically ill; but these serve our study little except when many follow the path of a languishing soul. For he says in his third book that the root of the sickness is found through the variation of the pulse at the naming of the beloved. Then, if the law allows, let them be joined in marriage, for they are thus healed when nature is obeyed. Or let there be an application of medicines, which he treats and teaches there. Or let the sick person turn their love from the beloved through provoked remedies toward loving another, whom they ought to prefer over the former, and thus flee the presence of the beloved.

However, by resisting manfully, as much as they felt themselves being pushed by the allure of these fantasies, they also overcame all the devil's machinations through the aforementioned protections.

For he who hates and carries it in his heart, if he is an adult, is not easily turned back to the love of his wife even through any pilgrimages. And it has been discovered from the reports of witches that such spells are worked through serpents...

### Remedies for those from whom the male organs are removed by magical illusion, and where humans are sometimes transformed into bestial forms. Chapter IV.

<margin>The Hammer of Witches</margin>
Regarding those who are mocked by magical illusion <term>prestigiosa arte; a term meaning "the art of glamour," where the devil deceives the senses so a person sees or feels something that is not physically there</term> so that they think they lack their male organ or have been transformed into animal shapes: the remedies by which they may be relieved are clearly drawn from the preceding arguments. For since such people are entirely destitute of divine grace—which is the fundamental starting point for the bewitched—it is not possible to apply a healing plaster while the iron remains in the wound <note>A medical metaphor: spiritual healing (the plaster) cannot work while sin (the iron) remains unconfessed</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the person first be reconciled to God through true confession. Finally, as was touched upon in the second part of this work, chapter seven, such members are never in truth torn away or separated from the body, but are only hidden from the senses of touch and sight by magical illusion. It was also clear that such illusions do not happen so easily, either actively or passively, to those established in grace—namely, that their members are taken away or that their visual power is mocked as if they were taken from others. Therefore, the remedy is expressed in that same chapter when the witch herself presents herself in a friendly manner. Finally, regarding those who think they have been transformed into animal shapes: it should be known that this kind of witchcraft is not practiced so much in Western kingdoms as it is in Eastern ones. Understand this in regards to "second persons" <note>Meaning the transformation of other people</note>, although regarding the personal shapes of

<column-break/>

witches themselves, this has more often been seen among us—namely, that the witches themselves have presented themselves to the eyes of onlookers in the likeness of animals, as recalled above in chapter eight. Therefore, the remedies which will be brought forward in the third part of this work concerning the extermination of witches by the secular arm <note>The "secular arm" refers to civil courts and executioners, as the Church could not legally shed blood</note> should be applied. And indeed, the way Easterners are accustomed to remedy such illusions is recounted as follows. For we have learned many things about these matters through the truthful report of the knightly brothers of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem in Rhodes. Especially, however, this case occurred in the city of Salamis in the kingdom of Cyprus. For since there is a seaport there, and a certain ship laden with merchandise arrived, the pilgrims <note>original: "peregrini"; can mean travelers or pilgrims</note> left the ship so that each might provide himself with victuals. A certain robust young man among them went to the house of a woman situated outside the city on the seashore and asked her if she had eggs for sale. But the woman, seeing a robust young man who was a foreigner and far from his country—whereby less suspicion of his disappearance might arise among the locals—said, "Wait a little, and you shall receive everything according to your wishes." And while she delayed, shut in the inner part of the house, the young man began to call out from outside so that she would hurry him along, lest the ship happen to leave him behind. Then the woman brought out some eggs and handed them to the youth, and enjoined him that in case he missed the ship, he should return to her. He then hurried with a fast run to the ship which was on the seashore; and before entering, because all his other companions had not yet gathered, he took care to eat the eggs and refresh himself. And behold, after an hour he was made mute and, as it were, changed in mind. As he himself was afterwards accustomed to relate regarding himself, wondering at what had happened to him, he could not guess the cause. Wanting therefore to enter the ship, he was driven back and beaten with sticks by those lingering there, all shouting: "Look, look! What is this in the donkey? Cursed beast, you shall never enter the ship!" Thus the young man, driven back and understanding the words of those who affirmed he was a donkey, pondered within himself and began to realize that he was infected by the woman's witchcraft—especially since he could form no word, although he understood everyone. And when he tried to board the ship again...

Hearing the ringing of the bell—since in that kingdom services are performed according to the <note>original: "more latinorum et non grecorum"</note> Latin rite and not the Greek—at the elevation of Christ's body, he turned toward the church. Although he did not dare to enter for fear of being beaten and expelled, from the outside he fixed his knees and hind legs on the ground and, raising his fore-

When certain Genoese merchants caught sight of this prodigy, they followed the donkey in wonder, discussing the miraculous work among themselves. Behold, the witch followed the donkey with a staff. Because, as promised, such witchcraft is practiced extensively in those parts, at the urging of the merchants the donkey was seized along with the witch. Having been interrogated and "exposed to the questions" <note>A standard legal euphemism for judicial torture</note>, she confessed the crime. To be allowed to return home, she promised to restore the youth to his true form. Thus released and having returned home, the youth was restored to his former shape, and she, being captured immediately afterward, received the punishment she deserved for her crimes, and the youth returned to his own people with joy.

### Remedies for those possessed through witchcraft. Chapter V.

<margin>
<image-desc>A wavy vertical ink line marks the start of this section in the right margin.</image-desc>
</margin>
That demons sometimes substantially inhabit certain men because of witchcraft was made sufficiently clear in chapters three and ten. For what reasons this happens—not only for their own grave crimes, but sometimes for their own greater merit, sometimes for another's light sin left unpunished, sometimes for their own venial sin, sometimes for another's grave sin, and sometimes for another's crime—is also clear. Various people are possessed in various ways, some more, some less, as <term>Nider</term> <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), a German Dominican whose work "Formicarius" or "The Anthill" provided many of the anecdotes used in the Malleus</note> also recounts in his *Formicarius*. It is no wonder if, through witchcraft or at the urging of a witch, God permitting, the demon substantially inhabits a man in the way declared there—namely, what is to be understood by "inhabiting by substance." Regarding the remedies by which they can be liberated: namely, through the exorcisms of the Church, accompanied by true contrition or even confession if one were possessed because of mortal sin, as was shown in the case of the Bohemian priest. But because beyond these two remedies, three others may also be of help: namely, the holy communion of the Eucharist, the application of the bodies of saints <note>referring to visiting the shrines of saints or touching their relics</note> or the prayer of vows, and the absolution from excommunication, according to the discourse of the aforementioned doctor, which it is also useful to recount here with a full supply of necessary treatises. For regarding the Holy Communion itself, <term>Cassian</term> <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), a monk whose "Conferences" or "Collationes" were foundational for Western monasticism</note>, the Abbot, speaks in the first of his *Conferences* in these words: "The Most Holy Communion [is not to be denied] to those spirits of wickedness..."

it is read from the Council of Carthage, and is held in

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual and physical remedies for demonic affliction, moving from the benefits of the Eucharist to the specific powers and risks involved in excommunication and the office of the exorcist. For such was the power of the Apostle, says the gloss, and such grace did he possess, that he could hand over those falling away from the faith to the devil by a single word. On this point, **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** in his writings <note>original: "i. iij. di. xviij."; referring to Thomas Aquinas’s commentary on the third book of the *Sentences*, distinction 18</note>, where the **Master** <note>referring to Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note> hands down three effects of excommunication, the same doctor explains them thus. By the very fact, he says, that someone is deprived of the suffrages <note>the intercessory prayers and spiritual benefits</note> of the Church, they incur a triple disadvantage corresponding to the three benefits one gains from those suffrages. First, they serve to increase grace in those who have it, or to merit it for those who do not; regarding this, the Master says that grace is withdrawn through excommunication. Second, they serve to guard virtue; regarding this, he says that protection is withdrawn—not that they are entirely excluded from God’s providence, but from that special way He guards the children of the Church. Third, they serve as a defense against the enemy; regarding this, he says that a greater power to rage against the person is given to the devil, both bodily and spiritually.

Hence, in the primitive Church, when it was necessary to invite men to the faith through signs, just as the Holy Spirit manifested through visible signs, so too the excommunicated person was made known through bodily torment by the devil. Nor is it inappropriate for a "daughter" who is not yet despaired of to be given to the enemy; for she is not given to him as one to be damned, but as one to be corrected, since it remains within the power of the Church to snatch her from his hand whenever she wishes. Thus says **Thomas**. In such cases, however, it does not seem inappropriate for an exorcist to absolve the possessed person as a precaution.

¶ **Nider** <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), a Dominican theologian and author of the *Formicarius*, one of the earliest works discussing witchcraft</note> adds that an exorcist must be very careful not to presume easily upon his own strength, nor to mix jokes or play into a serious work, nor to add anything superstitious or suspicious of witchcraft. Otherwise, he will hardly escape punishment, as is shown by examples. For regarding the first point, **Blessed Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604)</note> relates in his *Dialogues* of a certain woman who, against her conscience, granted her husband the "conjugal debt" <note>the traditional term for sexual relations between spouses</note> on the eve of the dedication of the Church of Saint Sebastian. Because she joined the church procession against her conscience, she was possessed and raged publicly. Seeing this, the priest of that church took a linen cloth <note>original: "syndonez"</note> from the altar and covered her with it. But the devil suddenly invaded this priest as well. Because he wished to presume anything beyond his strength, he was compelled to recognize who he was through his own torment. Thus says **Gregory**. Regarding the second point—that no one should make a joke

<column-break/>

<margin>Mo</margin>
concerning the holy order of the office of exorcism—**Nider** relates that he saw in the convent of Cologne a brother who was quite humorous in his speech, but famous for his grace in expelling demons. While this man was cornered by a demon in a possessed body at the boundaries of the Cologne convent, the demon asked the brother for a place to withdraw to. Rejoicing, the brother said in a joke: <note>original: "In cloacā meā vadas"</note> "Go into my latrine." That night, therefore, when the brother wished to "purge his belly" <note>use the toilet</note>, the demon tormented him so severely near the latrine that he barely escaped with his life.

And the cry of their distinct voices began to be heard. Her relatives finally confessed this and, wishing to rectify it, presented her to the holy **Bishop Fortunatus**, who through long prayers and fasting healed her completely.

For then he would fall into error, as if they could be forced by other herbs or words in the same way, as the error of necromancers <note>those who practice "black magic" or communication with the dead</note> claims, thinking they achieve their effects through the natural and inherent virtues of such things.
