<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into whether demonic power can be overcome by human strength or natural remedies. It transitions from the discussion of spiritual authority (excommunication) to the use of physical objects—herbs, music, and stones—in the practice of lawful exorcism, citing major medieval authorities like Thomas Aquinas and Nicolaus de Lyra.</meta>

All the preceding points seem to pertain to the refutation of the presumption of necromancers <note>original: "nigromanticor̃"; those who attempt to control spirits through magic</note> who strive to enter into pacts with demons and to subject them to themselves or to constrain them in any way. Having shown, therefore, that a man cannot overcome the devil by his own power, the author concludes by saying: **"Lay your hand upon him"** <note>Job 41:8 (Vulgate 40:27). The text implies a challenge: 'try it if you can.'</note>—understand "if you can"—as if to say: you can in no way do this by your own strength. Yet he is overcome by divine power; hence it follows: **"Remember the battle"** <note>original: "memẽto belli"</note>, namely the one in which I [God] fight against him. And it can be said that the present tense is used for the future; that is, "I will fight" on the cross, where **Leviathan** <note>a biblical sea monster often identified with the devil</note> shall be caught by a hook, namely by the divinity hidden under the bait of humanity, the devil thinking the Savior to be a mere man. Hence also later in chapter 41 it says: **"There is no power upon earth that can be compared to him."** By this, he says, it is signified that no bodily power can be equaled to the power of a demon, which is a power of a purely spiritual nature.

These are the views of **Thomas [Aquinas]**. But regarding how a person indirectly obsessed by a demon can be helped by melody—as **Saul** was by the harp of **David**—it is certainly possible to be relieved by the natural properties inherent in bodies or other things. Therefore, such things can be applied, as is deduced by authorities and reasons. Thus, in Question 26, it is said to one enduring a demon that it is lawful to have stones or herbs without incantation; these are the words of **Jerome**. Likewise, the **Master of Histories** <note>Peter Comestor (d. 1178), author of the "Historia Scholastica," a standard medieval history of the Bible</note> treating that passage in **Tobit chapter 6**, where the angel **Raphael** says to Tobias: "Regarding the heart and liver of the fish you caught, if you place a piece of it upon coals, its smoke will drive away every kind of demon, whether from a man or a woman, so that it no longer approaches them," he says: "Nor should we wonder at this, since the smoke of a certain burnt tree is seen to have the same power." Who also might contain a spiritual sense in himself, namely regarding the smoke of a spiritual order. On this same point, **Albertus [Magnus]** in his commentary on Luke 9, and **Nicolaus de Lyra** on 1 Samuel 16, and indeed **Paul of Burgos** <note>original: "paul’ burdegalñ"; a prominent 15th-century Jewish convert and bishop who wrote additions to De Lyra's work</note> on 1 Samuel 16, hold this conclusion: that it seems not only must it be granted that those afflicted by demons can be relieved by certain sensible <note>physical or perceptible by the senses</note> things, but even that they might be totally freed by certain sensible things. But this is to be understood when they are not too atrociously afflicted.

And he proves this by reason: Since demons cannot transform bodily matter according to their own will, but only by joining active agents to fitting passive subjects (as **Nicolaus** says), by that same reasoning, a disposition can be caused in the human body

<column-break/>

through some sensible thing, by which the body will not be fit to receive the action of the demon. For example: **mania** <note>in medieval medicine, an imbalance of "black bile" affecting the brain</note> is a condition that greatly disposes one toward the alienation of the mind, according to physicians, and consequently toward receiving demonic affliction. When this demonic suffering occurs, if the passive affliction in the possessed person were cured, the active affliction of the demon would recede. The same could be said of the fish's liver. The same of David's melody, by reason of which, although Saul was first refreshed and felt better, the spirit was nonetheless totally expelled. Hence the scripture says: **"The evil spirit departed from him."** <note>original: "Recedebat ab eo spũs malignus"</note> Nor is it consistent with the text to say that this happened solely because of the merit of David or his prayers, because it is not likely that Scripture would be silent about this if it were a notable thing said in his praise. These are the views of the aforementioned **Paul**.

Although we [the authors] have posited above, in the fifth question of the first part, that because the power of the Cross was prefigured by the stretching out of the veins of Christ’s body, Saul was therefore delivered—and many other things are contained there that can serve the present investigation—nonetheless, let us conclude that the application of sensible things in lawful exorcisms is not superstitious. Now, however, it is expedient to discuss some matters concerning the exorcisms themselves.

->Remedies through the lawful exorcisms of the Church against whatever infirmities are brought about by witchcraft, and concerning the method of exorcising those who are bewitched.<-

### Chapter VI

...whether he is to be exorcised and the demon adjured. 
### Second main point: what should be done when the grace of health is not obtained through exorcisms.
And third, regarding remedies involving deeds rather than words, with the resolution of certain arguments. Regarding the first point, we look to the **opinion of the Doctor, Thomas [Aquinas], in the fourth book of the Sentences, distinction 23**. He says that in the order of the **exorcist** <note>one of the "minor orders" of the medieval clergy, specifically tasked with performing rites to expel demons</note>, and in all other minor orders, power is received when they are conferred so that a person may perform those duties as part of their office—for example, to perform an exorcism. And he says the same can be done licitly by those who do not hold the order, because they do not perform it by office—just as a Mass can be said in a house that is not consecrated, since the consecration of a church is intended for the purpose of Mass being said there. But in the case of those without the office, this belongs more to **gratuitously given grace** <note>original: "gratiam gratis datam"; a spiritual gift given for the benefit of others rather than the personal holiness of the recipient</note> than to the **grace of the sacrament** <note>original: "gratiam sacramenti"</note>. From these words, it can be said that although it is good to seek an exorcist possessing the power to exorcise diseases caused by witchcraft <note>original: "morbos maleficiales"</note> to liberate the victim, sometimes even devout persons without formal exorcisms, or using them, can drive away such diseases. 

For it is told of a certain poor and therefore very devout virgin whose friend had been injured in the foot by **maleficium** <note>harmful magic or witchcraft</note>. It was clear by the judgment of doctors that he could not be cured by any medicines. It happened that the virgin visited the sick man, who immediately asked her to apply some blessing to his foot. She agreed and, in silence, applied only the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles' Creed, along with signs of the life-giving cross made twice. Then, immediately feeling himself cured, the sick man wanted to know what **charm** <note>original: "carminatōnis"; used here to mean a healing chant or rhythmic prayer</note> the virgin had applied as a remedy for the future. She replied: "You people of weak faith do not cling to the divine and approved exercises of the Church, and you frequently apply forbidden charms and remedies to your infirmities. Therefore, you are rarely cured in body, because you are always being harmed in your soul. But if you hoped in the efficacy of prayers and the signs of the cross, you would often be cured very easily. Truly, I applied nothing to you except the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles' Creed, and now you are healed." By the power of this example, it is argued whether other blessings, charms, or even adjurations through exorcisms have efficacy, since they seem to be rejected here. The answer is that this virgin did not reject anything...

<margin>Note: through exorcisms and devotions, diseases of witchcraft are cured.</margin>

<column-break/>

...except illicit charms with illicit adjurations and exorcisms. To understand this, one must consider where such things originated and how they came to be abused. For their beginning was most holy, but just as all things are corrupted by the instinct of the demon through the mediation of evil men, so too are the divine names. For the Apostles and holy men, according to the last chapter of **Mark**: **"In my name they shall cast out demons and visit the sick"** <note>Mark 16:17-18</note>, and they poured out prayers over them using sacred words. Then, as time passed, devout priests performed similar things in the proper rite. Because of this, most devout prayers and holy exorcisms are found in old churches today, applied by devout men in the past to everything humans could do or suffer, without any superstition. Likewise today, learned men and doctors of sacred theology are found who, visiting the sick, apply similar words to the infirm, and not only to those possessed by demons. 

But alas! Superstitious men have invented many vain and illicit things of their own in imitation of these, which are used today for the sick and for cattle. Nor does the clergy, out of their own laziness, use the licit words anymore when visiting the sick. Because of this, **William, called Durandus, the commentator on Raymond** <note>William Durandus (c. 1230–1296), a famous medieval jurist and liturgical writer</note>, says that a religious or discreet priest, or even a lay man or woman of excellent life and proven discretion, can perform such things by pouring out a licit prayer over the sick—not over a cloth or a belt or similar things <note>referring to common folk magic practices where items of clothing were used as proxies for healing</note>, but over the infirm themselves, according to that word of the Gospel: **"They shall lay hands upon the sick."** Nor should such persons be prohibited from these acts unless it is feared that, following their example, other indiscreet and superstitious people might usurp the abuse of **charms** for themselves, defending themselves by that example. Therefore, these superstitious chanters are rebuked by the aforementioned virgin, and she said those who would consult them have weak faith, or rather evil faith. Again, for the sake of this explanation, it is asked which words of charms and blessings are judged licit or superstitious, and about the manner in which they should be applied, and whether a demon is to be adjured and a disease exorcised? To the first point: it is said to be licit in the worship of the Christian religion that which is not superstitious; and it is called "superstitious," as noted in the gloss on **Colossians chapter two**, things that have a "show of wisdom in superstition"...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how spiritual healing and exorcism can be performed licitly. It moves from the qualifications of the person performing the rite to the specific conditions required for a prayer or blessing to be considered "religious" rather than "superstitious."</meta>

<margin>
The manner in which prayer does not become superstitious. See Question 92, Article 22. <note>This refers to Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologica*, specifically the section dealing with the vice of superstition.</note>
</margin>

...observes the measure of religion. For as it is said there, **superstition** is "religion observed beyond measure"—that is, religion practiced in ways or through circumstances that are evil or defective. Furthermore, anything that usurps the name of religion through human tradition without superior authority is superstitious. Examples include adding hymns to the Masses for the dead, interrupting the preface <note>The introductory prayer of the Canon of the Mass</note>, or similarly shortening the singing in the Mass. It is also superstitious to play the organ in the choir without a respondent in the Mass, and other similar things.

But to our purpose: when a work is performed by the virtue of Christian religion—as when someone wishes to help a sick person through some prayer or blessing using sacred words, which is the matter we now intend to discuss—such a person must consider **seven conditions**. If these are found, such a blessing is judged licit. And if it is done by way of adjuration <note>A solemn appeal or command, often used in exorcisms to command a demon to depart</note> through the power of the Divine Name and the power of the works of Christ—which were made known through His birth, precious passion, death, etc., and by which the devil was conquered and cast out—then the one speaking those blessings, charms, and exorcisms is licit, and those who practice them can be called licit exorcists or enchanters. According to **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar of the early Middle Ages</note> in the seventh book of his *Etymologies*: "Enchanters are those who perform some art through words."

The **first condition** to be considered is drawn from the teaching of **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** in the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 92: the words must not contain anything pertaining to the invocation of demons, whether express or tacit. What is "express" is clear; "tacit" invocation is judged by intent and by the work itself. By intent, as when the practitioner does not care whether they achieve their goal through God or the devil, provided they get the desired result. By the work, as when the act performed has no natural property to produce such an effect. Regarding this, not only doctors and astrologers but also theologians must judge. This is the way **necromancers** work, creating images, rings, and artificial stones which certainly have no natural inclination toward the effects they very often expect; hence, the devil involves himself in their works.

<margin>
How and when the judgment should hold. See Question 92.
</margin>

**Secondly**, it must be considered whether the blessings or charms contain any unknown names; because according to **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an Early Church Father</note>, such things are to be feared lest some superstition be hidden within them. **Thirdly**, the matter of the words must not contain any falsehood; because then its effect could not be expected from God, since 

<column-break/>

He is not a witness to falsehood. For instance, certain **old women** in their charms use rhythmic rhymes like: "The Blessed Virgin crossed the Jordan, and then Saint Stephen met her and questioned her," and many other such follies. <note>The author is criticizing apocryphal folk charms that invent non-biblical stories, such as the Virgin Mary meeting St. Stephen at the Jordan River.</note> **Fourthly**, they must not contain vain signs or written characters except for the **sign of the cross**. Thus, "briefs" <note>original: "brevia"; small written amulets or folded slips of paper worn for protection</note> carried by soldiers are to be rejected. **Fifthly**, no hope should be placed in the *manner* of writing or binding, or in any such vanity that does not pertain to divine reverence; otherwise, it will be judged entirely superstitious. **Sixthly**, in the binding or uttering of divine words or Sacred Scripture, regard should be had only to the sacred words themselves, their meaning, the reverence for the thing, or the divine power from which the effect is expected—or toward the relics of the saints, from whom the aforementioned is also expected secondarily, though principally from God. **Seventhly**, the expected effect must be committed to the **Divine Will**, which knows whether health or tribulation profits the petitioner more or less, or whether it might be harmful. Thomas places this condition in the *Prima Secundae*, in the matter concerning grace, and in Distinction 15 of the fourth book.

Therefore, we conclude that if none of the stated conditions infects the work, it will be licit. Thomas proves this based on the last chapter of **Mark**: *"These signs shall follow those who believe,"* and later, *"In my name they shall cast out demons... they shall take up serpents."* From this, he concludes that if the prescribed conditions are observed, it is licit to drive away serpents through divine words.

He further proves the preceding points: The words of God and the relics of saints are of no less holiness [than other sacraments]. As **Augustine** says: "The word of God is no less than the body of Christ." <note>A common medieval sentiment emphasizing that Christ is present in both Scripture and the Eucharist.</note> But according to all authorities, it is licit to carry the relics of saints reverently with oneself. Therefore, in whatever way the name of God is duly invoked—through the **Lord's Prayer**, through the **Angelic Salutation** <note>The "Hail Mary" (Ave Maria)</note>, through His birth, passion, five wounds, the seven words He spoke on the cross, through the **triumphal title** <note>The "INRI" inscription (Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews)</note>, through the three nails, and the other weapons of the military of Christ against the devil and his works—it will be entirely licit. Hope can be placed in these things by committing the effect to the Divine Will. And what has been said regarding the restraining of spirits, the same is understood...

</margin>

...read concerning other animals. When respect is given solely to the **sacred words** and to **divine power**, one must still act with great caution regarding incantations. For as the Doctor <note>A title usually referring to St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says, such enchanters often maintain illicit observances and achieve their effects through demons—especially in the case of **serpents**, because the serpent was the demon’s first instrument for deceiving humanity.

For in the city of **Salzburg**, there was a certain charmer. One day, for the spectacle of others, he wished to enchant all the snakes within the space of one mile (as it is told) into a certain pit and kill them. When the snakes had gathered from all sides while he stood over the pit, finally one huge and horrible serpent struggled to enter. The charmer frequently signaled with a motion as if he would permit it to leave and crawl freely wherever it wished. But because he would not desist from his enchantment—all the others having already been killed in the pit, for they died there instantly—it became necessary for that horrible snake to enter. Standing opposite the charmer, the snake made a leap over the pit and rushed upon the enchanter himself, binding his belly like a belt; it dragged the charmer into the pit with it and killed him.

From this event, it is understood that such things are not to be done except for the utility of driving away harm from human habitations, and they must be guarded by divine virtue and performed with the **fear and reverence of God**.

Regarding the second point—namely, how such exorcisms or charms <term>carmina: rhythmic chants or songs often used for healing</term> are to be carried, hung around the neck, or sewn into clothing: It appears that such things are illicit. For **Augustine** says in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*: "To superstition belongs a thousand magical arts, ligatures, and remedies which the discipline of physicians condemns, whether in incantations or in certain signs which they call 'characters,' or in certain things to be hung and tied." Likewise, **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father</note> says regarding Matthew: "Some carry a certain part of the Gospel written around their neck. But is the Gospel not read and heard daily by everyone in the church? If the Gospels placed in the ears do no profit, how can they save someone when hung around the neck? Furthermore, where is the power of the Gospel: in the shapes of the letters, or in the understanding of the senses?" If the power is in the shapes...

<column-break/>

<margin>Note</margin>
...then it is well to hang them around the neck; but if it is in the understanding, then they are more profitable when placed in the heart than when hung around the neck.

But here is the response of the Doctor, especially **Saint Thomas** [Aquinas] in the place cited above, Article 4, where he asks whether hanging divine words from the neck is illicit. He says that in all incantations or hung writings, two things must be avoided. First, what is written: if it clearly pertains to the **invocation of demons**, then it is judged not only superstitious but illicit and an apostasy from the faith, as has been touched upon often. Similarly, one must take care that it does not contain **unknown names** <note>Medieval theologians feared that strange, "gibberish" names in charms were actually secret names of demons</note>. Accept the conditions placed above, and then, just as it is licit to speak such things over the sick, it is licit to carry them.

Furthermore, the Doctors have regard for and condemn it when someone pays more attention and respect to the figures and written letters than to the **meaning of the words**. And if it is said that a layman, not understanding the words, cannot have regard for their meaning, the response is: let him have regard for the **divine power**, and let him commit that power to the divine will, so that God may do whatever is pleasing to His mercy.

Regarding the third point: whether the demon and the disease are to be adjured <note>Commanded or bound by an oath</note> at the same time, or vice versa, or one without the other. 
**Response:** Here, several things must be noted. First, whether a demon is always present when a person is afflicted by sorcery. Second, what kind of things can be exorcised or adjured. Third, the manner of exorcising.

To the first: since according to **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus</note> a demon is where he works, it seems that he is always present to the bewitched person when he afflicts them. Likewise, in the legend of **Blessed Bartholomew**, the demon is seen to "heal" only when he ceases from causing injury. The response is that the demon being "present" to the bewitched and afflicted person can be understood in two ways: either regarding his essence or regarding his effect. In the first way, he is present at the beginning while the sorcery is being introduced; in the second way, he himself is not said to be present, but his effect is. Just as when the Doctors ask whether the devil substantially inhabits a man through every mortal sin, it is said "not in himself," but through his effect—just as a lord is said to "inhabit" his servant in terms of his lordship. It is different, however, for those who are **possessed**.

Regarding the second point—what kind of things can be exorcised—it should be noted...

pertaining to works...

<insert>
**The method of exorcising an evil spirit (and adjuring the devil)**

<margin>
The method for exorcising a person possessed by the devil, and specifically for one who is bewitched <note>original: "maleficiato" — someone suffering from a curse or sorcery</note>.
</margin>
...the opinion of the Doctor Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, a 13th-century theologian whose writings became the gold standard for Church law and doctrine</note> in the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 6, where he says: because of human sin, the devil receives power over man and over all things that come into human use, to man's own detriment. And since there is no agreement between Christ and Belial <note>A name for the devil, referencing 2 Corinthians 6:15</note>, whenever something is to be sanctified for divine worship, it is first exorcised. This is done so that, once freed from the power of the devil (who could have used it to harm man), it may be consecrated to God. This is evident in the blessing of water, in the consecration of a temple, and in all such things. Since the first sanctification by which a person is consecrated to God occurs in baptism, it is necessary that the person also be exorcised before being baptized. This is required by a much stronger logic than for other things, because the cause for which the devil received power over other existing things lies within the human person—namely, due to original or actual sin. This is signified by the things said in the exorcism,
<margin>
Method
</margin>
such as when it is said: "Depart from him, Satan" <note>original: "recede ab eo sathana"</note> and other similar phrases and actions performed there. To the point, then: when it is asked whether a disease should be exorcised and a demon adjured, and which of these comes first, the answer is that the disease itself is not exorcised, but the diseased and bewitched person is. Just as in a child, the "tinder of sin" <note>original: "infectio fomitis" — the theological term for the inclination toward sin</note> is not exorcised, but the infected child is. Likewise, just as the child is first exorcised and afterward the devil is adjured to depart,
<margin>
Method
</margin>
so the bewitched person is first exorcised, and afterward the devil and his "works" <note>original: "facture" — referring to the specific spell or hex</note> are commanded to depart. Furthermore, just as salt and water are exorcised, it is very beneficial to exorcise and bless everything that might be put to the use of the bewitched person, such as food and pottage. Also,
<margin>
Method
</margin>
although the rite of exorcism is maintained in those to be baptized (such as the "exsufflation" <note>The ritual of blowing or breathing upon the candidate to drive away evil</note> toward the west and the renunciation; second, the lifting of hands to heaven with a sacred confession of faith and profession of the Christian religion; third, prayer, blessing, and the laying on of hands; and fourth, the stripping and anointing with holy oil, and after baptism, communion and the putting on of white garments), it is not necessary that all this be done here regarding the bewitched person. Rather, it is required that
<margin>
Method for the specific suffering...
</margin>
he first be purely and properly confessed, hold a lighted candle if he is able, and receive sacred communion.

<column-break/>

And in place of a white garment, let a blessed candle <note>Specifically, a strip or candle measured to a specific holy length</note> the length of the body of Christ or of the wood of the cross remain bound around his bare body. It may then be said: "I exorcise you, Peter (or Barbara), though infirm, yet reborn in the sacred font of baptism: by the living God + by the true God + by the holy God + by the God who redeemed you with His precious blood, that you may become an exorcised person; so that every fantasy and wickedness of diabolical fraud may flee and depart from you, and every unclean spirit, adjured by Him who is coming to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen."

> **Let us pray.** O merciful and clement God, who according to the multitude of Your mercies correct those whom You love, and mercifully restrain for their improvement those whom You receive: we invoke You, Lord, that You might deign to confer Your grace upon this servant who suffers in his body with a weakness of the limbs; so that whatever has been corrupted by earthly fragility, and whatever has been violated by diabolical fraud, You may bind back as a member of redemption to the unity of the body of the Church. Have mercy, Lord, on his groaning; have mercy on his tears, and admit him to the sacrament of Your reconciliation, since he has no confidence except in Your mercy. Through Christ our Lord, Amen.

"Therefore, accursed devil, recognize your sentence! Give honor to the living and true God; give honor to the Lord Jesus Christ, that you may depart from this servant with your 'work' <note>the spell/hex</note>, whom our Lord Jesus Christ redeemed with His precious blood." And let him be exorcised a second and third time in the same manner as said above. "Show favor to Your creature <note>original: "facture"</note> always with Your affection. Incline Your ear to our supplications, so that You may look upon Your servant with favor and visit him with Your healing from this adverse physical health; by Your heavenly grace, grant him medicine, through Christ our Lord. Amen." "Therefore, accursed devil [etc. as above]."

### Prayer for the third exorcism.
O God, the unique protection of human weakness: show Your power upon our sick one, so that, aided by Your help, he (or she) may deserve to be restored unharmed to Your holy Church, through Christ our Lord. Amen. (And always sprinkle him with holy water.) And note that this method is prescribed not because it must be done exactly this way in every case, or because other exorcisms might not be of greater efficacy...

<meta>This page continues the instructions for addressing supernatural afflictions, transitioning from the theoretical necessity of cleansing objects to the practical liturgical steps for performing an exorcism on a victim of witchcraft.</meta>

<insert>
**Note on the method of exorcising and the prayers that come before, then what should be read and done.**
</insert>

<margin>
Note on how the instruments of witchcraft <note>original: "maleficij"</note> should be treated.
</margin>

...but so that a method of exorcising and adjuring <note>original: "exorcizandi et adiurandi"</note> may be maintained. For in ancient histories and church books, more devout and effective exorcisms are sometimes found. But since the reverence of God must be prioritized in all things, let each person act according to what is expedient, following what has been concluded from the premises, except for simple folk.

This is the method of exorcising a bewitched person <note>original: "maleficiatum"</note>: first, they should make a pure confession. According to the chapter *Afflictis*, often. If it is through sorceries <note>original: "fortiarias"</note>. Then, let a diligent search be made in every corner, and in the bedding and pillows, and under the threshold of the door, to see if perhaps instruments of witchcraft might be cautiously found. If found, they are immediately to be thrown into the fire. It will also be helpful for all things in the bedding and clothing to be renewed; they should even change their residence.

In the case where nothing is found, then the person to be exorcised shall enter the church in the morning if possible, and the holier the days are—such as the feasts of the Blessed Virgin or vigils—the more effective it will be. The priest, having also confessed and being in a good state of grace, will accomplish more. Therefore, let the one to be exorcised hold a blessed candle in their hand as best they can, either sitting or kneeling; and let those present offer devout prayers for their liberation. And let him begin the Litany, starting with: "Our help is in the name of the Lord" <note>original: "Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini"</note>, and have someone respond. Let him sprinkle the person with holy water and place a stole around their neck, and then introduce the psalm: "God, [come] to my assistance," etc. <note>original: "Deus in adiutorium" — Psalm 70</note>. They continue the Litany as is customary for the sick, saying at the invocation of the saints: "Pray for him" or "Pray [for us]," and "Be merciful, deliver him, O Lord," following each part to the end. Where the prayers are to be said, then in place of the prayers let him begin the exorcism; and he shall continue in the prescribed manner or another better way as it seems to him.

Such exorcisms could also be continued at least three times a week, so that by multiplying the intercessors, the grace of health may be obtained. Truly, after all this, the person is to be given the sacrament of the Eucharist, although some think this should be done before the exorcism. And in the confession, the confessor should take note if the person is bound by any chain of excommunication, or if they had ever been rashly bound and had not received absolution from their judge. For then, although as a precaution...

<column-break/>

<margin>
Note on what an exorcist should be and how he should prepare himself.
</margin>
<margin>
Note on exorcisms.
</margin>
<margin>
Note.
</margin>

...he may absolve him, yet once health is restored, he should seek out the judge who had bound him.

It should be noted that where the exorcist does not have the formal order of "exorcist" <note>One of the "minor orders" in the medieval Church hierarchy, though priests also performed these duties</note>, he can then proceed through prayers; and if he knows how to read the scriptures, let him read the first four Gospels of the Evangelists. Also, the Gospel "The angel [Gabriel] was sent" <note>original: "Missus est angelus" — the Annunciation, Luke 1:26</note>. And the Passion of the Lord; all of which have great power for the expulsion of the works of the devil. Also, the Gospel of Saint John: "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original: "In principio erat verbum"</note> should be written down and hung from the neck of the sick person, and thus the grace of health should be expected from God.

Truly, if anyone were to ask about the difference between the sprinkling of holy water and exorcism, since both are ordered in effect against the harassment of the demon: Saint Thomas answers where mentioned above, Distinction 6, that the devil attacks us from without and from within. Holy water, therefore, is ordered against the attack of the devil which is from without. But exorcism is against the attack of the devil which is from within. Hence those against whom a demon is said to be "energumen" <note>original: "energumeni" — a term for those possessed by spirits</note> are named from *en* (which is "within") and *geron* (carried), as if they are hiding within. In exorcising a bewitched person, therefore, both are used, since they are harassed from both sides.

Truly, as to the second main point: what should be done when the grace of health is not obtained through exorcisms? The answer is that although this can happen for six reasons, there is a seventh upon which our judgment is suspended. For if someone is not delivered, it is either because of the lack of faith of the bystanders or of those presenting the sick person; or because of the sins of those suffering the witchcraft; or because of those neglecting to apply appropriate remedies; or because of some flaw <note>original: "vitium"</note> in the faith of the exorcist; or out of reverence for the virtues existing in another; or for the purification or merit of those suffering the witchcraft.

Of the first four, the Gospel truth teaches in Matthew 17 and Mark 9, in the presence of the only son, a lunatic, and the disciples of Christ; for first, those presenting him and the crowd lacked faith. Wherefore the father prayed with tears: "I believe, Lord; help my unbelief." And Jesus said to the crowd: "O faithless and perverse generation, how long..."

<margin>
Note on the reasons why witchcraft is not cured by exorcisms.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual and physical requirements for a successful exorcism, detailing the six specific impediments that might prevent a victim from being healed and introducing the controversial remedy of conditional re-baptism.</meta>

<margin>
The manner in which, by [divine] permission <unclear>in itself...</unclear> from sins.
</margin>

...I will be with you. Regarding the second point, namely concerning the one who sustains and warns: Jesus rebuked him, that is, the son. For as the Blessed Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 342–420 AD) was a priest and scholar best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says in that place, he had been oppressed by a demon because of his own sins. Regarding the third point, the neglect of the required remedies, it is clear because good and perfect men were not present. Hence Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan teacher and influential biblical commentator.</note> says there: the pillars of faith, namely Peter, James, and John, were not present, just as they had been present at the Transfiguration of Christ. Nor were prayer and fasting present, without which Christ said, "This kind of demon will not go out." Regarding this, Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> says: if it should be necessary for someone to remain involved in the cure of any sufferers, let us not wonder, nor ask, nor speak, as if to a spirit listening in the world; rather, let us drive out our own evil spirits with fasting and prayers. And the gloss <note>A standard marginal commentary on the Bible.</note> says: "This kind of demon," that is, this instability of carnal lusts—to which that spirit was inclining—is not conquered unless the spirit is strengthened by prayer and the flesh <note>original: "caro"</note> is weakened by fasting. Regarding the fourth point, the fault of the exorcist, especially in faith, it is clear in that same passage concerning the disciples of Christ who were present. For afterwards, the disciples asked secretly about the cause of their own impotence, and He replied: "Because of your unbelief. Truly I say to you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'move yourself.'" Regarding this, Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a bishop and theologian.</note> says: the Apostles had indeed believed, but they were not yet perfect in faith. For while the Lord stayed on the mountain with the other three, and those others remained with the crowd, the faith of some of them had slackened during that time. Regarding the fifth point, it is clear in the *Lives of the Desert Fathers*, where we read that sometimes the possessed were not freed by Saint Anthony, but were freed by his disciple Paul. Regarding the sixth point, it was clear above: because a person is not always freed from the penalty when they are freed from the guilt; rather, a penalty sometimes remains as a vengeance and a satisfaction for the preceding offense.

<margin>
The manner in which some have to be baptized anew.
</margin>

And there is yet another remedy of which it is told, that many have been freed, namely that the bewitched <note>original: "maleficiati"</note> were baptized anew, though under condition <note>A "conditional baptism" is performed if there is doubt whether the first baptism was valid; it avoids the sin of "re-baptism."</note>. Regarding this, as I promised, I dare to determine nothing. Yet it shines out most clearly that when someone was not properly exorcised before baptism, by divine permission the devil always receives greater power over such a person.

<column-break/>

It is clear from the premises, and it is not doubtful that many negligences are committed, either by priests who are not well-disposed—where the fourth previously noted impediment is touched upon, namely the fault of the exorcist—or by old women <note>likely referring to midwives or laypeople performing emergency baptisms</note> who do not observe the proper way of baptizing in times of necessity. Yet I do not wish to assert that sacraments cannot be conferred by wicked men. Indeed, whoever is wicked and baptizes, he performs it, provided that he is ordained and intends to perform it, using the proper matter and the proper form of words with the intention of baptizing. Likewise, in exorcising, let him proceed rightly, not being confused or violent. Would that they might not stumble or omit necessary words by involving themselves in such sacred offices without actual or habitual intention! In truth, just as four essentials serve to complete the act—namely matter, form, intention, and order <note>In Catholic theology, these four elements must be present for a sacrament to be "valid" or "work."</note>—where one is lacking, it cannot be performed; thus one must assert the same concerning exorcisms in their own way. Nor is the objection valid that people were baptized in the early Church without exorcisms, or even that a baptized person can now receive the "character" of baptism without them. For if that were so, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> would have instituted exorcisms in vain, and the Church would rather be in error in her ceremonies. Therefore, I have not dared to completely rebuke those who wish to re-baptize the bewitched under condition, perhaps to recover what was neglected. It is also told of those who are accustomed to walk at night in their sleep through high buildings without injury, which many assert is surely the work of an evil spirit carrying them. These people are known to be better once they are re-baptized; and it is a wonder that when they are called by their own names, they suddenly fall to the ground, as if perhaps that name had not been properly bestowed in baptism. It is expedient for the reader to be attentive to those six impediments. For although they sound like they refer to the "energumenoi" <note>a Greek term for the possessed</note> or the possessed and not the bewitched, nevertheless, because equal divine power is required in both—indeed it is said to be of greater difficulty to cure a bewitched person than a possessed one—therefore, those impediments, if they can have a place there, apply even more strongly to the bewitched.

</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the impediments to successful exorcism, moving from the personal failings of the victim or the exorcist to the nature of diabolical possession itself. It explores the difference between external physical possession and the more dangerous internal possession of the soul through sin, before transitioning into a discussion of lawful versus "suspect" remedies for witchcraft.</meta>

<margin>The manner in which [one is] possessed by the devil not for one's own crime [but] for another... <unclear>through divine permission</unclear></margin>

<margin>Ma</margin>
It is proven: for as was clear above in the tenth chapter, some are occasionally possessed through no personal fault, but for a minor fault of another, and for various other reasons. In the case of witchcraft <term>maleficium; the act of causing harm through magic or demonic intervention</term>, however, when adults are bewitched, it most often happens to them that they are possessed internally to the destruction of the soul, because they are most gravely possessed by a demon from within. Hence, a double burden is required concerning those bewitched, whereas a simple burden is required for those possessed from the outside. Regarding this most grave possession, Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), a monk and theologian whose "Conferences" (Collationes) were foundational to Western monasticism.</note>, in his conferences with Abbot Serenus, says: "Those are to be judged truly miserable and wretched who, while they defile themselves with all manner of crimes and outrages, show no sign of diabolical possession <note>original: "suppletionis," likely intended as "repletionis" or "suppressionis" in context of demonic influence</note>; nor is any temptation worthy of their deeds or any scourge of correction brought against them. For they do not deserve the swift and ready medicine of this present time; their hardness and impenitent heart, exceeding the punishment of this present life, treasures up for itself wrath and indignation on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, in which their worm shall not be extinguished."

And again, the same Cassian, comparing physical possession to that of the soul through sin, says a little earlier: "It is established that those are much more seriously and ultimately vexed who, though they do not seem to be physically afflicted by demons, are nevertheless more ruinously possessed in their soul, being entangled, namely, in their vices and pleasures." For according to the Apostle's <note>Referring to 2 Peter 2:19</note> sentence: "for by whatever a man is overcome, by this he is made a slave," except that these people are more desperately ill in this regard: because they are the slaves of those demons, they neither recognize that they are being attacked by them, nor that they are bearing their lordship. From which it is gathered that, by a stronger reason, those bewitched in the body—yet not possessed by a demon from the outside, but from within as to the destruction of the soul—

<margin>Ma</margin>
are healed with greater difficulty because of the many impediments. Regarding the third main point, namely concerning remedies not of words but of deeds: regarding such remedies, it must be noted that because those works are twofold—either entirely lawful and not suspect, or suspect and not entirely lawful—we spoke of the first kind

<column-break/>

immediately above at the end of the fifth chapter, where a doubt was raised concerning herbs or stones used to repel witchcraft, and how this might be lawful. ¶ Concerning the second kind of remedies, however, which seem to be suspect but are not entirely unlawful, we must now treat them. One should pay attention to those things touched upon in the second main part of this second part of the work concerning four remedies, three of which are judged unlawful. The fourth, however, is not entirely unlawful but "vain," regarding which even the canonists <note>Experts in Canon Law, the internal religious law of the Catholic Church.</note> speak, saying that it is lawful "to beat down vanities with vanities" <note>original: "vana vanis contundere," a legal principle suggesting that a minor superstition might be used to counteract a greater evil like witchcraft.</note>. ¶ But because we inquisitors hold this opinion along with the holy doctors: that in the event that remedies through sacred words and lawful exorcisms do not suffice—and this because of the six or seven impediments touched upon above—then such bewitched persons are to be exhorted to patience, to tolerate the evils of this present life with equanimity for the purging of their crimes, and not to seek further any superstitious and vain remedies by any means. ¶ Therefore, if anyone, not content with the aforementioned lawful exorcisms, wishes to turn to at least these "vain" remedies which were touched upon above, let him know that this is not done by our will or admission. Rather, such remedies were placed and explained there so that the sayings of such great doctors as Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Medieval philosopher-theologian.</note>, Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), an influential canonist known as Hostiensis.</note>, and others on one side, and the sayings of other theologians on the other, might be harmonized in some way. We confess, therefore, with Saint Augustine in a certain sermon against sorcerers and diviners—and the sermon is titled *On Auguries*—where he says: "Brothers, you know that I have frequently entreated you that you should not observe the customs of pagans and sorcerers <term>malefici; those who perform harmful magic</term> at all, but this benefits some people very little. And because if I do not tell you, I shall have to give an account for myself and for you on the day of judgment, and it will be necessary for me to endure eternal punishments with you. Therefore, I absolve myself before God while I warn and attest to you again and again: that none of you should seek out diviners or sorcerers, nor [consult] them..."

<meta>This page continues a theological inquiry into the nature of witchcraft and demonic influence. It specifically addresses the "remedies" people use to remove curses—distinguishing between legitimate natural medicine and illicit superstitious practices. For whoever performs this evil immediately violates <note>original: "bibit," literally "drinks," but used here to imply consuming or being steeped in the consequences of an action</note> the sacrament of baptism and is instantly made a sacrilegious pagan. Unless penance comes to their aid, they immediately "drink" eternal damnation. And afterward, the text adds: no one should observe specific days for going out or returning. For God made all things "very good," and while He established one day and another, whenever the necessity of doing something or traveling arises, you should sign yourselves in the name of Christ and faithfully recite the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer; then, secure in God’s help, you may go about your business. 

However, certain superstitious people and "sons of this world," not content with these instructions and wishing to pile error upon error, attempt to defend themselves with arguments beyond the understanding and intention of Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan priest and philosopher of the High Middle Ages.</note> and the canon lawyers. They argue that because natural things possess certain hidden powers <term>virtutes occultas; "occult virtues" or properties of objects that are not immediately obvious to the senses, like magnetism</term> whose logic cannot be assigned by man—such as the way a magnet <note>original: "adamas," which can mean diamond or magnet; here it refers to the magnetic property of attracting iron</note> draws iron, and many other examples that Augustine enumerates in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*—it should therefore not be illicit to seek out such things to acquire health when exorcisms and natural medicines fail. 

This might be done, for instance, where someone wishes to procure health for themselves or another through images—not necromantic ones, but "astrological" ones—or through small pieces of cloth. Likewise, they argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies <note>The stars and planets</note>, so too do artificial bodies—namely, carved images—
<margin>Love</margin>
obtain certain hidden powers following their form from the influence of the celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies like images receive a hidden power from the heavens to cause certain effects; thus, using them and other such things is not illicit. Furthermore, they argue that demons are able to transform bodies in many ways, as Augustine says in the tenth book of *On the Trinity* and as is evident in those who are bewitched; therefore, it should be permitted to even use the power of demons to remove those curses. 

But in truth, the sayings of all the holy doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theological teachers like Augustine and Aquinas.</note> stand in opposition to this, as has been made clear here and there. To the first argument, it is said that if natural things are used simply to produce effects for which they are thought to have a natural power, it is not illicit. If, however, there are added either

<column-break/>

certain characters <note>mystical signs or symbols</note> or any other unknown and vain observations—which clearly have no natural efficacy for the task—it will be superstitious and illicit. Hence Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 96, article 2, while treating this matter at the base of the question, says that in those things which are done to induce corporal effects—such as health or something of that kind—it must be considered whether they seem to be able to cause such effects naturally. Because it is permitted to apply natural causes to their effects, doing so is not illicit. 

If, however, they do not seem to be able to cause such effects naturally, it follows that they are not being used as causes, but only as signs; and thus they belong to the "compacts of signs" <note>An implied "silent pact" or agreement where the user relies on a demonic response to a symbol rather than a natural physical process.</note> entered into with demons. Hence Augustine says in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*: demons are lured through creatures which not they, but God, created; they are delighted by various things, not as animals are by food, but as spirits are by signs—through various kinds of stones, herbs, wood, animals, charms, and rituals. 

<margin>Note</margin>
To the second argument, the same doctor <note>Aquinas</note> says that the natural powers of physical bodies follow their "substantial forms," which they receive from the influence of the celestial bodies; therefore, from that same influence, they obtain certain active powers. But the forms of artificial things <note>Man-made objects like statues or talismans.</note> proceed from the conception of the craftsman; and since they are nothing other than composition, order, and figure (as stated in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle’s "Physics."</note>), they cannot have a natural power for acting. Thus it is that they obtain no power from the influence of celestial bodies insofar as they are artificial, but only according to their natural material. 

<margin>Note</margin>
Therefore, what Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) often cited by Augustine.</note> believed is false, as Augustine notes in the tenth book of *The City of God*: that by certain herbs, stones, animals, sounds, and even certain voices and figures—and by observing the movements of the stars in the heavens—men on earth could manufacture "powers" fit to execute various effects of the stars, as if the effects of the magical arts proceeded from the power of the celestial bodies. But as Augustine adds there: all of this belongs to the demons, the deceivers of the souls subject to them. Thus, even the images that are called "astrological"...

The proof of this is that it is necessary to inscribe certain characters <note>original: "caracteres," referring here to magical signs or sigils</note> upon them which naturally perform nothing; for a mere shape is not a principle of natural action. However, astronomical images <term>astronomice imagines; talismans intended to capture celestial influence</term> differ from necromantic ones in that in necromantic practices, express invocations <note>direct, spoken requests to spirits</note> are made. Regarding the third point: man does not have power over demons such that he might lawfully use them for whatever he wishes; rather, a war has been declared against them. Let him pray that his debt be forgiven and that he be led no further into temptation, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note> says at the end of his Rule.

## Remedies against hailstorms and for bewitched livestock. Chapter VII

Finally, how bewitched livestock <term>iumenta maleficiata; farm animals like horses or oxen targeted by a curse</term> can be cured, and similarly regarding storms in the atmosphere. 
<margin>
Note.
</margin>
First, certain illicit remedies practiced by some must be noted. For some use superstitious words or deeds, such as those who treat worms in the fingers or limbs through certain illicit words and charms <note>original: "carmina"</note>. Regarding how these charms are recognized as lawful or not was touched upon in the preceding chapter. There are others who, for bewitched livestock, do not merely sprinkle holy water, but pour it into the animal's mouth. 

That the first remedy of words is illicit, beyond what was said before, William <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and philosopher</note>—who is often cited—demonstrates it thus: if there were power in words, and we speak of words as words, then it would have to come from one of four ways: from the matter (that is, the air), from the form (the sound), from the mode of meaning, or from all of these together. It is not the first, because air 

<column-break/>

does not kill unless it is poisonous; nor is it the sound, because an excessive sensory object destroys the power of the sense. Nor is it the third, for then the names "devil," "death," or "hell" would always cause harm, and "health" and "goodness" would always be beneficial. Likewise, it is not all of them together, because a whole composed of powerless parts is itself powerless. This argument holds if a defendant claims he "bestowed power upon the words," just as power exists in herbs and stones. For if any virtues <note>original: "virtutes," meaning inherent powers or properties</note> exist in certain words—whether in the sacraments or in other blessings and lawful charms—the words do not have these in themselves as words, but from divine institution, the ordering of God, and from God's pact. It is as if the Lord said: "Whoever does this, I shall grant him this grace." In this way, the words in the sacraments effect what they signify. While others believe words have an intrinsic power, the first opinion is the one commonly followed and embraced. 

Regarding other words and charms, it is clear from what has been said that as words—whether composed, spoken, or shaped—they effect nothing. However, the invocation of the Divine Name and prayer through certain sacred things, which leaves the outcome to the Divine Will, are beneficial. 
<margin>
Note regarding superstition.
</margin>
There are also remedies of works that seem illicit, as touched upon above. For instance, in parts of Swabia <note>original: "sueuie," a region in southwestern Germany</note> it is widely practiced that on the first day of May, before sunrise, village women go out and bring willow branches or other foliage from the woods or thickets. They weave these into a circle and hang them at the entrance of the stable, asserting that for the entire year all the livestock will remain unharmed and preserved from witchcraft. This remedy, according to the opinion of those who say "vanity can be used to blunt vanity," would not be illicit; 
<margin>
Manuscript note.
</margin>
nor would those who expel diseases through unknown charms. But proceeding without offense, let us say that if on the first or second day, a woman or anyone else goes out—not out of respect for the sun's rising or setting—and gathers herbs, foliage, or branches while saying the Lord's Prayer or the Creed, and hangs them over the stable door in good faith, committing the outcome of the protection to the Divine Will, this shall not be blameworthy, as noted in the preceding chapter from the words of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for his Bible translation</note>.

Moreover, as stated lastly, it is permissible to possess herbs and stones for the sake of sustaining the spirit <note>original: "animū," referring here to the psychological or spiritual state of the person</note> without the use of incantations.

To the same effect, there are those who, within vineyards or grain fields, erect the sign of the cross, or branches or flowers blessed on Palm Sunday; they assert that while crops everywhere else were damaged by hail, the grains in their fields remained unharmed. Regarding these practices, it seems one must judge according to the distinction previously touched upon <note>referring to whether the intent is pious or relies on a hidden pact with demons</note>. To the same effect: there are those who, for the preservation of milk—lest cows be deprived of it through sorcery <term>maleficia; harmful magic or spells</term>—distribute the whole quantity of milk collected on the Sabbath to the poor for free for God's sake. They assert that through this kind of alms, the cows are preserved from sorcery and even yield an increased abundance of milk. In this work, nothing is judged to be suspicious, provided that for the sake of the piety which they show the poor, they also implore divine mercy for the preservation of the animals, yet leave the outcome of the guardianship to divine providence according to His good pleasure.

Furthermore, Nider <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), a Dominican theologian whose writings on witchcraft preceded the Malleus Maleficarum</note> in his *Preceptorium* <note>a commentary on the Ten Commandments</note>, first commandment, chapter 11, says that it is permissible to bless livestock—just like sick people—using written charms <note>original: "carmina," which can mean hymns or poems, but here refers to written sacred words used as protective amulets</note> and sacred words. He says that although these seem to have the appearance of incantations, they are permissible provided the seven aforementioned conditions are observed. He also says that devout persons and virgins have had the experience that when the sign of the cross is applied to a cow, and the Lord’s Prayer along with the Angelic Salutation <note>The "Hail Mary" prayer</note> is said three times or thereabouts, the work of the demon ceases if it is caused by sorcery. 

And in his *Formicarius* <note>The Ant Hill, a famous work by Nider discussing the dangers of witchcraft</note>, it is established that sorcerers confess their sorcery is hindered by the venerated and observed rites of the Church, such as the sprinkling of holy water, the taking of consecrated salt, and the lawful use of candles consecrated on the Day of Purification <note>Candlemas</note> and palms on Palm Sunday; for the Church exorcises such things for this purpose: so that the powers of the demon might be diminished. 

Furthermore, when witches want to deprive livestock of their milk supply, they are often accustomed to ask for a little milk or butter churned from that animal from the house where the animal stays, so that consequently they might be able to bewitch the animal through their art. Therefore, let women be cautious when suspect persons of this kind ask for such things,

<column-break/>

lest they lend or give to them even the smallest amount. Furthermore, there are certain women who, when they sense they are making no progress in churning butter (as they are accustomed to wash it in oblong vessels fit for this purpose), then, if they can suddenly obtain a little butter from the house of a suspected witch, they make three pieces or lumps out of that butter, and under the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—they throw those pieces into the vessel, and thus all sorcery is put to flight. 

Whereupon they happen again to hammer a nail into the vessel—yet in a brazen way <note>referring to a folk-remedy involving metal to drive out spirits</note>, since one must borrow butter from a suspected witch. But if without this borrowing, adding the Lord’s Prayer under the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity, she were to put in three pieces—even from her own butter, or another's if she does not have her own—committing the result to the divine will, she would remain blameless. However, she might not be commended for the three pieces of butter specifically; she would be more commended if she put the sorcery to flight through the sprinkling of holy water and the mixing of exorcised salt with prayer as mentioned above. 

Furthermore, because often all livestock are killed by sorceries, those to whom such things happen should take care that the earth be removed from under the threshold of the stable door, or the manger, or where the animals are watered, and other earth replaced in those spots with the sprinkling of holy water. Because often witches have confessed that they have hidden some instruments of sorcery <note>objects used to anchor a spell</note> in those places. They confessed that at the instance of demons they only had to make a hole; the demon, however, placed the spell-object <term>maleficium; here used to mean the physical object used as a focus for a curse</term> there. This spell-object was often a very common thing, such as a stone, wood, or a mouse, or some snake. For it is clear that the devil works the sorceries by himself and does not need those things; rather, he seeks the consent or perdition of the witch, and so he compels her to cooperate in some way. 

Against hailstorms and tempests, besides those things mentioned above regarding the erected sign of the cross, this remedy is practiced: three little stones of hail are thrown into the fire under the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity, and the Lord’s Prayer with the Angelic Salutation is added two or three times. <margin>Gospel of John</margin> "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original: "In principio erat verbum," the opening of the Gospel of John</note> is used with the sign of the cross on all sides against a storm, in front and behind, and is placed in every part of the land. And then, when at the end one repeats three times "the Word was made flesh" <note>original: "verbum caro factum est"</note> and afterwards says three times that through these evangelical words this storm is put to flight, the storm will cease immediately—provided it was procured through sorcery <term>maleficium; harmful magic</term>. They judge these to be the truest experiences and not suspicious. This very act, such as when pebbles <term>lapilli; small stones</term> are thrown into the fire, would be considered superstitious if it were done without the invocation of the divine name. Regarding whether the storm could be stilled without those pebbles, the answer is: certainly, through other sacred words. By throwing them, one intends to harass the devil while attempting to destroy his handiwork through the invocation of the most Holy Trinity. One throws them into fire rather than water because they are destroyed more quickly, and thus the devil's work is destroyed more swiftly. Nevertheless, one commits the outcome of the protection to the divine will. On this matter, a certain woman accused of sorcery <term>malefica; a witch or female sorcerer</term> was asked by a judge whether storms stirred up by sorcerers could be stilled in any way. She responded: "They can, namely through this: 'I adjure you, hail <term>gradines; hailstones</term> and winds, by the five wounds of Christ and by the three nails which pierced his hands and feet, and by the four holy evangelists Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, that you descend having been dissolved into water.'" Many also confess—some voluntarily, some under torture and with difficulty—that there are five things by which they are greatly hindered: sometimes entirely, sometimes in part; sometimes so that they cannot harm a person, and sometimes so they cannot harm their friends. These are: those who keep their faith whole or observe God's commandments; those who fortify themselves with the sign of the cross and prayer; those who cherish the rites and ceremonies of the Church; those who properly execute public justice; and those who meditate on the passion of Christ in word or mind. Hence, as Nider says above: For that reason, bells are rung universally or commonly in the Church against the air <note>meaning against bad weather or "the power of the air"</note>. Then, the demons may withdraw from their sorceries as if from trumpets consecrated to God, and also so that the people, having been stirred up, may invoke the Lord against the storms. And for the same reason, one proceeds with the Sacrament of the Altar <note>the consecrated Host/Eucharist</note> and sacred words to calm the air.

Through these, anyone can recognize whether a work offered to God is superstitious (that is, observed beyond the measure of the Christian religion) or whether it pertains to the due worship and honor to be shown to God, proceeding from the true virtue of religion in both the acts of the heart and the body. Therefore, in every work pertaining to the Christian religion, let one attend to whether the work is for the glory of God, and let the person in that work give glory principally to God, so that through the work itself the mind of the person is subjected to God. And indeed, although because of this rule the ceremonies or even the judicial laws of the Old Testament are no longer practiced in the New, since we know those were under a figure but these have now been revealed in truth; nevertheless, the carrying of the Sacrament or of relics to calm the air does not seem to fight against this rule. Likewise, since the second rule is that one should attend to whether the work being done is for the exercise of the body or the restraining of lust or bodily abstinence—yet in a manner due to virtue, that is, according to the rite of the Church or according to moral teaching. For the Apostle says in Romans 12: "Let your service be reasonable." And because of this second rule, they act foolishly who vow not to comb their head on the Sabbath, or to fast on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> as if it were a "better" day, and similar things. Again, it does not seem that the carrying of the Sacrament is such a superstition. # Certain hidden remedies against certain hidden infestations of demons.

### Chapter VIII

**B**ut now once again judgment is suspended to write remedies against certain harms to the fruits of the earth, which are sometimes inflicted by worms and caterpillars <term>canifes; likely referring to locusts or destructive beetles</term> in swarms flying through the air across vast spaces of land, so that they seem to cover the earth from sight and consume from the roots up all green things, both in vineyards and in grain fields and grasses. Likewise, remedies against children changed by the work of demons <term>cambitos; 'exchanged' or 'swapped' children</term>. To the first point, however, it must be said according to Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century theologian</note> in the Second Part of the Second Part, question ninety, where he asks whether it is permitted to adjure an irrational creature. He responded that it is indeed permitted, yet by way of compulsion, which then ought to be directed toward the devil who uses irrational creatures for our harm. Such is the method of adjuring in the exorcisms of the Church, through which the power of the demons is excluded from irrational creatures. For if the intention were directed toward the irrational creature itself, which understands nothing, it would be vain. From this, it is given to be understood that through lawful exorcisms and adjurations, they can be repelled—with divine mercy assisting, however—in such a way that fasts, processions, and other devotions are first enjoined upon the people. For on account of adulteries and the multiplication of crimes, evils of this kind are sent; hence, men are to be led to confessions. In several provinces they even hurl excommunications, but then they obtain the force of adjuration over the demons. There is also another horrible permission of God over men where sometimes, after their own children have been taken away from women, other children are substituted by demons. And these children are commonly called "exchangers" <term>campsores; those who have been swapped</term>, named in German as <term>wechselkind</term> <gloss>changeling</gloss>, in a threefold difference. For some are always thin and wailing, even though four women with no shortage of milk could not satisfy one...

Some, however, are produced by the work of **incubus demons** <note>original: "incuborum demonum"; demons believed to have sexual intercourse with women</note>, although they are not actually the children of the demons, but properly belong to the man and woman from whom the demons received the seed—acting as **succubi** <note>original: "succubi"; demons taking female form to collect seed from men</note> or polluting men in their sleep. For by divine permission, demons sometimes substitute these children, having taken away the parents' own children. There is also a third kind, where sometimes demons appearing in the form of small children join themselves to nurses. Common to all three types is that they are very heavy, gaunt, do not grow, and no abundance of milk can satisfy them, as was mentioned before. And it is often said that they simply vanish.

But why does **Divine Piety** permit such things? It can be said that it is for a twofold cause. First, because parents love their children too much; therefore, for their own benefit, God permits such things. Second, because it must be presumed that the women to whom such things happen are for the most part superstitious and are seduced by demons in many other ways. Hence the Lord, who is a true **jealous lover** <note>original: "zelotes"; from the Greek "zelos," implying a passionate, protective guardianship</note> according to a righteous zeal—which is a vehement love for His own bride <note>the human soul</note>—will not only refuse to allow another to approach her, but, like a jealous husband, cannot even endure signs of adultery or suspicion regarding the soul He bought with His precious blood and betrothed through faith. He cannot tolerate this in touch, in conversation, or in any kind of approach with the enemy, the devil, the adversary of salvation. And if a jealous husband cannot endure the signs of adultery, how much then is He troubled when adultery is actually committed? Thus, it is no wonder if a person's own children are taken away and "adulterous" ones are substituted. 

Indeed, so that these things may be more strongly impressed, and to show how much He watches over the soul and refuses to endure even signs that cause suspicion, He gave the **Ancient Law**. In that law, to distance His people thoroughly from idolatry, He prohibited not only idolatry itself but many other things which could provide an occasion for idolatry. These things might not seem to have a practical use in themselves, yet they wonderfully retain a mystical sense. Thus, He not only said in Exodus 22: "You shall not permit sorcerers <note>original: "maleficos"</note> to live upon the earth," but He also added: "Let them not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin." Just as a woman who facilitates adultery <note>original: "copulatrix"</note> is killed and is not permitted to be cleansed among men.

<column-break/>

Note the zeal of God in Deuteronomy 22, where He commanded that if you find a nest with eggs or chicks with the mother bird sitting upon them, you shall not take the mother and the young together, but you must let the mother fly away. He commanded this because the pagans used to turn such signs toward fertility or sterility; the Lord, as a **jealous lover** of His people, would not endure such a sign of adultery. In the same way today, old women judge the finding of a coin to be a sign of great luck, and the opposite when they dream of treasure.

Likewise, He commanded all vessels to be covered, and any vessel not having a lid was considered "unclean." This was to counter an error, for some thought that at night demons—or as the old women say, **the blessed ones** <note>original: "die seligen"; a folk euphemism for spirits or witches</note>, though they are actually witches or demons in their likeness—must consume everything so that they might later bestow things more abundantly. <margin>Summaries</margin> Some people try to color this and say they are **goblins** <term>schretel; a Germanic term for a wood spirit or kobold</term>, but this goes against the determination of the Doctors of the Church, who state that there are no other rational creatures besides humans and angels; therefore, they are nothing but demons.

Likewise, in Leviticus 19 <note>OCR says 18</note>: "You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard." For the idolaters used to do those things in veneration of idols. Likewise, in Deuteronomy 22, it was commanded that men should not wear women's clothing, nor vice-versa, because the former was done in veneration of **Venus**, and the latter in veneration of **Mars** and the god **Priapus**. For that same reason, He ordered the altars of idols to be destroyed; and **Hezekiah** destroyed the bronze serpent when the people wanted to offer sacrifices to it, saying "it is only copper." 

For that same reason, He forbade dreams to be observed or omens to be taken, and commanded that any man or woman in whom there was a "divining spirit" <note>original: "phitonicus spiritus"; referencing the Pythian spirit of Delphi</note> should be put to death—just as those now called **fortune tellers** <term>warsegerin; a German term for a female soothsayer</term>. All these things He forbade because they generate suspicion of **spiritual adultery**; thus, as was said, it is out of the zeal God has for the souls betrothed to Him, like a groom for a bride. So also we, the preachers and governors of souls, ought to take heed that no sacrifice is more acceptable to God than a **zeal for souls** <note>original: "zelus animarum"</note>, as Jerome testifies in his commentary on Ezekiel. Consequently, this will be discussed in the third part of this work, regarding the **extermination of witches**...

¶ One Remedy
Regarding someone who, for the sake of temporal benefit, devoted themselves entirely to a demon: as experience has often shown, although they were liberated from the power of the devil through a true confession, they were nevertheless very severely troubled for a long time afterward, especially during the night.
