### The third part of the entire work follows, concerning the methods of exterminating or at least punishing witches through due justice in the ecclesiastical and civil courts. This part will contain various questions, and five general and introductory points are placed first.

**Whether witches and those who favor, receive, and defend them are so subject to the judgment of the diocesan ecclesiastical and civil courts that the inquisitors of heretical depravity can be relieved of the duty of inquiring into them.** And it is argued that they are:

<margin>See the chapter "Accusatus," section "Sane," in the Sixth Book of Decretals.</margin>
Indeed, since the business of faith—which is highly privileged—should not be hindered by other occupations, the inquisitors of heresy appointed by the **Apostolic See** <note>The Papacy</note> should not involve themselves in divinations or sorceries unless they clearly **savor of heresy**; <note>original: "heresim sapent"; a legal term meaning the act implies a rejection of Catholic dogma</note> nor should they punish those who practice such things, but rather leave them to be punished by their own judges. Nor does it seem to stand in the way that the heresy of witches is not explicitly mentioned here; for both are punished with the same penalties in the **court of conscience.** <note>term: "court of conscience" (foro cōscie); the internal realm of sin and confession, as opposed to the public legal court</note> According to the laws regarding consecration: if the sin of diviners and sorcerers is hidden, a penance of forty days is imposed; if it is notorious, the Eucharist is denied. Thus, the same judgment is decreed for those under the same penalty, and the fault appears to be the same in both cases. For just as

<column-break/>

sorcerers <note>original: "sortilegi"; specifically those who cast lots or use "sortilege"</note> wait for the outcome of their lots, so witches <note>original: "malefice"</note> expect and demand the harming of creatures from demons; in both cases, they seek illicitly from a creature what should be sought from God alone. Hence, in both cases, there is the sin of **idolatry**. To this point, Ezekiel 21 notes that the King of Babylon stood at the crossroad, at the head of two ways, mixing arrows and consulting idols. Furthermore, if it is said that the law restricts diviners and sorcerers to the crime of heresy (for which they must be under the judgment of inquisitors) when it says, "unless they clearly savor of heresy," it would mean that at least heretical diviners and sorcerers are subject to them. On the contrary, this would mean one would have to acknowledge "artificial" diviners, who are mentioned nowhere in the scriptures.

Furthermore, if witches are subject to the judgment of inquisitors, it would be because of the crime of heresy. But the deeds of witches can be done without heresy. This is proven: for just as trampling the Body of Christ in the mud—which is a truly horrifying sin—can be done without an error in the intellect, and consequently without heresy (since someone might firmly believe Christ's body is present there, yet throw it into the mud to please a demon because of a pact, perhaps to obtain a desired end like finding treasure), so too the acts of witches can be done without an error of faith, though not without great sin. Therefore, in that case, they escape the judgment of the inquisitor and are left to their own judges.

Furthermore, just as Solomon showed reverence to the gods of his wives for the sake of pleasing them, yet did not therefore incur the **apostasy of perfidy** <note>original: "apostasiam perfidie"; the total rejection of the faith</note> because he remained faithful in his mind and always retained the true faith, so too witches, because of the reverence they show the devil on account of a pact they have entered, are not to be called heretics if they retain the faith in their minds. Furthermore, if it is said that all witches must deny the faith—and thus are to be judged as heretics—this is countered: for even in a case where someone denies the faith in mind and heart, they are still not called heretics, but **apostates.** And since there is a difference

For where the chapter <note>referring to a specific section of Canon Law</note> says, as was brought up in the first argument, that **inquisitors of heretical depravity** <note>original: "inquisitores heretice prauitatis"</note> ought not to involve themselves in cases of **sorcery and divination** unless it clearly **smacks of heresy** <note>original: "heresim sapiat manifeste"</note>, they say that sorcerers or diviners are of two kinds: namely, **artificial** and **heretical**. 

The first kind are called **pure diviners** because they act purely through a practiced art. The chapter *Ex tenore* in the Decretals <note>a collection of papal decrees</note> regarding sorcerers speaks of these; it mentions a priest named **Udalricus** who went with a certain "infamous person"—that is, a diviner, as the **gloss** <note>a scholarly explanation in the margin of a legal text</note> says—to a secret place. He did this not with the intention of **invoking demons** (the text implies that would have been heretical), but so that by inspecting an **astrolabe** <note>an ancient astronomical instrument used here to find lost items</note> he might locate a certain stolen item. This is considered pure divination or sorcery.

The second kind are called **heretical diviners**. These are people who, in the course of their art, offer some honor of **worship** <note>original: "latrie"; the highest form of worship due to God alone</note> or **veneration** <note>original: "dulie"; honor typically given to saints</note> to demons while attempting to predict the future. Or, they perform something similar that clearly "smacks of heresy." Such people fall under the judgment of the inquisitors just as other heretics do. 

That this is the intent of the chapter is proven by the **canonists** <note>legal scholars of Church law</note> commenting on the word "smack" <note>original: "saperent"</note>. For **Johannes Andreae** <note>a famous 14th-century legal scholar</note>, commenting on the chapter *Accusatus*, says they "smack of heresy" when they do things such as:
* Uttering wicked prayers around an altar of idols.
* Offering sacrifices.
* Consulting demons and receiving their responses.
* Associating with heretics to perform lots.
* Performing the aforementioned acts with blood, or with the **Body of Christ** <note>the consecrated Host</note>, or using lots to get answers.
* Rebaptizing children or similar acts.

To this same effect, they cite the **Archdeacon** <note>referring to Guido de Baysio</note> on that same chapter and the section *Sane*, regarding that same word "smack."

<insert>Red Paragraph Mark</insert> Likewise, they cite **Johannes Monachus**, **Raymond**, and **William of Mont-Lauzun**. They also prove this by the determination of the Church and from the **Council of Agde** <note>original: "acauire"; likely a corruption of "Agathense"</note> in the section *Episcopi*, where such suspicious women are called **infidels**. It says they "dwell in their own perfidy," and in a Christian, **perfidy** is called **heresy**. Therefore, they are subject to the judgment of the inquisitors of heretics. Furthermore, they prove this through the **theologians**. First, through **Saint Thomas Aquinas** in the second book of the *Sentences*, distinction 7, where he asks

whether using the help of a demon is a sin. Among other things, he says the following regarding the passage in **Isaiah 8**: *"Should not a people seek a vision from its God?"* In all matters where the completion of a task is expected through the power of a demon, there is **apostasy** <note>a total rejection of the Christian faith</note> from the faith. This is because of a **pact** entered into with the demon, whether by words (if an invocation is used) or by some physical deed, even if actual sacrifices are missing.

To the same point, they cite **Albert the Great** in his same writing and distinction. Likewise, **Peter of Tarentaise**—recently canonized—though he is not called Peter here since his name as **Pope** <note>Innocent V</note> was used. Likewise, **Alexander of Hales** and **Guido of the Carmelite Order**, who all say that those **invoking demons** are apostates and consequently heretics; thus, they are subject to the judgment of the inquisitors of heretics.

But the aforementioned inquisitors, through these and whatever else they have cited, cannot sufficiently prove that the aforementioned sorcerers and their kind do not continue to be subject to the judgment of the **ordinaries** or **bishops** <note>the local church authorities</note>, to the exclusion of the inquisitors. Indeed, inquisitors can excuse themselves from dealing with such diviners, **necromancers** <note>original: "nigromāticozū"</note>, or even **evildoers** <note>original: "maleficorum"; here referring to those who practice harmful magic</note>. This is not to say that those inquisitors do wrong by investigating such people in cases where the bishops fail to do so—in which case the inquisitors should rather be commended. 

The proof is as follows: Inquisitors ought not to involve themselves unless the crime is **heresy**, and even then, the crime must be **manifest** <note>obvious or proven</note>. This is clear from the frequently cited chapter *Accusatus*. This being the case, the argument is made again: when someone commits acts that can be committed without the vice of heresy—no matter how grave or enormous those acts are—that person is not yet to be judged as a heretic, even if they must be punished. From this, it follows that where someone is not to be judged as a heretic but punished as a <term>malefactor</term> <note>a criminal or worker of harmful magic</note>, the inquisitor should not involve himself. Instead, he should leave such a person to their own judges for punishment according to the meaning of the canon law. 

This being the case, it follows that all the points brought forward by the commentators, canonists, and theologians—such as invoking demons, sacrificing to them, and so forth...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological distinction between acts of sorcery and the formal crime of heresy. It moves from general definitions into specific criteria used by the Inquisitors of Germany to determine if a suspect falls under their jurisdiction or that of a local bishop.</meta>

As was touched upon above, unless these acts proceed from the **vice of heresy** <note>original: "vicio heresis"</note>, the **inquisitors** <note>specialized church officials tasked with investigating and prosecuting heresy</note> ought not to involve themselves, but should leave the matters to the proper judges, as stated previously. This being the case, since the aforementioned acts can very often occur without the vice of heresy—in which case those doing such things are not to be held as heretics or condemned as such—this is proved by the following authorities and reasons.

For a person to be **properly considered a heretic**, five things are required:

1.  The first is that there must be an **error in reason** <note>an intellectual mistake in understanding Church doctrine</note>.
2.  The second is that the error must concern those things which are of the **faith**, or must be against the truth of the **Church’s determination** in matters pertaining to faith or good morals and those things necessary for the attainment of eternal life.
3.  The third is that such an error must exist in one who has **professed the Catholic faith**; otherwise, they would be a Jew or a pagan, not a heretic.
4.  The fourth is that such an error in one who has received the faith must be of such a kind that they still **confess some truth about Christ** pertaining to His divinity or humanity; otherwise, if they disbelieved everything, they would be an **apostate** <note>one who completely renounces their religion</note>.
5.  The fifth is that they must choose and follow such an error with a **stubborn will and an obstinate mind** <note>original: "pertinaci voluntate et obstinata"</note>.

This definition of heresy and the heretic is taken from the chapter *Accusatus* <note>a section of Canon Law</note> and the "word of the wise," without rejecting the **glosses** <note>interpretative comments written in the margins of legal texts</note> of the canon lawyers, but rather upholding them. Thus it is proved: for it to be required first that there be an error in the intellect is known to all by the common rule.

Two things are required for someone to be called a heretic: one is **material**, namely the error in reason; the other is **formal**, namely **stubbornness** <note>original: "pertinacia"</note> in the will. This is clear according to **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, a foundational Church Father</note>: "A heretic is one who either creates or follows new and false opinions." The reason is also present because heresy is a species of **unbelief** <note>original: "infidelitatis"</note>, and unbelief exists subjectively in the intellect, just as faith (its contrary and opposite) must concern the same thing.

This being the case, any act or work performed without error does not make a person a heretic. For example, if someone commits fornication or **adultery** <note>original: "mechař," from "moechari"</note>, even though they act against the truth which says "thou shalt not commit adultery," they are not a heretic because of this, unless they believe or hold the opinion that fornicating is lawful. And the reason is this: whenever two things are necessarily required for the constitution of something, if one of them is missing, it is impossible for that thing to exist. For if it could exist without that part,

<column-break/>

it would no longer be a necessary requirement for its constitution. Just as a foundation, walls, and a roof are necessarily required for the construction of a house, if any of these are missing, one does not have a house.

So, therefore, because an error in the intellect is necessarily required to constitute heresy, no act performed absolutely without an error in the intellect makes a person a heretic. And because of this, we, the **inquisitors of Germany** <note>original: "nos inquisitores germanie"</note>, say—along with **Blessed Antoninus** <note>Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), a Dominican friar and archbishop known for his works on moral theology</note> in the second part of his *Summa* where he treats this matter—that **baptizing an image**, **worshiping demons**, **offering incense to them**, or **trampling the body of Christ** <note>the consecrated Host/Eucharist</note> in the mud, and all such things which are truly horrific sins, do not make a person a heretic unless there is an error in the intellect.

And therefore, if someone were to do these things—for instance, if they baptized an image but did not hold a wrong view regarding the **sacrament of baptism**, nor its effect, nor believed that this [mock] baptism was anything or had any power of its own, but did this to achieve some end through a **demon** who sought to be pleased by it—then they would be acting by some **pact**, either implicit or explicit, only so that the demon might do what they ask. This is similar to how, according to the **magical arts**, demons are invoked by men through characters and figures, by an expressed or silent pact, to fulfill their desires.

Provided that they do not ask the demon for something beyond its faculty—neither in terms of its power nor its knowledge—and provided they do not hold a wrong view about the power or knowledge of the demon. Such wrong views would be held by those who believe a demon can **constrain the free will** of a human, or those who believe a demon could fulfill a request by such a pact in every event, even if not permitted by God, or those who believe a demon could know the truth of **future contingencies** <note>events that may or may not happen, which theology holds only God can know for certain</note>, or produce some effect which is proper to God alone. In such cases, there is no doubt that they would have an error in the intellect and hold a wrong view of the demon's power. Consequently, assuming the other conditions required for heresy are met, they would be heretics and subject to the judgment of both the **Ordinary** <note>the local bishop</note> and the Inquisitor. But if, for the reasons mentioned, they did these things without holding a wrong view of baptism...

This is because, by that very fact, **sorcerers** <note>original: "malefici"</note> and **necromancers** <note>those who practice magic involving communication with the dead or demons</note>, since they know the devil himself to be the enemy of the faith and the adversary of salvation, are forced to feel in their hearts a great power in the faith—which can be subject to no falsehood, even though the **father of lies** <note>the devil</note> is known to preside over it. Therefore, although those doing such things sin most gravely, they would not necessarily be heretics. The reason is that they do not hold a wrong opinion regarding the **sacrament**, even though they use it wickedly and sacrilegiously; hence they are more properly **sorcerers** than heretics.

Concerning the number of those mentioned in the chapter *Accusatus* <note>a reference to a specific chapter in Canon Law</note>, it is claimed that they do not fall under the judgment of the inquisitors, since they do not manifestly taste of heresy—indeed, barely in secret, and almost not at all. But if they do these things without holding such views about the demon, but rather so that by some **pact** with the demon they might more easily carry out through him what they intend, such people are not heretics by the nature of the act, although they sin gravely. Regarding this, for a greater declaration, certain objections must be raised. For it seems to be an obstacle that, according to the laws, a **simoniac** <note>original: "symoniacus"; one who buys or sells sacred things or church offices</note> is not a heretic (as in question 1, *Quisquis per pecuniam*), and yet he does not have an error in his intellect. For a simoniac is not a heretic in the proper sense, but in a broad sense due to a certain similarity; because when he sells or buys sacred things, he acts as if he estimated that the gift of grace could be possessed for money, according to **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note>. But if he does not actually estimate this—as commonly happens—he is not a heretic because he does not believe this; though he would indeed be a heretic if he believed that the gift of grace could be possessed for money. 

Likewise, it seems to be an obstacle what is said concerning heretics in the chapter *Accusatus*: that one who **worships a heretic** is a heretic. But he who worships a demon sins more gravely than he who worships a heretic; therefore, etc. Likewise, he who is to be judged as a heretic seems to be a heretic, because judgment ought to follow the truth of the matter; but such a person is to be judged a hereti-

<column-break/>

-tic. For the Church cannot judge except regarding those things which are evident; for the knowledge of hidden things belongs to God as judge (distinction 33, *Erubescant*). But those things which are in the intellect cannot be evident except from external deeds seen or proved. Therefore, one performing such acts is to be judged a heretic. 

Furthermore, it seems impossible that anyone performing such things—namely, by **trampling on the Body of Christ** <note>desecrating the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> and the like—could do so unless he held a wrong opinion about the Body of Christ. This is proved because it is impossible for malice to be in the will without there being an error in the intellect, since, according to **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note>, "every evil person is ignorant or erring." Since, therefore, those performing such acts have malice in their will, they must have an error in their intellect.

One responds to these points, and first to the first and third because they coincide: There is a **double judgment**. Namely, God’s, who sees internal things; and men’s, who cannot judge internal things except through external signs, as the third argument admits. But he who is judged as a heretic by God’s judgment is truly a heretic by the nature of the thing. For God judges no one a heretic unless they have an error of faith in their intellect. 

However, he who is judged a heretic by the judgment of men does not necessarily have to be a heretic by the nature of the thing, but rather because he has committed such an act through which he appears to hold a wrong opinion about the faith; and consequently, by **presumption of law**, he is considered a heretic. And if you ask whether the Church must immediately judge such people who thus worship demons, or **baptize images**, as heretics and punish them as heretics, note the responses. 

First, that discerning this belongs more to the **canonists** <note>lawyers specializing in Church law</note> than to the **theologians**. The canonists will say that by presumption of law he is considered a heretic and is to be punished as a heretic. The theologian will say (initially, under the correction of the Apostolic See) that it is not so by the nature of the thing, whatever the presumption of law may be. And this can be the reason: because whenever any effect can depend on a double cause, one can never judge precisely which of the two causes it is by the nature of the thing from that effect alone. 

Since, therefore, this effect—which is to worship a demon, or to ask for his help for sorcery by **baptizing an image**, or by **offering or killing a living infant**, or other such things—can proceed from a double cause: namely, either by believing the demon...

Another response to our proposition is that, whatever the case may be among all these arguments and citations, it is established that all **diviners** and **sorcerers** <note>original: "malefici"</note> who are judged as heretics by **presumption of law** <term>presumption of law: a legal assumption that something is true unless proven otherwise</term>—and not by the very nature of the act—fall under the judgment of the local **ordinaries** and not the **inquisitors**. Furthermore, the aforementioned inquisitors of other kingdoms cannot defend themselves by citing the **canons** <note>church laws</note> and **glossators** <note>legal scholars who wrote commentaries on law</note>, because they judge those sacrificing to and worshiping demons as heretics by legal presumption, and not by the nature of the act itself. 

A third opinion, however, says that they must **manifestly savor of heresy** <note>original: "sapere heresim manifeste"</note>, which is to say, they must hold it inwardly and by the nature of the act. It will be enough for us, as **inquisitors of heretics**, to involve ourselves with those infected by the nature of the act, leaving others to their own judges. And since it was said that one must inquire into the cause—whether they did this from an error of faith or not—this will certainly be easy to determine. For just as the **habit of faith** is known through an act of faith (which is to believe and confess those things which belong to the faith), and the habit of chastity is known by living chastely, so the Church can judge someone a heretic by inquiring if they have performed an act of discerning or **feeling wrongly** about any article of faith. 

Thus, regarding a **female sorcerer** <note>original: "malefica"</note> who has denied the faith in whole or in part, or who has treated the **Body of Christ** <note>the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note> most vilely, or has performed **homage** [to the demon]: the question is whether she did such things only to please the demon. Indeed, if she has denied the faith entirely, even in her heart, she shall now be judged as an **apostate** <term>apostate: someone who totally renounces their religion</term>, and the fourth condition required for someone to be properly called a heretic will be met. 

<column-break/>

If an objection is raised against this determination regarding the **Bull** <term>Bull: an official decree issued by a Pope, named after the lead seal (bulla) attached to it</term> and commission granted to us by **Innocent VIII** <note>Pope Innocent VIII, who issued the famous bull "Summis desiderantes affectibus" in 1484, which authorized inquisitors to act against witchcraft</note>, wherein **sorcerers** are subjected to the judgment of the inquisitors, the answer is that the **diocesans** <note>local bishops</note> are not excluded by that decree. They may still proceed against such persons even up to a definitive sentence by virtue of those ancient laws mentioned previously. This is because this Bull was entrusted to us inquisitors more as a **share of the responsibility** <note>original: "in partem sollicitudinis"; a legal term meaning shared administrative care rather than absolute power</note>, which work we carry out as much as we can with God’s help. 

Therefore, the first argument does not support those inquisitors, but rather concludes the opposite, since **Simonists** <term>Simonists: people who buy or sell church offices or sacred things</term> are considered heretics only by **presumption of law**, and the ordinaries can judge them by themselves without requiring the inquisitors. Indeed, inquisitors do not have to involve themselves in various cases of **Simony**, and by the same reasoning, they should not involve themselves with others who are judged heretics only by legal presumption. 

For they cannot proceed against **schismatic bishops** or other superior prelates, as is shown in the constitutions regarding heresy in the **Sixth Book** <note>the "Liber Sextus," a collection of canon law</note>, where it says: "Inquisitors of heretical depravity, whether deputized by the Apostolic See or any others, cannot inquire into such a crime against [bishops], nor proceed against them under that pretext, unless it is expressly contained in the letters of commission from the Apostolic See that they may do so." 

However, if the inquisitors themselves know or find that **bishops** or other superior prelates have committed crimes concerning heresy, or that they are defamed or suspected of such things, they are bound to report this to the **Apostolic See** <note>the Vatican/the Pope's office</note>. 

The response to the second point is similarly clear from what was discussed before. For one who **worships a heretic** is a heretic only if they worship him believing that he *should* be worshiped or honored because of his doctrine and opinion. If, however, one honors him for some **temporal reason** <note>for social, political, or financial gain</note> without any intellectual error regarding the faith, he is not properly a heretic, but is only so by **legal fiction** or presumption, or by way of resemblance—because he acts as if he feels wrongly about the faith, just as the one he worships does. Therefore, he shall not be subject to the judgment of the inquisitors. The answer to the third point is clear from the premises...

This heresy involves an error in the intellect, and four other subsequent annexed conditions. 

The **second** of these is that such an error must concern those things which are of the faith, or be against the truth of the **determination of the Church** in matters pertaining to faith, good morals, and those things necessary for the attainment of eternal life. For if an error is made concerning things that do not pertain to the faith—for example, if one believes the **sun is not larger than the earth**—this is not a dangerous error. However, an error against **Holy Scripture**, against the **articles of faith**, or against the determination of the Church is, as stated above, heresy. (See Canon Law: 24. q. 1. *Haec est fides*). Furthermore, the determination of doubts concerning the faith belongs principally to the Church and especially to the **Supreme Pontiff**, the **Vicar of Christ** and successor of Peter, as stated expressly in 24. q. 1. *Quotiens*. And against the determination...

<column-break/>

...of the Church, no **Doctor** <note>original: "doctor"; an eminent teacher of the Church</note> or Saint defends his own opinion, as **Thomas [Aquinas]** says in the *Secunda Secundae*. Not Jerome, nor Augustine, nor any other. Therefore, just as one who stubbornly asserts something against the faith is a heretic, so too is one who stubbornly asserts something against the determination of the Church in those matters pertaining to the faith that are necessary for salvation. For the Church herself **never errs** <note>original: "nunquam errat"</note> in the faith, as is proven in 24. q. 1. *A recta* and other chapters. 

It is specifically said, however, that one asserting something against the Church's determination is a heretic only in those matters that pertain to faith and salvation. For in other matters, one holding a contrary view is not a heretic. For example, regarding whether a **legal right** can be separated from **usage** in things consumed by use—which **Pope John XXII** declared and determined in the decree *Ad Conditorem*—he says those contradicting this opinion are **contumacious** <term>contumacious: stubbornly disobedient to authority</term> and rebels against the Church, but not heretics.

The **third** requirement is that the error must exist in one who has **professed the Catholic truth**. For if someone had never professed the Christian faith, they would not properly be a heretic but simply an **infidel**, such as a Jew or a Gentile who are "outside." Hence **Augustine** in *The City of God* says: the devil, seeing the human race being liberated from the worship of idols and demons, moved heretics so that, under the **Christian name**, they might resist Christian doctrine. It is necessary, therefore, that the error be in one who has received the Christian faith in **baptism** in order for it to be heresy.

The **fourth** requirement is that such an error be in one who has received the faith in such a way that they confess some truth about Christ pertaining to His **divinity or humanity**. For if they confessed no truth at all, they would be considered more properly an **apostate** <term>apostate: one who totally renounces their religion</term> rather than a heretic, like **Julian the Apostate**. One is distinguished from the other, although sometimes one term is used for the other. Under this condition, certain people are found who, occasionally afflicted by poverty and various troubles, surrender their **body and soul** to the devil and abjure the faith, provided that the devil assists them in their needs and in possessing riches and honors. We ourselves, as inquisitors, have known certain such people, and later as penitents, who acted entirely without an error of faith in the intellect, but only for the sake of **temporal advantage**...

And here one term is used for the other, as was touched upon before. And he adds: Truly, those who deny the faith out of fear of death—take this to mean those who deny the faith to the devil for the sake of **temporal advantage** <note>worldly or material gain, such as wealth or power</note> and do not actually believe in the errors—note here that they are not strictly heretics. He adds: Since they do not have the error in their minds, they are nevertheless to be held as heretics by the judgment of the Church, which must judge internal matters by external signs. Note here that this is by a **legal fiction** <term>legal fiction: an assumption made by a court that something is true (even if it might not be) to allow a law to be applied</term>. Thus, if they return as penitents, they are to be received as heretics. For the fear of death is not a fear that should cause a steadfast man to deny the faith of Christ; likewise, you should understand this regarding temporal advantages. Hence **Augustine** concludes: It is holier to die than to deny [the faith] or to eat food offered to idols, as is recited in the Decree, case 22, question 3. ¶ A similar judgment would apply to **sorcerers** <note>original: "maleficis"; those who practice harmful magic or witchcraft</note> who deny the faith: if they wish to turn back, they should be received as penitents without being abandoned to the secular court. In every way, they are received into the bosom of the Church when they ask for it. But if they do not, they are left to the secular court, and this is because of the temporal damage they have caused, as will be clear in the methods of passing sentence. The aforementioned **ordinary** <term>ordinary: a Church official, usually a bishop, who has standard jurisdiction over a territory</term> executes all these things, so that even an **inquisitor** can delegate his duties to the bishop in this specific case of apostasy. It is different in other cases involving sorcerers. ¶ The fifth thing required for someone to be strictly a heretic is that they choose such an error with a firm and obstinate will, and that they follow these opinions **pertinaciously** <term>pertinaciously: with stubborn persistence, especially in a way that is wrong or annoying</term>. ¶ According to

**Jerome**, heresy is named after the word for "choice." And therefore, according to **Augustine**, it is not the person who creates or follows false opinions, but the one who defends them pertinaciously, who is to be judged a heretic. Hence, if someone does not believe something against the faith out of stubborn malice, but out of ignorance, and is ready to be corrected if what they believe is shown to be false or against the faith, the Holy Scripture, or the determination of the Church (as stated in case 23, question 3), the Apostle said this. And therefore Augustine himself used to say: **"I may err, but I will not be a heretic"** <note>original: "Errare potero hereticus non ero"</note> because, namely, he was ready to be corrected once his error was shown to him. And it is a fact that every day there are various and sometimes contradictory opinions among the **Doctors of Theology** concerning divine matters, so that it is necessary for one side to be false; yet neither of them is considered false heresy until it has been defined by the Church. See case 23, question 2, "Those in the Church." From all of this, it is concluded that the attempt to prove that sorcerers fall under the judgment of inquisitors (or any others) simply by the fact that they invoke demons—based on the phrase **"tasting of heresy"** <note>original: "verbum saperent"; a legal standard where an action "smacks of" or suggests heresy</note> in the canon *Accusatus*—is not sufficiently proven. For such people are judged as heretics by a certain **legal fiction**, and the aforementioned arguments of the theologians do not prove it either, since they themselves call such people apostates in word or deed, but not in mind and heart (which is what the phrase "tasting of" implies). And although they are judged *as* heretics, it does not follow from this that a bishop cannot proceed to a definitive sentence against them, or assign them to prison for punishment, or expose them to **torture** without an inquisitor. Indeed, in cases where the evidence does not seem sufficient for us inquisitors to be relieved of the duty of investigating sorcerers, we nevertheless do not wish to establish this as a binding rule of law, since we can delegate our authority in passing sentence to the **diocesan bishops** themselves. ¶ For this is found in the chapter *Multorum* at the beginning, regarding heretics, in the **Clementines** <note>a collection of Church laws issued by Pope Clement V in the early 14th century</note>. Where it is said: "The complaint of many," and so on, so that the business of this kind of inquiry may be completed more successfully, and henceforth the investigation of this same stain...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological discussion regarding the jurisdiction of the Inquisition. The previous page established that while some may deny the faith for worldly gain, they are to be treated with the same legal rigor as heretics or apostates. This page transitions into the "Third Part" of the manual, detailing the specific legal procedures for arresting, questioning, and sentencing those accused of witchcraft.</meta>

### The Legal Procedure for the Inquiry into Witches

The third part of this work shall be carried out more diligently and cautiously. We decree that the investigation itself is to be exercised both by the **diocesan bishops** <term>diocesan bishop: the high-ranking priest in charge of a specific geographic district or "diocese"</term> and by the **inquisitors** <term>inquisitor: an official authorized by the Pope to investigate and suppress heresy</term> commissioned by the **Apostolic See** <note>original: "a sede apostolica"; the authority of the Pope in Rome</note>. All human hatred, fear, or any kind of partiality for personal gain must be set aside. Thus, any of the aforementioned officials may, without the other, summon and arrest or seize a person and commit them to safe custody, even placing them in **leg irons and iron handcuffs** <note>original: "compedibus et manicis ferreis"</note> if it seems appropriate to them—a matter for which we charge their own conscience. Furthermore, they may inquire against those for whom it seems expedient for such business according to God and justice. 

However, they are not permitted to hand someone over to a **harsh prison** <note>original: "duro tradere carceri"</note>—which is intended for punishment rather than mere custody—or to subject them to **tortures** <note>original: "tormentis"</note>, or to proceed to a final sentence against them, unless they act together. The Bishop cannot act without the Inquisitor, nor the Inquisitor without the Bishop (or, if the bishop’s seat is vacant, a representative delegated by the **cathedral chapter** <note>original: "capituli"; the governing body of a cathedral</note>), provided they are able to reach one another within eight days of a request. If they presume to act otherwise, the proceeding shall be null and void by law.

What follows pertains to our main purpose: Moreover, if the Bishop (or the chapter’s delegate) and the Inquisitor cannot or will not meet in person for the reasons mentioned above, the Bishop can delegate his authority to the Inquisitor, or the Inquisitor to the Bishop, or they may signify their counsel and consent through letters. From this, it is clear that while there are five cases where one may proceed without the other, there are three cases where they absolutely cannot. Yet, because one can delegate his role to the other—especially regarding the **passing of a sentence** <note>original: "sententiam ferendam"</note>—we have decreed that this can be done, while the other inquisitors remain within their own assigned boundaries. 

Therefore, in responding to the arguments: the decision regarding the first six arguments favoring the inquisitors is clear from what has been said—namely, that it does not seem that **witches** <note>original: "malefici"</note> and **sorcerers** <note>original: "sortilegi"</note> are exempt from their inquiry.

<column-break/>

As for the other arguments on behalf of the **diocesan bishops** <note>the local church leaders</note>, in the event that they might wish to excuse themselves from the investigation of witches and leave it entirely to the **civil court** <note>original: "ciuili iudicio"</note>: it is clear they cannot do this as easily as the inquisitors might. This is because in the **crime of heresy** <term>heresy: the holding of religious beliefs that contradict the official doctrine of the Church</term>, according to the canon laws *Ad abolendam*, *Vergentis*, and *Excommunicamus* found in the section on heretics, it is the role of the **ecclesiastical judge** <note>Church judge</note> to investigate and judge, and the role of the **secular judge** <note>civil or government judge</note> to carry out the punishment, specifically where the sentence involves **blood vengeance** <term>blood vengeance: a legal term for the death penalty or physical execution</term>. 

It is different, however, when dealing with other **penitential punishments** <note>spiritual or symbolic punishments, like public shaming or pilgrimages</note>. It is also argued that in the case of the heresy of witches—though perhaps not in other forms of heresy—the local bishops may delegate their duty of investigation and judgment to the civil court. This is because, as mentioned in the arguments, the crime of witchcraft is not purely a Church matter; indeed, it is also a civil matter because of the **temporal damages** <note>physical, agricultural, or financial harm caused to people and property</note> that witches inflict. Furthermore, special laws have been issued specifically for the punishment of witches. 

Finally, this combined path serves most effectively to exterminate witches and provides the greatest relief to the **ordinaries** <note>bishops with standard jurisdiction</note when they must stand before the "Tremendous Judge" for their strict examination. For, as Scripture witnesses, a **most harsh judgment** <note>original: "iudicium durissimum"</note> threatens those who are in authority. According to this distinction, we shall proceed: namely, that the secular judge can investigate and judge up to the **final sentence** <note>original: "sententiam diffinitiuam"</note> regarding the penance (which he receives from the church authorities), but he can carry out judgments regarding **blood** <note>the death penalty</note> on his own authority.

Therefore, so that judges in both the **ecclesiastical and civil courts** may always have the methods of investigating, judging, and sentencing ready at hand, we must proceed regarding three principal stages:
1. The method of **beginning a trial of faith** <note>original: "processus fidei"</note>.
2. The method of continuing the trial.
3. The method of concluding and sentencing in this matter of witches.

Regarding the first stage, there are five difficulties to address:
- First: Which of the three methods of legal proceeding is most appropriate?
- Second: The required number of witnesses.
- Third: Whether witnesses can be compelled to swear an oath.
- Fourth: The status and condition of the witnesses.
- Fifth: Whether **deadly enemies** <note>original: "inimici capitales"</note> of the accused should be allowed to testify.

The second part <note>referring to the second section of the judicial instructions</note> contains eleven questions. First, how witnesses are to be examined and why five persons should always be present. Also, how witches are to be interrogated in general and in particular. This will be the sixth in the order of the book, though the numbering is changed so that the reader may more easily find the desired material. The second question clarifies various doubts regarding negative responses <note>when a prisoner denies the charges</note>, when she should be imprisoned, and when she is clearly caught in the **heresy of witches** <note>original: "heresi maleficarum"</note>. The third covers the method of arresting witches. The fourth concerns two things the judge must do after the arrest: whether the names of the informants should be revealed to the accused and whether legal defenses should be granted. 

The fifth explains how defenses should be granted along with the appointment of an **advocate** <term>advocate: a legal representative or lawyer provided to the accused</term>. The sixth concerns what the advocate should do when the names of witnesses are not made public to him, and when he alleges "capital enmity" <note>an argument that a witness is a mortal enemy of the accused and therefore unreliable</note> before the judge. The seventh covers how the judge must investigate such capital enmity. The eighth concerns those things the judge must consider before he exposes the accused to **tortures** <note>original: "tormentis"</note>. The ninth concerns the method of sentencing for questioning and tortures. The tenth concerns the continuation of tortures, how they are to be tortured, and the cautions and signs against the **spell of silence** <term>spell of silence: the belief that witches could use magic to remain silent and feel no pain during torture</term>. The eleventh concerns the final interrogations and the precautions to be observed by the judge.

The third part contains first three questions which the judge must consider, and from which every definitive sentence must proceed. First, whether a sentence can be passed based on the **trial by red-hot iron** <note>original: "examen cadentis ferri"; an ancient form of ordeal that the Church was increasingly skeptical of by this period</note>. Second, the manner in which every sentence is to be delivered. Third, on what suspicions he can judge and how he should sentence based on each type of suspicion. Finally, the last part covers twenty modes of sentencing, thirteen of which are common to all heresy, while the rest are specific to the **heresy of witches**. Because these will be clear in their own places, they are not assigned here for the sake of brevity.

### Question one regarding the 
### method of starting the process

<column-break/>

It is asked first: what is the proper way to begin a **process of the faith** <note>original: "processum fidei"; a formal inquisitorial trial</note> against witches? It is answered: There are three modes touched upon in the laws <note>referring to Canon Law</note>: **denunciation**, **inquisition**, and **accusation**. 

The first mode <note>Accusation</note> is when someone accuses another of the crime of heresy or of protecting heretics before a judge, offering to prove it and submitting themselves to the **penalty of talion** <term>talion: the "law of retaliation" where a false accuser receives the same punishment the accused would have faced if the proof fails</term> unless they prove it. 

The second mode <note>Denunciation</note> is when someone denounces another, yet does not offer to prove it nor wishes to be a party to the case, but says they denounce them out of **zeal for the faith** <note>original: "zelo fidei"</note>, or by reason of a sentence of excommunication issued by the Ordinary or his vicar, or by reason of the temporal penalty which a secular judge issues against those who do not denounce. 

The third mode is through **inquisition** <note>original: "per inquisitionem"</note>. This is when there is no accuser or denouncer, but **public rumor** <note>original: "fama"</note> is at work in some city or place that there are witches; then the judge must proceed not at the instance of a party, but by virtue of his office. 

Therefore, it should be noted that the judge should not willingly admit the first mode of proceeding <note>Accusation</note>, partly because it is not common in cases of faith nor in the case of witches (who perform their witchcraft in secret), and partly because it is very dangerous for the accuser due to the **penalty of talion** they would suffer if they failed in their proof; and also because it is very litigious. He should begin the process with a general citation, posting it on the doors of the parish church or the courthouse in the following manner: 

"Since we, the Vicar of such an Ordinary, or the Judge of such a Lord, desiring with all our hearts and seeking with all our souls that the Christian people committed to us be nurtured in the unity and serenity of the Catholic faith and be inwardly removed from every plague of **heretical pravity** <note>original: "pravitatis heretice"; a standard term for the "wickedness" of heresy</note>. Therefore, we the aforementioned Judge, upon whom these duties fall by joined office, for the glory and honor of the venerable name of Jesus Christ, and for the exaltation of the holy Orthodox faith and the suppression of heretical pravity—especially in all and singular witches of whatever condition or status..."

## The third mode of beginning a trial, which is also a common and used method, and besides this, it is secret; it is where no accuser or denouncer offers themselves, but rumor is active in some city or place regarding some witch, and specifically such a rumor that the judge can or should proceed "by virtue of office" <note>original: "ex officio"; a legal procedure where the judge acts on his own authority without a formal accuser</note> without the general citation mentioned above or a warning, because such frequent outcry reaches his ears. ### Second question regarding the number of witnesses.

Because it was mentioned in the second mode how the statements of witnesses ought to be recorded, it is necessary to know their number and status. It is asked whether a judge, based on the testimony of two legitimate witnesses who are not "singular" <note>original: "singularium"; witnesses who report different specific incidents rather than the same event</note>, can lawfully condemn someone for the heresy of witches, or whether more than two are necessarily required. Witnesses are called "singular" when they are partial in their statements but agree in the substance or effect of the matter—for example, if one said "she bewitched my cow" and another "she bewitched my child," they would agree on the fact of the harmful magic. However, the question here is where the witnesses are not partial but agree entirely. And it is answered that although they may seem to suffice...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the standard of proof required for a conviction. The previous page detailed the interrogation process for informants; this page moves into the legal theory of whether two witnesses are sufficient for a conviction in cases of heresy or witchcraft, considering the severity of the crime and the rights of the accused.</meta>

sig n 3

Two witnesses are required by the strictness of the law, because the rule is that "by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand" <note>This is a reference to Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16, a cornerstone of medieval legal evidence</note>. However, according to legal equity, it does not seem that two witnesses are sufficient in this specific crime, partly because of the immensity of the crime itself. For in criminal cases, proofs ought to be **clearer than light** <note>original: "luce clariores," a famous legal maxim meaning evidence must be indisputable</note> (Digest, *On Proofs*, law "si autem"). Heresy, especially of this kind, is numbered among the greatest crimes. 

And if it is argued that lighter proofs suffice in this crime—because someone might reveal themselves as a heretic by a "slight argument" (Code, *On Heretics*, law 2), such as by withdrawing from the judgment and path of the Catholic religion—the response is that this "slight argument" is sufficient for *presuming* guilt, but not for *condemning* the person. 

This is also due to the "curtailment" of the legal order in this crime. In this type of trial, the judicial order is shortened or "truncated" in favor of the faith; for the accused does not see the witnesses swear their oaths, nor are their names made public to the accused, because grave danger might threaten the witnesses if their identities were known (as stated in the chapter *Statuta*, *On Heretics*, Book VI). Because of this, the accused cannot guess who is testifying against them. Therefore, the judge is bound by his own office to diligently inquire into any **enmity** <note>In legal terms, "inimicicia" or personal hatred would disqualify a witness's testimony</note> of the witnesses, which would exclude them from testifying, as will be seen below. 

Furthermore, if the witnesses have testified vaguely regarding the "source of their knowledge" <term>source of knowledge: the legal requirement for a witness to explain exactly how they know a fact—e.g., they saw it personally rather than heard a rumor</term>, the judge must interrogate them again. This is because the more the path of defense is taken away from the accused, the more the burden falls upon the judge to investigate with greater diligence. 

Where two consistent and legitimate witnesses are found against someone, I would not wish to condemn him for such a great crime on that alone; rather, I would order him to undergo **purgation** <term>purgation: a formal process where an accused person clears their name by swearing their innocence along with a group of "oath-helpers"</term> if he has a bad reputation, or make him **abjure** <term>abjure: to formally renounce a heretical belief under oath</term> or undergo questioning <note>likely a euphemism for judicial torture</note> or delay the sentence due to the "vehement suspicion" arising from the words of the two witnesses. For it does not seem safe to condemn a person of good reputation for such a great crime solely on the voice of two witnesses. It is different, however, if the person already has a **bad reputation** <term>bad reputation: known in Latin as "mala fama," this was a specific legal status that lowered the threshold for proof required for conviction</term>. The Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous 13th-century canon lawyer</note> treats this more fully in his commentary on the chapter *Ut officium*, and Johannes Andreae <note>A renowned 14th-century legal scholar</note> says the same. Also, in the chapter *Excommunicamus*, it is said that the Bishop should make three or 

<column-break/>

more men of good testimony swear to tell the truth if they know of any such heretics in the parish.

The same is asked: Whether a judge, through **singular witnesses** <term>singular witnesses: witnesses who testify to different, isolated incidents rather than the same specific event</term> alone, or at least in combination with a bad reputation, could justly condemn someone for such heresy. The answer is no; not by singular witnesses alone, nor even with the presence of a bad reputation (as in *Extra. On Witnesses*, chapter *Cum litteris*), especially since in criminal matters, proofs must be **clearer than light**, as shown above. In this crime, no one should be damned based on presumption. Therefore, such a person is ordered to undergo **purgation** by reason of their bad reputation, and **abjuration** by reason of the "vehement suspicion" arising from the witnesses' statements. However, where witnesses are singular but agree on the "substance of the fact" and the "evidence of the fact" aligns, then the judge's conscience operates indirectly regarding the question of how often witnesses can be examined.

### Third Question

The question is: Whether a judge can compel witnesses to swear to tell the truth to him in a case concerning the faith or **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficarum," referring specifically to female practitioners of harmful magic</term>. And also whether he can examine them multiple times. 

The answer is yes, especially for an ecclesiastical judge, as shown above in the chapter *Ut officium*. Witnesses are compelled to give their testimony in ecclesiastical cases under oath (as in *Extra. On Compelling Witnesses*, chapter *Pervenit*); otherwise, the testimony will not be valid. 

Furthermore, in the chapter *Excommunicamus*, it is said that the Archbishop or Bishop should travel through the parish where there is a rumor that heretics live, and there he should compel three or more men of good testimony—or even the entire neighborhood if it seems expedient—to swear an oath. It follows below: "If any of these, through damnable obstinacy, refuse to swear by the sanctity of the oath, they shall by that very fact be **reputed as heretics**." 

Regarding whether they can be examined multiple times, the Archdeacon says this in his commentary on the chapter *Ut officium*. He states: "Here the Inquisitor, or the judge, ought to..."

the judge must be diligent so that if witnesses have testified in a confused manner, or if they were insufficiently questioned regarding the **basis of their knowledge** <note>original: "causa scientie" — a legal requirement for a witness to explain how they know what they claim to know, such as through sight or hearing</note>, he should inquire with them again. ### Fourth Question: On the Status of Witnesses.

**Regarding** the status of witnesses: 
Note that excommunicated persons, <note>Those officially excluded from the communion of the Church</note> as well as accomplices and partners in the crime, may be admitted. Likewise, the infamous <note>original: "infames" — those who have lost their legal standing or "fama" due to previous crimes or shameful professions</note> and criminals, and even servants, are admitted to bring charges and testify against their masters in any cause of faith. 
<margin>B.</margin> Furthermore, just as one heretic is admitted to testify against another heretic, so too is a **sorcerer** <note>original: "maleficus"</note> admitted against another sorcerer. However, this is only in the absence of other proofs, and they may always testify *against* the accused, but never *for* them. Wives, children, and household members are also permitted to testify *against* but not *for* the accused, based on the chapter *Filij* (*On Heretics*, Book VI); this is because their testimony is considered more effective for proving the truth <note>Since they are "insiders" who would know the accused's private behavior</note>. 

Regarding the first groups, it is clear in the chapter:
<margin>c.</margin> *In fidei* (*On Heretics*), where it states: "In favor of the faith, we grant that in the business of the inquisition into heretical depravity, excommunicated persons and accomplices or partners in the crime may be admitted to testimony in the absence of other proofs against heretics, believers, harborers, supporters, and their defenders." This applies if—based on likely conjectures, the number of witnesses, the quality of the persons testifying and those being testified against, or other circumstances—those so testifying are not presumed to be speaking falsely. 

Regarding perjurers: they may be admitted when it is presumed they testify out of zeal for the faith. This is clear in the chapter *Accusatus*, section *licet* (cited above), where it is said: "Although perjurers are rejected even after they have performed penance... yet if it appears from manifest signs that such people act not out of levity of mind, the fuel of hatred, or the corruption of money, but out of zeal for the orthodox faith, wishing to correct their previous statement and reveal what they had previously kept silent, then in favor of the faith—unless another obstacle stands in the way—their testimony must stand both against themselves and others." 

And regarding the fact that the infamous, the criminal, and servants are admitted against their masters, the **Archdeacon** <note>Guido de Baysio (c. 1250–1313), a famous canon lawyer</note> says the following on the word "excepted" in the aforementioned chapter *Accusatus*:

<column-break/>

"So great is the stain of the crime of heresy that for its prosecution even servants are admitted against their masters, and any criminal or infamous person is admitted against anyone else." (As found in the Decretum, 2. q. 7. § *huic opponitur*).

### Fifth Question: Whether Mortal Enemies are Admitted to Testify.

**If** it is asked: whether a judge can admit **mortal enemies** <note>original: "inimicos capitales" — literally "head-enemies," those whose enmity is so great it seeks the life of the other</note> of an accused person to testify or bring charges against them in such a case: 
We respond that he cannot. Hence the Archdeacon says in the place cited above: "Do not understand this to mean that in this crime a mortal enemy is admitted to the action." **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), one of the most influential canonists of the Middle Ages</note> also notes this sufficiently in his *Summa* (*On Accusations*, section "Who can [accuse]"). 

But who are called "mortal enemies"? 
Note that because someone is rejected solely by reason of enmity—and not just any enmity, but specifically "mortal"—it must be understood as a situation where death was either actually inflicted between them, or was attempted, or things leading toward death were set in motion, or grave and lethal wounds followed, or similar things which clearly prove the malice of the accuser against the victim. For it is presumed that just as he intended the person's **physical death** by means of wounding, he would also intend to cause it by falsely imposing the crime of heresy. And just as he wished to take away the man's life, he would wish to take away his **reputation** <note>original: "fama" — in medieval law, one's public reputation was a legal asset as valuable as physical life</note>. Therefore, such mortal enemies are lawfully excluded from testifying. 

Other enmities, however—especially those that are serious, and noting that women are easily moved to enmities—even if they do not disqualify a witness entirely, they do weaken their statement somewhat, so that full faith is not to be placed in their testimony. However, with other supports and the statements of other witnesses, they can provide full proof. This is especially true where the judge asks the accused whether he thinks he has an enemy who would dare to falsely charge him with such a capital crime out of hatred. If the accused says "yes," the judge shall ask who that person is; and then the judge will observe if that person...

<summary>This page explains that while heresy trials allow witnesses who are normally disqualified (such as criminals, servants, or accomplices), "mortal enemies" are strictly excluded to prevent people from using the Inquisition to settle deadly personal vendettas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal instructions for an inquisitor. The previous page discussed how a judge must be careful with witness testimony, especially regarding the "basis of knowledge" for their claims. This page addresses how to handle potential bias or personal grudges against the accused and transitions into the formal rules for a "summary" trial, which bypasses many standard legal delays.</meta>

concerning whom there is a suspicion that they have testified out of enmity <note>original: "inimicicia" — personal hatred or a grudge</note>, the judge has noted this. In such a case, where the judge can be informed by other honest people about the cause of this enmity, and if no other supporting evidence appears, he may securely reject such a witness based on the statements of the other witnesses. 

But if a "veiled person" <note>original: "velata persona" — a witness whose identity is kept hidden from the accused to protect them from retaliation</note> says: "I do not expect to have any such enemy, although I have sometimes had quarrels with women," or if they say "I have an enemy" but do not properly identify them (perhaps naming someone else who did not actually testify), then even if others say the testimony was given out of enmity, the judge ought not to reject the witness. Instead, he should preserve the testimony as part of the full proof alongside other supporting evidence.

There are many people who are less prudent and circumspect who seek to refute and annihilate these depositions made by women, claiming they should not be upheld because women are very often spiteful and accustomed to testifying out of envy. Those who say this are ignorant of the "astuteness and precautions" <note>original: "astutias et cautelas"</note> used by judges; they speak and judge like blind men discussing colors. These judicial precautions will be made clear in the eleventh and twelfth questions.

### Second part: how the process is to be continued, sixth question. And how witnesses are to be examined in the presence of four other persons, and how the accused is to be interrogated twice.

Now, sixthly, it is asked how this kind of process against **witches** <note>original: "maleficas"</note> in a **case of faith** <note>original: "causa fidei" — a legal trial concerning heresy or religious crimes</note> is to be continued. 

It must first be considered that in a case of faith, one proceeds **summarily, simply, and plainly** <note>original: "summarie simpliciter et de plano" — a legal term for an expedited trial that bypasses formal, time-consuming court procedures</note> and without the "noise and pageantry" of lawyers and formal judgments, as is clear in the chapter *Statuta* (Book VI). How these words are to be understood is clear from the title *On the Meaning of Words*, in the chapter *Saepe Contingit* (in the Clementine decrees), where it says: "It often happens that we commit cases... to be proceeded with simply and plainly, and without the noise and pageantry of judgments." Many people argue over the meaning of these words and doubt how the procedure should go. We, desiring to settle this doubt as much as possible, decree by this perpetual constitution: the judge to whom we commit such a case does not necessarily require a formal bill of complaint 

<column-break/>

or demand a formal "joinder of issue" <note>original: "litis contestationem" — the formal beginning of a trial where both sides agree on the points of dispute</note>. He may proceed during court holidays—granted by law due to human necessity—and should cut off delays. He should make the matter as brief as possible, rejecting frivolous exceptions, appeals, and delays. He should restrain the contentions and quarrels of the advocates and procurators <note>legal representatives</note> and the superfluous multitude of witnesses. 

However, the judge must not overwhelm the case so much that necessary proofs are excluded. We understand that formal summons, the protestation of the oath of "calumny" <note>An oath taken by both parties that they are acting in good faith and not bringing a false or malicious suit</note>, or the oath to tell the truth (so that truth is not hidden) are not excluded by this commission.

And since the process, as seen above, can be started in three ways—by the instance of an accuser, by the zeal of a denouncer, or by the outcry of public fame—the judge in this matter should not accept the process at the instance of an accusing party. This is because the deeds of witches are hidden by the work of demons, and an accuser cannot proceed and defend their case through evidence of the fact as easily as in other criminal cases. 

Indeed, the judge ought to advise the accuser to withdraw the word "accusation" and substitute "denunciation." This is done for the grave danger of the accuser <note>Under the law of "talion," an accuser who failed to prove a capital crime could be forced to suffer the punishment intended for the accused</note>. Therefore, we focus on the second method, which is the most used, and similarly the third, in which one proceeds not at the instance of a party. 

It should be noted that, as said previously, the judge must specifically interrogate the denouncer as to who else knows about the case. Therefore, the judge has those witnesses cited whom the denouncer indicated and those who seem to know the most about the fact. The scribe will continue the process by writing as follows: "After which, the judge himself, attending to the aforementioned heretical things denounced to him—which by their nature are so grave they cannot and should not be tolerated with closed eyes, as they result in the reproach of the Divine Majesty and the detriment of both the Catholic faith and the republic—proceeded to inform himself and to examine witnesses in the following manner."

Such a witness from such a place, having been summoned, sworn, and questioned as to whether he knows the accused, expressing the name of the accused <note>original: "delati" — the person who has been denounced or accused</note>. And he says that he does. ¶ Likewise, he is questioned about the length of time he has known the person, and he says it has been ten years, or however many.

And he said [the answer]. ¶ Likewise, he is questioned whether he had a close familiarity with the suspected sorcerer. And he said [the answer].
¶ Likewise, he is questioned concerning the manner and reason that these things were said. And he said: for that reason and in such a manner.
¶ Likewise, he is questioned whether it seems to him that the person spoke or acted in jest <term>trufatorie</term> <note>original: "trufatorie" — mockingly or as a trick</note>, or as a recital, or with an unreflective mind, or rather assertively and with a deliberate mind. And he said that he believes the person did the aforementioned things jokingly and in jest, or as a recital, and not with the intention of actually believing it or asserting it as truth.
¶ Likewise, he is questioned about the reason for this belief. And he said he believes it is so because the person who spoke was laughing as they said it. And concerning these matters, one must inquire very diligently, because sometimes people say things while reciting the words of others, or joking, or conversing so as to entice or incite others, even though they may also sometimes say them by way of assertion or affirmation.
¶ Likewise, he is questioned if he reports these things out of hatred or resentment, or if he omits anything out of love or favor.

These things were done in such a place, on such a day, in the presence of such witnesses, summoned and requested, and by me, the notary or scribe. Here it must always be noted that in such an examination at least five people ought to be present: namely, the investigating judge; the witness or denouncer; the respondent, or the accused themselves appearing later; the third is the notary or scribe, and where a notary is lacking, let him then join to himself another honest man so that the two may fulfill the role of the notary as touched upon above, acting by apostolic authority which they then exercise in that act, as seen above in the chapter *Ut officium* regarding heretics in the Sixth Book <note>original: "li. vi." refers to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a collection of canon law published in 1298</note>. And two honest men act as witnesses to the things they testify. Likewise, it must be noted that a summoned witness must also be sworn—that is, he must take an oath in the manner described above to tell the truth—otherwise it would be falsely recorded as "summoned and sworn."
¶ Other witnesses shall be examined in a similar fashion. When these have been examined, if the judge sees the fact is fully proven, or if not fully, yet there are very great signs and "vehement suspicions"—and note that we are not speaking of a "slight suspicion" which arises from trivial conjectures, but that the person is heavily defamed regarding the bewitching of children, beasts of burden, etc.—then the judge, if he fears the flight of the accused man or woman, should have them seized. If, however, he does not fear flight, let him have the person summoned. And whether they are seized or not, the judge should first have the person’s house searched unexpectedly, and all chests opened, and small boxes <note>original: "pirides," likely a spelling of "pyxides" — small containers used for ointments or charms</note> in corners and all instruments found there should be taken away. He shall conduct the inquiry having the notary with him, as above, after a bodily oath has first been sworn upon the four Gospels of God to tell the truth, both about themselves and about others. And in the following manner, each point shall be written down.

And she said [her answer]. ¶ And note that this question is necessary so that one may reach the root of the enmity, because in the end the accused will allege enmity <note>original: "inimiciciam" — personal hatred or a legal feud, which could sometimes disqualify a witness's testimony</note> as a defense. They are driven to make this manifestation at the urging of demons <note>original: "instantia demonum"</note> so that the sins of the judges may be made worse while the witches remain unpunished. ¶ Note also that they do such things when no one else is present, so that if the witness wished to produce other witnesses, he would not have any. ¶ Likewise, if she denies everything, let her be questioned about other acts of witchcraft reported by other witnesses, for instance regarding beasts or children. ¶ Likewise, question: why was she seen in the fields or in the stable touching the beasts, as she is sometimes accustomed to do? And she said [her answer].
¶ Likewise, question: why did she touch the child and why was he afterwards ill? And she said [her answer]. ¶ Likewise, question: what did she do in the fields at the time of the storms? And so concerning many other things.
¶ Likewise: how is it that since she has only one or two cows, they abound more in milk than those of her neighbors who have four or six? <note>This refers to the common folk belief that witches could magically "steal" milk from neighboring cattle.</note> ¶ Likewise: why does she remain in a state of adultery or concubinage? Although these do not directly pertain to the matter at hand, yet they generate greater suspicion than for those accused who are upright and honest. <meta>This page continues the legal and procedural instructions for the trial of a suspected witch, transitioning from the initial questioning (the "first act") to the weighing of evidence and imprisonment (the "second act").
