## ¶ Seventh question in which various doubts are clarified regarding the previous interrogations and negative responses: whether the accused should be imprisoned and when she should be considered as manifestly caught in the heresy of witches. And this is the second act.

It is first asked what should be done if, as most often happens, the accused person denies everything. The response is that the Judge must attend to three things: namely, the ill-repute <note>original: "infamiam" — a person's public reputation, which carried legal weight in canon law</note>, the evidence of the fact <note>original: "indicia facti"</note>, and the statements of the witnesses; specifically, whether all of these concur at once or not. If all concur at once—as most often happens because witches are immediately brought into ill-repute on account of deeds done in some village or city—then the evidence of the fact is also before one's eyes. This might include, for instance, bewitched children or beasts of burden which they often infect or deprive of milk. The number of witnesses is also recorded; though their testimonies may be "singular" <note>original: "singulares" — meaning each witness describes a different event rather than multiple witnesses seeing the same single act</note>—for example, one testifies that she bewitched a child, another a beast, and a third testifies to her general ill-repute, and so on—nevertheless, they agree on the substance of the fact: namely, in the acts of witchcraft <note>original: "maleficiis"</note> and that she is suspected of being a witch. 

And these witnesses—although they may not be sufficient for condemnation without ill-repute, or even with ill-repute (as was touched upon above in the third question)—yet along with the evidence of the fact, she could be considered from these three things together not merely as "vehemently" or "violently" suspected (about which degrees of suspicion it will be explained below), but considered as **manifestly caught** in the heresy of witches. This applies where fit witnesses—meaning those not acting out of personal enmity—and a sufficient number of them (for instance six, eight, or ten sworn men) should concur. Consequently, she ought to be subject to the penalties in the chapter *Ad abolendam* <note>A famous papal bull from 1184 issued by Lucius III, foundational for the prosecution of heretics</note>, the section beginning "Presenti," under the title "Of Heretics," and the chapter *Excommunicamus*, the second part. And this is so whether she has confessed to the crime or not. 

These things are proved thus: when it is said that where all three aforementioned conditions concur, she must be considered as "manifestly caught" in heresy, it is not to be understood that all three must necessarily concur together. Rather, it is proved by an argument *a fortiori* <note>original: "argumentum a fortiori" — a logical argument that if a lesser condition is true, then a greater one must certainly be true</note>. For if each one by itself—between the evidence of the fact and the legitimate production of witnesses—can render someone as "caught" in

<column-break/>

heretical depravity, how much more so when both proofs concur equally. For the jurists, when they ask in how many ways someone is legally considered as "manifestly caught" in heretical depravity, respond that it is in three ways, as noted by Bernard <note>likely Bernard of Parma, a major 13th-century legal commentator</note> in the *Ordinary Gloss* on the chapter *Ad abolendam*, the section "Presenti," and on the word "deprehensi" <note>meaning "the apprehended" or "those caught"</note> in the *Decretals* under the heading "Of Heretics." 

And this was touched upon above in the first question at the beginning of the work: namely, the "evidence of the fact," for instance, because a person publicly preached heresy. But here <note>in cases of witchcraft</note> we define the "evidence of the fact" because of the public threats she made, saying *“you shall never have another healthy day,”* or similar, and the effects followed. Next follows either legitimate proof by witnesses, or thirdly, from one's own confession. Hence, if each of these by itself makes and renders someone as if "manifestly suspected," how much more so by joining together the ill-repute and the evidence of the fact with the deposition of witnesses. 

Although in general heresy cases the law says "evident fact," and here we say "evidence of the fact," this is because the devil does not work openly but in secret. However, the damages and the "instruments of witchcraft" <note>original: "instrumenta maleficii" — physical objects like charms or potions found in a suspect's possession</note> which are discovered provide the evidence of the fact. Therefore, where an "evident fact" alone would suffice in another heresy, here we require all three things. 

Concerning the second point, namely that such a person caught, even if she denies it, should nevertheless be punished according to those legal chapters, it is proved thus: for one caught by evidence of the fact or by witnesses either confesses the crime or does not. If she confesses and is penitent, she is to be handed over to the **secular arm** <note>The civil authorities, who carried out physical punishments like execution which the Church officially could not perform</note> to be struck with the final punishment according to the chapter *Ad abolendam*, or as stated above, she is to be thrust into perpetual prison according to the second part of the chapter *Excommunicamus*. 

¶ But if she does not confess but stands in her denial, she is to be handed over as an impenitent person to the power of the secular court to be punished with the **due penalty** <note>original: "animadversione debita" — a standard legal euphemism for the death penalty</note>, as noted by Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio, a preeminent canon lawyer of the 13th century</note> in his *Summa* under the title "Of Heretics," in the section "How they are caught." Thus it is concluded that if the judge were to proceed in this manner—following the interrogatories and the depositions of witnesses, since in cases of faith one can proceed "summarily, simply, and plainly"—and were to commit the accused to prison for a time or for several years, he would be acting justly. If perhaps after a year, depressed by the "squalor of the prison," she should confess her crimes, he would not be proceeding unjustly. However, lest he should seem to rush his sentence, but rather to proceed according to all equity, it is asked what must be done next.

It explains how a judge must combine public reputation, physical evidence (like threats followed by misfortune), and witness testimony to justify life imprisonment or execution.</summary>

## ¶ Question eight, annexed to the preceding: whether she should be imprisoned, and regarding the manner of arrest. And this is the third act of the judge.

Whether, following negative responses <note>original: "negativas responsiones" — when the accused denies all charges</note>, a witch should be committed to prison for custody. This occurs where the aforementioned three factors concur: namely, reputation <note>original: "fama"</note>, evidence of the fact <note>original: "indicia facti"</note>, and the production of witnesses. Alternatively, should she be released under the security of guarantors <note>original: "cautione fideiussorum" — essentially a form of bail provided by others</note> so that she may respond when summoned again?

The response can be found in three opinions. First, the opinion of some is that she must be committed to prison and under no circumstances released on bail. They rely on the reasoning touched upon in the previous question: that she is considered **manifestly caught** <note>original: "manifeste deprehensa"</note> when those three factors align.

Others, however, say that before imprisonment she can be left to the security of guarantors, such that if she flees, she would then be held as convicted. However, after imprisonment, following her denials, she should not be left to bail or a "raised hand" <note>original: "manu levata" — a legal gesture of release or oath-taking</note> when those three factors mentioned above concur. This is because she could not then be sentenced and punished with death. This view relies on custom.

The third group says that no infallible rule can be given; instead, it should be left to the judge to decide based on the witness statements, the depth of her ill-repute, and the evidence of the facts. He should judge more severely as more factors concur, following the customs of the land. They conclude that if she cannot provide notable guarantors or is perhaps suspected of fleeing, she should then be committed to prison. This third view is seen as more reasonable, provided the proper manner of arrest is followed, which consists of three points.

First, her house should be searched as thoroughly as possible, above and below, in all corners, pits, and chests. If she is indeed a notorious witch, various instruments <note>original: "instrumenta" — tools of the trade such as charms, potions, or effigies</note> will undoubtedly be found unless she has hidden them previously, as touched upon above.

Second, if she has maidservants or companions, they should be detained separately, even if they haven't been accused. It is presumed that the secrets of the accused would not be hidden from them.

Third, when she is arrested in her own home, she must not be given time to enter her chamber, because they then usually take certain witchcrafts 

<column-break/>

and carry them with them to ensure **taciturnity** <note>original: "taciturnitas" — a magical silence believed to prevent a suspect from confessing under torture</note>.

On this point, a doubt arises: is the method of arresting witches used by some—where they are suddenly lifted from the ground by servants and carried in a chair or on litters so they do not touch the earth further—lawful?

It is answered that, according to the opinion of canonists and certain theologians, this is lawful for three reasons. First, as shown in the introductory question of this third part, many doctors whose words no one dares to reject—such as **Hostiensis** <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent expert in Church law</note> and **Gofridus** <note>Goffredus de Trano (c. 1200–1245), another influential legal scholar</note>—state that it is lawful to **shatter vanities with vanities** <note>original: "vana vanis contundere" — a legal principle allowing the use of seemingly superstitious methods to counter actual magic</note>.

Furthermore, experience and the confessions of witches show that those caught in such a manner often lose their spell of silence. Indeed, many who were to be burned <note>original: "incinerande" — literally "those to be reduced to ashes"</note> have asked to touch the ground with at least one foot; when refused, they eventually confessed. When asked why they had wished to touch the earth, they responded that if they had touched it, they would have freed themselves from the arrest through various "thunderbolts" <note>original: "fulminibus" — likely referring to magical bursts or escapes</note>.

Another reason is that this truth is manifest, as shown in the second part of this work: all powers of witchcraft are broken by public justice regarding past deeds. Regarding future deeds, unless the devil aids her anew with a silence spell, she will confess all crimes. We say therefore with the Apostle: *“Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”* If she is innocent, this manner of arrest will not harm her.

In the third respect, doctors agree it is lawful to remove witchcraft through "vain works" <note>original: "vana opera"</note>, provided they are not "illicit." This is the gloss on Hostiensis's phrase: "shatter vanities with vanities," noting he says *vanities* but not *illicities*. Thus, it is especially lawful to impede witchcraft, as this practice aims at prevention rather than any illicit exercise.

Finally, the judge should note there are two types of imprisonment: one for **punishment** <note>original: "ad poenam"</note> where criminals are placed, and another solely for **custody** <note>original: "ad custodiam"</note>, which occurs in the **praetorium** <note>the judgment hall or administrative court</note>. These two types of custody are noted in the legal chapter *Multorum querela* <note>A reference to a specific chapter in the Decretals of Pope Gregory IX concerning legal complaints</note>.

as stated above. Therefore, at the very least, she is to be imprisoned for custody. However, if the matters for which she was accused were light, such that she was not ill-reputed <note>original: "infamata" — meaning someone whose reputation was not already ruined in the community</note>, nor were there evidences of the deed in children or livestock, then she may be sent back home. But because she perhaps had familiarity with evildoers and knew their secrets, she should be bound by **guarantors** <note>original: "fideiussores" — people who would provide a financial or legal pledge for her appearance</note>—whom if she cannot provide, she must be bound by oaths and penalties—not to leave her home unless summoned. As for handmaids and domestic servants, of whom we spoke above, they should be detained for custody and not for punishment.

## Question nine: what should be done after capture, and whether the names of the deponents <note>original: "deponentium" — the witnesses giving testimony</note> should be made known to her. And this is the fourth act.

Two things are done after capture. The first among these is left to the judge's discretion: namely, the **granting of defenses**, and [the matter of] the place of torture—though not yet the examination by torture itself. The first is not granted unless she asks for it. The second does not happen unless the handmaids or companions she had in the house are first examined. Let us proceed, however, in the established order. If the accused says she is innocent and that she has been falsely accused, and that she would gladly look upon such accusers and hear them, then it is a sign that she is seeking her defense.

But is the judge bound to reveal the deponents to her and present them to her sight? Here the judge should take note that he is bound to do neither of those things: neither to reveal the names, nor to present them for a face-to-face meeting, unless the deponents offer themselves for this voluntarily and of their own accord—that is, to be presented before their [the accused's] eyes and to charge them to their faces with what they have deposed. That the judge is not bound to do this is proved by the **danger to the deponents**. For although various Supreme Pontiffs have held different views, none has ever held that a judge is bound in such a case to reveal the names of the deponents to the accused, nor even to an accuser (though we are not proceeding here by way of formal accusation, but rather by inquisition). Some held that it was permitted in no case; others in some cases; finally, however, **Boniface VIII** <note>Pope Boniface VIII (r. 1294–1303), a major figure in the development of Canon Law.</note> decreed this, as appears in the chapter *Statuta*, section *Inhibemus*, in the sixth book [of the Decretals], where it is said: "We nonetheless forbid that if, to the accusers or witnesses in a case of heresy who are discovering or deposing, a grave danger appears to be imminent on account of the power of the persons against whom you are inquiring..." Note that by "inquisitor and bishop" you should understand any judge

<column-break/>

proceeding against witches <note>original: "maleficas"</note> with the consent of the bishop and the inquisitor. For it is the same, and they can delegate their roles, as was clear in the introductory question. Hence, even such a judge—even a secular one—endowed with apostolic authority and not only imperial authority, follows this: [if] a grave danger is imminent if it happens that a publication [of the names] is made, then their names should not be published, etc. And it follows further: "But when the aforementioned danger ceases, the names of the accusers or witnesses shall be published, as is done in other trials."

The circumspect judge should also pay attention to the **power of the persons** involved, for that power is threefold: namely, the power of lineage and family; the power of money; and the power of malice—which is to be feared more than the other two. For because of that malice, grave dangers could be imminent for the witnesses if their names were published to those against whom they deposed. And the reason is this: there is a greater danger in publishing the names of witnesses to an accused person who is poor but has rebellious and murderous accomplices in evil who have nothing to lose but their lives, than to a nobleman or a wealthy person who is abundant in temporal goods.

What this grave danger is, and of what kind, **Johannes Andreae** <note>Giovanni d'Andrea (c. 1270–1348), an influential Italian canonist.</note> declares regarding the aforementioned word "danger," saying thus: "danger that death is feared, or the mutilation of themselves, or their children, or their parents, or the devastation of their property, or things similar to these." Furthermore, the judge should take note that since he proceeds by apostolic authority with the good pleasure of the <term>Ordinary</term> <note>The "Ordinary" usually refers to the local Bishop who has immediate jurisdiction.</note> in these matters, regarding that secret—namely, of not revealing the names of those testifying—both he himself and all other assessors who were present at the depositions of the witnesses, or who may be present in the future concerning the passing of the sentence, are bound under penalty of **excommunication**. The bishop can strike them with this penalty if they do the opposite; and thus, to prevent them from revealing anything, he has, at least implicitly, issued this threat from the beginning of the process.

Hence, in the aforementioned chapter *Statuta*, in the section *Et ut eorundem*, it is said: "And so that the dangers to those same accusers and witnesses may be more effectively met, and the business of the inquisition may proceed more cautiously, by the authority of this present constitution we permit that the bishop and the inquisitors (understand this as above) may impose [silence] upon those to whom they explain such a process, as has been mentioned, and upon those [they may issue excommunication]."

## Question 10: How defenses are to be granted with the appointment of an advocate. And this is the fifth act.

If, therefore, she seeks defenses, how
can they be granted when the names of the witnesses
are entirely hidden? It must be said that
the defense consists in three things. First,
that an **advocate** <note>original: "aduocatus" — a legal representative or defense lawyer</note> be appointed for her. Second, that
to that advocate the names of the witnesses shall not be published,
nor is he even bound to keep a secret under

<column-break/>

a sworn oath, but he is to be informed of each individual point contained in the process. Third, that the cause of the **accused** <note>original: "delati" — the person who has been reported or denounced</note> be interpreted in the best possible light, as far as it can be, yet without scandal to the faith and damage to justice, as will be seen. A **procurator** <note>original: "ꝓcuratoꝛ" — a legal agent who acts on behalf of another</note> should be granted in like form, to whom a copy of the entire process is given, though with the names of the witnesses and deponents suppressed. The same advocate may also proceed in the name of a procurator. Regarding the first point: Note that an advocate is not appointed at the whim of the accused. For instance, if she wished to have someone of her own choosing, the judge must be entirely careful not to grant a litigious or malevolent person, or one who could easily be corrupted by money—as such men are often found. Instead, the judge should grant her an upright man who is not suspected of legal dishonesty. The judge must note four things in an advocate; if these are observed by the advocate, the judge should permit him to plead; otherwise, he has the right to refuse him. For an advocate must first examine the quality of the case, and if he sees the cause is just, then if he wishes, he may take it up. But if it is unjust, he should refuse it. Hence, he must diligently beware lest he take up an unjust and desperate cause. Furthermore, if he ignorantly accepted the case at the start and received money for it, but during the process recognized the cause as desperate, then if he did not advise his "little client"—that is, the accused for whom he took the case—to yield, he is bound to restore the salary received, according to **Goffredus** <note>original: "Gof." — Goffredus de Trano, a 13th-century canonist</note>, which seems to be proven by the **Law concerning judgments on a matter not new** <note>original: "L. de iudi. rē nō noua" — a reference to the Corpus Iuris Civilis</note>. Although **Hostiensis** <note>original: "Hostiñ." — Henricus de Segusio, a preeminent medieval canonist</note> says the opposite—namely, regarding the restitution of the salary—unless the advocate acted with fraudulent industry. Hence, if a wicked advocate knowingly induces his little client to defend an unjust cause, he is held liable for damages and expenses under the **Law concerning the administration of tutelage** <note>original: "L. de admi. tu."</note>. The second thing he must observe is that he maintains three things in his advocacy: First, **modesty**, so that he does not present his case impudently, nor by insulting, nor by shouting, according to the Law "Since..." Second, **truth**, namely that he does not lie by introducing false reasons or proofs, nor false witnesses or laws (if he were an expert), nor should he seek delays—especially in this cause where proceedings are **summary, simple, and plain** <note>original: "sūmarie simpliciter et de plano" — a legal term for a fast-tracked trial without the usual formal complexities of a full lawsuit</note>, as was touched upon above in question six. And these three things are touched upon in [Canon Law] Case 3, Question 7. And the third thing that is observed is on the part [of the court...]

<meta>This page continues the legal instructions for the "Fifth Act" of a trial, focusing on the strict conditions under which a defense advocate must operate and how they should proceed when witness names are withheld to protect the safety of the accusers.</meta>

The **salary** <note>original: "salarij"</note> of the advocate should be regulated according to the custom of the region, a matter discussed in the canon law <note>original: "iij. q. vij. §. arcens. et .§. tria" — references to the Decretum Gratiani concerning legal fees and conduct</note>. But returning to our purpose, the Judge should propose the following conditions to the advocate, adding at the end that he must not incur the charge of being a **supporter of heretics** <note>original: "fautoriaz heresis" — a serious crime where one aids or protects a suspected heretic</note>, for then he would be excommunicated. This is in accordance with the chapter **Excommunicamus** <note>original: "c. excommunicamus" — a fundamental decree in Canon Law (Extra, v. 7. 10) regarding the punishment of heretics and their supporters</note>, specifically the section beginning "Believers."

It is not a valid defense if he tells the judge that he is not defending the error itself, but only the person. This is because he must not defend them in any way that prevents the case from proceeding **summarily, simply, and plainly** <note>original: "summarie simpliciter et de plano" — a legal term meaning the case should be handled quickly without the usual formal delays of a full civil trial</note>. He would be doing exactly that if he were to seek long delays or interpose appeals, all of which are rejected as stated in the sixth question. For although he might not defend the heresy itself, by acting thus he would be more damnable than the **witches** <note>original: "maleficis"</note> themselves, and would be considered a **heresiarch** <note>original: "heresiarcha" — a leader or founder of a heretical movement</note> rather than merely a heretical witch. As is clear from canon law, by unduly defending one already suspected of heresy, he makes himself a supporter. He must then publicly **abjure** <note>original: "abiura/re" — to formally renounce a belief or association under oath</note> before the bishop. A judge should not consider these matters lightly, for many dangers often arise from an advocate or **procurator** <note>original: "ꝓcuratoꝛe" — a legal representative</note> who strives to proceed falsely. Therefore, a judge must altogether reject such a person and proceed according to the facts and evidence whenever the advocate is found to be reprehensible. However, if the judge has an irreproachable advocate who is zealous for the truth and a lover of justice, he may reveal the names of the witnesses to him, provided he is bound by a sworn oath to maintain total secrecy.

### Question 11: What shall the advocate do when the names of the witnesses are not published to him? The Sixth Act.

It is asked: What then shall the advocate do (even when acting as a procurator for the accused) when the names of the witnesses are not made public to him or his poor client? This publication is something the accused would greatly desire.

**The Answer:** He should receive information from the judge regarding every detail contained in the process. If he wishes to have a copy of the records, it should be given to him with the names of the witnesses suppressed. Thus informed, he should go to the accused and present each point. If the matter demands it—for instance, if the evidence is very 

<column-break/>

burdensome to the accused—he should exhort them to patience as much as possible. And when the accused repeatedly insists that the witnesses be revealed, the advocate can answer: "You can guess the witnesses from the facts that have been disclosed. For example, the child or the beast of such-and-such a person was **bewitched** <note>original: "maleficiat'"</note>; or you said to such a man or woman, because they would not lend you something you asked for, 'You will find it would have been better to have accommodated me.' After those words, that person suddenly fell ill, just as the testimonies cry out." These facts carry more weight than the mere words of witnesses. 

The advocate might also say: "You know you are **ill-famed** <note>original: "infamatā"</note> and have long been suspected of many witchcrafts and harms brought upon people." By going back and forth in this way, it will finally come to one of two things: either the accused will allege **enmities** <note>original: "inimicicias" — legal grounds for dismissing a witness if it can be proven they are acting out of a personal grudge</note>, asserting that the charges were brought out of hatred, or she will say, "I admit I said those words, but not with the intent of harming." 

Therefore, the advocate should then propose the matter of "enmity" to the judge and his advisors, and the judge must investigate it. If a **mortal enmity** <note>original: "capital' [inimicicia]" — a deep-seated hatred involving a threat to life</note> is found—such as an attempted death between husbands or kinsmen, or an accusation of a crime that would lead to public execution, or serious wounds inflicted with clubs—then the provident judge and his advisors shall discuss whether the enmity is more severe on the side of the accused or the witness. For instance, if the husband or friends of the accused had unjustly oppressed the witness, then, if there is no physical evidence of witchcraft (in children or animals) and no other witnesses or public ill-fame, it is presumed that the witness testified out of a desire for revenge. In such a case, the accused is to be entirely acquitted and set free, under a suitable bond to not seek further vengeance, as is the custom of the court. 

But a question arises: Suppose **Catherine** <note>original: "katherina" — used here as a generic name for a female defendant</note> has a bewitched child, or is bewitched herself, or has suffered many losses among her livestock, and she suspects a woman whose husband or kinsmen have recently and unjustly oppressed Catherine's own husband or kin in a public trial. Here there is a **double enmity** <note>original: "dupler... inimicicia"</note>: on the part of the witness (who feels wronged by the lawsuit) and on the side of the accused (who is suspected of the witchcraft). In this case, should the witness's testimony be rejected or not? Indeed, on one hand...

On one hand, it seems that this is the case, because **enmity** <note>original: "inimicicia"</note> exists there. On the other hand, it is argued not, because he brings forward evidence of the deed. It is answered that in a case where there are no other witnesses testifying, and there is no **public infamy** <note>original: "publica laborat infamia" — a legal status where a person is widely rumored to be guilty</note> working against the accused, then the testimony of the enemy does not stand alone, but is rejected. Nevertheless, the accused is rendered suspect if and insofar as the illness is of a harmful, magical nature and does not arise from a natural defect. How this is recognized will appear below, and she must be **canonically purged** <note>original: "canonice est purganda" — a legal process where the accused clears themselves by taking a solemn oath, often with character witnesses called 'compurgators'</note>. 

But if it is asked again whether other witnesses, even if they have testified about the evidence of the deed which happened to themselves or others, can testify only regarding the infamy: It is answered that if they testify regarding some **evidence of the deed** <note>original: "indicia facti"</note>, it is well and good. However, if they testify only regarding the infamy, and such a state of affairs exists, then the judge—although he may have rejected the witness on account of enmity—shall take the evidence of the deed which that witness brought forward and showed to the judge. This, along with the other witnesses who testified regarding the infamy, shall be taken as a sign of **vehement suspicion** <note>original: "suspicionem vhementem"</note>. From this, the detained accused can be judged by the judge under a three-fold penalty:

First, **canonical purgation** because of the infamy, according to the chapter *Inter sollicitudines* <note>original: "c. Inter sollicitudines" — a specific decretal in Canon Law concerning the procedure for purgation</note>. Second, **abjuration** <note>original: "abiurationem" — a formal renunciation of heresy under oath</note> on account of the suspicion, according to the chapter *Accusatus* in the beginning; and according to the various degrees of suspicion, there are various forms of abjuration, as will appear in the fourth mode of sentencing. Third, on account of the evidence of the deed, if she confesses the crime and repents, she is not left to the **secular arm** <note>original: "brachio seculari" — the civil authorities who carried out physical punishments the Church could not</note> for the punishment of blood, but is judged by the ecclesiastical judge to **perpetual imprisonment** <note>original: "perpetuos carceres"</note>. 

However, she can still be judged by the secular judge, notwithstanding that she was sentenced to perpetual prison by the ecclesiastical judge; the secular judge can deliver her to the **fire** on account of temporal damages, according to the chapter *Ad abolendam* and the chapter *Excommunicamus* <note>original: "c. ad abolendam... excommunicamus" — key papal decrees establishing the punishment for heretics</note>. All these things will appear below regarding the sixth mode of sentencing.

In summary: the judge should first take care that he is not easy in believing the **advocate** <note>original: "aduocato"</note> when he alleges "capital enmity" on behalf of the accused. This is because it is extremely rare in such a crime for anyone to testify without enmity, since **witches** <note>original: "malefice"</note> are always held in hatred by everyone. Second, he should observe that a witch can be convicted in four ways: namely, by witnesses, by evidence of the deed, by indicators of the 

<column-break/>

deed, and by her **own confession** <note>original: "confessionem propriam"</note>. This may be regarding the infamy alone (which would be done through witnesses), or regarding suspicion (which would be done through evidence or indicators of the deed). From these, the suspicion can be judged as light, vehement, or violent. All this can proceed even without her own confession, though if that were present, one would proceed as stated.

Third, the judge should apply the aforementioned points to the person's advantage or disadvantage in order to counter the advocate. For example, consider whether she is accused only regarding infamy, or whether some indicators concur where she is rendered vehemently or lightly suspect; then he can answer the advocate regarding the alleged enmity.

This addresses that part where the advocate alleges enmity of the witnesses on behalf of the accused. But where he alleges the second point—namely, regarding those words she spoke against the witness, such as: "You will feel shortly what will happen to you," or "You will not have many more healthy days," or "The time will soon come when you wish you had lent or sold me such a thing," and similar threats—then the advocate may add that although some evil subsequently happened to the witness's property or body, it does not follow that the accused was the cause of this **witchcraft** <note>original: "malificie"</note> as a witch. This is because illnesses can happen in various ways. Likewise, he alleges that it is common for women to quarrel with one another using such words.

Against these allegations, the judge has to counter in this manner: if indeed the illness happened from a **natural defect** <note>original: "defectu nature"</note>, then the excuse could have a place. But because the opposite is clear from signs and experiences—for instance, because it could be cured by no natural remedy—the excuse fails. Likewise, it is judged so because of the judgment of **physicians** who identify it as a "witch-illness," commonly called <term>nightly harm</term> <note>original: "nachtschaden" — a German term for a blight or injury attributed to magic or nocturnal spirits</note>. Likewise, it may be judged by the opinion of other **enchantresses** <note>original: "incantatricum"</note> who assert that the disease is magical. Likewise, because it came on suddenly without any previous weakening, whereas natural illnesses usually weaken the body gradually. Likewise, because perhaps she was cured because certain **instruments** <note>original: "instrumenta" — charms, dolls, or ritual objects</note> were found under the bed or in her clothing or other places, and when those were removed, she was suddenly restored to health, as very often happens. As mentioned above in the second part.

### There follows on the same matter the twelfth question, further declaring how capital enmity is to be investigated. The seventh act.

Considering that witnesses are only rejected from providing testimony if they are **capital enemies** <note>original: "inimici capitales" — enemies who seek the life or total ruin of the accused</note>, as was touched upon above in the fifth question. However, to clarify such enmity from those things discussed in the preceding chapter perhaps seems too obscure and difficult to the judge, especially considering that the accused or his **advocate** <note>original: "procurator" — a legal representative or lawyer</note> would not easily acquiesce to a decision on what is called capital enmity and what is not. Therefore, other ways must be expressed by which the judge might arrive at the knowledge of such enmity, so that he might avoid condemning the innocent while still punishing the guilty with due justice. And although these ways are cautious or even deceptive, nevertheless the judge can practice them for the good of the faith and the state, since even the Apostle says: *Since I was crafty, I caught them with guile* <note>original: "cum essem astutus dolo eos cepi" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 12:16, used here to justify legal entrapment</note>. These methods are practiced especially upon accused persons who are not publicly defamed, or those not yet marked by any **evidence of the deed** <note>original: "indicium facti"</note>; though the judge may also use them upon any accused persons who allege enmities against those **deposing** <note>original: "deponentes" — witnesses giving sworn testimony</note> and who wish to know the names of the witnesses. The first way is this: a copy of the **legal process** <note>original: "processus"</note> is given to the accused or his advocate in one part—that is, separately—and the names of those deposing or accusing are given in another part. However, they are not listed in the order in which they gave their testimony, but in this way: the name of the witness who is first in the copy is listed as sixth or seventh on the schedule, and the one who is second is listed as second-to-last or 

<column-break/>

last. And thus the accused is asked: who deposes this or that? And who is first or second in his copy? In this situation, he will either claim all of them are his enemies, or he will not. If he claims all, the accused is more quickly caught in a lie when the cause of the enmity is scrutinized by the judge. If he only names some, then the cause of the enmity will be more easily investigated. The second way would be similar: where a copy of the process is given to the advocate on one side and the names of the deponents on the other, but with other extraneous matters added—things that were perpetrated elsewhere by witches but were not actually deposed by the deponents or the recorded witnesses. In this way, the accused will not be able to assertively claim that this or that person is a capital enemy, because he does not know which specific charges were deposed against him by whom. The third way is that which was also touched upon above in chapter five: when the accused is examined at the end of the second examination—before he requests his defense and before an advocate is assigned to him—let him be interrogated whether he considers himself to have capital enemies who, having set aside all fear of God, would falsely accuse him of the stain of **witchcraft heresy**. And then perhaps, being unprepared and caught unawares, and not having seen the witnesses' statements, he will respond that he does not believe he has such enemies. Or, if he says "I think I have some," then let them be named, and let those names be written down along with the cause of the enmity, so that the judge may later investigate with greater certainty after the copy of the process and the names have been handed over separately in the ways mentioned above. There is also a fourth way: again at the end of the second examination or **confession** <note>original: "confessio"</note> (discussed in the sixth question regarding the second interrogatories), before the defense is presented, he is interrogated about the witnesses who deposed most gravely against him in this manner: "Do you know such a one?"—naming one of the witnesses who gave the most serious evidence. And then he will say "yes" or "no." If he says "no," then he cannot later, when his defense and advocate are granted, list that person as a capital enemy, since he previously stated the opposite under oath—namely, that he did not know him. But if he says "yes," then let him be interrogated if he knows or has heard that this person has done anything against the faith, just as witches are accustomed to do. If he says yes, such...

In fact, those accused of witchcraft <note>original: "malefice" — specifically female witches</note> quickly deduce from the copy of the process who testified against them. And because capital enmity is very rarely found in such a case—except that which arises from their own evil works—the judge can easily resolve the matter through the aforementioned modes, noting also that those testifying often desire to present themselves personally to the witches and object to their faces regarding the things that were inflicted on them through **witchcraft**.

Let him give the accused or his advocate a copy of the process of the deponents, yet with the names of those reporting suppressed. And because in his defense he says he has capital enemies, and perhaps alleges various causes of enmity—whether they be so in reality or not—let the judge nevertheless assemble a **council of experts** of whatever faculty <note>original: "cuiuscunq̄ facultatis" — referring to the faculties of law or theology</note> if he can conveniently have them, or at least from provident and honest persons, because he is bound to this by the law. 

He should have the whole process read to them integrally and perfectly by a **notary** or scribe. Then, let him publicly expose the names of the witnesses or deponents, yet in such a way that he binds all the experts by a sworn oath to keep the secret. He must first inquire of them whether they are willing to do this, because otherwise those names are not to be exposed to them at all. 

Afterward, let him explain how, by inquiring into the enmity through such and such a mode, he could find none. However, let him add that if it seems fit, let one of two things be done: either it be discerned by the council which of the deponents are to be rejected as capital enemies and why; or let three, four, or five be chosen from the village or town who know more about the friendship or enmity of the accused and the witnesses (and who are not present in the council). Let only the names of the accused and the witnesses be made public to those few, but not the specific **articles** <note>original: "articuli" — the specific points of accusation or evidence</note> of the process. Their judgment shall then be followed. 

By the first method, they will not easily be able to reject the witnesses, considering that the judge has already practiced his own modes of inquiry. But by the second method, the judge will make himself totally immune and shake off all sinister suspicion from himself. He is also bound to observe this last mode where the accused is captured in a foreign place or country. And let these things suffice for discerning regarding enmity.

# **Question Fourteen: Regarding those things to be proposed before interrogations in the place of imprisonment and torture. The judge must take heed, and this is a new stage of the proceedings.**

It is finally clear what must be done by the judge. For if, as common justice requires, no one is judged for the **penalty of blood** <note>original: "penā sanguinis" — the death penalty or capital punishment</note> unless they are convicted by their own confession, or when they are held by the other two means: being **manifestly caught** <note>original: "manifeste reprehensa" — a legal status where the crime is considered self-evident or undeniably proven</note> in heretical depravity—namely, from the evidence or indications of the fact and from the legitimate production of witnesses, as was touched upon above in Question Seven. And regarding such an accused person, the matter is currently being handled: then, certainly, they shall be exposed to **interrogations** <note>original: "questionibus" — in this legal context, this specifically refers to questioning under torture</note> and torments for the confession of their crimes. 

And so that the question may be clear, let a case be posed which frequently arises and comes to the notice of many: a certain honest man, while passing by, did not wish to satisfy a certain woman’s whim in the sale of a certain item for sale. She, being indignant, shouted after his back: "In a short time, you will wish you had agreed!" This is a common way for witches to speak, or from their keen sense when they wish to inflict **harmful magic** <note>original: "maleficium" — supernatural harm intended to cause injury, disease, or death</note> through warnings. Then the man, indignant and not without cause, turned his face back toward her to see with what spirit she had uttered those words. And behold! Suddenly struck by harmful magic, his mouth was stretched sideways in a horrible deformity all the way to his ears. He was unable to pull it back, but remained in that deformity for a long time. 

Here, an evident fact is proposed to the judge. We pose the case and ask whether she should be held as manifestly caught in the heresy of witches. It is necessary to answer from the words of Bernard in the ordinary gloss, and in the chapter *Ad abolendam* <note>A famous 1184 papal decree by Lucius III which served as a foundational legal text for the prosecution of heretics</note>, as noted in the question touched upon above: that she is indeed caught. This is because a person is judged as "caught" in three ways, as noted there; and these are not cumulative—meaning that all do not have to occur together—but each one by itself—namely, evidence of the fact, the legitimate production of witnesses, and one's own confession—renders a witch as being considered "manifestly caught." An **indication of the fact** <note>original: "indicium facti"</note>, however, differs from **evidence** <note>original: "evidentia"</note> because, while it is less than evidence, it is nevertheless also gathered from the words and works of

<column-break/>

witches, as is touched upon in that seventh question. It is judged from harms inflicted not so suddenly, but over a period of time, though preceded by threats. 

Thus let us conclude: that regarding similar accused witches—those who failed in their defense as promised, or those who did not fail because a defense was not granted (not granted because it was not requested)—our question now turns to what the judge must do, and how one should proceed to interrogations to conquer the truth for the punishment of blood. Here, there are several things for the judge to notice, on account of the immense labors against the **spell of silence** <note>original: "maleficium taciturnitatis" — a magical protection believed to be granted by the devil to prevent a witch from feeling pain or speaking the truth during torture</note>, which shall be reviewed successively through the chapters. 

The first point is that the judge should not be prone to questioning the witch by torture; yet he should pay attention to certain signs that follow. Why he should not be hasty, the cause is this: unless divine compulsion through a holy angel concurs—so that the devil's magic departs—the witch is made so insensible in those pains that she would sooner be torn limb from limb than be able to confess any of the truth. Yet, torture is not to be omitted for this reason; partly because not all are equally entangled in such spells, and partly because the devil sometimes, of his own accord and not forced by a holy angel, permits the witch to confess her crimes. To understand this, one must note those things which were written in the second part of this work regarding the manner of performing **homage to the devil** <note>original: "homagium diabolo" — the formal pact or oath of loyalty to Satan</note>. 

For there are some who first serve the devil for certain years—such as six, eight, or ten years—before they perform homage to him, namely by devoting themselves to them in body and soul; whereas others, from the beginning, perform homage immediately by offering a denial of the faith. Why does the devil accept this requested space of time? Surely for this reason: so that in that interval he may test whether the witch denies the faith only with her mouth and not her heart, and whether she would perform homage to him in a similar way. For since the devil cannot know the secrets of the heart except through external signs and conjectures—as discussed in the first part of this work under the difficulty of whether demons can change the minds of men toward hatred or love—many are also found who, led by some necessity or poverty through other witches, and under the hope of professions and escape...

<columns>
...men who are zealous for the faith should be brought in to lead the questioning, encouraging the accused to confess the truth freely. If the accused refuses to confess, the judge should command the officers to bind them with cords or apply them to other instruments of **torture** <note>original: "tormenta" — while translated as "questioning" in some contexts, the text explicitly refers to physical instruments of pain</note>. The officers should obey immediately, appearing not joyful but as if troubled by the necessity. Afterward, the accused should be released again at the request of certain persons, drawn aside, and persuaded to confess, being informed that they will not be sentenced to death. 

Here it is asked: Whether a judge can lawfully promise to preserve the life of an accused person who is notorious, infamous, and legally convicted by witnesses and evidence—where nothing is missing except a confession from their own mouth—even though the crime, if confessed, would normally be punished by the final penalty of death.

It is answered that various authorities hold various opinions. For some feel that if the accused is highly infamous and there is violent suspicion based on the evidence of the facts—especially if she is a danger to others as a teacher of other **witches** <note>original: "maleficarum" — those who perform harmful magic</note>—she could then be secured of her life under these circumstances: that she be sentenced to perpetual imprisonment on bread and water, provided she reveals other witches by certain and true signs. However, this penalty of imprisonment should not be revealed to her at the start; only the security of her life should be promised, though she might eventually be punished by exile or some other means. 

Undoubtedly, for famous witches—especially those who persist in using harmful medicines and "cure" those they have bewitched through superstitious acts—they should be handled in such a way that they either help those they have harmed or betray other witches. Yet their betrayal should not be relied upon alone, because the devil is a liar, unless other evidence of the facts and witnesses also concur. Others believe that in such a case, the promise of life should be kept for a time while she is assigned to prison, but after a space of time, she should be **burned to ashes** <note>original: "incineranda"</note>. 

There is a third group who say the judge can safely promise to preserve her life, provided that afterward he excuses himself from passing the final sentence and substitutes another judge in his place. Among these methods, although the first seems useful for the sake of curing those who have been bewitched, it is nevertheless not lawful to remove witchcraft by means of witchcraft or illicit works, as was made clear in the first and introductory question of this third part.

<column-break/>

It is the opinion of many that it is lawful to remove witchcraft through empty and superstitious works. But because in these matters the experience and practice of judges, along with the variety of cases, is seen more than any specific art or doctrine, this is left to the discretion of the judges. It is certain, however, as experience has many times taught, that many would confess the truth were they not held back by the fear of death. 

The third stage of the process is this: if the accused refuses to confess the truth despite these promises, then the officers should execute the sentence passed. They should be questioned in the usual ways, not with new or exquisite methods, more lightly or more strongly according to what the crime requires. While being questioned on specific **articles** <note>original: "articulis" — the specific points of the legal accusation</note> for which they are being interrogated, they should be asked frequently, starting from the lighter matters, because they will more quickly admit to minor things than grave ones. 

While this is being done, the **notary** <note>the official record-keeper of the court</note> should write everything down in the trial record: how the person is questioned, what they are asked, and how they respond. And note that if they confess under torture, they should be taken afterward to another place so that they may confirm the confession again, showing that it was not only because of the pain of the instruments. 

The fourth stage is this: if the accused, having been recently questioned, still refuses to confess the truth, other types of instruments should be placed before them, telling them that they must endure these unless they speak the truth. If they cannot be led to the truth even by this terror, then on the second or third day, they are to be questioned again for the **continuation** <note>original: "continuandum"</note> of the torture—not for its repetition. For torture must not be repeated unless new evidence has come to light. 

The sentence shall be read before them in the following manner: "And we, the aforementioned judge, assign to you, such-and-such person, such a day for the continuation of your questioning, so that the truth may arise from your own mouth." All of this must be recorded in the process by the notary. During that assigned time, the judge, either himself or through other upright men, should persuade the accused to confess the truth in the manner described above, with the promise of safety of life if it seems expedient. The judge must also ensure that guards are constantly with the accused during this time, so that they are never left alone, because they will be visited by a **demon** <note>original: "demone"</note> to induce them to take their own lives...

### **Question 15: Regarding the continuation of torture, and the precautions and signs by which a judge may recognize a witch, and how he should protect himself from their spells. Also, how they should be shaved and where they hide their charms, with various explanations for countering the "spell of silence." This is Action 11.**

What follows now concerns the judgments on continuing **torture** <note>original: "tormenta" — while often translated as "questioning," the text explicitly refers to the physical instruments of the "questioning room"</note>. First, it must be noted that just as the same medicine is not for all diseases—but rather there are diverse and specific medicines for diverse and individual cases—so too the same method of questioning, inquiring, and examining regarding the articles of faith is not to be maintained for all heretics or those accused of heresy. Rather, according to the variety of sects and persons, a various and diverse method of examination is used. Therefore, the prudent judge—like a doctor who strives to cut away and sequester rotten limbs and scabby sheep from the healthy flock—can already estimate if the accused is infected with the **spell of silence** <note>original: "maleficio taciturnitatis" — a supernatural enchantment believed to be granted by the devil to prevent a witch from confessing even under extreme pain</note>. This silence cannot be uprooted by one single or infallible rule or method; indeed, it would not be safe to provide one. For if the "children of darkness" foresaw such a standard method and general rule, they would avoid it or guard against it as a snare for their own betrayal. Therefore, let the prudent and industrious judge take the opportunity and method of questioning either from the responses of witnesses, or from their testimonies, or from what experience has taught him elsewhere, or from what the sharpness of his own natural wit reveals, by using the precautions written below.

For if he desires to investigate whether she is wrapped in the spell of silence, let him observe whether she is able to shed tears while standing before him, or when being exposed to torture. For this very thing has been found—from the ancient reports of trustworthy men and teaching from personal experience—to be a most certain sign. For even if she is exhorted and urged by **exorcisms** <note>original: "coniurationibus" — ritual commands or adjurations</note> to weep, if she is

<column-break/>

a witch, she cannot shed these tears. She will indeed give out piteous cries and will attempt to smear her cheeks and eyes with spit as if she were weeping. On this point, those standing around must be carefully observant. The method of **adjuring** <note>original: "adiurandi" — a formal religious command</note> for true tears—if she is innocent—and of restraining false tears, can be practiced by the judge or a priest in this or a similar sense, by placing his hand upon the head of the accused:

> I conjure you by the loving tears shed on the cross by our Savior Lord Jesus Christ for the salvation of the world; and by the most burning tears of His most glorious mother, the Virgin Mary, shed over His wounds in the evening hour; and by all the tears which all the saints and elect of God have shed here in this world, and from whose eyes He has now wiped away every tear: that if you are innocent, you shall shed tears; but if you are guilty, in no way. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. + Amen.

Experience has taught that the more they were adjured, the less they were able to weep, even though they violently stimulated themselves to weep and moistened their cheeks with spit. It is possible, however, that later, in the absence of the judge and outside the place and time of torture, they may be able to weep in front of their guards. If the cause for this hindrance of weeping in witches is sought, it can be said that because the grace of tears is ascribed as one of the chief gifts to the penitent—since St. Bernard asserts that a humble tear penetrates heaven and conquers the Invincible—there is no doubt that it is known to be greatly displeasing to the enemy of salvation. Therefore, let no one doubt that the devil strives with his greatest efforts to prevent tears, so that final impenitence might rather be introduced. But what if, by the craft of the devil and God permitting it, a witch should happen to weep—since it is said that "weeping, spinning, and deceiving" are the natural properties of women? It can be answered that since the judgments of God are hidden, if she cannot otherwise be convicted by legitimate witnesses upon any evidence of fact, nor is she even heavily or violently suspected, she should certainly be acquitted. But in cases of suspicion where she stands accused because of the ill repute reported by witnesses, she would have to abjure the heresy of witchcraft, as will be discussed in the second method of sentencing. The second precaution is to be observed not only after this first one, but...

It must also be noted by the judge and all the assessors at all times that they should not permit themselves to be touched by her <note>The accused woman</note> bodily, especially upon the bare joints of the hands and arms. Instead, they should always carry with them **exorcised salt** <note>original: "sal exorcizatum" — salt blessed by a priest to drive away demons</note> from Palm Sunday and **blessed herbs**. For these things, wrapped together with blessed wax and worn around the neck—as was shown above in the second part of this work concerning remedies against witchcraft-induced illnesses and defects—possess a wondrous efficacy for protection. This is known not only from the testimonies of witches themselves, but also from the use and custom of the Church, which exorcises and blesses such items for this very purpose, as is evident in the exorcism rites when it is said "to drive away all power of the enemy," and so forth.

And let it not seem strange to speak of the touch of joints or limbs; for by divine permission, witches are able to perform their sorcery through the operation of demons sometimes by touch, and sometimes by sight, or even by the hearing of words uttered by them—especially at that time when they are exposed to **questioning** <note>original: "questionibus" — a technical term for interrogation under torture</note>.

Experience has taught us this. We have known certain women detained in castles who begged nothing else from the castle guards with the most insistent prayers except that, upon the arrival of the judge or another presiding official, they might be brought forward so that they could direct their first gaze upon the judge himself before they were seen by him or others. From such a gaze, it happened—perhaps by chance—that the judge or his assessors became so alienated in their hearts that they lost whatever indignation they had previously felt; they no longer presumed to trouble the women in any way, but permitted them to go free. He who knows this and has experienced it gives true testimony. And would that they could not procure such things! Let judges not disregard such warnings and remedies, since the contempt of these measures after so many warnings will lead to their eternal damnation, according to the saying of the Savior: *If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin* <note>John 15:22</note>.

Therefore, let the judges fortify themselves with the aforementioned things according to the institution of the Church. If it can be conveniently done, let the accused be introduced **backwards**, with her back turned toward the judges and assessors. Not only in the present act, but in all preceding and following acts, by fortifying themselves with the **sign of the cross** and attacking manfully, the strengths of the "ancient serpent" <note>The Devil</note> shall be broken with God's help.

<column-break/>

Nor should anyone deem it superstitious that she is introduced from behind. As has often been mentioned, the experts in canon law agree that to remove and hinder greater sorceries, it is sometimes lawful to "beat down vanities with vanities" <note>original: "vana vanis protundere" — a legal maxim suggesting that a minor unconventional act is permissible to prevent a major spiritual crime</note>.

The third precaution to be observed in this eleventh action is that the hair from every part of the body be **shaved off**. The reason for this is the same as mentioned above regarding the removal of clothes: for the sake of the **spell of silence** <note>original: "maleficio taciturnitatis"</note>, they sometimes have certain superstitious charms hidden either in their clothes, or in the hair of their body, or sometimes in the most secret places not to be named.

But if it were objected: Could not the devil, without such physical charms, harden the mind of the witch so that she is unable to confess her crimes? For other wicked men are often found who, under the greatest tortures, refuse to speak, no matter how much they are convicted by evidence or witnesses. 

The answer is that it is certainly true that the demon is able to procure such silence without any physical objects; nevertheless, he uses those things for the destruction of souls and as a greater offense to the Divine Majesty. To make this clearer: a certain witch in the town of **Haguenau** <note>original: "hagesnouie" — Modern Haguenau in Alsace</note>, who was also mentioned in the second part of this work, knew how to procure such a spell of silence in the following way: a male child, recently born and not baptized—and moreover a firstborn—was killed and roasted in an oven, and then, together with other things which it is not appropriate to describe, was turned into ash and powder. If any witch or criminal carried any of this powder with them, they could in no way be made to confess their crimes.

Here it is clear that even if a hundred thousand boys were used, they could never, by any natural property, cause such an effect of silence. Yet the devil uses such means, as is clear to any intelligent person, for the perdition of souls and the offense of the Divine Majesty. 

But as for the claim that often wicked men who are not witches maintain such silence, it must be said that such silence can arise from three causes. First, from a certain natural **hardness of mind**. For just as some are soft of heart or faint-hearted, so that at a light torture they would betray everything, even things that are false, so some are so hard that no matter how much they are burned by the truth...

When this was devoutly completed, it was revealed to someone that in a certain part of the body—namely, under the arm—they had a certain spell sewn between the skin and the flesh. Once this was found and removed, they were immediately consumed by the fire. Although others believe that a certain necromancer, through the counsel of a demon who had revealed this to him, had disclosed it; but in whatever way it happened, it is likely that the demon was compelled by divine power to reveal this, even though he always schemes for the subversion of the faith. From this, what should be done if such a legal case occurs can be deduced: namely, to recur to divine protection, so that through the fasts and prayers of devout persons, this kind of demon may be expelled from the witches in cases where they cannot be induced to confess the truth under torture, either through a change of clothing or the shaving of hair.

And although in the regions of **Germany** <note>original: "alemanie"</note> such shaving, especially in secret places, is considered highly indecent—for which reason we inquisitors have not made use of it—instead, having shaved the hair of the head, we have removed the spell of silence from many by the grace of God, by placing a drop of blessed wax in a chalice or cup of holy water,

If it is asked whether, in a time of necessity when the spell cannot be removed by any suitable remedies as mentioned, it would be lawful to consult female diviners—who are also accustomed to cure and remove spells—regarding the removal of such a spell: The **Answer** is that, whatever the case may be regarding the business at Regensburg, we exhort in the Lord that in no case, no matter how necessary for the public good, should diviners be consulted. This is especially because of the great offense to the Divine Majesty, since so many other remedies have been granted to us through which we can certainly attain our goal—either in the specific form requested or in an equivalent one—so that the truth will be snatched from her mouth so she may be burned, or God will take her from our midst by permitting another death to come upon her. 

These remedies are proposed to us: first, that a man should do what he can through his own industry and the exercise of his own strength, persisting in the ways touched upon above multiple times, and especially on certain days, as will be clear in the following question; as stated in **2 Corinthians 9**: *Abounding in every good work.* Second, if he fails, let him seek counsel from other men, so that perhaps a remedy which he had never thought of may be obtained for him, since there are various ways to remove spells. Third, if the aforesaid fail, let him have recourse to devout persons, according to that saying in **Ecclesiasticus 37**: *Be continually with a holy man, whomsoever thou shalt know to be a keeper of the fear of God.* Likewise, let the saints in the fatherland be invoked for them. If all these should fail, let the judge and all the people have recourse immediately to God with fasts and prayers, so that such a spell may be removed by His mercy. Just as **Jehoshaphat** said in **2 Chronicles 20**: *As we know not what we should do, we have this only [recourse: to turn our eyes to Thee].*

### Question 16. Concerning the time and the second manner of interrogation, and this is the twelfth action regarding the final cautions to be observed by the judge.

Regarding the aforementioned, some things must be noted. Second, those things touched upon above—concerning salt and other blessed items, along with the "seven words" that Christ spoke on the cross written on a slip of paper and tied together—should be bound around her neck. then the judge should ask if she would be willing to confess if the witnesses were presented to her face. And if she seeks grace in such a veiled way and reveals her deeds, let general words be said that more will be done for her than she has asked.

<meta>This page transitions from the practical interrogation tactics of the previous page to a legal and theological debate regarding "trial by ordeal." It specifically addresses whether a person accused of witchcraft can appeal to ancient tests like the red-hot iron to prove their innocence.</meta>

First, it should be noted that this heresy—as mentioned at the beginning of this final part—differs from other heresies in a simple way: it is not a "pure" religious crime, but a <term>mixed crime</term> <note>original: "mixta crimie ecclesiastico et ciuili"</note>, involving both Church law and civil law. This is self-evident. Therefore, in discussing the methods of passing sentence, we must first deal with a specific type of sentence to which witches often appeal: one where a secular judge acts on his own without consulting the <term>Ordinary</term> <note>The "Ordinary" refers to an ecclesiastical official with immediate jurisdiction, such as a Bishop.</note>. Secondly, we will discuss cases where the judge cannot act without the Ordinary, and thirdly, how the Ordinaries can fulfill their duties.

### Question 17. Regarding the Common Ordeal,
### and especially the trial by red-hot iron,
### to which witches often appeal.

The question here is whether a witch, when being tried for her crimes, ought to be tested by <term>common purgation</term> <note>original: "purgatoē vulgari"; this refers to "trial by ordeal," a medieval practice where God was called upon to reveal the truth through a physical test.</note>—as discussed in Canon Law—and whether a secular judge should compel her or allow her to undergo the **judgment of the red-hot iron** if she appeals for it. It would seem that this is permissible. For just as a **judicial duel** <note>original: "duellū"</note> is organized to protect one's life in a criminal case or one's property in a civil case, so too is the judgment of the red-hot iron by touch, or the judgment of boiling water by drinking it. Indeed, the first of these (the duel) is considered lawful in certain cases according to **Saint Thomas Aquinas** in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 95, at the end of the final article. There, he says a duel can be lawful when it closely resembles a fair contest of strength; therefore, in some cases, the judgment of red-hot iron should also be lawful. Furthermore, many princes of holy life and honorable character have used such tests; for example, **Saint Henry the Emperor** used it to test his wife, the virgin **Cunigunde**, whom he suspected of adultery. Additionally, just as a judge who cares for the community may lawfully permit minor evils to avoid greater ones—such as allowing prostitutes in cities so that society is not thrown into chaos by unchecked lust, following **Augustine** in his book *On Free Will*—so too should such a judgment be allowed where someone could be freed from the attacks and injuries of a community in a criminal or civil case. Finally, it is argued that burning one's hands with red-hot iron is a lesser harm than being killed in a duel; therefore, if a duel is permitted where it is custom, the trial by red-hot iron should be permitted even more so. However, the opposite view is found in Canon Law, where it is stated that those who follow such practices seem to be **tempting God**. 

<column-break/>

Where this is concerned, the Doctors of the Church say we must pay attention to the words of the Apostle <note>1 Thessalonians 5:22</note>: "Abstain not only from evil, but from everything that has the **appearance of evil**." <note>original: "ab hñte spēm mali abstinendū est"</note> Therefore, the law does not say everyone following these practices *is* tempting God, but that they *seem* to be tempting Him. This implies that even if someone practicing such things has a good intention, because the outward appearance is evil, it must be avoided. 

**I respond:** Such a judgment or trial is unlawful, especially the ordeal of the red-hot iron. This is deduced from two points. First, it is designed to judge **hidden things** <note>original: "iudicādū occulta"</note>, which are reserved for the judgment of God alone. Second, this type of judgment is not authorized by divine authority or by the recorded writings of the Holy Fathers. Indeed, in the decrees of the Church, it is stated that whatever is not sanctioned by the teaching of the Holy Fathers must be presumed a **superstitious invention**. **Pope Stephen** stated in the same chapter that crimes should be judged by spontaneous confession or the testimony of witnesses; truly hidden and unknown things are to be left to Him who alone knows the hearts of men. 

However, there is a difference between a **judicial duel** and the ordeal of the red-hot iron or boiling water. Duels more closely resemble a rational contest of strength, as the fighters are usually equal in skill and power. But in the trial of the red-hot iron, a **miraculous effect** is expected, whereas in a duel, the only outcome is the death of one or both parties. Therefore, the iron ordeal is entirely unlawful, even if the duel is considered less so. 

Incidentally, regarding whether princes and secular judges should permit duels, we should note the words of Saint Thomas, who makes this distinction. **Nicholas of Lyra**, in his commentary on the Bible (specifically on 1 Samuel 17, regarding the conflict between **David and Goliath**), suggests that in some cases a duel can be lawful. However, **Paul of Burgos** <note>original: "paulus burdegalēf."</note> argues against Nicholas, proving that this was not actually Thomas's intent. Secular princes and judges should pay close attention to Paul's proof. His first point is that the duel, like the other ordeal, is designed to judge hidden things which are reserved for God's judgment, as touched upon above.

It cannot be said that this practice <note>referring to judicial duels or ordeals</note> holds its institution from the conflict of David <note>The biblical battle between David and Goliath.</note>. For it was revealed to him by the Lord through an interior instinct that he should enter such a contest, and that he wished to avenge the injury brought upon him by that Philistine. This is elicited from the words of David: "I come against you in the name of the living God." Thus, he was not properly a **duelist**, but an **executor of divine justice**. 

Secondly, this point must be especially noted by judges: that in a duel, power is given—or at least permission is premeditated—for both parties to kill one another. Since one of them may be innocent, authority or at least permission is granted to kill an innocent person. Because this is simply illicit and contrary to the dictates of natural law and the divine commandment <note>original: "non occides" — Thou shalt not kill.</note>, it is entirely illicit on the part of the accuser, the recipient, the judge, and those providing counsel, all of whom are considered homicides. 

Thirdly, since a duel is a single combat between two people so that through the victory of one, justice appears—as if through a divine judgment—and in the other, injustice, this nonetheless constitutes a **tempting of God**. While it is rendered illicit on the part of the accuser and the recipient, the judges themselves are also at fault. When they could procure a just judgment or a termination of the suit by other means, yet do not do so—instead advising or entirely permitting it when they could have forbidden it—they surely consent to the killing of an innocent person. 

It is clear that it is not likely that the <term>Postillator</term> <note>A commentator on the Bible; here referring to Nicolaus de Lyra (c. 1270–1349).</note> Nicolaus de Lyra was unaware of this. Therefore, where he says that in some cases a duel may be committed without mortal sin, he is speaking from the perspective of the judges or advisors in cases where the duel is practiced not through their inducement or counsel, but by the accuser and the recipient themselves, or in some other respect. However, it is not our purpose to linger on these speculations, but to discuss the witches themselves. 

It is clearly evident that if such an examination is forbidden in other criminal cases regarding theft or robbery, it is much more forbidden here, where it is established that **witches** procure all their evil deeds through the help of demons, whether in inflicting injuries, or in curing, removing, or hindering them. Nor is it a wonder that witches are preserved from injuries in such an examination by the work of demons. For as natural philosophers hand down, the juice of a certain herb, when smeared on the hands, can preserve them from burning; and since the virtues of herbs are 

<column-break/>

least of all hidden from the demon himself, even if he did not intercept the injury by placing some body between the hands and the iron, he could still achieve this through such natural properties of things. 

Hence, witches—more than any other evildoers—should not be purged by such an examination because of the intimate familiarity they hold with demons. Indeed, by the very fact that they appeal to this test, they are already to be held as suspect witches. 

A fact serves this point which is said to have happened in the **Diocese of Constance** within the last three years. In the domain of the Counts of **Fürstenberg**, near the **Black Forest**, there was a certain notorious witch who was greatly defamed by the inhabitants. When she had been apprehended by the Count at the instance of many people, and charged with various crimes of witchcraft based on many pieces of evidence, she was finally interrogated through tortures and <term>questions</term> <note>original: "questiones"; a legal term for interrogation under torture.</note>. Wishing to escape the hands of all, she appealed to the **ordeal of the red-hot iron**. 

The young Count, not being very experienced in these matters, admitted the examination. When she was judged to carry the red-hot iron for only three paces, she carried it and brought it back, even offering to carry it again for a longer distance. Because of this, they should have judged the matter as a manifest sign of witchcraft, for no saint would have presumed to tempt divine assistance in such a way. Nevertheless, she was released from her chains and remained unharmed, and she persists to the present day—certainly not without a small scandal to the faith.
