**Regarding the first.** Since according to <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, whose writings formed the basis of much medieval law</note>, as found in Causa 2, Question 1, Chapter 1: "We cannot pass sentence against anyone unless they are either convicted or have confessed of their own accord." And the sentence is threefold, as the summary gloss says at the beginning of the question: namely, **Interlocutory, Definitive, and of Precept.** And <term>Raymond</term> <note>Raymond of Penyafort (c. 1175–1275), a prominent canonist and compiler of the Decretals of Gregory IX</note>, giving examples, says: An **Interlocutory** sentence is that which is pronounced not on the principal matter but on other questions emerging between the start of the case and the end, such as regarding the rejection of a witness, or whether a delay should be granted or not, and things of this sort. Or perhaps it is called interlocutory because it is delivered by speaking between the parties without the solemnity of writing. A **Definitive** sentence, however, is so called when the principal question is decided (as in the Digest <note>original: "ff." is the standard abbreviation for the Digest of Justinian's Corpus Iuris Civilis</note>, regarding *res iudicata*, Law 1). A **Sentence of Precept** is when a superior commands an inferior. Our investigation will consequently concern the first two, especially regarding the definitive sentence.

**It should be noted secondly** that although it is said in the aforementioned gloss that if a definitive sentence was passed with the legal order omitted, it is null by the law itself (Causa 2, Question 6, *Si quando*, section *diffinitiva*). And afterwards it is said: know that there is a twofold <term>legal order</term> <note>original: "ordo iuris" — the formal sequence of a trial</note>. One concerns the necessary substance of judgments, such as that the <term>joining of the issue</term> <note>original: "litis contestatio" — the formal start of a trial when the defendant denies the charge</note> takes place and witnesses are received. If a sentence is passed against this order, it does not hold. There is another order which does not concern the substance of judgments, namely that a sentence should not be passed under a condition, and that one should not pronounce on possession before ownership; if however this is not observed, the sentence still holds (as in Causa 2, Question 6, *Anteriorum*, section *biduum*). In this case, however, because it is a case of faith and the crime of heresy (though a mixed one), the procedure is <term>summary</term>,

simple, and straightforward <note>original: "summarie simpliciter et de plano" — a legal phrase meaning a fast-tracked trial without the usual lengthy formalities</note>, as is clear in the chapter *Statuta*, Book VI; and how these words are to be understood you have above in Question Six. And as is deduced there: the judge need not necessarily demand a formal petition, nor require the formal joining of the issue, etc. It follows, however, that he should admit necessary proofs, likewise the citation and the protestation of the <term>oath of calumny</term> <note>original: "iuramenti de calumnia" — an oath where parties swear they are acting in good faith and not bringing a false suit</note>, etc. Whence another mode of proceeding is now declared by the new laws.

**Regarding the second**, however, how the sentence is to be passed: **Note** that it must be delivered by the judge and not by another, otherwise it is not valid. Also, it must be in a public and honorable place, and while seated (as in Causa 3, Question 3, *Inducie*, section *spacium*). And similarly, it must be by day and not in darkness, and so with many things noted there; also because it is contained there that it should not be on holidays, and that it should be delivered in writing.

**It should be noted** that because here the procedure is summary, simple, and straightforward, as touched upon above; and in the chapter *Saepe contingit* in the Clementines <note>original: "in clemen." refers to the Clementine Constitutions, a collection of canon law</note> regarding the meaning of words, it is said: that in times of holidays, granted due to human necessities, one may proceed by law, and that the judge may cut short any delay. Therefore, if the judge is free, he can observe those things. Nor is he bound to deliver it in writing, since according to <term>Joannes Andreae</term> <note>A famous 14th-century canonist known as "the fountain and trumpeter of the law"</note> there are several cases in which a sentence is valid without writing, and among those is listed the custom of the place or the court (Book VI, regarding custom). A Bishop, even if he is the judge, can have the sentence read by another, after the fashion of illustrious persons.

Also note that although in criminal actions the execution of the sentence should not be delayed, this fails <note>i.e., there is an exception</note> in certain cases, especially four. But for this matter, two are taken: the first, if it is passed on a **pregnant woman**, for it is deferred until the time of birth (Digest, *De re iudicata*, Law *Pregnantes*). Also, when someone has confessed to a crime and afterwards denies it; understand this if the prior confession was not repeated in the manner touched upon above in Question 15.

**Regarding the third**, namely in how many ways it is to be passed: we shall treat of these things consequently until the end of the work. There are, however, still some things to be put forward regarding the ways in which a reported person is rendered suspect, because different sentences must be passed based on different suspicions.

# Question nineteen. In how many ways suspicion is understood for the purpose of passing sentence.

In how many ways and by what criteria should those suspected of heresy or another crime be described? And in such cases, should they be judged and sentenced for such a crime based on those suspicions? This must be answered according to both ancient and new <term>laws</term> <note>The author refers to "iura," the body of canon and civil laws used in ecclesiastical courts</note>. For the gloss on the chapter *Nos in quenque* <note>original: "c. nos in quenque"; a reference to a specific section of the Decretum Gratiani, the foundational collection of canon law</note> cited in the preceding question says that there are four ways to overcome <note>meaning to legally convict</note> a defendant: either by law, such as through legal documents and witnesses; or by the evidence of the fact <note>original: "facti euidentia"</note>; or by the interpretation of the law, such as when a defendant has been summoned multiple times and fails to appear; or by **violent suspicion**.

The <term>canonists</term> <note>Legal experts in Church law</note> also note that suspicion is threefold. The first is **rash** <note>original: "temeraria"</note>, concerning which the canon says: "You shall judge no one by the whim of suspicion." The second is **probable**, and this leads to a <term>purgation</term> <note>A legal process where the accused must formally swear their innocence and provide "oath-helpers" to vouch for them</note>, though the first type does not. The third is **violent**, which leads to condemnation. It is in this sense that the saying of <term>Jerome</term> <note>St. Jerome, an early Church Father</note> is understood: that a wife can be dismissed on account of fornication or the *suspicion* of fornication. Note further that the second type, which is probable suspicion, is admitted as "half-full proof" <note>original: "semiplenam pꝛobatōem"; a legal term meaning the evidence is suggestive but not yet conclusive on its own</note>. Thus, it assists in proof if other supporting evidence is present, and it is not only admitted for the purpose of ordering a purgation. 

Regarding **violent suspicion**, which suffices for condemnation, note that it is of two kinds. One is "of law and by law" <note>original: "iuris et de iure"</note>, where the law assumes and establishes something as a fact, and against this, no counter-proof is admitted. For example, if a man gives his word to a woman to contract marriage with her and physical union follows, it is presumed to be a marriage, and proof to the contrary is not allowed. The other kind is "of law but not by law" <note>original: "iuris sed non de iure"</note>, such as if a man has lived with a woman for a long time, it is presumed he has known her intimately. And against this

<column-break/>

proof is admitted. Applying this to our proposal regarding the **heresy of witches** and according to the new laws, we say that in law there is a triple suspicion regarding the crime of heresy: the first is **slight**, the second is **grave**, and the third is **very grave**.

The first, which is slight, is called "light suspicion" in law. This is found in the chapter *Accusatus* <note>original: "c. Accusatus. li. vi. de here." refers to the Book Six of the Decretals</note> at the beginning, where it is said: "If, however, that suspicion was light and slight, although the person should be severely punished for it, they should not be punished with the penalty for relapsed heretics." This suspicion is called slight or light both because it is removed by a slight defense and because it arises from slight and light conjectures. Thus, it is called slight because of slight signs <note>original: "modicis indicijs"</note> and light because of light conjectures. 

For instance, in cases of simple heresy concerning the faith, this applies if some are found holding secret meetings, or deviating in their life or habits from the common social life of the faithful. Regarding the **heresy of witches**, it is a similar case where they might meet in narrow places or at more sacred times of the year, in fields or woods, whether by day or by night; or if some are found apart from others; or if they do not frequent divine services at the accustomed times and in the accustomed ways; or if they contract secret familiarities with suspected witches. For such people are at the very least lightly suspected of heresy, because it is proven that such heretics frequently do these things. Regarding this light suspicion, it is also found in the Code of Laws <note>original: "C. de here. l. ij."; referring to the Code of Justinian</note> where it is said: "They are included under the name of heretics, and must succumb to the sentences passed against them, who are detected to deviate even by a light argument from the judgment and path of the Catholic religion." And <term>Hostiensis</term> <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a hugely influential canon lawyer</note> agrees with this opinion in his summary, saying: "It should be noted that someone may be detected as a heretic by a light argument, but to the end that they be held as *suspected*; they ought not yet be treated as [convicted] heretics." The second suspicion, which is **grave**...

Whether the devil, without the sight or touch of women, could cause **harmful magic** <note>original: "maleficiare"; the act of performing *maleficia*, or harmful witchcraft</note> to humans or beasts. The answer is: certainly, if God permits. But because there is a greater "promise" <note>likely referring to the contractual or spiritual yield of the act</note> where a creature dedicated to God concurs through the denial of the faith and other horrific crimes, the devil more greatly desires such a way of harming creatures. Indeed, it can also be said that even if the devil could perform such things without a witch, he still strongly desires to exercise them through a witch for various reasons, as was made clear in the preceding sections.

Summarizing our purpose regarding the methods of judging based on presumptions, it should be said that, according to the aforementioned distinction, those suspected of the **heresy of witches** are of three kinds: those **lightly**, those **vehemently**, and those **violently** suspected.

Those are **lightly suspected** who perform such small or light acts that only a minor or light suspicion of such heresy arises against them. And although, as stated, where someone is found so suspected they are not to be considered a heretic, they must still be ordered to undergo **canonical purgation** <note>A formal legal process where the accused clears their name by swearing an oath of innocence, often supported by character witnesses called "compurgators"</note> or be enjoined to perform an **abjuration** <note>A formal public renunciation of heresy under oath</note> as one lightly suspected. And indeed, that purgation can be ordered for them is found in the chapter *Excommunicamus* <note>original: "c. excoīca mus"; a famous decree in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding the handling of heretics</note>, at the beginning, in the section on heretics, where it says: "But those who are found notable by suspicion alone—by probable suspicion, which is light and appears lightly, as **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Segusio (d. 1271), a preeminent canonist whose commentaries were legal standards</note> says—unless they demonstrate their own innocence by a fitting purgation according to the nature of the suspicion and the quality of the person, they shall be struck with the sword of anathema <note>excommunication</note> and avoided by all until they have made worthy satisfaction." Thus, if they persist in excommunication for a year, they are thereafter condemned as heretics.

And note that in the canonical purgation assigned to them, whether they consent or not, or whether they fail or not, judgment must be passed in all respects as if they were one defamed of heresy to whom canonical purgation must be assigned. But also, that abjuration can be assigned to such a person as one "lightly suspected" of heresy is clear from the chapter *Accusatus* <note>original: "c. Accusatus"</note>, at the beginning, where it is said: "One accused of heresy or suspected, against whom a greater and vehement suspicion of this crime had arisen, if they abjured the heresy in court and—

<column-break/>

—afterward commits it, they ought to be deemed **relapsed** <note>original: "relapsus"; a legal status for those who return to heresy after swearing it off. Under the Inquisition, relapsed heretics were typically handed over to the secular authorities for execution</note> by a certain jurisdiction, even if the crime of heresy had not been proven against them before their abjuration." If, however, that suspicion was minor and light, although they are to be heavily punished for it, they should not be punished with the penalty for those relapsed into heresy.

There are some, however, who are **vehemently suspected**, and these are the ones who perform such vehement and strong acts that a vehement and great suspicion arises from them. Such people, although they are not heretics nor to be condemned as heretics (because, as explicitly held in the section on presumptions <note>original: "extra de pꝛer sumpt. c. literas"</note>, in the paragraph "Wherefore": "No one is to be condemned for so great a crime on the basis of vehement suspicion alone"), for it says there: "Wherefore we command that, since we do not wish anyone to be condemned for so grave a crime because of suspicion alone, even if it be vehement," nevertheless, one so vehemently suspected must be ordered to **abjure** all heresy generally, and specifically that into which they fell as a vehement suspect. This is supported by the aforementioned chapter *Accusatus* at the beginning, as stated, and by the chapter *Inter sollicitudines* <note>In the section on canonical purgation</note> and the chapter *Literas* regarding presumptions.

If such a person afterward relapses, either into their former error or into another, or associates with, visits, or shelters those they know to be witches or heretics, or gives them counsel by donating gifts, or sends them, or bestows favor upon them, they shall not escape the penalty of the **relapsed**. This is according to the cited chapter *Accusatus*, where it says: "Truly, when one who has committed an offense in one species or sect of heresy, or has erred in one article of faith or sacrament of the church, and afterward abjured heresy simply or generally—if from then on they commit an offense in another species of heresy or sect, or regarding another article or sacrament, we will them to be judged as **relapsed into heresy**." Therefore, he whose fall into heresy was established before abjuration, or is established now, if after that abjuration he receives heretics, shelters them, visits them, or associates with them, or gives or sends gifts or favors to them...

...or sends aid or bestows favor upon them. And further down: they should rightly be judged as **relapsed** <note>original: "relapsus"; a legal term for a heretic who returns to their errors after a previous formal renunciation</note>, since there is no doubt that they committed the act after having previously renounced that error. From these words, it appears that in three general cases, one who is **vehemently suspected** of heresy—after they have already abjured—is struck with the penalty for the relapsed.

The **first** case is when one falls back into the same and original heresy for which they were vehemently suspected. The **second** is when they have abjured heresy simply or generally, yet they fall back into a different heresy, even if they were never previously suspected or accused of that specific one. The **third** is when they harbor heretics, mislead others, or bestow favor upon them. And this case encompasses many specific situations and has many outcomes, as is clear in the cited section "But truly" in the chapter *The Accused*, which is frequently cited.

But it is asked what should be done if such a vehemently suspected person does not consent to abjure continuously at the command of their judge. Should they be handed over to the **secular power** <note>The civil government or local authorities, who carried out physical executions that the Church itself was forbidden from performing</note> to be punished with the due penalty according to the chapter *To Abolish*? The answer is: by no means. For that chapter and its section speak expressly not of those who are merely suspected, but of those **manifestly caught** in heresy, and one must act more rigorously against those clearly caught than against those who are only suspected.

If it is asked how one should then proceed against such a person, the answer is that they are proceeded against according to the chapter *We Excommunicate*, and specifically the section "those who by suspicion alone," as inserted above. They shall be excommunicated; if they remain in that state of excommunication for a year, they are to be condemned as a heretic.

However, some are **violently suspected**. These are individuals who commit such violent acts <note>In this legal context, "violent" refers to evidence so strong and compelling that it creates a nearly certain presumption of guilt</note> that a violent suspicion arises against them. Such a person is to be treated as a heretic, and judgment is to be passed as if they were caught in the act of heresy, according to the chapter *We Excommunicate* and the chapter *With Contumacy* in the sixth book. For they either confess the crime or they do not. If they do, and they wish to return and abjure the heresy, they are to be received for penance according to the chapter *To Abolish*. But if they do not consent to abjure, they are to be handed over to the secular court for the due

<column-break/>

punishment, as cited in the first section of *To Abolish*. If, however, they do not confess the crime after they have been convicted, and yet do not consent to abjure, they are to be condemned as an impenitent heretic. For **violent suspicion** is sufficient for condemnation and does not admit any proof to the contrary, as held in the chapters *Letters* and *Bring Forward* regarding presumptions.

And while this discussion applies to simple heresy—where there is no outward evidence or proof of the deed—how much more does it apply to the **heresy of witches** <note>original: "heresim maleficarum"</note>? In these cases, there is always either an evident deed, such as bewitched children, men, or cattle, or evidence of the fact, such as the discovery of the "instruments" <note>Physical items used for charms or curses, like wax dolls, bones, or sachets</note> of their craft.

And although in cases of simple heresy, those who are penitent and abjure are received for penance and sent to **perpetual prison** <note>original: "pretuous carceres"; a standard sentence for repentant heretics</note> as mentioned, in this specific heresy of witchcraft, the rules differ. Although the ecclesiastical judge may receive the person for penance to save their soul, the **civil judge** <note>original: "ciuilis [iudex]"</note>—on account of the crimes committed regarding physical harm and temporal losses—can still punish the person with the **ultimate penalty** <note>Death, usually by burning</note>. Nor shall the ecclesiastical judge hinder the civil judge, for though the Church may not directly hand the person over to be killed, it can simply "leave" them to the secular court's judgment.

### Question Twenty on the First Method of Passing Sentence

Since, therefore, the accused person:
->Is either found innocent and to be totally acquitted.<-
->Or is found only generally defamed of heresy.<-
->Or is found, beyond defamation, to be somewhat exposed to interrogations and **tortures** <note>original: "tormētis"; the judicial use of physical pain to extract a confession</note>.<-
->Or is found **lightly suspected** of heresy.<-
->Or is found **vehemently suspected** of heresy.<-
->Or is found **violently suspected** of heresy.<-
->Or is found both defamed and suspected of heresy together and commonly.<-
->Or is found truly having confessed heresy and being penitent and not relapsed.<-
->Or is found probably having confessed heresy and being penitent, but relapsed.<-

¶ Or they are found to have confessed to heresy and are unrepentant, but are not actually relapsed <note>original: "relapsa"; someone who has fallen back into heresy after a formal renunciation</note>.
¶ Or they are found to have confessed to heresy and are unrepentant, and are certainly relapsed.
¶ Or they are found not to have confessed, but are convicted of heresy by legitimate witnesses and other judicial means.

¶ Or they are found to be a witch-midwife <note>original: "malefica obstetrix"</note> who hostilely consecrates infants to demons.
¶ Or they are found to be defending themselves through the remedy of appeal in a frivolous and fraudulent manner.

And if indeed the person is found to be totally innocent <note>original: "immunis"</note>, they shall be finally sentenced in the following manner. It should be noted that an accused person <note>original: "persona delata"</note> is found totally innocent when the merits of the process—having been diligently discussed with the good counsel of experts—do not convict them, neither by their own confession, nor by evidence of the fact, nor by the production of legitimate witnesses (because they disagree on the main point), nor was that person otherwise publicly suspected or defamed of the aforementioned crime. It would be otherwise if they were defamed of some other crime; nor are there signs of the fact against such a person. For such a person, this practice is observed: they must be absolved by the bishop or the judge through a sentence of the following tenor:

**We**, [Name], by divine mercy Bishop of such a city, or Judge of such a place, etc. Considering that you, [Name], of such a place and such a diocese, were accused before us of such heretical pravity, namely witchcraft <note>original: "maleficarium"</note>. Considering also that these matters were such that we could not, nor should we, pass over them with closed eyes, we proceeded to inquire if the aforesaid accusations were supported by any truth, by receiving witnesses, examining you, and performing other actions

<column-break/>

which were appropriate according to canonical sanctions. For that reason, having seen and diligently examined all acts and proceedings in this case, and having taken the counsel of experts in law and also in the faculty of theology, and having reviewed this often, sitting as a tribunal in the manner of a judge judging, and having only God and the truth of the case before our eyes, with the Holy Gospels placed before us so that our judgment might proceed from the face of God and our eyes might see equity, we proceed to our final sentence in this manner, having invoked the name of Christ: Because by those things which we have seen and heard, and the acts and proceedings produced and offered before us in the present case, we have not found anything legitimately proved against you concerning those things for which you were accused before us. We pronounce, declare, and define by sentence that there has not been a legitimate case against you before us, on account of which you could or should be judged as a heretic or witch, nor be held in any way suspected of heretical pravity. Therefore, from the present instance of inquiry and judgment, we totally release you. This sentence was passed [at such a place/date]. Let the judge take care that it is not stated in the sentence that the accused is "guiltless" or "innocent," but rather that "it was not legitimately proved against him." This is because if later, in the course of time, he is accused again and it is legitimately proved, he can be condemned notwithstanding the aforementioned absolutory sentence. Note also that a person is to be absolved in the same way when they are accused of receiving, defending, or otherwise favoring heretical pravity where nothing is legitimately proved against them. A secular judge, acting by commission of the bishop, shall judge in his own manner.

<meta>This page continues the legal instructions for judges and inquisitors, specifically addressing how to handle an accused person when there is no concrete proof of a crime—such as a specific act of witchcraft—but the individual suffers from a widespread "bad reputation" or infamy in their community.</meta>

Other proven indicators against him do not exist, except for **infamy** alone, so that in particular no **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficium"; a harmful act of sorcery</note> is proven to have been committed. However, a judge can prove a vehement or violent suspicion when threatening words regarding an injury to be inflicted had been uttered, saying in effect or in meaning: "In a short time you will feel what will happen to you," and afterwards some effect followed in the form of an injury to bodies or to cattle. Regarding this person against whom nothing is proven except specifically infamy, the following practice must be observed. In such a case, since a sentence cannot be delivered by the official to absolve him—as was touched upon in the first method—but instead by enjoining upon him **canonical purgation** <note>a legal process where the accused clears their name by taking an oath of innocence supported by character witnesses</note>. Therefore, let the bishop or his official or the judge first take note that in a cause of heresy, it does not matter if someone is defamed among "good and grave" persons; indeed, it is observed here that one may even be defamed among any "vile and simple" persons. And the reason is: because anyone who can be an accuser in a crime of heresy is also someone among whom one can be defamed. But any heretic can be accused by any persons whatsoever, since only "capital enemies" are excepted, as was shown above; therefore, among such people, one can be defamed.

---

The bishop or judge shall therefore deliver the sentence regarding canonical purgation in this manner, or one very similar:

**We, [Name]**, by divine mercy Bishop of such-and-such a city, or such-and-such a judge, etc. Considering that, having diligently discussed the merits of the process of the deed performed by us against you, [Name], of such-and-such a diocese, reported to us concerning such heretical depravity, etc. We find you have neither confessed nor been convicted of the aforementioned stain, nor otherwise suspected even lightly, except that we find you legitimately and truly publicly defamed in such-and-law village, city, or diocese, both among the good and the bad. Therefore, to purge this infamy, and so that a "good odor" <note>a metaphor for a clean reputation</note> may exist in the assembly of the faithful, we enjoin upon you canonical purgation as is according to the law, assigning to you such a day of such a month and such an hour of such a day. On which you shall appear personally before us so that you may purge your infamy with such-and-such a **hand** <note>original: "manu"; referring to the number of supporting witnesses required</note> of your order. These **compurgators** <note>character witnesses who swear to the innocence of the accused</note> shall be men of the Catholic faith and of proven life, who have known your conversation and life

<column-break/>

not only in recent times but in the past. Signifying that if you fail in the purgation, we will hold you as convicted, just as the canonical sanctions will.

**Here**, however, it must be considered that when someone is found legitimately publicly defamed regarding some heresy, and nothing is proven against him except the infamy itself, canonical purgation is enjoined upon him. This means he must have some men—seven, thirteen, or twenty, or thirty, according to whether he has been defamed more or less, or in more or fewer places—who are of his own condition or order. For example, if a member of a religious order is defamed, then those men should be of a religious order; if a secular cleric, then those should be secular clerics; if knights, then those should be knights who purge him from the crime of which he is defamed. These are called "compurgators," and they must be men of the Catholic faith and proven life, who have known his conversation and life not only in recent times but in the past, as is held in the decretal *Extra de purgatione canonica, inter sollicitudines* <note>a reference to Canon Law regarding the requirements for character witnesses</note>. If, however, he refuses to purge himself, he shall be excommunicated. If he sustains this excommunication for a year with a hardened soul, he is from then on condemned as a heretic, according to the chapter *Excommunicamus*, in the section *itaque*, paragraph *quantit*.

If, however, he has agreed to purge himself but fails in the purgation—that is, he does not find such and so many compurgators as were enjoined upon him to purge him—he is held as convicted, and thus is condemned as a heretic, as is held in the decretal *Extra de hereticis, excommunicamus*, section 1, paragraph *adjicimus*, and the verse *qui non se*, and in *de purgatione, chapter Cum dilectus*.

It must be considered here that when it is said that the defamed person is enjoined to purge himself with a "third or fourth hand" of his order, the term "order" is taken there in a general sense and not specifically. Hence, if a bishop is to be purged, it is not denied that he may be admitted to be purged with other bishops. Abbots and religious priests follow in a similar form, according to *de purgatione, chapter Quoties*. A defamed person shall purge himself in the manner that follows, as is gathered from *Extra de purgatione, chapter quoties*, paragraph *porro*, and the chapter *accepimus*. Regarding the second part:

**When the term** assigned to the same defamed person for purging himself canonically arrives, the person to be purged shall appear personally with his compurgators before the bishop and inquisitor in the place...

...where he is known to be ill-famed, and he who has been defamed, placing his hand upon the book of the Gospels set before him, shall say thus: "I swear upon these four holy Gospels of God that—expressing that heresy for which I am defamed—I never held, nor believed, nor taught it, nor do I now hold or believe it." He shall, in short, deny with an oath whatever it is for which he is defamed. Once this is done, all the **compurgators** <note>character witnesses, usually neighbors or peers, who swear to their belief in the defendant's honesty rather than the facts of the case</note> shall place their hands upon the aforementioned book of the Gospels, and each shall say as follows: "And I swear upon these holy Gospels of God that I believe he has sworn the truth." And then he is **canonically purged** <note>legally cleared of the charge through this ritual oath</note>.

It must also be considered that a person defamed of heresy must be purged in the place where he is known to be defamed. And if he has been ill-famed in many places, it should be required of him that in all those places he publicly professes the Catholic faith and detests the heresy for which he is known to be ill-famed, according to the chapter *Inter sollicitudines* <note>original: "de purga. ca. inter sollicitudines"; a reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding the procedure for clearing one's name</note>. Nor should he look down upon the fact that he has canonically purged himself of heresy. For if, after purgation, he falls into the heresy for which he was already purged, he is considered a **lapser** <note>original: "per lapso"; one who has fallen back into a crime</note> and, as a **relapsed** person, he is to be handed over to the **secular court** <note>original: "curie seculari"; the civil authorities, as the Church could not shed blood and thus handed "unredeemable" heretics to the state for execution</note>, according to the chapter *Excommunicamus*, section *Adicimus*, and the verse "or if after purgation," and the chapter *Ad abolendam*, section *Illos quoque*. However, it is otherwise if he falls into a different heresy for which he had not previously purged himself, according to another chapter.

### Question 23: On the third method of sentencing the defamed, and on subjecting them to questioning.

The third method of finishing and concluding a **trial of the faith** <note>original: "processus fidei"; an inquisitorial proceeding</note> occurs when a person accused of heresy—after the merits of the case have been diligently considered with the advice of experts—is found to be **inconsistent** <note>original: "varius"; giving contradictory or changing testimony</note> or having evidence against them that warrants **questioning** <note>original: "questiones"; a standard legal term for judicial torture used to extract a confession</note>, so that they may be subjected to examinations and torments. This is done so that if, while being questioned, he concedes nothing, he may be considered immune and innocent. This happens when the accused is not convicted either by their own confession, nor by the evidence of the fact, nor by the legitimate production of witnesses, nor are there signs of such strong suspicion that he must **abjure** <note>formally renounce</note> heresy. Yet, he is inconsistent in his confessions. Or otherwise, there are sufficient indicators for questioning and torments. Regarding such a person, the following practice is to be followed. In such a 

<column-break/>

case, however, because an **interlocutory sentence** <note>a provisional decree made during a case that does not resolve the main issue but orders a specific action, in this case, torture</note> must be delivered against the accused and not in his favor, it must be delivered by the Inquisitor jointly [with the Bishop] and not separately, according to the chapter *Multorum*. First, if such a person remains firm in their denial and, although urged by pious men, refuses in any way to confess the truth, a sentence shall be delivered which appears to have the force of a definitive sentence, following the tenor of the text below:

**We, [Name]**, by divine mercy Bishop of such a city, or judge in the lands subject to the jurisdiction of such a lord: Having considered the merits of the case conducted by us against you, [Name], of such a place and such a diocese, and having diligently examined them, we find that you are inconsistent in your confessions, and nonetheless there are many indicators that are sufficient for subjecting you to **questioning and torments**. Therefore, so that the truth may be had from your own mouth, and that hereafter you do not offend the ears of the judges, we declare, judge, and sentence by this interlocutory decree that on this present day and at such an hour you are to be subjected to questioning and torments. This sentence was thus delivered.

¶ If the person to be questioned is found to be inconsistent and at the same time there are other indicators sufficient for questioning, both shall be placed in the sentence, as was set down in the aforementioned text. If, however, these two do not concur—but only one, such as inconsistency without other indicators, or other indicators without inconsistency—only that which is found shall be placed in the sentence. However, once the sentence is delivered, let it be executed immediately, or let the execution be simulated. Yet, let the judge not be too eager to question anyone; for questioning and torments are not employed except in the absence of other proofs. And therefore, let him seek other proofs; but if he does not find them, and he holds it as probable that the accused is guilty but denies the truth out of fear, let him use good and sometimes cautious methods, occasionally employing the person's friends to urge them to speak the truth. Let him use his diligence so that he may have the truth from the person’s mouth, and let him not hasten the business. For frequent meditation, the misery of prison, and repeated instruction by upright men dispose one toward learning the truth. If it happens to the accused...

...having waited for the appropriate time and having granted many delays for information. If the Bishop and the Judge believe in good faith, having considered everything, that the accused is denying the truth, they should **interrogate** <note>original: "questionent"; in this legal context, "questioning" refers specifically to judicial interrogation under torture</note> him moderately, yet without the shedding of blood, knowing that such interrogations are often deceptive and ineffective. For some are so soft-hearted and weak of mind that at the slightest torture they would admit to anything, even if false. Others, however, are so stubborn that no matter how much they are tormented, the truth cannot be wrung from them. There are some who have been interrogated before; of these, some endure the questioning better because their limbs are more easily stretched and bent, while others remain weaker and thus endure the questioning less. Some are even **bewitched** <note>original: "maleficiati"</note> and use sorcery during the questioning so that they would die before they would confess anything, for they are made as if insensible to pain. Therefore, in these interrogations, one must act with the greatest prudence, paying close attention to the manner of questioning. When the order has been given, the officials should immediately prepare themselves to question the accused. While they are preparing, the Bishop or the Judge, both by themselves and through other good men zealous for the faith, should persuade the one to be questioned to confess freely, even promising to spare his life if necessary, as was done above. And if he cannot be induced by terror or by the truth to confess, they may assign a day or a third day to **continue** the torments, not to **repeat** <note>original: "non ad iterandum... sed continuari"; medieval law forbade repeating torture without new evidence. To circumvent this, judges would "suspend" the session and "continue" it later, legally treating multiple days as a single session</note> them, for they should not be repeated unless new evidence comes to light; however, continuing them is not forbidden. They shall say thus: "And we, Bishop N. and Judge M., if present, assign you such a day for the **continuation** of your questioning, so that the truth may be drawn from your own mouth," and they shall record the whole matter in the process. And within the time assigned to him, they shall, by themselves and through other honest men, induce him to speak the truth. And if he refuses to confess on the assigned day, the questioning may be continued, and thus he may be questioned with the same or other more severe torments, more or less strongly according to the gravity of the crimes. And the judges may use many lawful deceptions, both in words and in deeds, so that the truth may be obtained—things which experience, practice, and the variety of cases teach better than any art or doctrine. But where one recently questioned and exposed to

<column-break/>

torments has refused to reveal the truth, he shall not be harassed further but shall be allowed to go free. If, however, he persists in his confession and reveals the truth, acknowledging his own guilt and asking pardon from the Church as one caught in heresy by his own profession but repentant, then according to the chapter *Absolenda*, paragraph *Praesenti* <note>references to the Decretals, the body of canon law</note>, he shall **abjure** <note>formally renounce his errors</note> and be sentenced as one publicly convicted, in the same manner as those convicted of heresy by their own confession, as will be discussed below in the eighth method of dealing with such convicts. But where he reveals the truth and does not repent but persists obstinately in heresy and has not relapsed, he shall be condemned according to the chapter *Ad abolendam*, paragraph *Praesenti*. After being waited for and properly informed, he shall be handed over to the **secular arm** <note>the civil authorities; the Church technically did not execute people, but "relaxed" them to the state for the death penalty</note> to be struck with the ultimate punishment, as is said below in the tenth method. If, however, he has relapsed, he shall be condemned in the manner described below in the tenth method of concluding a process.

Here it must be diligently noted that sometimes a person who is to be questioned has confessed nothing against himself before the questioning, and nothing is proven for which he could or should **abjure** <note>renounce</note> heresy or be condemned for heresy; it is such people who are being dealt with here, as has just been said. At other times, however, he is already caught in a veiled heresy, or there are other proven pieces of evidence against him for which he ought to abjure—for instance, if he is lightly or vehemently suspected of heresy—for which he should not be questioned; but if beyond this he denies other things which are not proven but for which there is sufficient evidence for questioning, and when he is questioned for such things he confesses nothing because of the questioning, he is nevertheless not to be acquitted according to the first method. Instead, he shall be proceeded against according to what has been proven against him, and he shall abjure either as a suspect or as a convicted person, as the merits of the case demand and require. If, however, because of the questioning he confesses those things or any of them for which he was questioned, then he shall abjure both the heresy and those specific things, and sentence shall be passed against him for both.

<meta>This page continues the legal procedures for concluding a trial. While the previous page discussed the use of torture for those who refuse to confess, this section details the protocol for a defendant who is found to be "lightly suspected" of heresy rather than "vehemently" or "violently" suspected. It provides the specific oaths and sentencing formulas used to reconcile such individuals to the Church.</meta>

After things have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those skilled in law, if a person is found only **lightly suspected of heresy**, <note>original: "suspectus de heresi leuiter." In inquisitorial law, there were three degrees of suspicion: light (levis), vehement (vehemens), and violent (violenta), each carrying different legal consequences.</note> it occurs when one accused of heresy is not convicted by their own confession, nor by the evidence of the fact, nor by the legitimate production of witnesses, nor are there other strong or vehement indications against them. Instead, there are only small and light indications, which have been judged as such by counsel. Because of this, as one lightly suspected of heresy, they can and ought to abjure the heresy of which they were accused. Such a person, if they should **relapse**, <note>A "relapsed" heretic was someone who fell back into heresy after a previous formal abjuration. Under canon law, relapsed heretics were generally handed over to the state for execution.</note> is not punished with the penalty due to a relapsed person, although they should then be punished more severely than if they had not abjured beforehand. This is according to the chapter *Accusatus* at the end of the section on heresy in **Book VI**. <note>original: "li. vi." refers to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a collection of canon law promulgated in 1298.</note> Concerning such a person, the following practice is to be observed: if they are held suspected publicly, they shall abjure publicly in the church according to the manner that follows in the sentence:

> I, [Name], of such a diocese, inhabitant of such a city or place, placed in judgment before you, Lord Bishop of such a city, with the holy Gospels placed before me and touched by my own hands, swear that I believe in my heart and profess with my mouth that holy Catholic and Apostolic faith which the holy Roman Church believes, confesses, preaches, and observes. Likewise, I swear that I believe in my heart and profess with my mouth that the Lord Jesus Christ with all the saints detests the most evil **heresy of witches**, <note>original: "heresim pessimam maleficarum"</note> and that all those following or adhering to it shall be tortured with eternal fires with the devil and his angels forever, unless they repent and are reconciled to the holy Church through penance. And consequently, I abjure, deny, and revoke that heresy of which you, Lord Bishop and official vicars, hold me suspected—because I had familiarity with witches, or ignorantly defended their error, or held hatred toward the inquisitors who prosecute them, or even because I did not reveal their crimes. Likewise, I swear that I never believed the aforesaid heresy, nor do I believe it, nor have I adhered to it, nor do I adhere to it, nor will I ever believe it; nor am I a heretic, nor have I taught it, nor do I intend to teach it. If I should do any of the aforementioned things in the future—which may God forbid—I submit myself with a ready mind to the penalties of the law. Being thus abjured, I am prepared to undergo all penance which you wish to enjoin upon me for those things I have done and said, for which you rightly hold me suspected; I swear

<column-break/>

to fulfill this to the best of my strength, so that I in no way contravene it, so help me God and these holy Gospels.

The aforesaid abjuration should be done in the **vernacular** <note>original: "in vulgari"; the common spoken language (such as German or French) rather than Latin, ensuring the defendant and the public fully understood the gravity of the oath.</note> so that it may be understood by all. Once this is done, the judge, if he is present, or the official can say to the person publicly in the vernacular these or similar words: "Son (or daughter), you have abjured the suspicion we had of you—not without cause—and have cleared yourself through the aforementioned abjuration. From now on, take care that you do not fall into this abjured heresy. For although, if you were to repent, you would not be handed over to the **secular arm** <note>original: "brachio seculari." The Church technically could not shed blood, so "handing over to the secular arm" was the legal phrasing for delivering a condemned person to civil authorities for execution.</note> because you abjured as one lightly suspected and not vehemently suspected, you would nevertheless be punished much more strongly than if you had not abjured. Furthermore, henceforth for even a small matter you would be held vehemently suspected, and if you were to abjure as such, you would be punished with the penalty due to the relapsed, and without mercy you would be handed over to the secular court to be struck with the ultimate punishment." If, however, they abjure secretly in the chamber of the Bishop or the Judge (namely when the matter has not been made public), they shall abjure in a similar manner. Once these things are done, the sentence shall be delivered in this way:

> We, by divine mercy Bishop of such a city—or the judge if he is present in the lands subject to the jurisdiction of such a lord—having attended to and diligently considered the merits of the process conducted by us against you, [Name], who were accused before us of heretical pravity, we find that you have committed such and such things <note>Here they state the specific actions that make the person lightly suspected.</note> which render you lightly suspected of heresy. Because of these things, rightly holding you as such, we have made you abjure that same heresy as one lightly suspected of the aforementioned stain. But lest the things committed in the past remain unpunished, and so that you may be made more cautious in the future, by the counsel of many and great men skilled in law and also religious men, having held a mature and thorough deliberation upon these matters, and having before our eyes only God and the irrefragable truth of the holy Catholic faith, with the holy Gospels placed before us: So that our judgment may go forth from the face of God and our eyes may see equity, sitting as a tribunal in the manner of judges passing judgment, we condemn you, [Name], here personally present in our presence, in the manner that follows...

## Question XXIV. On the fifth mode
## of sentencing one vehemently suspected.

The fifth mode of finishing and terminating a process of faith is when, after the merits of the process have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those skilled in law, the accused is found to be **vehemently suspected of heresy**. And this occurs when the person accused of heretical depravity is not found to be legitimately convicted by their own confession, nor by the evidence of the fact, nor by the legitimate production of witnesses, but there are great and grave indications proven against them. These are such indications as are judged by counsel to render the person **vehemently suspected** <note>original: "suspecta vehementer." This level of suspicion was reached when the evidence, though not a direct confession or multiple eyewitness accounts, was so overwhelming that a reasonable person could not doubt the guilt.</note> of the aforementioned heretical depravity.

Regarding such a person, this practice is to be observed: Such a person must abjure that heretical depravity as one vehemently suspected of such heresy, so that if they later **relapse**, they shall be punished with the penalty due to a relapsed person. This means they shall be **handed over to the secular arm** <note>original: "tradari brachio seculari." A euphemism for the Church handing a prisoner to the civil authorities to be executed, as the Church itself was forbidden from shedding blood.</note> to be struck with the ultimate punishment. According to the chapter *Accusatus* at the end of the section on heresy in **Book VI**. <note>Refers to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a key collection of Canon Law.</note> And they shall abjure publicly or secretly, depending on whether they were held suspected publicly or secretly, and before many or few people, and people of high or low status, as was just said concerning one who is lightly suspected of heresy.

The method of preparing for the abjuration is as follows: When the Sunday arrives for making the abjuration and for hearing the sentence or penance to be imposed, the preacher shall deliver a general sermon. When this is finished, let the notary or cleric read publicly those things of which the person is to abjure—those things of which he was convicted and other things from which he is held vehemently suspected of heresy. Afterward, the judge or official shall say to him: "Behold, from these things recited, you are vehemently suspected by us of such heresy..."

<column-break/>

"...wherefore it is necessary that you **purge** yourself <note>original: "purges te." Canonical purgation was a formal process of proving one's innocence or clearing one's name from suspicion.</note> and abjure the aforementioned heresy." And then let a book of the Gospels be placed before the one abjuring, and he shall place his hand upon it. If he knows how to read competently, the following abjuration shall be handed to him in writing, and he shall read it before all the people. If, however, he does not know how to read well, the notary shall read it slowly and the one abjuring shall respond in a high and intelligible voice in this manner: For the notary or cleric shall say, "I, so-and-so, from such-and-such a place," and the person shall respond with the same words. And the person shall always respond with the same words in the **vernacular** <note>original: "in vulgari." It was essential that the suspect understood exactly what they were saying, and that the public understood the renunciation, so the oath was translated from Latin into the local language (e.g., German or French).</note> while established in the court. And so on until the abjuration is finished; and he shall abjure through the form of the following tenor:

> I, [Name], of [Place], of [Name] Diocese, personally established in judgment before you, the Reverend Lords, the Bishop of [City] and [Name], the judge in the lands subject to the jurisdiction of [Lord Name], with the holy Gospels placed before me and touched by my own hands, I swear that I believe in my heart and profess with my mouth that holy Catholic and Apostolic faith which the Holy Roman Church teaches, professes, preaches, and holds.
>
> Likewise, I swear that I believe in my heart and profess with my mouth that [etc.]. <note>At this point, the specific Catholic article of faith that contradicts the person's suspected heresy is recited.</note>
>
> For example: if it concerns the **heresy of witches**, it shall be said thus: I swear that I believe that not only simple heretics or schismatics will be tortured with eternal fires, but above all those infected with the heresy of witches. These are they who, denying the faith they received in the sacred font of baptism, follow diabolical filthiness to fulfill their depraved desires, inflicting many injuries upon men, cattle, and the fruits of the earth. And consequently, I abjure, deny, and revoke that heresy, or rather that **infidelity**, <note>original: "infidelitatem." In this context, infidelity refers to a total lack of faith or a betrayal of the Christian faith.</note> which falsely and lyingly asserts that there are no witches on earth and that no one ought to believe they can inflict injuries with the help of demons. For such infidelity expressly fights, as I now recognize, against the determination of Holy Mother Church and of all Catholic doctors, and even against the **imperial laws** which have decreed that such women are to be burned. Likewise, I swear that never the aforementioned...

Nevertheless, it can be imposed upon them that they stand on certain solemn days at the doors of such churches, or around the altars while the solemnities of the Masses are celebrated, holding in their hands a burning wax candle of a certain weight, or that they go on such a pilgrimage, and similar things, as the quality of the business demands and requires.

<meta>This page transitions from the "vehement suspicion" discussed on the previous page to the even more serious "violent suspicion." It outlines the legal definitions and the specific procedures for dealing with individuals—particularly witches—who fall under this category of evidence.</meta>

### The Third Mode of Concluding a Trial of the Faith

The third way of concluding a process of the faith occurs when, after the merits of the case of **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica pravitate." A standard legal term for heresy.</note> have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of legal experts, the accused is found to be **violently suspected** of heresy. 

This happens when the accused is not legally caught by their own confession, nor by the clear evidence of the fact, nor by the legal production of witnesses, but there are signs that are not merely light or vehement, but are very strong and most violent. These signs deservedly render the accused **violently suspected** of the said heresy, and because of them, such a person must be judged as one who is violently suspected. 

To ensure this method is understood more clearly, we shall provide examples both of simple heresy regarding the faith and of the **heresy of witches** <note>original: "maleficarium." Referring specifically to those who practice harmful magic or sorcery.</note>. In a case of simple heresy, it occurs when the accused is not legally caught by their own confession and so forth, as stated above, but because of something they said or did—for instance, if they remained under excommunication for a year or more in a case not involving faith—such a person is then **lightly suspected** of heresy. This is because such a delay is not free from the suspicion of heretical depravity, according to the chapter *Gravis* <note>A reference to a specific chapter in Canon Law regarding penalties.</note>. However, if someone is cited to answer regarding their faith and does not appear, but obstinately refuses to appear and is thus excommunicated, they then become **vehemently suspected** of heresy; for then a light suspicion passes into a vehement one. If they remain under that excommunication for a year with an obstinate mind, they then become **violently suspected** of heresy. 

For at that point, a vehement suspicion passes into a violent one, against which no defense is admitted; rather, from then on, such a person is to be condemned as a heretic, as is clear from the chapter *Cum contumacia* <note>Chapter in the "Sext," a book of Canon Law, regarding obstinacy.</note>. 

In the **heresy of witches**, an example of violent suspicion was given above: when someone has said or done things that are practiced by witches when they wish to bewitch someone. It is common for them to manifest themselves through threatening words or actions, whether by sight or touch. This happens for three reasons: so that their sin may be aggravated in the eyes of judges, so that simple people may be more easily seduced, and so that God may be more greatly offended and a greater power of raging against men be left to the devil. Therefore, a witch is **violently suspected** when, after using threatening words such as "I will do something to you that you will feel shortly," or similar phrases, some effect follows in that person or another. In such a case, she is not lightly suspected, as are those who were suspected merely because of 

<column-break/>

familiarity with witches, or those who wished to provoke someone to inordinate love. See above regarding the three levels of suspicion: **light**, **vehement**, and **violent**. 

Now we must see what kind of practice should be followed with such people. Regarding one violently suspected of simple heresy, this practice is observed: even if in reality they might not be a heretic—inasmuch as they may not hold error in their mind nor have obstinacy in their will, as the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous medieval canonist.</note> notes—they are nevertheless to be condemned as a heretic because of the aforementioned violent suspicion, against which no proof is admitted. They are condemned as a heretic in this way: if they refuse to turn back, abjure the heresy, and perform worthy satisfaction, they are handed over to the **secular arm** <note>The civil authorities, who carried out the death penalty since the Church could not shed blood.</note> to be punished with the due penalty, according to the chapter *Ad abolendam* <note>A famous papal bull/decree from 1184 that established the foundations for inquisitorial procedure.</note>. If, however, they are willing and effectively consent to abjure the heresy, they are consigned to **perpetual prison**, according to the chapter *Excommunicamus*. The same form applies to one who is thus violently suspected of heresy. 

However, regarding one violently suspected of the **heresy of witches**, although the same method should be observed, one may proceed in a milder way. It should be noted that if she stands by her denial, asserting (as they usually do) that she did not speak those words with that intent, but out of vehement and womanly passion, and if the judge does not think she should be sentenced to the fire despite the violent suspicion, then the judge should keep her in prison. He should inquire or have it proclaimed whether she had been noted for such things in the past, and if so, whether she is publicly **defamed** <note>original: "diffamata." Having a widespread bad reputation for a specific crime.</note> of such heresy. From these findings, he may proceed further, specifically by exposing her to **questions and tortures** <note>original: "questionibus tormentis." Formal judicial torture to extract a confession.</note>.

If signs appear regarding such heresy or regarding a **silence-spell** <note>original: "maleficium taciturnitatem." Witches were believed to use magic to remain silent or insensitive to pain during torture.</note>—for instance, if she does not shed tears, or if she is found to be as if insensible to the tortures because she recovers all her strength quickly after the torture—then he should proceed through various **cautions** <note>Tricks or strategies used by inquisitors to break a suspect's will or reveal their magical protection.</note> as laid out above. In the event that all these fail, he should consider whether she has perpetrated similar things in the past. If so, she is by no means to be released, but is to be consigned to the **squalor of prison** for at least a year and tormented, and very frequently examined, especially on the more sacred days. If she is defamed alongside these signs, then the judge, following what was mentioned regarding simple heresy, could sentence her to the fire, especially on account of a multitude of witnesses and because she was frequently noted for these or other acts of witchcraft.

So that such a person, being suspect, must generally and publicly abjure all heresy, just as the canonical sanctions <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership (canons).</note> command us. ### Question XXVI. Regarding the proper mode of sentencing one who is suspected and defamed.

<note>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'S' printed in red ink, decorated with foliate patterns.</note>

The seventh mode of finishing and concluding a trial of the faith is when one accused of heretical depravity, after the merits of the case have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those learned in the law, is found to be suspect of heresy and also defamed <note>original: "diffamatus." Concerning this person, the following practice is to be observed: such a person, so publicly defamed of heresy and, beyond infamy, held suspect of heretical depravity by other indications, shall first purge themselves publicly in the manner touched upon in the second mode. He shall abjure in this manner:

¶ And I, [Name], from [Place] of [Name] diocese, appearing personally before you, my venerable lords, [Name], Bishop of [City], and the judge in the lands of [Name of Lord], having been placed in judgment, and having before me the most holy Gospels, which I touch corporally with my own hands, I swear that I believe in my heart and profess with my mouth that holy Catholic faith which the Roman Church believes, professes, preaches, and observes. And consequently, I abjure, detest, deny, and revoke every heresy that exalts itself against the holy and Apostolic Church, of whatever sect or error it may be. <note>The standard formula for the "Abjuratio," where the accused must explicitly renounce all beliefs contrary to Church doctrine.</note> And afterward, as touched upon above: Likewise, I swear and promise that regarding [such and such things] which I have done, for which I have been deservedly defamed <note>original: "diffamatus." So help me God and these most holy Gospels. ¶ It should be noted here, however, that if the evidence is so strong that, whether with the aforesaid infamy or without it, they render the aforementioned defamed person "vehemently suspect" <note>original: "suspectum de heresi vehementer." And if they relapse into any heresy whatsoever, they shall be punished with the penalty due to a relapsed person, as found in the chapter *Inter sollicitudines* regarding procurators, and in the chapter *Accusatus* concerning heretics in the Sixth Book of Decretals.

¶ If, however, that evidence is so small and slight that even with the aforesaid infamy it does not render him vehemently suspect of heresy, but only "lightly suspect," then it will suffice that he abjure not generally nor simply, but specifically the heresy of which he was held suspect. Thus, if he relapses into another species of heresy, he shall not be punished with the penalty due to the relapsed. But if he relapses into the same species for which he abjured—specifically because he abjured while lightly suspect—he shall not be punished with the penalty of the relapsed, although

<column-break/>

more harshly than if he had not abjured at another time, as all these things are clear in the chapter *Accusatus* at the beginning, concerning heretics in the Sixth Book. One suspected of heresy is said to abjure all heresy if he has abjured as one **vehemently suspected**, or the aforementioned specific heresy if he has abjured as one **lightly suspected**. <note>The severity of the penance depended on whether the evidence against the accused made them "lightly" or "vehemently" suspected of the crime.</note> But because we cannot and should not tolerate in any way such things as you have done, but are compelled to avoid them—as justice persuades us—so that you may be rendered more cautious in the future, and that crimes do not remain unpunished, and so that others are not rendered more dangerous by promising similar things, and so that injuries to the Creator are not tolerated with indifference: Therefore, regarding such a person who has been previously purged and has abjured, being personally present here in our presence in this place and at this hour assigned to you from this time forward: We, the Bishop or the aforementioned judge, sitting as a tribunal in the manner of those judging, with the most holy Gospels placed before us so that our judgment may proceed from the face of God and our eyes may see equity, we sentence or enjoin penance in the following manner: namely, that you be bound, etc. Let those things be imposed which shall be seen to be more for the honor of the faith and the extermination of heretical depravity. <note>original: "hereticæ pravitatis." ### Question 27. On the manner of sentencing
### one who has confessed to heresy but is penitent.

**T**he eighth mode of concluding and finishing a trial of faith is when a person accused of heretical depravity—after the merits of the process have been diligently discussed with good counsel from those skilled in the law—is found to have confessed to heresy but is truly penitent and has not otherwise relapsed. And this is when the accused himself con-

<column-break/>

fesses judicially before the Bishop and the Inquisitor, under oath, that it is true that he stood and persevered for such a time in that or another heretical depravity of which he was accused; and that he believed in and adhered to it, but afterward, through the instruction of the Bishop and others, he wishes to withdraw and return to the bosom of the Church. And he wishes to abjure that and every other heresy, and to make satisfaction just as they wish to ordain. It is not found that he ever previously abjured any heresy, but now he is prepared to abjure with a prompt mind. Concerning this case, the practice to be followed is this: for even if such a person has stood for many years in the aforesaid heresy and also in any others whatsoever, and has believed them, practiced them, and induced many into errors—if finally he confesses those heresies with effect, abjures them, and offers suitable satisfaction at the discretion of the Bishop and the ecclesiastical judge, he is **not to be handed over to the secular arm** to be struck with the ultimate punishment, <note>The "secular arm" refers to civil authorities. The Church itself could not shed blood; if it "relaxed" a prisoner to the secular arm, it was a death sentence.</note> nor, if he is a cleric, is he to be degraded; but he is to be admitted to mercy. <note>original: "ad misericordiam admittendus." A legal principle where a first-time offender who repents is spared the death penalty.</note> According to the chapter "To Abolish," <note>original: "ad abolendam." A reference to a famous decretal by Pope Lucius III.</note> and once the heretical depravity has first been abjured, he is to be thrust into perpetual prison. <note>original: "in perpetuum carcerem retrudendus." Life imprisonment was the standard "merciful" alternative to execution for repentant heretics.</note> According to the chapter "We Excommunicate," after the benefit of absolution has been bestowed upon him and the penance enjoined which is customary to be enjoined on such people. According to the chapter "That the Office," though he must be watched skillfully lest he return fraudulently through a feigned fiction. The secular arm also cannot prevent this. The method of abjuring, however, is as touched upon above; only this much is added: that before the people on a feast day in the church, he shall confess his crimes with his own mouth. This is done so that while he is questioned by the official: "Did you persevere for so many years in such heresy and sorcery?" he shall respond, "Yes." And afterward: "Did you do this and that as you have confessed?" and he shall respond, "Yes," and so on. And then after everything, he shall abjure on bended knees. And let them by no means be held as suspected of heresy [thereafter]. And because this person who was thus caught in heretical depravity was excommunicated, and has returned to the bosom of the Church through abjuration, therefore the benefit of absolution must be bestowed upon him. According to the chapter "That the Office" in the beginning, in the sixth book; wherefore after the aforesaid abjuration, he is to be absolved according to the manner Bishops have for absolving from the greater [excommunication].

A relapsed heretic is someone who has previously sworn off heresy but has fallen back into it; under the law of this period, such individuals were almost invariably executed, even if they repented a second time.</meta>

Immediately, the aforementioned garment <note>original: "vestis predicta," likely a "sanbenito" or penitential tunic embroidered with crosses or flames</note> should be put on him, and he should be placed high on a ladder so that he may be prominently seen by those departing, with the officials of the **secular court** <term>secular court: the civil or royal legal system, as opposed to the church's ecclesiastical courts</term> standing around him. At the hour of the midday meal, he shall be led by the officials to the prison, and afterwards, other things shall be done as set forth in the sentence. ->Question XVIII. Regarding the method of sentencing a heretic who is confessed but relapsed, even if penitent<-

**T**he ninth mode of concluding a trial of faith and delivering a sentence is when the merits of the case against a person reported for **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica pravitate," the standard legal term for the crime of heresy</note> have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those skilled in the law. This occurs when the person is a confessed heretic and is penitent, but is a **relapsed heretic** <term>relapsed heretic: a person who previously abjured (renounced) heresy under oath but has since returned to heretical beliefs or practices</term> in actual fact. This is the case when the accused person judicially confesses before the bishop or other judges that they had previously abjured all heresy and had done so legally. And that afterwards, they believed in such heresy or error; or that they specifically abjured the heresy of **sorcery** <note>original: "maleficarum"</note> and later returned to the same. But if, following better counsel, they repent and believe in the Catholic way and return to the unity of the Church—to such a person, if they humbly ask for it, the sacraments of **penance** and the **Eucharist** are not to be denied. However, no matter how much they repent, because they are relapsed, they are nonetheless to be handed over to the **secular arm** <term>secular arm: the civil authorities responsible for carrying out physical punishments, including the death penalty, which the Church itself did not perform</term> to be struck with the final punishment. This is understood to apply when it is legally established that they abjured as one caught in heresy, or as one vehemently—not merely lightly—suspected of heresy. Regarding such a person, the following practice is to be observed: when it has been concluded in a mature council of experts and digested—and if necessary, repeated—that the aforementioned accused is legally relapsed, the Bishop or the judge shall send to the said relapsed accused, confined in prison, two or three upright men, and especially **religious** <note>original: "religiosos," meaning members of a religious order like monks or friars</note> or clerics

<column-break/>

who are zealots for the faith and are not suspected or unwelcome to the relapsed person, but are familiar and pleasing to him. These men shall enter to him at a suitable hour and speak to him about the contempt of the world, the miseries of this present life, and the joys and glory of paradise. Finally, after these things have been promised, they shall indicate to him on behalf of the bishop or judge that he cannot escape **temporal death** <note>original: "mortem temporalem," referring to his upcoming execution</note>, and therefore he should take care for the salvation of his soul and arrange for the confession of his sins and the reception of the sacrament of the Eucharist. These men shall frequent his company, inducing him to penance and also to patience, strengthening him as much as they can in the Catholic truth, so that they diligently cause him to confess and humbly grant him the sacrament of the Eucharist if he asks for it; for such sacraments are not to be denied to such persons, according to the chapter *Super eo* on Heretics in the Sixth Book. Once these sacraments have been received, and because he is well-disposed toward salvation in the judgment of the aforementioned men after two or three days—during which he is confirmed in the Catholic faith and induced toward patience by the aforementioned men—the Bishop or the judge of the place shall command the **bailiff** of the place or the **podestà** <term>podestà: a high-ranking civil magistrate or city official</term> of the secular court that on such a day and hour (specifically not a feast day), he should be present with his staff in such a square or place outside the church to receive from their jurisdiction a certain relapsed person whom the bishop and judge will hand over to him. And nonetheless, on the preceding morning or before, let him cause it to be publicly announced by a crier through the city or place, in those accustomed places where other proclamations are usually made, that on such a day and hour, in such a place, a sermon for the faith will be preached, and the bishop and other judges will condemn a certain person relapsed into heretical depravity, handing him over to the secular arm.
¶ It must be considered here that if this person who is thus relapsed is established in **holy orders**, or is otherwise a priest, or is protected by the shadow of any order or religion, he must first be stripped of the prerogative of the entire ecclesiastical order. Thus, having been despoiled of every office and ecclesiastical **benefice** <term>benefice: a church office that provides an income</term>, he is left to the judgment of the secular power to be punished with the due penalty, as in the chapter *Ad abolendum*, paragraph *Praesenti*, regarding heretics. Therefore, one who is such is to be **degraded** from his orders.
