...to be handed over and relinquished to the **secular court** <term>secular court: the civil or royal legal system, which carried out physical punishments that the Church was forbidden from performing</term>.
The Bishop shall convoke the prelates and religious men of his diocese. Although it was not so in the past, now the Bishop alone, together with the prelates and other religious and skilled men of his diocese, has the power to **degrade** <term>degrade: a formal ritual stripping a member of the clergy of their titles and protections, effectively making them a layman again</term> someone established in holy orders when they are to be relinquished to the **secular arm** <note>original: "brachio seculari"</note> or to be perpetually imprisoned for **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica pravitate," the legal term for the crime of heresy</note>. This is according to the chapter *Quoniam* regarding heretics in the **Sixth Book of Decretals** <note>original: "li. vi.," referring to the *Liber Sextus*, a major collection of Canon Law issued in 1298</note>.

When the appointed day arrives for the degradation of the **relapsed** <term>relapsed: a "relapsus" is someone who returns to heresy after previously abjuring (swearing off) it</term> person who is to be handed over—if they are in holy orders—to the secular arm, or for the relinquishing of a layman to hear the definitive sentence, it shall take place in some square or location outside the church with the people gathered. A sermon shall be delivered by the inquisitor, with the relapsed person standing there in an elevated place. If the one to be degraded is a relapsed cleric, the Bishop, dressed in his **pontifical vestments** <note>original: "pontificalibus indutus," the formal ceremonial robes of a bishop</note> and assisted by the prelates of his diocese, shall degrade him while he stands before him, dressed and prepared as if he were about to minister in his order. He shall degrade him starting from the highest order and proceeding step by step down to the lowest. In doing so, the Bishop uses the words ordained by the Church for this purpose; in each removal—the **chasuble** <note>the outermost liturgical robe</note>, the **stole** <note>the long silk band worn over the shoulders</note>, and so on—he may use words contrary to those used during ordination.

When this degradation has been performed where necessary, according to the manner established by law or custom, the official shall command a notary, a monk, or a cleric to read the sentence. This sentence, whether the relapsed person is a layman or a degraded cleric, shall be delivered in the following form:

**We**, [Name], by divine mercy Bishop of such a city and judge in the territories of such a lord, considering that we are legally informed that you, [Name], of such a place and diocese, were brought before us (or before such bishops and judges) for such heretical depravity. In these heresies, it was legally discovered that you were involved, as proven by your own confession and the testimony of witnesses. And because you persisted in them for a long time with a hardened heart, as was the case,

<column-break/>

but afterward, following sounder counsel, you publicly **abjured** <term>abjured: to formally and under oath renounce a belief or heresy</term> those heresies in the customary form of the Church, and you denied and revoked them. Therefore, the aforementioned bishops and inquisitors—believing you to be truly converted to the bosom of the Church—absolved you from the sentence of excommunication by which you were bound (provided you had returned to the unity of the Holy Church with a true heart and unfeigned faith) and they imposed a **salutary penance** <note>a spiritual punishment intended for the health of the soul</note> upon you.

However, after all the aforementioned things and after the passage of so many years, you have now recently been reported to us again for having fallen back into those same abjured heresies (which should be specified). Although we heard such things about you with displeasure, justice compelled us to proceed with an inquiry, to examine witnesses, and to summon and question you under oath, as well as to do everything else that was required of us according to the **canonical statutes** <note>the established laws of the Church</note>.

Indeed, wishing to conclude the present cases without undue delay, we ordered a formal council of experts to be gathered, both from the faculty of theology and from those skilled in **canon and civil law** <term>canon and civil law: "ius canonicum" refers to Church law, while "ius civile" refers to the secular legal system inherited from Rome</term>. Having received the mature and well-considered advice of these experts, and having carefully discussed and weighed all the acts, records, and merits of the process in a balance of equity as the situation required, we find legally—both through witnesses and through your own confession received in court—that you have relapsed into the heresies you previously abjured. Moreover, we find that you said or did such and such things (here, all details should be explained).

Because of these things, and deservedly so, based on the advice of the aforementioned council, we have held and do hold you to be a **relapsed heretic**, according to the canonical statutes which we further refer to and uphold. But because, by the inspiration of divine grace, you have again returned to our information and to the presence of Catholic men, returning to the bosom of the Church and to the truth of the same faith by detesting the aforementioned errors and heresies and professing the Catholic faith, we have admitted you to receive the ecclesiastical **sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist** as you humbly requested. Nevertheless, since the Church has nothing more it can do for you or regarding you, seeing as it has acted so mercifully toward you as we have said, and you have abused that mercy...

...by falling back into abjured <note>original: "abiuratas," meaning heresies the person previously swore to renounce</note> heresies. Therefore, we, the bishop and the judges, sitting as a tribunal in the manner of judges judging, with the holy Gospels placed before us so that our judgment might proceed from the face of God and our eyes might see equity, having before our eyes only God and the irrefragable truth of the holy faith and the extirpation of **heretical depravity** <note>original: "hereticæ pravitatis"</note>, do here in this place, day, and hour previously assigned to you for hearing your definitive sentence, judicially judge that you have truly **relapsed** <term>relapsed: a legal status for someone who returns to heresy after a formal reconciliation with the Church</term> into heretical depravity, although you are now penitent. And because you have truly relapsed into the same, we cast you out from our **ecclesiastical court** <note>original: "foro nostro ecclesiastico"</note> and relinquish you, to be handed over to the **secular arm** <term>secular arm: the civil or royal government, which carried out physical punishments that the Church was forbidden from performing</term>. We nonetheless effectively pray that the said secular court may moderate its sentence regarding you, so that it stops short of the shedding of blood and the danger of death. <note>This "mercy clause" was a standard legal formula used by the Church to avoid the appearance of "irregularity" caused by causing a death, though it was understood the secular court would proceed with execution.</note> And thus the bishop and his assessors shall withdraw, and the secular court shall execute its office.

¶ It should be noted that although the bishop and the **inquisitor** <note>original: "inquisitor"</note> ought to be most diligent, both by themselves and through others, to ensure that the relapsed person repents and is converted to the Catholic faith, nevertheless—once they have repented and it has been concluded in council that although they are penitent, they are still truly relapsed and must be handed over to the secular arm as such—they themselves should not personally inform the prisoner of the sentence. This is because the face of a judge terrifies the condemned. Their words might lead the condemned person toward despair rather than patience. Therefore, neither at that time, nor before the sentence, nor after, should they have the person presented to them, lest the prisoner's mind be moved against them; for in such a case of death, diligence must be carefully maintained. Instead, as has been said, they should send certain upright men, especially **religious** <term>religious: members of holy orders, such as monks or friars</term> or clerics who are not unpleasant to the prisoner, but rather welcome, who may announce the coming sentence and imminent death, confirm them in the faith, and exhort them to patience. After the sentence, they should accompany the person, comforting them and praying with them, and they should not leave until the person has returned their spirit to the Creator. Let them therefore be cautious and advised not not to do or say anything by which the relapsed person's death might be hastened, lest they themselves be made **irregular** <term>irregular: a canonical penalty where a cleric becomes unfit for their duties because they were responsible for a person's death</term>. For where they ought to report

<column-break/>

merit, they might instead bring back upon themselves both punishment and guilt. It should also be considered that such sentences of handing someone over to the secular court are not usually carried out on a feast day or a solemn holiday, nor even inside a church, but outside in some square. This is because it is a sentence that leads to death, and it is more decent that it be carried out on a workday and outside the church, since feast days and the church are dedicated to the Lord.

### **¶ Question XIX. On the manner of sentencing a confessed but impenitent heretic, who is nonetheless relapsed.** <note>The heading says "relapsed," but the following text clarifies this section is actually about those who are NOT yet relapsed (first-time offenders who refuse to repent).</note>

The tenth way of concluding and sentencing a trial of faith is when, the merits of the trial for **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica pravitate"</note> having been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those skilled in the law, the accused is found to have confessed to heresy and is **impenitent** <term>impenitent: someone who admits they hold heretical views but refuses to renounce them</term> but is not yet relapsed. However, because such a case is very rarely found—though it has occasionally happened to us inquisitors—the bishop and the judges should not hurry with such a person. Rather, they should keep them well-guarded and shackled to induce conversion, even for several months, warning them that they will be damned in both body and soul if they remain thus impenitent. If, at last, they cannot be softened by prayers, hardships, threats, or flatteries so that they recoil from their errors, and they have been waited upon for the aforementioned suitable time, the bishop and the judges shall prepare themselves to hand them over or relinquish them to the **secular arm** <note>original: "brachio seculari"</note>. They shall send a notice to the messenger, bailiff, or provost of the secular court, stating that on such a day (not a feast day) and at such an hour, they should be in such a place outside the church with their staff, and the judges will hand over to them a certain impenitent heretic. Furthermore, they shall have it publicly proclaimed by a crier in those neighborhoods or places where other proclamations are usually made, that on the predicted day, hour, and place, a preacher will deliver a sermon on behalf of the faith and hand over a certain heretic to the secular arm. Therefore, everyone should come and be present, and they will receive the customary **indulgence** <term>indulgence: a grant of remission from the temporal punishment for sin, often given to those attending important religious events or sermons</term>. When these things are completed, the prisoner shall be handed over to the secular court according to the following tenor, having been frequently warned beforehand to recoil and repent. If they absolutely will not, the sentence shall be carried out.

We, [Name], by divine mercy Bishop of [City], and judge on earth for [Lord Name], observing that you, [Name] from [Place] in the [Diocese], were reported to us by public fame and the information of trustworthy people regarding **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica prauitate"; a standard legal term for heresy in the Middle Ages</note>. We, upon whom the duty of extirpating heretical depravity was laid by our office, wishing—as we were bound—to be more certainly informed on these matters and to see whether you walked in darkness or in light, diligently investigated the aforementioned things. Having cited you and interrogated you effectively, we find you infected with the said heretical depravity. Truly, since above all the desires of our mind it urges our heart to plant the holy Catholic faith in the hearts of the people once heretical depravity has been rooted out, we have employed various and appropriate methods, both through ourselves and through others, so that you might recoil from the heresies and errors mentioned above, in which you have stood and still stand even now, contumaciously and pertinaciously with a hardened soul. It is certain that since the enemy of the human race <note>Refers to the Devil</note> is assisting your heart, and involves and entangles you in the said errors, you have not wished and do not wish to recoil from the often-mentioned heresies, choosing rather to incur the death of the soul in Hell <note>original: "gehennalē"</note> and of the body in time, rather than to abjure the aforementioned heresies and fly to the bosom of the Church and gain your soul, being given over to a reprobate sense. For that reason, since you are bound by the holy Church with the bond of excommunication, and deservedly and numerically separated from the Lord's flock and deprived of participation in the goods of the Church, and since the Church has nothing further it can do concerning you, having done everything in its power to convert you: We, the bishop and the judges separated in the cause of the faith, sitting as a tribunal in the manner of judges judging, with the holy Gospels placed before us so that our judgment might proceed from the face of God and our eyes might see equity, having before our eyes only God and the truth of the holy faith and the extirpation of heretical depravity, on this day, hour, and place previously assigned to you for hearing the definitive sentence, we condemn

<column-break/>

and judicially judge you to be truly an **unrepentant heretic** <term>unrepentant: "impenitens"; a legal status for one who refuses to renounce their beliefs even after being proven a heretic</term>, and as such, you are truly to be delivered and relinquished to the **secular arm** <term>secular arm: the civil authorities, as the Church was legally forbidden from carrying out executions</term>. And so, as an unrepentant heretic, through this our sentence, we cast you out from our entire ecclesiastical court and deliver or relinquish you to the secular arm and the power of the secular court, effectively praying that the said secular court may moderate its sentence concerning you, so that it stops short of the shedding of blood and the danger of death. <note>This "mercy clause" was a standard legal formula; while it asked for no blood to be shed, it was understood that the secular authority would execute the condemned, often by burning.</note> This sentence was passed.

# Question 30: Concerning confessed, relapsed, and unrepentant heresy.

The eleventh way of terminating and finishing a process of faith is when, after a report of heretical depravity and after the merits of the process have been diligently discussed with good counsel from those skilled in the law, a person is found to be a **confessed heretic** who is both **unrepentant** and **relapsed**. This occurs when the accused confesses with their own mouth in court to believe in such and such things and to have performed such practices—as mentioned above—and the sentence is to be delivered before the bishop and judges, for things which are clearly heretical, according to the form of the following text:

We, [Name], by divine mercy Bishop of [City], or judge on earth for [Lord Name], observing that you, [Name] from [Place] in the [Diocese], were reported to us or to our predecessors regarding heretical depravity (here let the heresies be explained). In these, as has been legally revealed, you were caught by your own judicial confession and by trustworthy witnesses; and that you persisted in them for so long a time with a hardened soul (let it be said as the case was). But because afterward, adhering to sound counsel, you publicly **abjured** <note>original: "abiurasti"; a formal oath renouncing heresy</note> those heresies in such a place in the customary form of the Church, the aforementioned bishop and judge—believing that you had truly recoiled from the aforementioned errors and had flown to the bosom of the Church by believing catholically—imparted to you the benefit of **absolution** <note>original: "absolutōnis"</note>, absolving you from the sentence of excommunication by which you were previously bound, provided that you had turned to the unity of the holy Church with a true heart and unfeigned faith, and they enjoined upon you a salutary penance.

<insert>Question 22 regarding one convicted and caught, yet denying everything.</insert>

The twelfth way of terminating and finishing a process of faith is when a person reported for **heretical depravity**, after the merits of the process have been diligently discussed with the full council of legal experts, is found to be caught in heresy by evidence of the deed or by legitimate production of witnesses, yet not by his own confession. This occurs when the accused is legitimately convicted of some heretical depravity or by the evidence of the fact—for example, because he practiced heresy publicly, or through legitimate witnesses against whom the accused could not legitimately object—yet he, thus convicted and caught, persists firmly in denial and constantly maintains his innocence, according to the notes by Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous canon lawyer known as Hostiensis because he was the Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia.</note> in the *Summa*, under the title "On Heretics," in the section "How one is caught in heresy," and as appeared above in Question 24. Regarding such a person, this practice is to be followed: Such a person is to be held in a harsh prison in leg-irons and chains, frequently visited by officials...

jointly and separately, and by himself or through others, he must be effectively warned to reveal the truth to them, judging for him that he should do so by confessing his error, so that by abjuring that heretical depravity <note>original: "hereticam pravitatem"</note>, he may be admitted to mercy. If, however, he refuses but persists in denial, he will at the end be abandoned to the secular arm <note>The "secular arm" refers to civil authorities, as the Church was forbidden from shedding blood; handing someone over was a euphemism for execution</note> and will not be able to escape temporal death. But if, having been long defamed and waited upon, he persists in denial, the bishop and officials—now jointly, now separately, now by themselves, now through others—should bring before them through [qualified] men now one witness, now another, informing the witness to consider what he has testified. They should ask whether he spoke the truth or not; for he should not damn himself eternally [by lying] and another temporally [by causing their death]; and he should be moved to tell them the truth at least secretly, lest the accused die unjustly. They should strive to speak such words to him so that he may clearly see whether he has presented the truth or not. If it happens that the witnesses, as instructed, stand by their affirmation and the accused by his denial, the bishop and officials should not immediately wish to determine the business by sentence and by handing over the one so convicted to the secular arm. Instead, they should hold him longer, now inducing the convicted man to affirm the truth, now the witnesses separately, however, to thoroughly examine their consciences. And the bishop and officials should pay particular attention to that witness whom they see is better disposed toward the good and who seems to have a better conscience; they should press him longer as to whether the matter was as he testified or not, burdening his soul. And if they see any witness waver, or if there are other indications against him for which it is suspected that he told a falsehood, they should, with the good counsel of experts, arrest him and proceed as justice shall persuade. For it is found frequently, and more frequently still, that one thus convicted by trustworthy witnesses, after he has long persisted in denial, is brought back to his heart—especially if truthfully informed that he will not be handed over to the secular arm but admitted to mercy—he reveals his depravity and then freely confesses the truth which he had for so long denied. And it is frequently found that witnesses, driven by malice and overcome by enmity, have conspired together to impose heretical depravity upon an innocent person. After frequent instruction, such witnesses, fatigued by the remorse of conscience

<column-break/>

and divinely inspired, revoke what they said and confess that they maliciously imposed such a great stain [upon the accused]. For this reason, such a person, so accused, is not to be rushed to sentence, but should be waited upon for a long time—even for a year or more—before he is thus handed over to the secular court. When that time has passed, and fitting diligence has been applied, if the one thus accused and lawfully convicted acknowledges his fault and has judicially confessed that he was ensnared for such a time in the aforementioned heretical depravity, and has consented to abjure it and every heresy, and to provide fitting satisfaction at the discretion of the bishop and the inquisitor <note>original: "inquisitoris" — the official investigator of heresy</note>, he is treated as one convicted of heresy both by his own confession and by the lawful production of witnesses. And the heretic shall utterly abjure every heresy publicly, according to the form discussed in the Eighth Mode of concluding a process of faith, as treated above. If, however, having thus confessed that he fell into heresy, he persists in it with a stubborn mind, as one impenitent, he shall be abandoned to the secular arm; and one should proceed against him in the manner discussed above in the Tenth Mode of concluding a process of faith. If, however, the accused himself has stood firmly in denial, but the witnesses themselves have recoiled from their affirmation, revoking their testimony and acknowledging their guilt—because, driven by rancor and hatred or seduced by a bribe, they imposed such a great stain upon an innocent man—the accused himself shall be released from judgment as immune. Those witnesses shall be punished as false witnesses, as Paul notes regarding the chapter *Multorum* and the word *illos* in the beginning, concerning heretics in the Clementines <note>original: "de here. in cle." — the Clementine Constitutions, a collection of Church laws promulgated by Pope Clement V</note>. And a sentence or penance shall be brought against them at the discretion of the bishop and the judge, condemning such false witnesses absolutely to perpetual prison, and placing them on a penance of bread and water for the days of their lives, and also afterwards placing them at the steps before the church doors [for public shaming]. Nevertheless, the bishops have the power to mitigate or even aggravate the sentence after a year and other times, according to the form of the following tenor.

And nonetheless, the bishop and the official should send word to the bailiff or the magistrate of the secular court that on such a day and hour, and in such a place—outside the church, however—he should come with his staff to receive a certain impenitent heretic whom they will hand over to him. And they shall also have it publicly proclaimed in the usual places where other proclamations are made, that everyone should be present on such a day and hour in such a place to hear the "Sermon on the Faith" <note>The *sermo generalis*, later known as the *Auto-da-fé*, a public ceremony where sentences were read</note> which the preacher shall deliver, and that the bishop or official will hand over a certain obstinate heretic to the secular arm. When the predicted day for delivering the assigned sentence arrives, the bishop and official shall be in the aforementioned place for the handing over, with the accused being present there in a high place <note>To be visible to the crowd</note> before the assembled clergy and people so that he may be seen prominently by all, and with the power of the secular court standing by for the handing over. Once these things have been read, the sentence shall be delivered in this manner:

**W**e, by divine mercy Bishop of such a city, or judge in the lands of such a lord: Considering that you, [Name], from such a place in such a diocese, were brought before us for such **heretical depravity** <note>original: "heretica pravitate," the standard term for the "wickedness" of heresy</note>. Let the facts be stated <note>original: "Experimantur," a placeholder indicating where the specific charges should be inserted</note>. And we wished to be certain whether the things that had been said to us about you and against you were supported by any truth, and whether you were walking in darkness or in the light. We stepped down to inform ourselves, diligently examining witnesses, and calling and interrogating you many times under oath, and allowing the presentation of defenses as was required by canonical sanctions. Since we wished to terminate your present business with a due end, we caused a solemn council of those expert in the faculty of theology as well as in canon and civil law to be assembled before us. Having seen and diligently discussed the merits of the process and all and singular things produced and brought forth in the present case, and with the acts and proceedings of the aforementioned council having been digested and matured, we find against you;

<column-break/>

it is legitimately proven that you were for such a time infected with heretical depravity, and we have also found that you did and said such and such things. <note>original: "Experimantur," another placeholder for the specific evidence</note> From which it appears manifest that you are legitimately caught in the aforementioned heretical depravity. Although we desired, and still desire, that you—by confessing the truth—might turn away from the aforesaid heresy and be led back to the bosom of the Holy Church and to the unity of the holy faith, so that you might save your soul and escape both the death of the soul and the **hellish death** <note>original: "gehiennalem," referring to Gehenna or Hell</note> of the body, exercising our diligence both through ourselves and through others, and waiting for you for a long time; yet you, given over to a **reprobate sense** <note>original: "reprobum sensum," a biblical reference to a mind that can no longer discern right from wrong</note>, have scorned to acquiesce to our healthier counsel. Indeed, you have persisted and do persist in a negative obstinacy and contumacy with a hardened soul, which we report with sorrow, and reporting it, we grieve and mourn. Furthermore, since the Church of God has waited so long for you to turn back by recognizing your own fault, and you have not wished and do not wish to do so, the Church has nothing further it can do for you by way of grace or reward. Therefore, so that you may be an example to others, and others may be deterred from such heresy, and such great crimes do not remain unpunished: We, the mentioned Bishop and judges in the cause of the faith, sitting **from the judgment seat** <note>original: "pro tribunali," indicating a formal judicial pronouncement</note> in the manner of judges judging, with the Holy Gospels placed before us, so that our judgment may proceed from the face of God and our eyes may see equity; having before our eyes only God and the glory and honor of the holy faith; we define, declare, and sentence you, [Name], being present here before us on this day, hour, and place assigned for hearing the definitive sentence, to be an **impenitent heretic** to be handed over or relinquished as such to the secular arm. And by our sentence, as a truly obstinate and impenitent heretic, we cast you out from the ecclesiastical court and hand you over or relinquish you to the secular arm and to the power of the secular court. Effectively beseeching the same secular court that it should moderate its sentence concerning you **this side of the shedding of blood and the danger of death.** <note>A standard legal formula. While the Church technically asked the state not to kill the prisoner, it was understood that the state's "moderate" sentence for an unrepentant heretic was execution, usually by burning</note> This sentence was passed.

**T**he bishops and judges will also be able to arrange that some upright men, zealous for the faith, should remain with the person relinquished to the court...

Concerning this: if perhaps after the sentence and even after being taken back to the place where he is to be burned <note>The stake</note>, he says he wishes to confess the truth and acknowledge his fault, and does so and is ready to abjure this heresy and all others—even though it might be presumed that he does this more out of fear of death than love of truth—I would believe that out of mercy he could be received as a penitent heretic and be permanently immured <note>Term: *immurari* — strictly confined or imprisoned for life within walls, usually a cell in a monastery or prison</note>. ### Question 32. Concerning the convicted person, or a fugitive, or one who is contumaciously absent.

The thirteenth and final way of concluding and sentencing a process of the faith is when a person reported for heretical depravity, after the merits of the process have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those learned in the law, is found guilty of heretical depravity but is nonetheless a fugitive or contumaciously absent <note>Willfully refusing to obey a legal summons to appear in court</note>, though having been waited for for a suitable time. And this occurs in three cases. The first is when the accused has been proven guilty of heresy either by his own confession, or by the evidence of the fact, or by the legitimate production of witnesses, but has fled or absented himself and, though legitimately summoned, has refused to appear. The second case is when someone is reported and, after some information has been received against him, is held to be somewhat or lightly suspected, and is thus summoned to answer concerning the faith; and because he contumaciously refuses to appear, he is excommunicated. If he sustains that excommunication with a persistent mind and always contumaciously absents himself. The third case is when someone has directly obstructed the sentence or the process of the faith of the bishop or judge,

<column-break/>

or who has given aid, counsel, or favor to this end; such a person is struck by the blade of excommunication. If he endures this for a year with a hardened heart, from then on he is to be condemned as a heretic, according to the chapter *Ut inquisitionis*, paragraph *Philemus*, concerning heretics, Book VI, and has contumaciously absented himself. In the first case, such a person is an impenitent heretic to be condemned, according to the chapter *Ad abolendam*, paragraph *presenti*. In the second and third cases, he is not to be judged as an impenitent heretic, but is to be determined as if he were a penitent heretic, according to the chapter *Cum contumacia* and the chapter *Ut inquisitionis*, paragraph *Philemus*, regarding heretics, Book VI. Regarding any of these, the following practice is to be observed. Such a person, having been waited for for a suitable time, shall be summoned by the bishop and official in the cathedral church of that diocese which he left, and in other churches of that place where he maintained his residence, and especially from where he fled; and he shall be summoned according to the form of the following tenor:

We, [M.], by divine mercy Bishop of such-and-such a city, etc., or judge of such-and-such a diocese, [wish for] the spirit of sounder counsel. Furthermore, this is fixed most especially in our heart above all the desires of our mind: that in our times, in the said diocese, the flourishing and fertile Church—a vineyard, I say, of the Lord of Sabaoth <note>A biblical title for God, usually translated as "Lord of Hosts"</note>, which the right hand of the Highest Father planted with His virtues, which the Son of the same Father watered more abundantly with the wave of His own life-giving blood, which the same Holy Spirit the Comforter fertilized within by sending ineffable gifts, and which the whole incomprehensible and unattainable Blessed Trinity sanctified and likewise enriched with the greatest and various privileges—[that this vineyard] not be swallowed up and grazed upon by the wild boar of the forest <note>original: *aper de silva*; a metaphor for the heretic based on Psalm 80:13</note>, who is and is called a heretic, devastating the fertile fruits of the faith and tearing them by introducing the briars of heresy into the branches. Nor indeed should the crooked serpent, our wicked enemy of the human race, who is Satan and the devil, infect the branches of the same vineyard of the Lord and its fruits by injecting the poison of heretical depravity. Nor indeed should the Lord’s field itself—the Catholic people, I say—for whose cultivation and sowing the Son of God descended from the height of the highest heavens...

...the only-begotten and first-born of the Father sowed with holy walls and preachings. He traveled through villages and fortified towns teaching, not without great fatigue. But the little foxes of Samson <note>A reference to Judges 15:4. In medieval theology, these foxes—tied tail-to-tail with torches—symbolized heretics who might hold different faces/opinions but were united by the "fire" of their destructive intent toward the Church.</note> are entangled, plainly depraved by heretical ruin; though they have different faces, they have their tails tied together with fire. Because of their variety of flame, they come together for the same purpose: to destroy the Lord’s harvest, which is already white for reaping, with the most bitter bite of those who resist the faith. With the most subtle movement they go forth, and with the most powerful force they attack together, setting fire to, dissipating, and devastating the sincerity of the holy Catholic faith by subtly and damnably subverting it. 

Therefore, since you, [Name], have fallen into the damned heresies of sorceresses <note>Original: *maleficarum*—specifically referring here to practitioners of harmful magic or witchcraft</note>, practicing them publicly in such a place (or as it may be said), or having been convicted of heretical depravity by legitimate witnesses, or having been caught by your own confession received in judgment by us, and having afterwards fled as a captive, refusing the medicine of salvation—we have summoned you so that you might respond clearly before us regarding these matters. You, led and seduced by an evil spirit, have refused to appear.

Or in this way: Therefore, since you, [Name], were reported to us for heretical depravity, and information having been received against you, you were otherwise slightly suspected by us of the same, as you were infected by the aforementioned ruin. We summoned you to appear personally before us to answer concerning the Catholic faith, and when summoned you refused to appear, and we contumaciously excommunicated <note>Term: *excommunicatus* — formally excluded from the sacraments and the community of the Church</note> you and caused that excommunication to be published. In this state you have remained for a year (or so many years) with a stubborn mind, hiding away, so that we now do not know where that evil spirit has led you. Since we have waited for you mercifully and kindly so that you might return to the bosom of the unity of the holy faith, and you have scorned to do so, being given over to a reprobate sense. <column-break/>

to terminate your case of this kind without delay; nor can we tolerate such nefarious crimes with closed eyes. We, the bishop and judges in the aforementioned cases of the faith, by our present public edict, require and peremptorily summon you, such a person who has often acted as a hider, a runaway, and a fugitive. On such a day, of such a month, in such a year, in such a cathedral church of such a diocese, at the hour of tierce <note>The third hour of the day, roughly 9:00 AM</note>, you are to appear personally before us to hear the definitive sentence <note>Term: *diffinitiva sententia* — the final legal judgment that concludes a trial</note>. We signify that whether you appear or not, we will proceed to our definitive sentence against you as law and justice shall persuade. And so that our summons may reach your notice, and you may not be able to protect yourself with a veil of ignorance, we will and command these letters, containing our requirements and summons, to be affixed to the public doors of the aforementioned cathedral church. In testimony of which, we have ordered our present letters to be secured with the impression of our seals. Given on [Date].

When the appointed day for hearing the assigned definitive sentence arrives, if the fugitive appears and consents to abjure <note>Term: *abiurare* — to formally renounce a belief or heresy under oath</note> all heresies publicly, and humbly asks to be admitted to mercy, he shall be admitted, provided he is not relapsed <note>A "relapsed" heretic is one who had previously abjured but fell back into heresy; they were usually denied mercy and executed</note>. If he has been convicted by his own confession or by the production of legitimate witnesses, he shall abjure and do penance as a penitent heretic, according to the manner discussed above in the eighth method of concluding a process of the faith. 

If he is strongly suspected, such that when summoned to answer concerning the faith he refused to appear and was therefore excommunicated and remained in that excommunication for a year with a stubborn mind, and then repents, he shall be admitted and shall abjure all heresy and do penance as a heretic strongly suspected of heresy, according to the manner discussed above in the sixth method of concluding a process of the faith. 

If, however, he appears but does not consent to abjure, he shall be handed over as an impenitent heretic to the secular arm <note>Term: *brachio seculari* — the civil authorities who carried out the death penalty, as the Church itself could not shed blood</note>, in the manner said above and discussed in the tenth method of concluding a process of the faith. But if he contumaciously refuses to appear, then the sentence shall be formed in the manner of the following text:

We, [Name], bishop by divine mercy of such city, considering that you, [Name], of such a place and such a diocese, were before us...

# Regarding Heretical Depravity

Reported by public rumor or by the suggestion of trustworthy people, you have been accused of **heretical depravity** <note>original: *heretica pravitas* — a standard legal term used in the Middle Ages and Early Modern period to describe heresy as a moral and social corruption.</note>. We, to whom it is incumbent by our office, have come down to see and to inquire whether the outcry that had reached our ears was supported by any truth. Indeed, when we found you caught in heresy—many trustworthy witnesses testifying against you—we commanded that you be summoned before us and detained. Let it be stated as it was done: whether, for instance, you appeared and, being interrogated under oath, confessed or not.

But later, led and seduced by the counsel of an evil spirit, fearing that your wounds would be healthfully tended with **wine and oil** <note>A reference to the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:34); the Church viewed its legal process not just as punishment, but as a "medicine" for the soul.</note>, you fled. Or let it be stated, if it is so: you broke prison and arrest and likewise fled, hiding here and there; and where that aforementioned evil spirit has led you, we are entirely ignorant.

**Or thus:** Indeed, when we found many signs of heretical depravity reported to us against you as described above—on account of which we rightly held you lightly suspected of the aforementioned heretical depravity—we summoned you by public edict in such-and-such churches of such-and-such a diocese. This was done so that, within a certain fixed term set by us, you might appear personally before us in such a place to respond to the matters set forth against you and regarding other points of the Catholic faith and its articles. You, however, by insane counsel and by sticking to your refusal, have been stubbornly defiant in your actions. Justice demanding it, we excommunicated you and caused that **excommunication** <note>A formal exclusion from the sacraments and the community of the Church, intended to pressure the suspect into appearing.</note> to be publicly announced. You reject this saving medicine: you have endured said excommunication for more than a year and still endure it, given over to a **reprobate mind** <note>original: *reprobum sensum* — a biblical reference to Romans 1:28, implying a mind that can no longer distinguish right from wrong.</note> with an obstinate spirit, a fugitive hiding here and there, so that we know not where the evil spirit has led you.

Truly, since for a long time—for so many days—the Holy Church of God has waited for you mercifully and kindly, so that you might fly back to the bosom of its mercy by recoiling from your errors and acting according to the Catholic faith you professed, and so that she might nourish you with the breasts of her clemency. Yet, seduced by the counsel of the wicked, you have refused to comply, persevering in your obstinacy.

<column-break/>

Since we wish, as we both want and ought to do—justice compelling us—to terminate your case with a due end by a **definitive sentence** <note>original: *sententia definitiva* — the final, binding judgment in a legal proceeding.</note>, we summoned you to appear personally before us on this day, at this hour, and in this place, to hear the definitive sentence. And because you have stubbornly refused to appear, you rightly show that you wish to remain forever in your heresies and errors. We report this unwillingly, and we grieve in the reporting. But since we cannot and will not evade justice, nor tolerate such great disobedience and defiance toward the Church of God; for the exaltation of the **orthodox faith** <note>original: *fidei orthodoxe* — literally "right-believing" faith, meaning the officially sanctioned doctrines of the Catholic Church.</note> and for the extirpation of heretical depravity; justice demanding it and your disobedience and defiance requiring it; this day, hour, and place having been assigned to you peremptorily to hear the definitive sentence:

Having previously taken the counsel of many experts <note>original: *peritorum* — legal and theological consultants who advised the judges.</note> both in the faculty of theology and in **canon and civil law** <note>original: *iure canonico et civili* — the "two laws" (Utrumque Ius) that formed the basis of the medieval legal system.</note>, and having seen and diligently discussed the merits of the process; sitting on the **tribunal** <note>original: *pro tribunali* — a formal legal phrase indicating the judge is acting in an official capacity from the bench.</note> in the manner of judges judging; with the holy Gospels placed before us so that our judgment may proceed from the face of God and our eyes may see equity; having before our eyes only God and the irrefragable truth of the holy faith against you—who are absent as if you were present—imitating the footsteps of the Blessed Apostle Paul, we deliver the definitive sentence in these writings, having invoked the name of Christ:

We, the bishop and judges mentioned in this cause of the faith, observing that the order of law has been served in this cause of the faith and in the records produced therefrom; observing also that, though legitimately summoned, you did not appear, nor did you excuse yourself in any way through yourself or through another; observing also that you have persisted stubbornly in the aforementioned heresies for a long time and even still persevere, and have endured excommunication for so many years in this cause of faith, as you even now endure it with a hardened spirit; observing also that the Holy Church of God has nothing more it can do for you since you persevere and wish to persevere in excommunication and the aforementioned heresies: Therefore, following the footsteps of the Blessed Apostle Paul, we declare...

<meta>This page continues the procedural templates for sentencing heretics. The previous page discussed the summons of a suspect who had fled. This page provides the final sentencing formula for those who remain absent (contumacious) and introduces a new section on how to handle suspects who have been implicated by a convicted witch who has already been executed or is awaiting execution.</meta>

...we define and pass sentence that you, though absent, are to be considered as if present: an **obstinate heretic** <note>original: *hereticum pertinax* — a legal classification for a heretic who refuses to recant even after being shown their errors.</note>, and as such, you are to be relinquished to the **secular arm** <note>original: *brachio seculari* — the civil authorities. The Church court technically did not execute people; they "relaxed" or handed the prisoner to the state, which then carried out the death penalty, usually by burning.</note>. By our definitive sentence, we expel you from the ecclesiastical court and leave you to the present secular court. We affectionately entreat that same court that, should it ever have you in its power, it might moderate its sentence toward you **without the shedding of blood or the peril of death** <note>original: *citra sanguinis effusione; et mortis periculum* — a standard but ironic legal formula. By asking for "no blood," the Church technically avoided the "sin" of killing, while knowing full well the secular court would use fire (which does not shed blood) to execute the heretic.</note>. This sentence was passed, etc.

It should be considered here that if this fugitive and rebellious person was convicted of heresy—either by their own confession or by legitimate witnesses—and fled before they could renounce their errors, they are to be judged by sentence as a truly **impenitent heretic**, and must be recorded as such in the sentence. If, however, they were not otherwise convicted, but were merely reported and held as a suspect, and were summoned to respond regarding the faith, and because they refused to appear were excommunicated, and remained in that state of excommunication for more than a year with a hardened heart, and finally still refused to appear: this person is not to be judged as a heretic, but rather **as if** a heretic <note>original: *ut hereticus* — a legal distinction where the person is punished as a heretic because their refusal to answer the Church for a year creates a legal presumption of guilt.</note>, and must be condemned as such. And so it must be recorded in the sentence as was stated before.

### Question XXIII: Regarding a person reported by another witch who has been burned or is to be burned, and how they should be sentenced.

The fourteenth mode of concluding a trial of the faith and passing sentence occurs when a person reported for **heretical depravity**—after the merits of the process regarding the witness have been diligently discussed with the good counsel of those skilled in law—is found to be accused of such heretical depravity **only** by another witch who has been **burned or is to be burned** <note>original: *malefica incinerata vel incineranda* — literally "turned to ash." This refers to the practice of burning at the stake.</note>. 

This can occur in thirteen ways, through thirteen distinct cases. This is because the person so accused is either found innocent and to be totally absolved; or is found to be generally **defamed** <note>original: *diffamatus* — having a bad public reputation or "ill-repute" (*infamia*) regarding the crime.</note> of such heresy; or is found, beyond the ill-repute, to be subject to **questioning** <note>original: *questionibus exponendus* — a euphemism for judicial torture to extract a confession.</note> in some way; or is found to be lightly suspected of heresy; or is found to be vehemently suspected of heresy; or...

<column-break/>

...is found to be violently suspected of heresy; or is found to be both defamed and suspected together and commonly. And so it follows in the other cases, just as was touched upon in the twentieth question up to the thirteenth case inclusive. 

The **first mode** occurs when the person is accused only by the detained witch herself, and they are not convicted by their own confession, nor by the production of legitimate witnesses, nor are other signs found from which they could reasonably be judged as a suspect. Such a person is to be entirely absolved. Even the secular judge himself—who either burned the accuser or had the authority to do so, whether by his own power or by commission of the Bishop as the **ordinary judge** <note>original: *iudicis ordinarij* — the bishop or his deputy who held regular jurisdiction over the diocese.</note>—must do this. He shall grant absolution using the sentence contained in the first mode of concluding a trial of the faith, found near the twentieth question.

The **second mode** occurs when, in addition to being accused by the detained person, the suspect is also **defamed** throughout that entire village or city. In this case, they have suffered precisely and solely from ill-repute, although that ill-repute may have been made worse by the accusation from the detained witch. Regarding such a person, this practice is to be observed: the judge, considering that beyond the ill-repute nothing specific is proven against them by other trustworthy people in the village or town—even though the detained witch perhaps testified to certain grave things against them—must be cautious. This is because the witch lost her **credibility** <note>original: *fidez* / *fides*</note> by denying it to the devil; therefore, her words are only with great difficulty given credit by the judges, unless that ill-repute were supported by other circumstances. In that case, it would fall into the third mode. 

Therefore, **canonical purgation** <note>original: *purgatio canonica* — a legal process where a suspect proves their innocence by gathering a group of "compurgators" (character witnesses) to swear that the suspect is telling the truth.</note> must then be ordered, and the process will proceed according to the sentence found in the second mode of concluding a trial. If the civil judge accepts that this purgation be done solemnly before the bishop, it is well done; for if the suspect should fail in their purgation, they might then be punished by both the ecclesiastical and civil judges with a firmer sentence as an example to others. If, however, the judge wishes to carry this out himself, he should command that ten or twenty **compurgators**...

<meta>This page continues the procedural guidelines for the Inquisition's legal actions against those accused of witchcraft. It moves from general sentencing of fugitives to specific "modes" of handling suspects based on the level of evidence and the nature of their reputation or "infamy."</meta>

...of their order, and let him proceed as was touched upon in the **second mode of sentencing** such people. Except that, where someone is to be excommunicated, he should then have recourse to the **Ordinary** <note>The Ordinary is usually the local Bishop or a high-ranking official with the authority to exercise jurisdiction over a diocese.</note>. This would occur in a case where the person refuses to clear themselves of the charges.

**The Third Mode** occurs concerning such an accused person where, although they are not convicted by their own confession, nor by the legitimate production of witnesses, nor by the evidence of the fact, and there are not even signs regarding any deed for which they had ever been notorious among the other inhabitants of the village or town—nevertheless, they suffer from **ill-repute** <note>original: *infamia* — in medieval law, this was a specific legal status where a person’s public reputation was so damaged that it could trigger a trial even without a private accuser.</note> among them. Furthermore, this ill-repute is aggravated by the testimony of a detained witch who has asserted that he or she was an accomplice in everything and participated with her in her crimes. However, just as the accused person constantly denies this, so it is either unknown to the other inhabitants, or they are only aware of the person's honest conduct or association with others.

Regarding such a case, this practice is observed: First, they must be brought face-to-face to confront one another, and their mutual objections and responses must be diligently considered. And if indeed any inconsistency should arise in the words spoken, from which the judge can likely presume—based on what was admitted and what was denied—that the accused person deserves to be put to the **questions** <note>The "questions" is a legal euphemism for interrogation under torture.</note>, let him proceed according to the sentences contained in the **third mode of concluding a trial of the faith**, around the twenty-third question. He should subject her lightly to **torments** <note>original: *tormentis* — torture. The Malleus often suggests "light" torture initially as a psychological tactic.</note>, while employing many other very necessary precautions, as was explained at length above near the beginning of this third part. From these things, it is presumed whether such a person is innocent or guilty.

**The Fourth Mode** occurs when such an accused is found to be **lightly suspected** <note>original: *suspectus leviter* — the lowest of three grades of legal suspicion in Canon Law (light, vehement, and violent).</note>. This may be because of their own confession or the testimony of another person who is detained. There are some who reduce to this "light suspicion" those who have consulted witches in order to provoke women <note>Specifically, to provoke love or lust through magic.</note>, or where, among married people pursuing mutual hatred, they have procured "love" via magic, or even those who have worked with witches for some temporal advantage. But because such people are certainly excommunicated as **believers in heretics** <note>original: *hereticorum credentes* — those who do not necessarily hold heretical views themselves but act as though they believe in the power and efficacy of heretical or magical arts.</note> according to the chapter *Excommunicamus*, section *Credentes* in the fifth book of the Decretals on Heretics, where it says we judge those who believe in their errors to be heretics likewise...

<column-break/>

...because one's intent is presumed from one's actions (according to the legal rule "that which he has seen"). Therefore, it seems they should be punished and sentenced more sharply than those who are only lightly held as suspected of heresy. Some are to be judged based on light conjectures, such as if they had provided services to witches, delivered letters for them, or if they gave no credit to their errors yet did not report them, or if they accepted food from them.

But whether it be those or these, whatever is concluded in the council of experts regarding **light suspicion** must be pursued by the judge through the following practice: such a person shall either **abjure** <note>original: *abiurabit* — to formally renounce or recant a belief under oath.</note> or canonically clear themselves, according to what is touched upon in the **fourth mode of concluding a trial of the faith** under the twenty-fourth question. Nevertheless, it seems more appropriate that an abjuration should be enjoined, and this is because of the aforementioned chapter *Excommunicamus*, the first section, which says: "those who are found to be marked by suspicion alone," etc. However, if they lapse again, they ought not to be punished with the penalty for **relapsed heretics** <note>A "relapsed" heretic was someone who had already abjured their errors but was caught practicing them again. Relapse almost always resulted in execution.</note>. One shall proceed as was touched upon in the fourth mode of concluding a trial of faith regarding the twenty-fourth question.

**The Fifth Mode** occurs when such an accused is found to be **vehemently suspected** <note>original: *suspectus vehementer* — a high degree of suspicion that required a public and solemn renunciation.</note>. This happens in a similar way, either through their own confession or the testimony of another detained witch. And there are some who reduce to this category those who impede the judgment of the inquisitors, either directly or indirectly, by interfering in their office or hindering them from dealing with witches, provided they have done this sufficiently (from the chapter *Ut inquisitionis* in the sixth book of the Decretals). Likewise, they include all those who knowingly provide aid, counsel, or favor to those who impede the office. Likewise, they include those who, when heretics are summoned or captured, instruct them on how to hide the truth and how to withdraw it or assert a falsehood (from the chapter *Accusatus*). Likewise, they include all those who knowingly receive, visit, or associate with those they know to be heretics, or send them gifts or bestow favor upon them—all of which are done in favor not of the person, but of the crime, when done knowingly. And therefore they say that when an accused person participates in the aforementioned things, and this has been so judged by the council, then according to the **fifth mode of concluding a trial of the faith**...

<meta>This page continues the legal procedural guidelines of the Inquisition for sentencing individuals accused of witchcraft. It focuses on the transition between different levels of legal suspicion—light, vehement, and violent—and how the judge should handle defendants who refuse to confess, particularly when a "spell of silence" is suspected.</meta>

...sentence is given in the twenty-fifth question. It is given in such a way that they must abjure every heresy under penalty of relapse, should they fall back into it. We can, however, assert by adding that judges should have regard for the family, offspring, or even the lineage of every witch who is burned or detained. This is because very often such individuals are found to be infected, as witches are even known to offer their own infants to demons based on the demons' instruction. Wherefore, they are undoubtedly capable of being instructed in any crimes; these things are clear from the first part of this work. It is also proved from the fact that, just as in simple heresy, because of familiarity with known heretics, when someone stands defamed of heresy, they are consequently considered vehemently suspected of heresy by reason of that familiarity. So it is also in this heresy of witches. 

The aforementioned case is clear in the chapter *Among the Anxieties* <note>original: "Inter sollicitudines"</note> under the title *Of Canonical Purgation* <note>original: "de purgatione canonica" — a legal process where an accused person clears themselves by swearing an oath of innocence, often supported by character witnesses</note>, where it appears that by reason of ill-repute regarding heresy, a certain dean was ordered to undergo canonical purgation. And by reason of familiarity with heretics, he was ordered to perform a public abjuration; and by reason of the scandal, he was deprived of his benefice until the scandal should be put to rest.

**The Sixth Mode** occurs where such an accused person becomes **violently suspected** <term>violent suspicion: in canon law, this is the highest level of suspicion, often treated as equivalent to proof, leaving the judge with almost no doubt of guilt</term>. This happens not through a simple or naked accusation by another detained witch, but through the evidence of the fact derived from certain words and deeds perpetrated and uttered by the detained witch, in which at the very least the accused is asserted to have been present and to have shared in the works of demons. 

To understand these things, one must attend to what was touched upon above in the nineteenth question, especially concerning **violent suspicion**, how it arises from violent and convincing conjectures, and how a judge is compelled to believe, solely from suspicion, that someone is a heretic who perhaps nevertheless remains a good Catholic in their heart. This is as the canonists exemplify regarding simple heresy in the case of one who, having been summoned in a case of faith to answer, contumaciously <note>contumacy: a legal term for stubborn refusal to obey a court order or appear when summoned</note> refuses to appear. Because of this contumacy they are excommunicated; if they persevere in this state for a year, they become **violently suspected** of heresy. Therefore, by analogy, one must look for signs of the fact regarding such an accused person by which they are made violently suspected.

¶ Let a case be posed: a detained witch has asserted that she [the accused]

<column-break/>

was present at her evil deeds. Yet the accused person constantly denies it. What then shall the judge do? It will certainly be necessary to consider whether, from any other works, she is **vehemently suspected**, and whether a vehement suspicion can pass into a **violent** one. Just as in the aforementioned case, a person summoned to answer who does not appear but contumaciously refuses becomes **lightly suspected** of heresy, even if summoned in a case not involving faith. But if summoned in a case of faith they refuse to appear and are excommunicated for contumacy, then they become **vehemently suspected**, because then the light suspicion passes into a vehement one; and if they persist for a year, then the vehement passes into the violent. 

In the same way, the judge will consider whether, by reason of the familiarity contracted with the detained witch, the accused is **vehemently suspected**, as was touched upon just above in the fifth mode. Then it will be necessary to consider whether that vehement suspicion can pass into a violent one. For it is presumed that it can pass—that is, that the accused was present at the crimes of the detained person where she had frequent familiarity with her. Therefore, the judge must proceed according to the **third mode** of concluding a trial of faith, as touched upon in the twenty-sixth question.

¶ If it is asked: what should the judge do if such an accused person, denounced by another detained witch, persists entirely in her denial, notwithstanding whatever evidence the judge produces against her? 

The answer is: first, the judge must observe regarding the negative responses whether they arise from the vice or **spell of silence** <term>original: *maleficio taciturnitatis* — a magical charm or demonic influence believed to prevent a witch from confessing or even feeling pain during torture</term>, or not. And indeed, as was clear in the earlier questions, specifically question 15 and 17 of this third part, the judge can know this if she is unable to weep or shed tears. And where, during the interrogations <note>original: "quaestionibus" — in this context, the judicial examination often involved the application of torture</note>, she is rendered almost insensible so that she easily returns to her former strength, then indeed the violent suspicion is aggravated. She is by no means to be freely dismissed but, as was clear in the **sixth mode** of sentencing and concluding a trial of faith cited above, she should be assigned to perpetual prison to perform her penance. 

If, however, she is not infected by the spell of silence because of the vehement pains she truly and actually suffers during the interrogations—while others, as said, are rendered almost insensible by the spell of silence—then the final...

<meta>This page continues the legal procedural instructions for the Inquisition. It concludes the discussion on "violent suspicion" and transitions into the final "modes" of sentencing, specifically addressing how to handle those accused of using magic for healing or removal of spells (white magic), as well as specific categories of witches like midwives and magical archers.</meta>

...the final refuge <note>original: "modum refugium"</note> a judge can have is to rely on **canonical purgation** <note>A legal process where the accused clears themselves by swearing an oath of innocence, often supported by character witnesses called "compurgators."</note>. If this is ordered by a secular judge, it is lawful in place of "vulgar" purgation <note>original: "purgatione vulgari" — trial by ordeal, such as using hot iron or water, which the Church generally discouraged in favor of oaths.</note>, because it is not among the number of those common purgations discussed in the chapters *You have consulted* and *Single combat* <note>original: "consuluisti" and "monomachia"</note>. In this purgation, if the accused (male or female) fails, they shall be judged as guilty.

The **Seventh Mode** occurs when the accused person is not found to be legitimately caught—neither by their own confession, nor by the evidence of the deed, nor by the legitimate production of witnesses—but is only found to have been reported by an old **witch** <term>malefica: a female practitioner of harmful magic</term>. Along with this, clues <note>original: "indicia"</note> are found which render the person lightly or vehemently suspected, such as having had great familiarity with witches. Then, by reason of such ill-repute, canonical purgation must be ordered. According to the chapter *Among the Anxieties* <note>original: "inter sollicitudines"</note>, and by reason of suspicion, they must abjure heresy under the penalty for **relapsed heretics** <note>A "relapsed" person was someone who fell back into heresy after a previous trial; they were typically handed over to the secular authorities for execution.</note> if they were vehemently suspected, or without that penalty if they were lightly suspected. The process of the faith should then proceed to its conclusion, as was touched upon in the twenty-seventh question.

The **Eighth Mode** occurs where the accused is found to have confessed to that heresy but is penitent and has never relapsed before. You should note that in the following sections, where the text deals with those who have relapsed and those who have not, or those who are penitent and those who are not, such distinctions are made for the sake of **ecclesiastical judges** <note>Church officials</note>, who do not involve themselves in the infliction of the ultimate punishments <note>the death penalty</note>. Therefore, the **civil judge** <note>secular authority</note> can proceed as justice advises according to civil and imperial laws regarding those who have confessed—whether they are penitent or not, or whether they have relapsed or not. However, the judge can still have recourse to these thirteen modes of sentencing and resolve the case according to them whenever an ambiguity arises.

### Question 34: Concerning the method of sentencing a witch who removes spells. Furthermore, also concerning midwife witches and archer witches.

The **fifteenth mode** <note>The text jump from 8th to 15th mode reflects the complex organizational structure of the original manuscript's legal arguments.</note> of concluding a trial of the faith and sentencing is when the accused of **heretical pravity** <term>heretica pravitate: the ecclesiastical term for the "wickedness" of heresy</term> is found not to be inflicting spells, but removing them. Regarding such a person, the practice to be followed is this: they are using either

<column-break/>

lawful or unlawful remedies. If the remedies are indeed lawful, the person is to be judged not as a witch but as a **follower of Christ** <note>original: "christicola"</note>. Concerning these lawful remedies, it was explained at length above, near the beginning of this third part. 

If, however, the remedies are unlawful, then a distinction must be made: they are either simply unlawful or unlawful in a certain respect. If they are simply unlawful, there are two possibilities: they are done either to the harm of another or without harm to anyone; however, in both ways, it is always done with an express **invocation of demons**. 

If the remedies are "unlawful in a certain respect"—for example, because they are performed without an express invocation of demons, though not without a tacit one—such things are judged to be "vain" <note>superstitious but perhaps not intentionally diabolical</note> rather than being called "unlawful" by canonists and certain theologians, as appeared above in the first question of this final part of the whole work. 

Therefore, any judge, whether ecclesiastical or civil—though they ought not to reject the first and last types, and specifically should rather commend the first and tolerate the last (just as canonists assert it is lawful to "crush vanity with vanity")—must in no way tolerate those who remove **spells** <term>maleficia: harmful magic or charms</term> with an express invocation of demons. This is especially true for those who commit such acts to the harm of a neighbor. They are said to practice to the harm of a neighbor when a spell is removed from one person in such a way that it is inflicted on another. It does not matter if the person on whom it is newly inflicted is a witch themselves or not, or if they were the one who originally cast the spell or not, or if it is a human or any other creature. The acts and deeds concerning all these matters are clear from the first question cited above.

But it is asked: what shall the judge do where such a person asserts they remove spells by lawful and not unlawful remedies? Or how can the judge truly know such things? It is answered that, having summoned the person, they should be questioned as to what means they use. However, one should not rely solely on their words. Instead, the ecclesiastical judge, whose duty it is, should diligently inquire either by himself or through a parish priest. This priest can exactly inquire of individual parishioners, under a required oath, as to what remedies the person uses. And if they are found—as they commonly are—to use **superstitious remedies**, they are by no means to be tolerated because of the horrible punishments inflicted by the canons, as will appear below. And if it is asked how lawful remedies can be discerned from unlawful ones, since they always assert they use certain...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological classifications of witchcraft, moving from general suspicions to specific behaviors that identify witches posing as healers. It also introduces the high-risk categories of midwives and magical archers, and the legal consequences for their protectors.</meta>

...removing these things by prayers and the application of herbs. The response is that this would be easy, provided a diligent inquiry were made. For because they are obliged to hide their superstitious remedies—so that they are not rebuked, or so that they may more easily ensnare the minds of the simple—they therefore persist in such words or herbal applications. Nevertheless, they are clearly rebuked as **sorceresses** <term>sortilege: those who practice divination or lot-casting</term> and **witches** <term>malefice: those who perform harmful magic</term> by four of their superstitious acts.

First, where they divine hidden things and report matters that they cannot know except by the revelation of evil spirits. For example: where someone seeking to regain health visits them, they know how to reveal and make manifest the cause of the injury or the spell. If it happened by reason of a quarrel with a female neighbor or for some other cause, they know this perfectly and are accustomed to indicating it to those who visit them.

Second, where they involve themselves in the cure of a spell for one person's harm, but not at all for another's. For example, in the **Diocese of Speyer** <note>original: "dioc. spireñ"</note>, there exists a certain witch in a place called **Zun Hofen** who, although she seems to heal many, confesses that she is not at all able to cure certain ones. This is for no other reason than—as is reported by the inhabitants—the spell cast on them was so strongly impressed by other witches that she cannot remove it. This is because, as she asserts, by the power of demons, a demon cannot (or will not) always yield to another demon.

Third, where they are known to make specific exceptions regarding the spells cast. This is known to have happened in the city of Speyer itself, when a certain honest person afflicted by a spell in their legs called upon such a female diviner for the sake of health. Upon entering the house and looking at the person, she made this exception: "If," she said, "there are no scales or hairs in the wound, I will be able to extract everything else." She also revealed the causes of the injury, even though she had come from the countryside two miles away, saying: "Because you quarreled with a neighbor on such-and-such a day, this happened to you." Besides scales and hair, she extracted many other things of various kinds and restored the person to health.

Fourth, where they persist in superstitious ceremonies, or

<column-break/>

cause others to persist in them. For instance, if they wish to be visited before sunrise or at some other determined time, saying that they cannot heal illnesses brought on beyond a certain limit <note>original: "vltra angariā"</note>, or that they can only heal two or three people per year—even though they do not truly heal, but rather seem to heal by ceasing the injuries. 

Many other conditions can also be added, such as that they were usually of an evil and reprehensible life in the past, being of ill-repute, adulteresses, or the survivors of other witches; thus, this grace of healing was not granted by God through any holiness of life. Incidentally, **midwife-witches** <term>obstetrices malefice</term> are also mentioned, who exceed all other witches in their crimes, as was also mentioned in the first part of this work. Indeed, their number is so great that, as discovered from their confessions, it is thought there is no small village where they are not found. This danger should be remedied in part by the aforementioned authorities, so that none but **sworn midwives** should be recognized by those in charge, along with other remedies touched upon in the second part of the work.

The subject of **magical archers** <term>maleficis sagittarijs</term> also arises, certainly to the contempt of the Christian religion. These are all the more dangerous because they have more secure protectors, supporters, and defenders among the nobles and princes of the land. But how all such protectors and supporters of witches are often, in certain cases, more damnable than the witches themselves is explained as follows: For the defenders of such people are categorized by **canonists** <term>canonistis: experts in Church law</term> and **theologians** into two kinds.

Some defend them out of error; others defend the persons themselves. And those who defend them out of error are more damnable than the erring ones themselves, since they are to be considered not only **heretics** but **heresiarchs** <term>heresiarchi: leaders or founders of a heresy</term>, as is clear in [Canon Law] Question 23, Case 4. The laws do not usually speak of these defenders separately because they do not distinguish them from other heretics, in which case the chapter *Ad abolendam* <note>original: "c. Ad abolendā" — A famous papal bull by Lucius III (1184) against heresy</note> applies. 

There are others who, although they do not defend the error, nevertheless defend the person in error, such as those who resist with force and power so that such witches (or any other heretics) do not fall into the hands of the judges of the Faith for examination or punishment, and similar things.
