<meta>This page continues the legal classification of those who assist or protect witches and heretics. It shifts from identifying the witches themselves to the legal culpability of secular and spiritual authorities who fail to prosecute them.</meta>

In a similar way, those who support such people are of two types. For some are those who hold public authority—that is, public persons such as **secular** <term>temporal: relating to worldly or civil authority rather than the Church</term> or **spiritual** lords having secular jurisdiction—who can also be supporters in two ways: by **omission** and by **commission**. 

By **omission**, namely by failing to take action against **sorcerers** <term>maleficos: those who practice harmful magic or witchcraft</term> or suspects, those of ill-repute, or **believers** <note>original: "credentes" – a legal term for those who do not teach heresy but accept and believe the teachings of heretics</note>, harborers, defenders, and supporters, to which they are bound by their office. This applies when they are requested to act by bishops or inquisitors, or either one of them: for instance, if they do not arrest them, or do not guard them diligently once arrested, or do not lead them to the place commanded within their district, or do not carry out prompt execution upon them, and similar things. This is clear in the chapter **Concerning the Inquisition** <note>original: "c. Ut inquisitionis"</note> at the beginning of the **Sixth Book of Decretals** <note>original: "li. vi."</note> regarding heretics. 

By **commission**, for instance, if they free those arrested in this way from prison without the license or mandate of the bishop or his judge, or if they directly or indirectly hinder the legal process, the judgment, or their sentence, or do similar things as is clear in the aforementioned chapter **As the office** <note>original: "c. alle. vt officiū"</note> in the section **We prohibit**. General rules on these matters were declared in the preceding parts regarding the second principal point of this work, and near the end where **magical archers** <note>original: "maleficis sagittarijs" – soldiers or hunters believed to use demonic charms to ensure their arrows never miss</note> and other enchanters of weapons were touched upon. 

For the present, let it suffice that all such people are **excommunicated by the law itself** <note>original: "ipso iure" – a legal penalty that applies automatically when the act is committed, without needing a trial</note> and incur thirteen great penalties. This is clear in the **Decretals** <note>original: "extra"</note> under the title **On Heretics**, in the chapter **We Excommunicate** <note>original: "Excommunicamus"</note>, first section, **the believers**, and in the aforementioned chapter **Concerning the Inquisition**, section **We prohibit**. In this state of excommunication, if they persist for a year with a stubborn mind, they are then to be condemned as heretics, as in the same chapter and section cited. 

Now, as to who should be called **harborers** <term>receptatores: those who provide shelter or sanctuary to criminals or heretics</term> and whether they are to be treated as heretics: the response is that those receiving such magical archers, or any enchanters of weapons, **necromancers** <term>nigromāticis: those who communicate with the dead or demons</term>, or heretical sorcerers—who have been treated in this entire work—are of two types, just as was mentioned regarding their defenders and supporters. For some are those who receive such people not just once or twice, but many times and frequently; and these are properly called **harborers** according to the force of the word, from the word *to harbor*, which is a **frequentative** <term>frequentative: a type of verb that expresses repeated or habitual action</term> verb.

<column-break/>

And such **harborers** are sometimes without fault, such as if they do this out of ignorance and never suspected anything sinister about them. Others are at fault, namely when they know of their errors and are not ignorant of the fact that the Church always pursues such people as the most cruel enemies of the faith. Nevertheless, the **lords of the lands** harbor, keep, and defend them, etc. Such people are properly and are called **harborers of heretics**; and the laws also speak of these, and that they are excommunicated according to the chapter **We Excommunicate**, first section, **the believers**.

However, some have received such sorcerers or heretics not many times and frequently, but only once or twice; and these do not seem to be properly called **harborers** [receptatores] because they did not do it frequently, but rather **receivers** [receptores] because they received them and did not 'frequently harbor' them. Although the **Archdeacon** <note>original: "Archidiaconus" – likely referring to the medieval legal scholar Guido de Baysio</note> says the contrary in the chapter **Whosoever**, on the word *harborers*, not much weight is given to this because we must care for facts, not words. 

However, a difference is placed between **harborers** and **receivers** in this: that **lords of lands** are always called harborers of such people, whereas simple people, who do not have the power to expel them and cannot do so, even if they are receivers, are nevertheless without fault.

Lastly, concerning those who **hinder the office** of the inquisition of the bishops against such heretical sorcerers: who they are and if they should be called heretics. To this, it is answered that such **hinderers** are of two types. For some are those who hinder **directly**, such as those who, by their own audacity, free those arrested for the crime of heresy from prison, or tear up the records of the inquisition process, or wound witnesses in a case of faith because they have testified. Or if a **secular lord** <note>original: "dñs tp̄alis"</note> decrees that no one but himself may take notice of this crime, or that no one can be accused of this crime except to him, nor can anyone testify except before him, and similar things. These people hinder directly according to the notes of **Johannes Andreae** <note>Johannes Andreae was the most renowned 14th-century expert in Canon Law</note> in the chapter **The Statute**, on the word *directly*, in the **Fifth Book** <note>original: "li. v."</note> regarding heretics. And those who hinder directly, or those who have provided aid, counsel, or favor for these things to be done, although they are very much at fault...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding those who obstruct the work of the Inquisition against witches and heretics. The catchword "obstin-" from the previous page leads into the word "obstinacy" or "persistent will" regarding those who protect heretics.</meta>

...they are not, however, to be judged as heretics for this reason, unless it appears otherwise that they are entangled in similar errors of **witches** <term>maleficorum: those who perform harmful magic or sorcery</term> with a persistent will. Nevertheless, by the law itself, they are struck by the sword of **excommunication** <note>original: "excommunicationis mucrone" – being cut off from the Church community and sacraments</note>. This is according to the chapter **Concerning the Inquisition** <note>original: "c. Ut inquisitionis"</note> in the section **We prohibit** <note>original: "§. phibemus"</note>. Thus, if they remain under that excommunication for a year with a persistent spirit, they are then to be condemned as heretics, as is clear in the aforementioned chapter and section.

There are others who obstruct indirectly: for instance, those who decree that no one may carry arms to capture heretics except those of the temporal lord’s own household, and similar things, according to the notes of **Johannes Andreae** <note>A famous 14th-century expert in Canon Law</note> in the chapter **The Statute** <note>original: "ca. statutū"</note> regarding the word **indirectly**. Such people are less blameworthy than the first group; they are not heretics, but they are excommunicated according to the same chapter **Concerning the Inquisition**. 

This also applies to those providing counsel, help, or favor to this end. If they remain under that excommunication for a year with a persistent spirit, they are then to be condemned as if they were heretics, according to the second chapter in the section **We prohibit**. This is to be understood in this way: that heretics are condemned such that if they wish to return, they are received into **mercy** <note>original: "miām" (misericordiam) – the Church's forgiveness</note>, provided they first abjure their error. Otherwise, as impenitents, they are handed over to the **secular court** <note>original: "curie seculari" – the civil authorities, who usually carried out the death penalty</note>, as is clear in the chapter **To abolish** <note>original: "c. ad abolendā"</note> in the current section. 

In summary, **midwife-witches** <term>malefice obstetrices: midwives accused of using magic to harm or kill infants</term>, just like other witches who perform harmful magic, are condemned and sentenced according to the nature of their crimes. Similarly, those witches who superstitiously remove harmful magic by the help of the devil—for there is no doubt that just as they can take it away, so they can inflict it—are also condemned. Indeed, by a certain pact, such witches agree among themselves based on the demons' instruction: that some should harm, while others should heal, so that they may more easily ensnare the minds of the simple-minded and increase their **faithlessness** <note>original: "pfidiā" (perfidiam)</note>. 

As for **archers** <note>original: "Sagittarij" – likely referring to those who enchanted their weapons</note> and other witches who enchant armor—since they are only sustained by the favor, defense, and harboring provided by those in power—all such people are subject to the prescribed penalties. And any officials who hinder the work of the authorities against these witches or their supporters are likewise excommunicated. They are subject to all the same penalties as the supporters. Truly, where they have remained for a year under that excommunication

<column-break/>

with a persistent spirit, if they wish to return, they must abjure their obstruction and favor and are then admitted to mercy. Otherwise, as impenitent heretics, they are handed over to the **secular arm** <note>original: "brachio seculari" – civil authority</note>. And even where they have not stayed for a year, one can nonetheless proceed against such obstructors as one would against the supporters of heretics, based on the chapter **The Accused** <note>original: "c. Accusatus"</note> in the final section. 

What has been said regarding the supporters, defenders, harborers, and obstructors of archer-witches and so forth, is likewise and in all things to be understood regarding any witches (male or female) who bring various harms upon humans, livestock, and the fruits of the earth. 

Furthermore, any such witches who, in the **court of penance** <note>original: "foro penitētie" – the internal spiritual realm of confession and the soul</note>, with a contrite and humbled spirit, bewailing their sins and purely confessing, seek pardon, are received into mercy. Otherwise, where they become known, those whose duty it is must proceed against them by summoning, arresting, capturing, and proceeding in all things according to the nature of the crimes, up to and including the **final sentence** <note>original: "sententiam diffinitiuam"</note>, as has been touched upon. This must be done if and insofar as those in power wish to escape the snare of eternal damnation because of the excommunication inflicted upon them by the Church.

-> **concerning the methods of sentencing any witches** <-

As for the final resort to the remedy of **appeal** <note>original: "appellationis" – a legal challenge to a higher court</note>, the judge should observe: First, it must be noted that such an appeal is sometimes judged valid and just, and sometimes frivolous and void. For in matters of **faith** <note>original: "negociis fidei"</note>, the process should be summary, simple, and straightforward, as has been frequently touched upon in the preceding sections, following the chapter **The complaint of many** <note>original: "c. multorum querela"</note> in the **Clementines** <note>original: "Cle." – a collection of Canon Law by Pope Clement V</note>, where the remedy of appeal is also forbidden. 

However, because judges sometimes voluntarily prolong and delay the case because of its difficulty, they may take notice: if the accused person feels themselves truly and in fact burdened by the judge against law and justice—for instance, because the judge refused to admit them to their own defense, or because the judge acted alone without counsel...

...of others or even without the consent of the bishop or his vicar. He pronounced that the accused <term>delatus: the person who has been denounced or charged</term> was to be interrogated <note>original: "questionarẽ" – refers here to interrogation under torture</note> when he could have otherwise had sufficient evidence for and against him, and similar matters. In such a case, the appeal would indeed be just; otherwise, it would not.

**Second**, it should be noted that once such an appeal is presented to the judge, he must then, without agitation or disturbance, ask for a copy of the appeal, protesting verbally that time should not run against him. And when the accused has handed over the copy of the appeal, the judge should note that he still has two days to respond, and after these, thirty more to provide the letters of appeal <term>apostoli: formal letters issued by a lower judge to a higher court, either supporting or opposing an appeal</term>. And although he could respond immediately and provide these or those letters if he were very experienced and skilled, it is better to proceed more cautiously. He should assign a specific term of 10, 20, or 25 days for the accused to both give and receive the letters which the judge has decreed to provide, with the power to extend this deadline.

**Third**, the judge must note that within the legal timeframe and within the assigned term, he ought to diligently consider and discuss the causes of the appeal or the alleged grievances <term>grauamina: legal injuries or wrongs claimed by the person appealing</term>. And if he sees, after taking good counsel from experts <term>peritoruz: legal assessors or consultants</term>, that he has unjustly and unduly burdened the accused—by not admitting his defense or by exposing him to interrogation <note>original: "questionibus" – referring to the use of torture</note> at an improper time or similar things—he should, when the assigned term arrives, correct his error. He should return the process to the point and state in which it was when those defenses were first sought or the term for a middle judgment was assigned, and so on. He should remove the grievance, and once it is removed, proceed as before. For by the removal of the grievance, the appeal that existed becomes null, according to the chapter **Cessante** <note>A specific rule in Canon Law: "When the cause ceases, the effect ceases"</note> in the section **On Appeals** <note>original: "extra de appella."</note>. 

But here the circumspect and provident judge should take heed: some grievances are "repairable," and these are the ones just mentioned; in those cases, the instructions above apply. However, some are "irreparable." For instance, if the accused was interrogated <note>original: "questionatus" – tortured</note> in reality and in fact and afterwards escapes and appeals. Or if jewelry and other useful items, along with the vessels and instruments which

<column-break/>

**witches** <term>malefici: those who perform harmful magic or sorcery</term> use, were seized and burned, or the household <note>original: "familia" – the servants or family members of the accused</note> which cannot be restored or recalled. In such cases, the aforementioned method—returning the process to the state it was in before the grievance was inflicted—does not apply.

**Fourth**, the judge must note that although he has 30 days from the day of the response to provide the letters of appeal, according to the law <note>original: "iuxta .c. re appell’"</note>, and he can assign the very last legal day (the thirtieth) for receiving the letters, it is better not to do so. To avoid the appearance of wanting to harass the accused—which would make the judge suspect—and to avoid appearing to confirm the grievance for which the appeal was made, he should assign a reasonable term within the legal limit, such as the tenth or twentieth day. He can later, if he does not wish to proceed when that term arrives, extend it by saying he was busy with other business or similar reasons.

**Fifth**, the judge should note that when he sets a deadline for the appellant seeking the letters of appeal, he should not assign it only for the "giving" of letters, but for the giving and receiving of them equally. Because if he assigned it only for "giving," the judge would then have to send them to the appellant. He shall therefore assign a term—a specific day of a specific year—to give the letters to them and for them to receive from the judge such letters of appeal as he has decreed to give.

**Sixth**, he ought to note that in the assignment of this term, he should not say in his response whether he will give "negative" or "affirmative" letters <note>Negative letters (reuerendi) refuse the appeal; affirmative letters (dimissorii) grant it</note>. Instead, so that he may deliberate more fully, he should say that he will provide such letters as he then decrees should be provided. He should also take care that in assigning this term, to prevent any trickery or malice from the appellant, he assigns a specific place, day, and hour. For example, he might assign the 20th of August of the current year, at the hour of Vespers, in the judge's own chamber in a specific house in such a city, for the appellant to give and receive the letters.

...sets a deadline <term>terminus: a fixed legal period or date</term> and assigns such a date for giving or receiving the letters of appeal <term>apostoli: formal letters issued by a lower judge to a higher court, either supporting or opposing an appeal</term> in person. He should assign a place for the appellant to give and receive them, where the judge has the power to keep the appellant freely in custody. However, negative letters should be given immediately first, otherwise not.

**Seventh**, the judge notes that he must not change anything <note>original: "innouet"</note> concerning the appellant—such as seizing him, questioning him <note>original: "questionando" – often referring to interrogation under torture</note>, or releasing him from prison—from the hour the appeal was presented until the hour he delivers the negative letters of appeal. 

**In Summary.** Note that it often happens that a defendant, when they fear a sentence will be passed against them because they are aware of their own guilt, frequently resorts to the remedy of an appeal to escape the judge's sentence. For this reason, they appeal and assign "frivolous causes," such as claiming the judge held them captive and refused to grant them suitable bail <note>original: "cautioni idonee"</note>, and similar colorful excuses. 

Once this appeal has been presented to the judge, he should ask for a copy of it. Having received it, either immediately or after two days, he should set a day, hour, and place for the appellant to give and receive the letters of appeal that the judge has decreed. This must be within the legal timeframe—such as the 10th, 15th, or 20th day of the month. Within this assigned term, the judge should diligently discuss the copy of the appeal and the grievances or causes for the appeal, and deliberate with the good counsel of legal experts <term>iurisperitorum: men learned in the law who advised the court</term> whether he should provide the appellant with "negative letters"—that is, negative responses that do not admit the appeal—or "affirmative letters"—that is, affirmative and "reverential" responses to be sent to the higher judge to whom the person is appealing, thereby deferring to the appeal. 

For if he sees that the causes of the appeal are false, frivolous, or void, and that the appellant only wishes to escape or delay judgment, he should give negative or "refutatory" letters. If, however, he sees that the grievances are true and were unjustly inflicted upon the person and cannot be repaired, or if he is in doubt, or 

<column-break/>

otherwise exhausted by the malice of the appellant and wishes to be free of such a burden, he should grant the appellant affirmative or reverential letters. 

Therefore, when the assigned deadline arrives, if the judge has not yet drafted the letters or responses or is otherwise not prepared, he can peremptorily postpone the date, either all at once or successively, up to the 30th day, which is the final legal limit for providing the assigned letters. If he has drafted them and is ready, he can give the letters to the appellant immediately. If he has decreed to give negative or refutatory letters, then upon the arrival of the assigned final deadline, he should present them in writing in the following manner:

**E** <note>The large decorative 'E' marks the beginning of the formal legal response the judge is to read or provide.</note> And the said judge, dismissing <note>original: "ridens" — literally "laughing," but here used in a legal sense to mean "mocking" or "dismissing as trivial"</note> the aforementioned appeal—if it even deserves to be called an appeal—says that he has proceeded, and intends to proceed, justly and according to the canonical sanctions or even the imperial statutes and laws. He has not strayed from the path of either branch of law <note>original: "iuris vtriusqz" — referring to both Canon (Church) Law and Civil Law</note>, nor does he intend to. He has not burdened the appellant, nor does he intend or understand himself to have done so. 

This is made clear by judging each of the "colored" causes alleged. For he did not cause a grievance by seizing and holding the man; since the man was reported to him for such heretical depravity <term>heretica prauitate: the standard legal term for the crime of heresy or witchcraft</term> and the judge has many witnesses against him, he rightly should and must hold him as one convicted of heresy or at least vehemently suspected of it. Nor did he cause a grievance by refusing to grant him bail; for since the crime of heresy is among the "major crimes," and the appellant himself was convicted and was by no means in a state of denial, he is not to be granted bail, even for a very large sum. Rather, he is and was to be kept in prison. 

And thus the judge should proceed through the other reasons. Having done this, he should say: "Wherefore it appears that the judge proceeded duly and justly and has not deviated from the paths of the law, nor has he burdened the man in any way. Rather, the appellant himself, through colored and fictitious causes, strives to escape judgment by appealing unjustly and unduly. Because of this, his appeal is frivolous and void, as it is based on no actual grievance and is flawed in both matter and form." And since with frivolous appeals...

Once these negative letters have been provided to the appellant, the judge should immediately continue performing his office by ordering the person to be seized or detained, or by arresting them, or by assigning a deadline for them to appear before him, or something similar, so that it appears he has not ceased to be the judge. He shall continue his process against the appellant until he is prohibited from proceeding by the higher judge to whom the appeal was made. However, the judge must take care that he makes no "innovation" <note>original: "nullam nouitatem faciat" – a legal term meaning changing the status quo or the condition of the defendant</note> against the person of the appellant, neither by seizing him nor, if he is already seized, by releasing him from prison, nor otherwise, from the hour the appeal was presented to him until the time he has delivered the negative letters. "The judge, having been reached, responding to the aforementioned appeal (if it deserves to be called an appeal), says that he has processed the present case justly and as he ought, and not otherwise, nor does he intend to burden the person who claims to have been burdened <note>original: "aggrauatum" – meaning someone who has suffered a legal grievance or 'weight' from a ruling</note> by appealing. This is evident by examining each of the alleged reasons; for he did not burden him in this matter

in which he says, etc." (The judge should then run through each individual cause for the appeal in the best and most truthful way possible, responding and concluding thus:) "Wherefore it appears that the judge has in no way burdened the said appellant, nor did he give cause to the appellant, who fears that justice will proceed according to his demerits. For this reason, his appeal is frivolous and null, because it was introduced against no actual grievance, nor should it be referred by the judge by right. Nevertheless, out of reverence for the Apostolic See <note>The Papal court in Rome</note> to which the appeal was made, the judge says that he admits the said appeal, and he refers and intends to refer it, remitting the entire present business to our most holy lord the Pope and the holy Apostolic See. He assigns to the appellant a certain time, namely so many months immediately following, within which—with the records closed and sealed and delivered to him by the judge, or otherwise having given suitable security for presenting himself at the Roman Court <term>Romana curia: the administrative and legal body of the Pope</term>, or with faithful and safe custody provided for him by the judge—he must present himself to our lord the Pope at the Roman Court." The judge offers this response to the appellant in place of "affirmative apostles," and it is ordered to be inserted immediately after the appeal that was presented. He then hands it to the notary who presented the appeal.

A prudent judge should note, however, that as soon as he has issued "reverential apostles" to the appellant in the cause from which he appealed, he immediately ceases to be the judge of that case. He can no longer take notice of it unless the case is sent back to him by our most holy lord the Pope. Therefore, he should not involve himself further in that case, except by sending the said appellant in the manner described above to our lord the Pope, assigning him a competent deadline—such as one, two, or three months—so that in the meantime he can prepare himself and receive from him a guarantee of appearing and presenting himself in Rome.

...to the Curia within the same assigned deadline, provided with suitable security <note>original: "cautione" — a legal guarantee or bail intended to ensure the appellant actually appears at the higher court</note>. Or if the appellant cannot provide it, let him be sent under oath and safe custody. Or let him bind himself as best he can so that he presents himself within the assigned deadline in the Roman Curia to our lord the Pope, or at least that the failure to appear will not be on his part. 

If, however, the judge has another case and proceeds against the person in that other case, in which the appellant did not appeal, the judge remains the judge in that specific case just as before. Even if after the appeal has been admitted through the granting of reverential apostles <term>apostoli reverentiales: formal letters where a judge grants an appeal out of respect for the higher court, even if they believe the appeal lacks merit</term>, the appellant himself is accused or denounced to the judge regarding other crimes of heresy which are not part of the case for which he appealed, the judge does not cease to be the judge. Indeed, he can freely proceed to inform himself and examine witnesses as before. And once the first case is finished in the Roman Curia or remanded back to the judge, he can proceed freely in the second.

Furthermore, let the judges take care that they send the records <term>processus: the official trial documents and transcripts</term> closed and sealed to the Roman Curia, to the assigned judges who may do justice according to the merits of the proceedings. Nor should the inquisitors bother to act there against the appellants, but should leave them to be judged by their aforementioned judges. If the inquisitors do not wish to act as a party against the appellants, those judges will proceed *ex officio* <note>by virtue of their office, rather than at the instigation of an accuser</note> at the petition of the appellants if they wish to be discharged. 

Let the judges also take care that if they are personally summoned at the instance of the appellants and appear, they should nevertheless avoid swearing to the suit <note>original: "litem non iurare" — a legal technicality where the judge avoids becoming a personal litigant in the appeal, which would complicate his professional status</note>. Instead, let them see that the records exist and refer the whole case back to them, and let them take care to return as quickly as possible, lest they be damnably exhausted there by weariness, miseries, labors, and expenses. For damages to the Church follow from this, and heretics are emboldened; afterward, judges do not find as much favor and reverence, nor are they feared as much as their presence at home ensures. 

Likewise, the heretics themselves and any others, seeing the judges being exhausted and detained in the Roman Curia, will "lift up their horns" <note>a biblical metaphor for growing arrogant or aggressive</note> and will hold the judges in contempt and act maliciously and sow heresies more boldly; and where action is taken against them, they will appeal in a similar way. Other judges also become weaker in prosecuting the business of the faith and in extirpating 

<column-break/>

heretics, fearing lest they be exhausted by similar weariness and miseries through such appeals. All these things result in great prejudice to the faith and to the holy Church of God; from each of which may the Bridegroom of that same Church deign to preserve her.
